name: Invalid Command Opcode (SCT 0 / SC 0x01)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: SQE fetch, then an immediate CQE (a few µs) with no data TLPs.
What happens: The controller does not implement the opcode on that queue type (admin vs I/O), or the opcode is reserved. Nothing is executed.
How it shows up: CQE with SCT 0 / SC 0x01, normally DNR=1. Linux: NVME_SC_INVALID_OPCODE 0x001 → BLK_STS_NOTSUPP → -EOPNOTSUPP. dmesg "Invalid Command Opcode".
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Generic Command Status "Invalid Command Opcode". Commands Supported and Effects log (LID 05h) CSUPP bit says which opcodes the controller claims to support.
Typical causes: Optional command not supported (Compare, Write Zeroes, Copy, Verify, Write Uncorrectable); vendor tool sending a vendor opcode to a different model; I/O opcode sent on the admin queue; mismatch between Identify ONCS/OACS bits and actual support. QEMU: nvme_admin_cmd() , nvme_io_cmd_nvm() , nvme_io_cmd_zoned() reject opcodes whose effects entry lacks NVME_CMD_EFF_CSUPP .
How to detect / prove: Compare against nvme id-ctrl (OACS, ONCS) and nvme effects-log /dev/nvme0 . If the effects log says CSUPP=1 but the command returns 0x01, the controller contradicts itself (conformance bug).
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() (NOTSUPP); pr.c:nvme_status_to_pr_err() → -EINVAL for persistent reservations.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvme io-passthru /dev/nvme0n1 --opcode=0x7f --namespace-id=1 (a reserved I/O opcode) or nvme admin-passthru /dev/nvme0 --opcode=0x7f . Check that DNR=1.

name: Invalid Field in Command (SCT 0 / SC 0x02)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Immediate CQE after the SQE fetch. For PRP-based commands the device may first fetch the PRP list before rejecting.
What happens: A field in the SQE (CDW10–15, flags, PSDT, NSID-dependent fields, data length) holds a reserved or unsupported value. This is the catch-all argument error.
How it shows up: SCT 0 / SC 0x02, normally DNR=1. If the controller supports it, the Error Information log entry's Parameter Error Location names the byte and bit that was wrong. Linux 0x002 → BLK_STS_NOTSUPP → -EOPNOTSUPP.
Spec basis: Generic "Invalid Field in Command". Error Information log field Parameter Error Location (libnvme parm_error_location ).
Typical causes: Transfer larger than MDTS (QEMU nvme_check_mdts() ); unsupported Feature ID or log page offset (QEMU nvme_get_log() , nvme_set_feature() ); Identify CNS not supported; bad Abort SQID ( nvme_abort() ); reserved bits set; SGL requested when unsupported ( nvme_map_dptr() ); Flush to a bad NSID; DSM range count too large. QEMU returns this from about 86 sites, more than any other code.
How to detect / prove: nvme error-log /dev/nvme0 -e 16 : match SQID/CID, then read parm_error_location . Re-check the command against Identify limits (MDTS, ONCS, SGLS, DMRL/DMRSL).
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() ; core.c:nvme_scan_work() falls back to sequential namespace scanning when Identify NS List fails with DNR.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: Read with NLB larger than MDTS through nvme io-passthru ; nvme get-feature -f 0x7e on an unsupported FID; nvme get-log -i 0x02 -l 4096 -o 0x10000 (offset beyond the log).

name: Command ID Conflict (SCT 0 / SC 0x03)
In a PEX trace: Visible Visible as two SQE fetches (device MRd + CplD of the SQ slot) with the same CID on one SQ before the first CQE, and as the CQE status if the controller checks it. Pattern: Two SQEs on one SQ with the same CID and no CQE between them.
What happens: The host submitted a command whose CID is already outstanding on the same SQ. The controller may reject the new command.
How it shows up: SC 0x03. Many controllers do not check this and instead complete two commands with the same CID, which the host then confuses. Linux does not handle the code specially (→ -EIO).
Spec basis: Generic "Command ID Conflict". CIDs must be unique per SQ among outstanding commands.
Typical causes: Host driver bug (tag reuse before completion), a user-space driver (SPDK-style) with a broken tag allocator, or a duplicate completion making the host believe a tag is free. QEMU does not return it.
How to detect / prove: In an analyzer trace, list outstanding CIDs per SQ and flag a second SQE with the same CID before its CQE. Linux v7.2 adds a 4-bit generation counter to CID bits 15:12 ( nvme_cid_install_genctr() ) and warns on mismatching completions, which catches the host-side variant.
Linux v7.2 source: nvme.h:nvme_cid() , nvme_genctr_from_cid() ; quirk NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN disables the generation counter for devices that mishandle it.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: only from a user-space driver or a protocol exerciser that can submit duplicate CIDs.

name: Data Transfer Error (SCT 0 / SC 0x04)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. The cause is usually visible too: the device's MRd of a PRP address answered by a Cpl with UR/CA status, or no completion at all. Pattern: MRd from device → Cpl with status UR or CA (or no completion → device completion timeout), followed by a CQE with SC 0x04.
What happens: Moving data or metadata between host memory and the controller failed: a DMA read returned an error completion, a write could not be posted, or a transport failed in the middle of a transfer.
How it shows up: SC 0x04, DNR varies (QEMU uses both). Often there is a companion PCIe-level error: Unsupported Request or Completer Abort completion for the device's MRd, or an IOMMU fault on the host. Linux → -EIO.
Spec basis: Generic "Data Transfer Error". PCIe completion status UR/CA for the device's memory reads.
Typical causes: IOMMU blocks a PRP/SGL address (stale mapping, use-after-unmap in the host driver); a bad PRP entry pointing to non-existent memory; host memory poisoned (ECC) during the DMA read; link errors that corrupt the transfer. QEMU: nvme_map_addr() , nvme_map_prp() , nvme_map_sgl() , nvme_tx() return it when pci_dma_rw() fails or the address cannot be mapped.
How to detect / prove: dmesg for IOMMU/DMAR faults with the device's BDF at the same time; AER logs; analyzer: the device's MRd to the PRP address gets a UR/CA completion. Check lspci -vvv DevSta "UnsupReq+" / "AuxPwr".
Linux v7.2 source: No special handling. Mapped to BLK_STS_IOERR in core.c:nvme_error_status() .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: in a QEMU guest with a vIOMMU, unmap a buffer while a passthrough command is outstanding; or use a protocol exerciser to return UR to the device's data MRd.

name: Commands Aborted due to Power Loss Notification (SCT 0 / SC 0x05)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Also visible: the CC.SHN MWr to BAR0+14h before it. A real power loss ends the capture (link down). Pattern: MWr to CC (offset 14h) setting SHN, then a burst of CQEs with SC 0x05, then CSTS.SHST = 10b (shutdown complete).
What happens: The controller saw a power-loss notification (e.g. a shutdown notification by CC.SHN, or a platform power-fail signal) and aborted outstanding commands instead of finishing them.
How it shows up: SC 0x05 on the commands that were outstanding. Retryable after power returns. Linux → -EIO if the request ends there; usually the controller is being shut down anyway.
Spec basis: Generic "Commands Aborted due to Power Loss Notification". Shutdown via CC.SHN / CSTS.SHST.
Typical causes: Host issued a shutdown while I/O was still queued (driver ordering bug); surprise power loss with a hold-up circuit giving the firmware time to post completions; hot-unplug.
How to detect / prove: Correlate with SMART "Unsafe Shutdowns" increasing, the Persistent Event log "Power-on or Reset" event, and CC.SHN writes in the trace. The data from writes aborted this way is not guaranteed. Verify it with read-back.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux quiesces and drains queues before shutdown ( pci.c:nvme_dev_disable() ). Seeing 0x05 under Linux suggests an unexpected power event. No special case in nvme_error_status() .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: write CC.SHN through a user-space driver while I/O is queued (not with the kernel driver bound). EXPERT: a power-fail test fixture.

name: Internal Error (SCT 0 / SC 0x06)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. The CQE is visible, but the internal cause is not. Proof needs telemetry/Persistent Event log, which is visible only if read (Get Log Page data MWr) during the capture. Pattern: Normal SQE fetch, sometimes partial data transfer, then a CQE with SC 0x06. Latency is often abnormal (long internal retry before giving up).
What happens: The command failed because of something inside the controller that is not a media error and not the host's fault: a firmware exception, resource exhaustion, an internal bus or SRAM error.
How it shows up: SC 0x06; DNR=0 for transient problems, DNR=1 if the firmware knows it will repeat. Often comes with an Error-type AEN (Transient Internal Error 04h or Persistent Internal Error 03h) and a Persistent Event log "NVM Subsystem Hardware Error" event. Linux → -EIO after retries.
Spec basis: Generic "Internal Error". Asynchronous Event Information – Error Status values 03h/04h (see S-79 ).
Typical causes: Firmware bugs (assertion, corner-case state), DRAM ECC errors inside the SSD, thermal throttling edge cases, internal queue overflow. QEMU: returned when the backend block-status query fails ( nvme_check_dulbe() ), in zone-state checks for impossible states, and in nvme_map_addr() when too many SG entries are needed.
How to detect / prove: Read nvme error-log , nvme persistent-event-log and the vendor telemetry ( nvme telemetry-log --output-file=... ) right after the event. Repeat the same command: if it fails deterministically, record it as a firmware defect with the exact SQE.
Linux v7.2 source: Default branch of core.c:nvme_error_status() ; persistent internal error AEN → core.c:nvme_handle_aer_persistent_error() resets the controller.
Test to provoke it: Not reliably possible from the host. Use vendor error-injection commands, or QEMU with a backend whose block-status call fails while DULBE is enabled.

name: Command Abort Requested (SCT 0 / SC 0x07)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. The whole sequence is visible: the original SQE, a long silence, then an admin SQE opcode 08h and two CQEs. Pattern: Original SQE → long silence → admin SQE opcode 08h with CDW10 = SQID | CID<<16 → CQE for the target (SC 0x07) and a CQE for the Abort.
What happens: The command was aborted because the host sent an Abort (admin opcode 08h) naming its SQID and CID.
How it shows up: The aborted command completes with SC 0x07. The Abort command itself completes with Dword 0 bit 0 = 0 if the command was aborted, 1 if not. Linux prints "Abort status: 0x%x" from pci.c:abort_endio() .
Spec basis: Admin Abort command; Identify Controller ACL (Abort Command Limit, 0's based); Generic "Command Abort Requested".
Typical causes: Almost always a host timeout: Linux pci.c:nvme_timeout() sends Abort for an I/O command that exceeded nvme_core.io_timeout (default 30 s) the first time it times out. The real problem is whatever made the command slow or stuck.
How to detect / prove: dmesg "I/O tag N (cid) opcode ... QID q timeout, aborting" followed by "Abort status". If the command is not aborted and times out again, Linux resets the controller ("timeout, reset controller").
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_timeout() , pci.c:abort_endio() ; the limit ctrl->abort_limit is set to ACL+1 in core.c .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: in QEMU, cause a stalled backend I/O (for example a blkdebug rule with a delay); lower io_timeout (writable module parameter) to see the abort sooner. QEMU's nvme_abort() cancels the backend AIO, which completes it with 0x07.

name: Command Aborted due to SQ Deletion (SCT 0 / SC 0x08)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Admin SQE opcode 00h → CQEs on the I/O CQ with SC 0x08 → CQE for Delete SQ.
What happens: The host deleted an I/O SQ (admin opcode 00h) while commands were still outstanding on it. The controller aborts them.
How it shows up: SC 0x08 on each outstanding command, posted to the associated CQ before the Delete SQ completes. If the CQ has already been reaped, these completions can be lost.
Spec basis: Delete I/O Submission Queue; Generic "Command Aborted due to SQ Deletion".
Typical causes: Controller reset path, CPU hot-unplug changing queue count, driver unload. QEMU: nvme_del_sq() and nvme_ctrl_reset() set this status on in-flight requests.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: Delete SQ SQE followed by completions with SC 0x08. Linux normally cancels requests itself (0x371) before deleting queues, so seeing many 0x08 under Linux suggests a driver bypass or a non-Linux host.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:adapter_delete_sq() ; mapped to -EIO by default.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: user-space driver deleting a busy SQ.

name: Fused command aborted: Failed Fused (0x09) / Missing Fused (0x0A)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: SQE[n] FUSE=01b, SQE[n+1] FUSE=10b. On failure: CQE(n) Compare Failure, CQE(n+1) SC 0x09.
What happens: A fused pair (e.g. Compare + Write = atomic compare-and-write) did not run as a pair. 0x09: the other half failed, so this half was aborted. 0x0A: the adjacent SQE was not the expected fused partner.
How it shows up: One half gets the real error (e.g. Compare Failure 0x285), and the other gets 0x09. A mis-built pair gets 0x0A.
Spec basis: Fused Operation (FUSE field in CDW0: first/second command); Identify FUSES. Generic codes 0x09, 0x0A.
Typical causes: Compare miscompare (expected for CAS semantics); host submitting the two halves non-adjacently (another thread rang the doorbell in between); controller not supporting fused operations.
How to detect / prove: Trace: both SQEs must be consecutive slots in the same SQ, and the tail doorbell must cover both in one write.
Linux v7.2 source: The kernel block path does not issue fused commands. They come only through passthrough ( ioctl.c ). Status → -EIO.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: user-space (SPDK-style) compare-and-write with deliberately wrong compare data → 0x285 + 0x09.

name: Invalid Namespace or Format (SCT 0 / SC 0x0B)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Immediate CQE after the SQE fetch.
What happens: The NSID is not valid for this command (not allocated, not attached, 0 where not allowed, or FFFFFFFFh where broadcast is not allowed), or the namespace's current format does not support the command.
How it shows up: SC 0x0B, normally DNR=1. Linux 0x00B → BLK_STS_NOTSUPP → -EOPNOTSUPP. During a namespace rescan, Linux treats an Identify Namespace failure with DNR as "namespace gone" and removes the block device.
Spec basis: Generic "Invalid Namespace or Format". Identify NN (number of namespaces), Active Namespace ID list (CNS 02h).
Typical causes: Namespace deleted or detached by another host or a management tool; stale NSID after reformatting; tools using NSID 1 on a drive where it does not exist. QEMU: nvme_io_cmd() , nvme_identify_ns() , nvme_get_feature() , nvme_smart_info() (per-namespace SMART not supported) and about 15 other sites.
How to detect / prove: nvme list-ns /dev/nvme0 --all versus nvme list-ns /dev/nvme0 (allocated vs attached); look for a Namespace Attribute Changed AEN and the Changed Namespace List log (LID 04h).
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() ; core.c:nvme_validate_ns() starts with ret = NVME_SC_INVALID_NS | NVME_STATUS_DNR and calls nvme_ns_remove() on fatal (DNR) errors.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0 -n 0xfffe (an unused NSID). CAUTION: detach a namespace ( nvme detach-ns ) with I/O running and watch the block device disappear.

name: Command Sequence Error (SCT 0 / SC 0x0C)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Immediate CQE. The interesting part is the earlier commands.
What happens: The command is valid on its own but not allowed in the current state of a multi-command sequence or controller state.
How it shows up: SC 0x0C, usually DNR=1.
Spec basis: Generic "Command Sequence Error". Examples in the spec: Firmware Image Download sequencing, Set Features Number of Queues after queues exist, security protocol sequences.
Typical causes: Changing Number of Queues (FID 07h) after I/O queues were created (QEMU nvme_set_feature() : if (n->qs_created) return NVME_CMD_SEQ_ERROR ); changing FDP mode while namespaces exist in the endurance group (QEMU); Firmware Commit without a complete downloaded image; TCG/OPAL protocol out of order.
How to detect / prove: Reconstruct the admin command order from a trace or from the nvme_setup_cmd / nvme_complete_rq tracepoints; check which preceding command changed the state.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux sets Number of Queues once per reset ( core.c:nvme_set_queue_count() ) before creating queues, so it avoids this. A tool that sends the feature at runtime gets 0x0C.
Test to provoke it: SAFE on QEMU / CAUTION on hardware: nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 7 -v 0x00030003 while the driver has queues.

name: Data pointer descriptor errors: SGL 0x0D–0x11, 0x16, 0x1E; PRP Offset 0x13
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. The faulty descriptor is also visible: decode the SQE DPTR and the MRd of the PRP list/SGL segment by hand. Pattern: MRd of the PRP list or SGL segment (sometimes), then a CQE. No data TLPs.
What happens: The controller rejects the data pointer: an invalid SGL Segment/Last Segment descriptor (0x0D), a bad number of descriptors (0x0E), Data SGL length too short or too long (0x0F), Metadata SGL length invalid (0x10), unsupported SGL descriptor type (0x11), SGL offset invalid (0x16, mainly fabrics in-capsule data), SGL data block granularity invalid (0x1E), or PRP entry offset invalid (0x13).
How it shows up: One of these SCs, with DNR=1 in QEMU. Linux → -EIO. These almost always point to a host driver or IOMMU bug, not a drive problem.
Spec basis: PRP rules (PRP1 offset; PRP list entries must be page-aligned, Dword-aligned offsets); SGL descriptor types; Identify Controller SGLS field.
Typical causes: QEMU: nvme_map_sgl() → 0x0D for a misplaced segment descriptor; nvme_map_sgl_data() → 0x0E / 0x0F; nvme_map_mptr() → 0x10; 0x11 for unknown types (ctrl.c line ~1013); nvme_map_prp() , nvme_create_cq() / nvme_create_sq() → 0x13 for a non-page-aligned PRP. In real systems: a new driver (user-space or in-kernel) building PRP lists across page boundaries incorrectly, or MPS (CC.MPS) disagreeing with the host's assumed page size.
How to detect / prove: Decode the SQE's PSDT and DPTR in the trace and walk the PRP list or SGL by hand. Check that CC.MPS matches the host page size the driver uses.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux builds PRPs and SGLs in pci.c (e.g. nvme_pci_setup_data_prp() and the SGL counterpart). Errors are mapped to -EIO by nvme_error_status() .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: user-space driver with a deliberately misaligned PRP2; QEMU gives deterministic results.

name: Controller Memory Buffer misuse: Invalid Use of CMB (0x12), Command Not Supported for Queue in CMB (0x1F)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Addresses inside the device's own BAR in the DPTR. There is no MRd to host memory for those parts.
What happens: 0x12: a data pointer mixes CMB (or PMR) addresses and host-memory addresses in a way the controller does not support, or uses the CMB for something not enabled in CMBSZ. 0x1F: the command is not allowed when its SQ/CQ lives in the CMB.
How it shows up: SC 0x12 / 0x1F, DNR=1 in QEMU.
Spec basis: CMBLOC (38h), CMBSZ (3Ch) register capabilities (SQS, CQS, WDS, RDS); CMBMSC in newer revisions.
Typical causes: QEMU nvme_map_addr() : a scatter list that has started with DMA addresses then hits a CMB/PMR address (or the reverse). Peer-to-peer DMA setups with partly mapped buffers.
How to detect / prove: Compare every PRP/SGL address with the CMB BAR range from lspci -vvv and the CMBLOC offset.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c CMB support ( nvme_map_cmb() ; SQs in CMB with the use_cmb_sqes module parameter). The status itself is mapped to -EIO.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: QEMU -device nvme,cmb_size_mb=64 plus a user-space driver mixing CMB and host buffers.

name: Atomic Write Unit Exceeded (SCT 0 / SC 0x14)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: SQE for Write with NLB > limit → CQE 0x14, no data MRd.
What happens: The write is longer than the atomic write unit, and the controller is configured to reject such writes instead of executing them non-atomically.
How it shows up: SC 0x14. Linux → -EIO. Note that Linux's newer atomic-write support ( RWF_ATOMIC ) checks sizes before submission, so a drive returning this to the kernel path points to a mismatch between Identify limits and behaviour.
Spec basis: Identify Controller AWUN/AWUPF; Identify Namespace NAWUN/NAWUPF/NABSN; Write Atomicity Normal feature (FID 0Ah); QEMU nvme_set_feature_write_atomicity() .
Typical causes: Database or filesystem relying on atomic writes larger than the advertised unit; writes crossing an atomic boundary (NABO/NABSN).
How to detect / prove: Compare the write's SLBA/NLB with NAWUPF/NABSN from nvme id-ns -H . QEMU's nvme_atomic_write_check() shows how a controller decides whether a write is atomic.
Linux v7.2 source: Atomic limits come from Identify (NAWUPF/AWUPF) into queue limits in core.c:nvme_configure_atomic_write() ; core.c:nvme_valid_atomic_write() refuses, on the host side, REQ_ATOMIC writes that cross an atomic boundary before they reach the drive. The status itself → -EIO.
Test to provoke it: SAFE (data-destructive only for the target LBA range): enable the Write Atomicity Normal feature on QEMU and issue an oversized write with nvme write .

name: Operation Denied (SCT 0 / SC 0x15)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Immediate CQE; for SEDs, there are Security Send/Receive (81h/82h) exchanges earlier.
What happens: The command was denied for lack of access rights, as defined by a security specification (e.g. TCG Storage), or by a locking or lockdown rule.
How it shows up: SC 0x15. A read to a locked TCG range usually returns this or Access Denied 0x286, depending on the implementation impl .
Spec basis: Generic "Operation Denied"; Security Send/Receive; related Generic 0x23 "Command Prohibited by Command and Feature Lockdown" (libnvme NVME_SC_PROHIBITED_BY_CMD_AND_FEAT ).
Typical causes: Self-encrypting drive locked after power cycle (no unlock in initramfs); management commands blocked by lockdown; vendor-unique commands needing a key.
How to detect / prove: sedutil-cli --query or nvme security-recv to check locking state; repeat after unlock.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c OPAL hook ( nvme_sec_submit() ); the status itself → -EIO.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: lock a TCG Opal range on a test drive and read it.

name: Host Identifier Inconsistent Format (0x18), Keep Alive Timer Expired (0x19), Keep Alive Timeout Invalid (0x1A)
In a PEX trace: Not visible Not on PCIe at all: NVMe-oF statuses travel in TCP/RDMA/FC response capsules, so a PEX capture of the NIC/HBA link shows only encrypted or opaque network DMA. Use a network capture (Wireshark NVMe/TCP dissector) or target logs. Pattern: Missing Keep Alive (admin opcode 18h) commands for > KATO, then the association closes.
What happens: 0x18: the subsystem saw both 64-bit and 128-bit Host Identifiers used across controllers. 0x19: the Keep Alive Timer expired and the controller tears down the association; outstanding commands may complete with this status. 0x1A: Set Features Keep Alive Timer (FID 0Fh) with an unacceptable value.
How it shows up: On fabrics: 0x19 together with the controller disappearing; the host sees the connection reset and reconnect attempts. On PCIe keep-alive is optional and rarely enabled.
Spec basis: Host Identifier feature (FID 81h); Keep Alive Timer feature (FID 0Fh), KAS in Identify Controller.
Typical causes: 0x19: host stalled (CPU soft lockup, network partition), or a target too strict about KATO. 0x18: mixed host tooling on a shared subsystem. 0x1A: KATO outside the controller's range.
How to detect / prove: On the host: dmesg keep-alive messages from core.c:nvme_keep_alive_end_io() ; on the target, its log; on the network, a gap in Keep Alive capsules longer than KATO.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_keep_alive_work() , nvme_keep_alive_end_io() ; pr.c handles 0x18 ( NVME_SC_HOST_ID_INCONSIST ) for Reservation Report by retrying without the Extended Data Structure (128-bit Host ID) format.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: NVMe/TCP loopback target, then tc qdisc add ... netem loss 100% for longer than KATO.

name: Command Aborted due to Preempt and Abort (SCT 0 / SC 0x1B)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: On the other host's path: Reservation Acquire (opcode 11h) with RACQA=Preempt and Abort; on this host's path: CQEs with 0x1B.
What happens: Another host ran Reservation Acquire with the Preempt and Abort action. Commands from the preempted host that were in progress on the namespace are aborted.
How it shows up: SC 0x1B on in-flight commands of the preempted host. Later commands from that host get Reservation Conflict (0x83). A Reservation Notification log page (LID 80h) and an I/O Command Set–specific AEN (Reservation Log Page Available) may follow.
Spec basis: Reservations (Register/Acquire/Release/Report); Reservation Notification log.
Typical causes: Cluster fencing (pacemaker/STONITH with persistent reservations) evicting a node.
How to detect / prove: nvme resv-report /dev/nvme0n1 before and after; cluster logs; nvme get-log -i 0x80 .
Linux v7.2 source: pr.c implements the block pr_ops ; status → -EIO in the I/O path.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: two hosts (or two controllers) on a shared namespace; register both keys, acquire on A, then preempt-and-abort from B while A runs fio.

name: Sanitize Failed (SCT 0 / SC 0x1C)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Sanitize state itself is visible only via the Sanitize Status log read (Get Log Page LID 81h data MWr) if it happens during the capture. Pattern: Sanitize SQE earlier; reads now return 0x1C immediately.
What happens: The most recent sanitize operation failed and no recovery has completed yet. Until then, the controller rejects commands that would expose possibly un-sanitized data.
How it shows up: Media-access commands complete with SC 0x1C. Sanitize Status log (LID 81h) SSTAT status = 3h "completed with failure" (libnvme NVME_SANITIZE_SSTAT_STATUS_COMPLETED_FAILED ). See S-89 .
Spec basis: Sanitize command (84h), Sanitize Status log, "Exit Failure Mode" sanitize action.
Typical causes: Block erase failed on some dies; power lost during sanitize with an implementation that cannot resume; crypto erase key-store failure.
How to detect / prove: nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0 : SSTAT and SPROG; Persistent Event log Sanitize Start/Completion events (types 09h/0Ah).
Linux v7.2 source: No special handling (→ -EIO). The kernel does not issue Sanitize itself.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT/destructive: power-cycle during a sanitize on a sacrificial drive. Recovery: nvme sanitize -a 1 (Exit Failure Mode) or retry sanitize.

name: Sanitize In Progress (SCT 0 / SC 0x1D)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Every I/O SQE gets an immediate CQE 0x1D.
What happens: A sanitize is running. Commands that are prohibited during sanitize (I/O, most admin commands that touch media) are rejected.
How it shows up: SC 0x1D, typically DNR=0 (it will work once sanitize is done). Linux retries up to max_retries , which is far shorter than a sanitize, so the I/O ends with -EIO. Boot-time partition scans fail and the disk may look empty.
Spec basis: Sanitize; Sanitize Status log SPROG (progress /65536) and SSTAT = 2h "in progress"; sanitize persists across resets and power cycles.
Typical causes: A sanitize started by someone else (or by a previous boot, because sanitize resumes after power cycle); estimated times (ETBE/ETCE/ETO fields in LID 81h) of hours on large drives.
How to detect / prove: nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0 shows SSTAT=2 and SPROG increasing. Get Log Page for LID 81h is allowed during sanitize.
Linux v7.2 source: Generic retry in core.c:nvme_decide_disposition() ; the delay depends only on CRD.
Test to provoke it: DESTRUCTIVE / EXPERT: nvme sanitize /dev/nvme0 -a 2 (block erase) on a scratch drive, then dd from it.

name: Namespace is Write Protected (SCT 0 / SC 0x20)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Writes get immediate CQEs. Reads succeed.
What happens: The namespace is in a write-protected state (Namespace Write Protection Config feature: Write Protect, Write Protect Until Power Cycle, Permanent Write Protect), so writes and other modifying commands are refused.
How it shows up: SC 0x20 on writes. Linux → -EIO for that write. Linux also reads the namespace write-protect state at scan time and marks the disk read-only if Identify NS NSATTR has the write-protected bit set.
Spec basis: Namespace Write Protection Config feature (FID 84h); NSATTR in Identify Namespace.
Typical causes: Admin set write protection (forensics, golden images); permanent protection after end-of-life policies; feature set without the host noticing (no AEN for it).
How to detect / prove: nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -f 0x84 ; nvme id-ns -H NSATTR; blockdev --getro .
Linux v7.2 source: core.c namespace update path sets the disk read-only from NSATTR ( NVME_NS_ATTR_RO ). The status itself → -EIO.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -f 0x84 -v 1 (Write Protect, reversible), write, then set it back to 0. Never use the permanent value on a drive you want to keep.

name: Command Interrupted (SCT 0 / SC 0x21)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: CQE 0x21 → host waits the CRD time → same command re-submitted.
What happens: The controller stopped processing the command (internal event, ANA-related change, resource rebalance) and asks the host to retry, often with a Command Retry Delay.
How it shows up: SC 0x21 with DNR=0 by definition. If the retries run out, Linux maps it to BLK_STS_TARGET → -EREMOTEIO ("critical target error").
Spec basis: Generic "Command Interrupted": "the host should retry the command" (libnvme). CRD field + CRDT1–3 + ACRE.
Typical causes: Firmware busy with a background operation; controller-level events in dual-port arrays; QEMU returns it as an internal status for interrupted zone/atomic operations (defined as NVME_COMMAND_INTERRUPTED ).
How to detect / prove: Trace with nvme:nvme_complete_rq (status 0x21 with retries > 0) and command_retries_count . Check CRD values against nvme id-ctrl crdt1..3.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() → BLK_STS_TARGET; nvme_retry_req() CRD delay; nvme_configure_host_options() ACRE.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: fault-inject status 0x21 with dont_retry=0 (§II.1.5) to see the retry and errno behaviour.

name: Transient Transport Error (SCT 0 / SC 0x22)
In a PEX trace: Not visible Not on PCIe at all: NVMe-oF statuses travel in TCP/RDMA/FC response capsules, so a PEX capture of the NIC/HBA link shows only encrypted or opaque network DMA. Use a network capture (Wireshark NVMe/TCP dissector) or target logs. Pattern: On the network capture: retransmissions or digest mismatches just before the response capsule.
What happens: A short-lived transport problem made the command fail. Retrying on the same controller should work. libnvme quotes the spec: after four or more failures with this status, treat it as a persistent transport error.
How it shows up: SC 0x22, DNR=0. Linux retries (up to 5) and then gives -EIO. It is not in SCT 3, so Linux multipath does not fail over on it directly.
Spec basis: Generic "Transient Transport Error"; transport bindings (TCP, RDMA, FC).
Typical causes: Packet loss or digest errors (NVMe/TCP HDGST/DDGST), RDMA retry exhaustion, FC link resets.
How to detect / prove: Network counters ( ethtool -S , RDMA counters), NVMe/TCP digest error messages in dmesg; correlation with retries in the tracepoint.
Linux v7.2 source: Default retry/COMPLETE path in core.c ; transport drivers in tcp.c / rdma.c .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: NVMe/TCP with tc netem corrupt plus data digest enabled.

name: Admin Command Media Not Ready (SCT 0 / SC 0x24)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: CC write with CRIME=1 → CSTS.RDY=1 quickly → admin command → CQE 0x24.
What happens: The admin command needs the media, but the media is not ready yet. This can happen when the controller became ready early (CSTS.RDY) because the host set CC.CRIME (Controller Ready Independent of Media Enable).
How it shows up: SC 0x24 on admin commands such as Identify Namespace, Get Log Page of media-backed logs, Format.
Spec basis: CAP.CRMS (CRWMS/CRIMS), CC.CRIME, CRTO register (Controller Ready Timeouts).
Typical causes: Host using CRIME mode and sending media-dependent commands before media ready; large drives whose internal metadata load takes seconds.
How to detect / prove: Check CC.CRIME in a register dump or trace; compare time since CC.EN with CRTO.CRIMT.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_enable_ctrl() clears CRIME on purpose: "Setting CRIME results in CSTS.RDY before the media is ready. This makes it possible for media related commands to return the error NVME_SC_ADMIN_COMMAND_MEDIA_NOT_READY. Until the driver is restructured to handle retries, disable CC.CRIME." So Linux should never see this code.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: user-space driver enabling with CRIME=1 on a CAP.CRMS-capable drive and sending Identify NS at once.

name: I/O Command Set errors: Invalid I/O Command Set (0x2C) and the 0x29–0x2B group
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Identify with CNS 05h/06h and a CSI value → immediate CQE.
What happens: A command references a Command Set Identifier (CSI) that the controller does not support, has not enabled, or cannot combine with the others.
How it shows up: Linux defines NVME_SC_INVALID_IO_CMD_SET = 0x2C in the Generic range. QEMU ( NVME_INVALID_IOCS = 0x012c ) and libnvme ( NVME_SC_INVALID_IOCS = 0x2c under "Command Set Specific – Namespace Types") place it in SCT 1 , along with 0x29 I/O Command Set Not Supported, 0x2A Not Enabled, 0x2B Combination Rejected. uncertain Verify the SCT in the spec. A Linux string lookup of a real SCT 1 / 0x2C status prints "Unknown" because 0x12C has no entry.
Spec basis: I/O Command Set Profile feature (FID 19h), Identify I/O Command Set data structure (CNS 1Ch), CC.CSS.
Typical causes: QEMU: nvme_identify_ns() returns INVALID_IOCS for a namespace whose CSI is not enabled; nvme_set_feature() returns IOCS_NOT_SUPPORTED / COMBINATION_REJECTED. Real: tools asking for ZNS/KV identify data on an NVM-only controller.
How to detect / prove: nvme id-iocs /dev/nvme0 ; nvme get-feature -f 0x19 .
Linux v7.2 source: Linux sets CC.CSS to NVME_CC_CSS_CSI when CAP.CSS allows it ( core.c:nvme_enable_ctrl() ) and ignores namespaces with unsupported CSI during scan.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvme admin-passthru /dev/nvme0 --opcode=0x06 --cdw10=0x05 --cdw11=0x05000000 -r -l 4096 --namespace-id=1 (Identify CNS 05h with an unsupported CSI value).

name: LBA Out of Range (SCT 0 / SC 0x80)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: SQE with SLBA near the end of the namespace → immediate CQE.
What happens: SLBA + NLB goes past the namespace size (NSZE), or the arithmetic overflows. Nothing is transferred.
How it shows up: SC 0x80, DNR=1 in QEMU. Linux maps it to BLK_STS_TARGET → -EREMOTEIO ("critical target error"), not EIO, which surprises people searching logs.
Spec basis: Generic (I/O command set) "LBA Out of Range"; Identify Namespace NSZE.
Typical causes: Namespace shrunk/recreated while the host kept the old size (no rescan); partition table from a larger drive copied to a smaller one; block-layer sector-to-LBA conversion bugs with mixed 512/4096 formats. QEMU: nvme_check_bounds() : if (UINT64_MAX - slba < nlb || slba + nlb > nsze) .
How to detect / prove: dmesg error line shows "@ LBA x, n blocks". Compare with nvme id-ns NSZE and blockdev --getsize64 . A mismatch means a stale capacity.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() (BLK_STS_TARGET); capacity updates in nvme_update_ns_info() after rescans.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvme read /dev/nvme0n1 -s <NSZE> -c 0 -z 4096 (read the block just past the end).

name: Capacity Exceeded (SCT 0 / SC 0x81)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Write SQE → CQE 0x81, possibly after data transfer.
What happens: Running the command would make the namespace use more than its capacity (NCAP). This only matters for thin-provisioned namespaces, where NCAP < NSZE.
How it shows up: SC 0x81. Linux maps it to BLK_STS_NOSPC → -ENOSPC: the filesystem gets "no space" even though df shows free space.
Spec basis: Identify Namespace NSZE, NCAP, NUSE; thin provisioning (NSFEAT bit 0).
Typical causes: Over-subscribed thin namespace; host not sending Deallocate (discard), so NUSE never shrinks; deallocations the drive accepts but does not apply (see silent-failure part).
How to detect / prove: Watch NUSE vs NCAP with nvme id-ns over time; compare with filesystem usage. If NUSE stays high after fstrim , deallocation is not taking effect.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() → BLK_STS_NOSPC.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: thin namespace (QEMU or array) filled past NCAP with fio.

name: Namespace Not Ready (SCT 0 / SC 0x82)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Immediate CQE 0x82 to I/O shortly after controller enable.
What happens: The namespace cannot be accessed right now, for a reason other than an ANA state (libnvme wording). Examples: still coming up after reset, a background operation, or a namespace that is being created.
How it shows up: SC 0x82. DNR=0 means "try again later", DNR=1 means "will not become ready". Linux → BLK_STS_TARGET → -EREMOTEIO once retries are used up.
Spec basis: Generic "Namespace Not Ready"; Identify Namespace / I/O Command Set Independent NS data "Namespace Ready" indications in newer revisions (verify in spec).
Typical causes: Command sent right after reset or namespace attach on a drive that rebuilds mapping tables; a drive in a vendor "failure" mode returning 0x82 to everything.
How to detect / prove: Time since CSTS.RDY; check whether it clears by itself (poll with nvme read each second). Persistent 0x82 with DNR=1 is a dead namespace.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() → BLK_STS_TARGET.
Test to provoke it: SAFE via fault injection (status 0x082).

name: Reservation Conflict (SCT 0 / SC 0x83)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: I/O SQE → immediate CQE 0x83.
What happens: Another host holds a reservation on the namespace that does not allow this host's access (for example, Write Exclusive held by another host, and this host writes).
How it shows up: SC 0x83, normally DNR=1. Linux maps it to BLK_STS_RESV_CONFLICT → -EBADE; the persistent-reservation API returns PR_STS_RESERVATION_CONFLICT .
Spec basis: Reservation types (Write Exclusive, Exclusive Access, Registrants Only, All Registrants); Reservation Report.
Typical causes: Cluster software fenced this node; stale reservation left by a crashed node; a host that has not registered its key after reboot.
How to detect / prove: nvme resv-report /dev/nvme0n1 -c 1 shows holder, type and registrants; compare with this host's Host ID ( nvme get-feature -f 0x81 ).
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() ; pr.c:nvme_status_to_pr_err() .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: nvme resv-register + resv-acquire -t 1 (Write Exclusive) from controller A, write from controller B.

name: Format In Progress (SCT 0 / SC 0x84)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Format SQE without its CQE yet; I/O CQEs with 0x84.
What happens: A Format NVM is running on the namespace; I/O to it is rejected until it completes.
How it shows up: SC 0x84 on I/O, DNR typically 0. Linux retries a few times, then -EIO.
Spec basis: Format NVM (80h); Identify Controller FNA (Format NVM Attributes, e.g. whether a format applies to all namespaces). Some drives report progress in a vendor log.
Typical causes: Format issued by another tool or host on a shared namespace, or on a "format all namespaces" drive (FNA bit) where formatting one namespace blocks the others. QEMU: nvme_do_format() sets ns->status = NVME_FORMAT_IN_PROGRESS and I/O to that namespace returns it until done.
How to detect / prove: Look for an earlier Format SQE (opcode 80h) in the trace or in the admin nvme_setup_cmd tracepoint; Persistent Event log Format NVM Start/Completion events (07h/08h).
Linux v7.2 source: Default handling; the kernel itself never formats.
Test to provoke it: DESTRUCTIVE / CAUTION: on a scratch namespace in QEMU, nvme format /dev/nvme0n1 -s 1 (user-data erase; slower) and read from another shell.

name: Completion Queue Invalid (SCT 1 / SC 0x00)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Create SQ with CQID=n where no earlier successful Create CQ n exists.
What happens: Create I/O SQ named a CQID that does not exist (or is 0), or Delete I/O CQ named an invalid CQ.
How it shows up: Linux 0x100 "Completion Queue Invalid" on the admin command; queue setup continues with fewer queues (see callout above).
Spec basis: Create I/O Submission Queue (01h) CDW11 CQID; Delete I/O Completion Queue (04h).
Typical causes: Host creating the SQ before its CQ, or after a failed CQ creation; QEMU nvme_create_sq() and nvme_del_cq() : if (!cqid || nvme_check_cqid(n, cqid)) return NVME_INVALID_CQID | NVME_DNR .
How to detect / prove: Admin command order in the trace: Create CQ (05h) must complete successfully before Create SQ (01h) uses its ID.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_create_queue() → adapter_alloc_cq() then adapter_alloc_sq() .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: user-space driver creating SQ 1 bound to CQ 7 that was never created.

name: Invalid Queue Identifier (SCT 1 / SC 0x01)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Set Features FID 07h CQE DW0 = e.g. 0x00070007 (8 SQ + 8 CQ), then Create CQ with QID 9.
What happens: Create I/O SQ/CQ used a QID that is 0, already in use, or above the number of queues granted by Set Features Number of Queues. Also used by Delete I/O SQ for a bad SQID.
How it shows up: Linux 0x101; queue creation stops at that queue.
Spec basis: Number of Queues feature (FID 07h) result NSQA/NCQA (0's based); Create/Delete queue commands.
Typical causes: Host asked for N queues, got fewer in the Set Features result, and created N anyway; QID reuse without deleting. QEMU: nvme_create_sq() / nvme_create_cq() check qid > n->conf_ioqpairs || n->sq[qid] != NULL .
How to detect / prove: Decode the Number of Queues completion Dword 0 in the trace and compare with the highest QID created.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_set_queue_count() uses the granted count. pci.c:nvme_setup_io_queues() sizes the queues from it.
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: start with -device nvme,max_ioqpairs=4 and create queue 5 from a user-space driver.

name: Invalid Queue Size (SCT 1 / SC 0x02)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Create CQ CDW10 = (QSIZE<<16)|QID with QSIZE > MQES.
What happens: The queue size in Create I/O SQ/CQ is 0 or bigger than CAP.MQES+1, or (QEMU) the CC.IOSQES/IOCQES entry sizes are not 64/16 bytes.
How it shows up: Linux 0x102 "Invalid Queue Size".
Spec basis: CAP.MQES (0's based maximum queue entries); CAP.CQR (contiguous queues required); CC.IOSQES/IOCQES.
Typical causes: Host ignoring MQES; a device that reports MQES wrongly (Linux has quirks for this). QEMU: nvme_create_cq() / nvme_create_sq() return NVME_MAX_QSIZE_EXCEEDED | NVME_DNR .
How to detect / prove: Read CAP ( nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -H ) and the QSIZE field (CDW10 bits 31:16) of the Create command.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : queue depth is limited by NVME_CAP_MQES(cap) + 1 and the io_queue_depth module parameter (default 1024).
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: user-space driver creating a queue of MQES+2 entries.

name: Abort Command Limit Exceeded (0x03) / 0x04 "Abort Command Is Missing" (reserved)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: ACL+2 Abort SQEs without completions between them; the last one gets 0x103.
What happens: The host has more Abort commands outstanding than ACL+1 (Identify Controller ACL is 0's based). The extra Abort is rejected. 0x04 is listed by libnvme as "Abort command is missing". Linux names it NVME_SC_ABORT_MISSING but prints "Reserved" uncertain in current specs.
How it shows up: The Abort itself completes with 0x103. Linux logs "Abort status: 0x103" from pci.c:abort_endio() .
Spec basis: Abort command (08h); ACL in Identify Controller (spec recommends at least 4, i.e. ACL ≥ 3).
Typical causes: Many simultaneous timeouts from a non-Linux host. Linux sets ctrl->abort_limit = id->acl + 1 and, in nvme_timeout() , does not send more aborts than that (it re-arms the timer instead). Linux therefore should not trigger this code unless ACL is reported wrongly.
How to detect / prove: Count outstanding Abort SQEs (opcode 08h) in the trace vs ACL from nvme id-ctrl .
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_timeout() ( atomic_dec_return(&dev->ctrl.abort_limit) < 0 → BLK_EH_RESET_TIMER ).
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: user-space driver issuing ACL+2 aborts for commands stuck in a slow backend (QEMU).

name: Asynchronous Event Request Limit Exceeded (SCT 1 / SC 0x05)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: AER SQEs normally stay outstanding for hours. One that completes within microseconds with 0x105 is this error.
What happens: More AER commands are outstanding than the controller supports (Identify Controller AERL, 0's based). The extra AER completes at once with this status.
How it shows up: 0x105 on an AER (opcode 0Ch). Linux's nvme_complete_async_event() returns early for any non-success AER status ( if (le16_to_cpu(status) >> 1 != NVME_SC_SUCCESS) return; ) and does not resubmit, so the error is not logged.
Spec basis: Asynchronous Event Request command; AERL (spec recommends at least 4 supported).
Typical causes: A host or tool submitting AERs in a loop; a controller with AERL=0 meeting a host that posts several. Linux posts only one ( NVME_NR_AEN_COMMANDS = 1 ). QEMU: nvme_aer() : if (n->outstanding_aers > n->params.aerl) return NVME_AER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (no DNR).
How to detect / prove: Count outstanding opcode 0Ch commands in the trace; compare with AERL.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_complete_async_event() , pci.c:nvme_pci_submit_async_event() (fixed CID NVME_AQ_BLK_MQ_DEPTH ).
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: -device nvme,aerl=0 plus a second AER sent with nvme admin-passthru --opcode=0x0c (it blocks until an event if accepted).

name: Invalid Firmware Slot (SCT 1 / SC 0x06)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Firmware Commit SQE CDW10[2:0] slot value → immediate CQE.
What happens: Firmware Commit named a slot that does not exist, or a read-only slot (slot 1 when FRMW.S1RO is set) for a replace action.
How it shows up: 0x106 on Firmware Commit (opcode 10h). nvme-cli prints the status name.
Spec basis: Identify Controller FRMW: bit 0 slot 1 read-only, bits 3:1 number of slots, bit 4 activation without reset; Firmware Commit CDW10 FS (slot) and CA (commit action).
Typical causes: Update scripts written for a model with more slots; writing to slot 1 on drives where it holds the read-only factory image; slot 0 used with a CA that requires an explicit slot.
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ctrl -H /dev/nvme0 | grep -A5 frmw ; nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0 shows populated slots.
Linux v7.2 source: The kernel does not issue Firmware Commit. Only passthrough (status returned raw to nvme-cli).
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvme fw-commit /dev/nvme0 -s 7 -a 2 on a drive with fewer than 7 slots (CA 2 = activate existing image; no image is replaced).

name: Invalid Firmware Image (0x07) and Overlapping Range (0x14)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: A series of opcode 11h SQEs with OFST increasing by NUMD+1; a gap or overlap is visible directly.
What happens: 0x07: the downloaded image failed validation (signature, CRC, wrong model, incomplete) at commit time. 0x14: Firmware Image Download pieces overlapped (the same offset range sent twice in an incompatible way).
How it shows up: 0x107 on Firmware Commit, or 0x114 on Firmware Image Download/Commit. The running firmware is unchanged. Some drives also raise an Error AEN "Firmware Image Load Error" (05h) at a later activation.
Spec basis: Firmware Image Download (11h) NUMD/OFST in Dwords; FWUG (Firmware Update Granularity) in Identify Controller; Firmware Commit.
Typical causes: Wrong image file for the SKU; chunk size not a multiple of FWUG; tool retrying a chunk with a different offset; image signed for a different security version (anti-rollback).
How to detect / prove: Log every Firmware Image Download (offset, length) and check contiguity; compare nvme id-ctrl FWUG with the transfer size ( nvme fw-download --xfer ).
Linux v7.2 source: Passthrough only.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: download a truncated or foreign image, then commit with CA=0 (replace, no activation). The drive must reject it without bricking. Run this as a robustness test.

name: Invalid Interrupt Vector (SCT 1 / SC 0x08)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Create CQ CDW11[31:16] = vector ≥ table size.
What happens: Create I/O CQ named an interrupt vector the controller cannot use: beyond the MSI-X table size, or non-zero when MSI-X is disabled.
How it shows up: 0x108; Linux continues with fewer queues.
Spec basis: Create I/O CQ CDW11 IV and IEN; PCIe MSI-X capability Table Size.
Typical causes: MSI-X table smaller than the advertised queue count; host fell back to MSI/INTx but still assigns per-queue vectors. QEMU nvme_create_cq() : if (!msix_enabled(...) && vector) and if (vector >= n->conf_msix_qsize) .
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv MSI-X "Count=" vs number of I/O queues; /proc/interrupts nvme entries.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:adapter_alloc_cq() ; vector allocation in nvme_setup_irqs() .
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: -device nvme,msix_qsize=2 with more queues requested; boot with pci=nomsi to see the non-MSI-X case.

name: Invalid Log Page (SCT 1 / SC 0x09)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Get Log Page with CDW10[7:0]=LID → immediate CQE.
What happens: Get Log Page asked for an unsupported or reserved Log Identifier.
How it shows up: 0x109. QEMU, however, returns Invalid Field (0x002) from nvme_get_log() 's default case. Implementations differ on which code they use impl .
Spec basis: Get Log Page (02h) LID; Supported Log Pages log (LID 00h, Linux NVME_LOG_SUPPORTED ); LPA field in Identify Controller.
Typical causes: Tools asking for Persistent Event (0Dh), Telemetry (07h/08h) or vendor logs on drives without them.
How to detect / prove: nvme supported-log-pages /dev/nvme0 (if LID 00h is supported) and LPA bits in nvme id-ctrl -H .
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_get_log() ; the driver checks LPA before reading optional logs (e.g. command effects via NVME_CTRL_LPA_CMD_EFFECTS_LOG ).
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvme get-log /dev/nvme0 -i 0x30 -l 512 .

name: Invalid Format (SCT 1 / SC 0x0A)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Format SQE (80h) → fast CQE. A real format takes seconds to hours.
What happens: Format NVM asked for an LBA format index that does not exist, or for a PI/metadata combination the namespace cannot support.
How it shows up: 0x10A on Format NVM. The namespace is unchanged.
Spec basis: Identify Namespace NLBAF and LBAF[] table; Format NVM CDW10 LBAF, MSET, PI, PIL, SES.
Typical causes: LBAF index beyond NLBAF; PI type with a format whose metadata size is 0; extended LBA format index (above 15) without LBAFEE. QEMU: nvme_format_check() returns NVME_INVALID_FORMAT | NVME_DNR for lbaf > nlbaf and for PI on formats with metadata smaller than the PI size. nvme_copy() also uses it for formats it cannot copy between.
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ns -H /dev/nvme0n1 lists the LBA formats with "in use".
Linux v7.2 source: Passthrough only; Linux enables LBAFEE in Host Behavior Support when CTRATT.ELBAS is set ( core.c:nvme_configure_host_options() ).
Test to provoke it: SAFE (rejected before any erase): nvme format /dev/nvme0n1 -l 15 on a namespace with fewer formats.

name: Firmware Activation Requires Reset: Conventional (0x0B), NVM Subsystem (0x10), Controller Level (0x11)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Firmware Commit CQE with SCT 1 SC 0x0B/0x10/0x11; later CC.EN 1→0→1 (controller reset), PCIe hot/conventional reset, or a write of "NVMe" (4E564D65h) to NSSR.
What happens: These are successes reported as errors . The commit worked and the image is in the slot, but it will only run after the given type of reset. Until then the old firmware keeps running.
How it shows up: 0x10B / 0x110 / 0x111 on Firmware Commit. Firmware Slot log (LID 03h) AFI: the "next active" slot (bits 6:4) differs from the current slot (bits 2:0). Linux reports this at AEN time as "Firmware is activated after next Controller Level Reset".
Spec basis: Firmware Commit CA values (libnvme: 0 replace, 1 replace+activate at reset, 2 activate at reset, 3 replace+activate immediately, 6/7 boot partition); Firmware Slot Information log AFI; NSSR register (20h) for subsystem reset.
Typical causes: Image needs a full reset to load; CA=1/2 used (activation at next reset by design). Scripts that treat any non-zero status as failure roll back a successful update. Scripts that ignore it think the new firmware is running when it is not.
How to detect / prove: nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0 AFI before and after; cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/firmware_rev stays old until reset; after a reset, check the revision again.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_get_fw_slot_info() : if (!cur_fw_slot || (next_fw_slot && (cur_fw_slot != next_fw_slot))) → "Firmware is activated after next Controller Level Reset"; reset via nvme reset /dev/nvme0 ( NVME_IOCTL_RESET ) or subsystem reset ( NVME_IOCTL_SUBSYS_RESET , pci.c:nvme_pci_subsystem_reset() ).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: nvme fw-download a valid image, nvme fw-commit -s 2 -a 1 , read status, then nvme reset /dev/nvme0 and verify firmware_rev . Use a supported vendor image only.

name: Firmware Activation Requires Maximum Time Violation (0x12) / Activation Prohibited (0x13)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Commit CDW10[5:3]=3 → CQE 0x12.
What happens: 0x12: activating now (CA=3, immediate) would take longer than MTFA (Maximum Time for Firmware Activation, Identify Controller, 100 ms units), so the controller refuses. 0x13: the controller refuses this image for vendor-specific reasons (e.g. anti-rollback, a downgrade not allowed).
How it shows up: 0x112 / 0x113 on Firmware Commit; the running firmware is unchanged.
Spec basis: MTFA; FRMW bit 4 (activation without reset supported); Firmware Commit CA=3.
Typical causes: Immediate activation of an image that changes the media layout; downgrade blocked by security policy.
How to detect / prove: Retry with CA=1/2 and a reset. If it works, the immediate path was the problem. For 0x13, check the vendor's release notes for minimum versions.
Linux v7.2 source: MTFA is stored in ctrl->mtfa and used by core.c:nvme_fw_act_work() to bound the wait while CSTS.PP is set after a "Firmware Activation Starting" AEN ( S-81 ).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: commit with CA=3 an image the vendor says needs a reset.

name: Invalid Queue Deletion (SCT 1 / SC 0x0C)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: 04h before 00h.
What happens: Delete I/O CQ was sent for a CQ that still has SQs attached (they must be deleted first), or for the admin CQ.
How it shows up: 0x10C on Delete I/O CQ (opcode 04h). QEMU returns it without DNR, so retrying after deleting the SQ is expected.
Spec basis: Delete I/O Completion Queue; queue deletion order (SQs before their CQ).
Typical causes: Teardown order bug in a host driver. QEMU nvme_del_cq() : if (!QTAILQ_EMPTY(&cq->sq_list)) return NVME_INVALID_QUEUE_DEL .
How to detect / prove: Trace order: Delete CQ (04h) issued before Delete SQ (00h) for an SQ mapped to that CQ.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_delete_io_queues() deletes SQs first, then CQs (passes of nvme_admin_delete_sq then nvme_admin_delete_cq ).
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: user-space driver deleting the CQ first.

name: Feature errors: Not Saveable (0x0D), Not Changeable (0x0E), Not Namespace Specific (0x0F)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Set Features CDW10 bit 31 (SV) set → CQE 0x10D.
What happens: Set Features with SV=1 for a feature that cannot be saved (0x0D); a write to a read-only feature (0x0E); a namespace-specific NSID used with a controller-wide feature (0x0F).
How it shows up: 0x10D/0x10E/0x10F with DNR=1 (QEMU). The current value is unchanged.
Spec basis: Set/Get Features, SV bit, Get Features SEL=11b "supported capabilities" (saveable, namespace-specific, changeable). ONCS bit "Save field in Set/Get Features".
Typical causes: Tools blindly setting --save . QEMU: nvme_set_feature() returns NVME_FID_NOT_SAVEABLE when save is set on any feature, NVME_FEAT_NOT_NS_SPEC for NSID ≠ 0/FFFFFFFFh on controller-scope features, NVME_FEAT_NOT_CHANGEABLE for fixed features.
How to detect / prove: nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f <fid> -s 3 (capabilities) before setting.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_set_features() never sets SV. Errors come only from passthrough tools.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -v 0 --save (Interrupt Coalescing, saved) on a drive without saveable support.

name: Namespace management/attachment errors: 0x15, 0x16, 0x18, 0x19, 0x1A, 0x1B, 0x1C, 0x24, 0x25
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Admin 0Dh/15h with a 4 KiB data buffer (namespace data or controller list) → CQE.
What happens: Namespace Management (0Dh) or Namespace Attachment (15h) refused: Namespace Insufficient Capacity (0x15), Namespace Identifier Unavailable (0x16, no free NSIDs), Namespace Already Attached (0x18), Namespace Is Private (0x19, already attached to another controller), Namespace Not Attached (0x1A, detach of a non-attached namespace), Thin Provisioning Not Supported (0x1B, NCAP < NSZE requested), Controller List Invalid (0x1C), ANA Group Identifier Invalid (0x24), ANA Attach Failed (0x25).
How it shows up: The matching 0x1xx status. Nothing changes.
Spec basis: Namespace Management create/delete; Namespace Attachment attach/detach with a Controller List; Identify TNVMCAP/UNVMCAP, NN, MNAN, ANAGRPMAX.
Typical causes: Provisioning scripts not checking UNVMCAP; wrong controller IDs (CNTLID) in the list; creating private namespaces on dual-port drives then attaching to both ports. QEMU nvme_ns_attachment() returns NS_ALREADY_ATTACHED, NS_PRIVATE, NS_NOT_ATTACHED, NS_CTRL_LIST_INVALID.
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ctrl (tnvmcap, unvmcap, nn, cntlid), nvme list-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -n <nsid> , nvme list-ns --all .
Linux v7.2 source: Passthrough only. After a successful change Linux rescans on the Namespace Attribute Changed AEN ( core.c:nvme_handle_aen_notice() → nvme_queue_scan() ).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION (the creates and deletes are destructive): on QEMU with -device nvme-subsys and nvme-ns,detached=true , attach the same namespace twice → 0x118.

name: Device Self-test In Progress (SCT 1 / SC 0x1D)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Two opcode 14h commands; the second gets 0x11D.
What happens: A Device Self-test (opcode 14h) was started while another self-test is running.
How it shows up: 0x11D. Device Self-test log (LID 06h) byte 0 shows the current operation (1h short, 2h extended) and byte 1 the percent complete.
Spec basis: Device Self-test command STC (1h short, 2h extended, Fh abort); Device Self-test log; EDSTT (extended test time, minutes).
Typical causes: Monitoring agents (smartd, vendor tools) starting tests on a schedule while a manual test runs.
How to detect / prove: nvme self-test-log /dev/nvme0 ; abort with nvme device-self-test -s 0xf .
Linux v7.2 source: Passthrough only.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvme device-self-test /dev/nvme0 -s 2 twice in a row.

name: Boot Partition Write Prohibited (SCT 1 / SC 0x1E)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Firmware Commit CA=6 → CQE 0x11E.
What happens: An attempt to change a locked Boot Partition (Firmware Image Download/Commit with boot-partition commit actions 6/7).
Spec basis: Boot Partitions (CAP.BPS, BPINFO/BPRSEL/BPMBL registers), Boot Partition Write Protection Config feature in newer revisions.
Typical causes: Platform locked the boot partition; tool writing the wrong partition.
How to detect / prove: nvme show-regs -H BPINFO; Boot Partition log (LID 15h).
Linux v7.2 source: Passthrough only.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: platform with boot-partition lock.

name: Virtualization management errors: 0x1F Invalid Controller Identifier, 0x20 Invalid Secondary Controller State, 0x21 Invalid Number of Controller Resources, 0x22 Invalid Resource Identifier
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Admin 1Ch → CQE.
What happens: Virtualization Management (1Ch) refused: unknown secondary controller, secondary controller in the wrong state (online vs offline) for the action, resources (VQ/VI) over the flexible limit, or bad resource type.
How it shows up: 0x11F–0x122 with DNR=1 (QEMU).
Spec basis: Virtualization Enhancements; Primary Controller Capabilities (CNS 14h), Secondary Controller List (CNS 15h).
Typical causes: Assigning resources to a VF that is online; asking for more queues than VQFRSM. QEMU: nvme_assign_virt_res_to_sec() , nvme_virt_set_state() , nvme_virt_mngmt() .
How to detect / prove: nvme primary-ctrl-caps , nvme list-secondary .
Linux v7.2 source: Passthrough only.
Test to provoke it: SAFE on QEMU with sriov_max_vfs : assign resources to a secondary controller that is online.

name: Sanitize Prohibited While Persistent Memory Region is Enabled (SCT 1 / SC 0x23)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Sanitize SQE → immediate CQE.
What happens: Sanitize was requested while the PMR is enabled (PMRCTL.EN=1).
How it shows up: 0x123. Linux prints "Sanitize Prohibited".
Spec basis: Persistent Memory Region (CAP.PMRS, PMRCAP/PMRCTL registers); Sanitize.
Typical causes: Decommissioning scripts not disabling the PMR first.
How to detect / prove: nvme show-regs -H PMRCTL.
Linux v7.2 source: Passthrough only.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: a PMR-capable controller (QEMU pmrdev= ) with PMR enabled.

name: Conflicting Attributes (SCT 1 / SC 0x80)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: DSM (09h) SQE, MRd of the range list, CQE 0x180.
What happens: Dataset Management (or another NVM command) carries attribute bits that contradict each other or that the controller cannot honour together.
How it shows up: 0x180 → Linux BLK_STS_NOTSUPP → -EOPNOTSUPP (a discard that fails this way looks like "discard not supported"). Persistent reservations map it to -EINVAL.
Spec basis: NVM Command Set: Dataset Management attributes (AD deallocate, IDR, IDW) and context attributes.
Typical causes: DSM with a combination the firmware does not implement; reservation commands with conflicting options.
How to detect / prove: Decode CDW11 of the DSM in the trace; repeat with only AD set.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() ; pr.c:nvme_status_to_pr_err() .
Test to provoke it: SAFE via fault injection; on hardware, nvme dsm /dev/nvme0n1 -a 1 -d -w -r combinations (illustrative; check the nvme-cli syntax for your version).

name: Invalid Protection Information (SCT 1 / SC 0x81)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Immediate CQE, no data.
What happens: The PRINFO field (PRACT, PRCHK bits) is not valid for the namespace's PI type, or PI was requested on a namespace without PI.
How it shows up: 0x181 → Linux BLK_STS_PROTECTION → -EILSEQ.
Spec basis: End-to-end Data Protection: Identify Namespace DPS/DPC, PRINFO in Read/Write/Compare/Verify CDW12.
Typical causes: Host sends PRCHK for Type 3 reference tag; PRACT with metadata size larger than the PI size in a mode the controller rejects. QEMU: nvme_do_write() , nvme_compare() , nvme_verify() return NVME_INVALID_PROT_INFO | NVME_DNR (e.g. Compare with PRACT set).
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ns -H DPS/DPC; decode CDW12[29:26] in the trace.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() ; PRINFO built in core.c:nvme_setup_rw() from the integrity profile.
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU (PI namespace -device nvme-ns,pi=1,ms=8 ): nvme compare with PRACT set.

name: Attempted Write to Read Only Range (SCT 1 / SC 0x82)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Write → CQE 0x182 (may follow data transfer).
What happens: A write touched an LBA range that the host previously marked read-only through the LBA Range Type feature (FID 03h).
How it shows up: 0x182 → Linux BLK_STS_MEDIUM → -ENODATA ("critical medium error"). This is misleading: the media is fine and the cause is configuration.
Spec basis: LBA Range Type feature (attributes: read-only / hidden ranges). QEMU defines NVME_WRITE_TO_RO but never returns it.
Typical causes: OEM BIOS/firmware marked ranges read-only; old tools.
How to detect / prove: nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -f 3 -H .
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() (BLK_STS_MEDIUM).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: set an LBA Range Type entry with the read-only attribute on a test drive that supports FID 03h.

name: Command Size Limits Exceeded (0x83) and Copy-related 0x85/0x86/0x87/0x89
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Copy SQE → MRd of the source range descriptors → CQE.
What happens: A Copy (19h) or similar command exceeds MSSRL (max single source range length), MCL (max copy length) or MSRC (max source range count): 0x83. libnvme and QEMU add 0x85 Incompatible Namespace or Format, 0x86 Fast Copy Not Possible, 0x87 Overlapping I/O Range, 0x89 Insufficient Resources. These are not in Linux's nvme.h , so Linux prints them as "Unknown".
How it shows up: 0x183 (Linux text "Command Size Limits Exceeded"); 0x185/0x187 from QEMU's nvme_do_copy() .
Spec basis: NVM Command Set Copy command; Identify Namespace MSSRL/MCL/MSRC; ONCS Copy bit.
Typical causes: Copy offload with ranges built from filesystem extents larger than MSSRL; cross-namespace copy between different LBA formats (0x85); source overlapping destination (0x87). QEMU: nvme_check_copy_mcl() , nvme_copy() .
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ns -H mssrl/mcl/msrc, then the Copy range list contents.
Linux v7.2 source: Default mapping (-EIO); Linux v7.2 does not issue Copy from the block layer in the paths examined here uncertain , so Copy errors come from passthrough.
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: nvme copy with a range longer than MSSRL.

name: Fabrics Connect/Discovery statuses: 0x80–0x84, 0x90 Discovery Restart, 0x91 Authentication Required
In a PEX trace: Not visible Not on PCIe at all: NVMe-oF statuses travel in TCP/RDMA/FC response capsules, so a PEX capture of the NIC/HBA link shows only encrypted or opaque network DMA. Use a network capture (Wireshark NVMe/TCP dissector) or target logs. Pattern: Network capture: Fabrics command capsule (opcode 7Fh, fctype Connect) → response capsule with the status.
What happens: Fabrics Connect rejected: Incompatible Format (0x180), Controller Busy (0x181), Connect Invalid Parameters (0x182), Connect Restart Discovery (0x183), Connect Invalid Host (0x184). Also Discovery Restart (0x190) and Authentication Required (0x191). libnvme also lists 0x85 Invalid Queue Type for Disconnect.
How it shows up: Connect fails; nvme connect reports the error. dmesg from fabrics.c:nvmf_log_connect_error() . For 0x182 it decodes which parameter failed using the Connect response's IATTR/IPO fields. 0x191 on I/O → Linux disposition AUTHENTICATE → re-authentication work, then retry.
Spec basis: NVMe over Fabrics: Connect command and response, Discovery log, DH-HMAC-CHAP in-band authentication.
Typical causes: Host NQN not on the target's allow list (0x184); wrong subsystem NQN or CNTLID (0x182); dynamic controller already associated (0x181); keys not configured (0x191).
How to detect / prove: dmesg "Connect Invalid Host"/"Connect command failed ..." lines; target-side logs; nvme discover output.
Linux v7.2 source: fabrics.c:nvmf_log_connect_error() , nvmf_should_reconnect() path stops reconnecting when status & NVME_STATUS_DNR ; core.c:nvme_decide_disposition() AUTHENTICATE branch. Note the string-table collision with NVM codes (§II.1.4.3).
Test to provoke it: SAFE: Linux nvmet loopback target without the host NQN in allowed_hosts → 0x184.

name: Zone Boundary Error (SCT 1 / SC 0xB8)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Write SQE near a zone end → CQE 0x1B8.
What happens: A command's LBA range spans more than one zone. For reads this is only an error if the namespace forbids cross-zone reads (Read Across Zone Boundaries, OZCS.RAZB=0).
How it shows up: 0x1B8 → -EIO.
Spec basis: ZNS Command Set: zone size (ZSZE), OZCS RAZB.
Typical causes: Host splitting logic ignoring zone size (non-power-of-2 zone sizes are a classic trap). QEMU: nvme_check_zone_write() , nvme_check_zone_read() .
How to detect / prove: nvme zns id-ns (zsze); compute slba / zsze and (slba+nlb-1) / zsze .
Linux v7.2 source: Block layer splits at chunk_sectors (zone size) so in-kernel I/O should not cross; default mapping in nvme_error_status() .
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU ZNS: nvme read across a zone boundary.

name: Zone Is Full (0xB9) / Zone Is Read Only (0xBA) / Zone Is Offline (0xBB)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Write SQE → immediate CQE.
What happens: A write to a zone in ZSF:Full (0xB9) or ZSRO:Read Only (0xBA), or any access to a zone in ZSO:Offline (0xBB). Read Only and Offline are device-initiated states: the drive moved the zone there because of media problems. That makes them media-health events disguised as state errors.
How it shows up: 0x1B9/0x1BA/0x1BB → -EIO. A zone report shows the zone state. The drive may also raise a Zone Descriptor Changed notice (ZNS-specific AEN) verify in spec .
Spec basis: ZNS zone states ZSE/ZSIO/ZSEO/ZSC/ZSF/ZSRO/ZSO; Zone Management Receive (report zones).
Typical causes: Host lost track of the write pointer after a crash (Full); worn or failed dies (Read Only, Offline). QEMU: nvme_check_zone_state_for_write() , nvme_check_zone_state_for_read() .
How to detect / prove: nvme zns report-zones /dev/nvme0n1 -d 10 ; blkzone report ; count zones in RO/Offline over time as a health metric.
Linux v7.2 source: zns.c ( nvme_ns_report_zones() ) converts zone states for the block layer; status → -EIO.
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: fill a zone, then write again (0xB9). QEMU's Offline send action works only from Read Only ( nvme_offline_zone() ). Read Only and Offline must be entered by the device, so test 0xBA/0xBB with vendor injection or fault injection on the host.

name: Zone Invalid Write (SCT 1 / SC 0xBC)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Two Writes to the same zone completing out of order, or a re-submission after a host timeout.
What happens: A Write to a sequential-write-required zone did not start at the zone's write pointer.
How it shows up: 0x1BC → -EIO. The most common ZNS error in the field.
