Spec basis: ZNS sequential write requirement; Zone Append (opcode 7Dh) avoids it by letting the device choose the LBA.
Typical causes: Reordered writes (multiple queues, no zone write locking or plugging); retry of a write that actually succeeded (write pointer already advanced); host write-pointer cache stale after power loss. QEMU nvme_check_zone_write() : if (slba != zone->w_ptr) return NVME_ZONE_INVALID_WRITE .
How to detect / prove: Trace per-zone SLBA order and compare with the reported write pointer. A write that is reported failed but whose data is present means the earlier attempt succeeded.
Linux v7.2 source: Block layer zone write plugging keeps order. The NVMe driver maps the status to -EIO. Note the danger of nvme_decide_disposition() retries for zoned writes when DNR is clear derived .
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: nvme write to zslba + 8 on an empty zone.

name: Too Many Active Zones (0xBD) / Too Many Open Zones (0xBE)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: A write to an empty zone → CQE 0x1BE.
What happens: Opening or writing a zone would exceed MAR (Maximum Active Resources) or MOR (Maximum Open Resources), both 0's based.
How it shows up: 0x1BD → BLK_STS_ZONE_ACTIVE_RESOURCE → -EOVERFLOW; 0x1BE → BLK_STS_ZONE_OPEN_RESOURCE → -ETOOMANYREFS. These are the only zone codes with dedicated Linux errnos, so the filesystem can tell them apart and close zones.
Spec basis: ZNS Identify Namespace MAR/MOR; implicit vs explicit open.
Typical causes: Too many concurrent writers or log streams; not finishing zones. QEMU: nvme_zns_check_resources() (with DNR).
How to detect / prove: cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/max_open_zones and max_active_zones ; count zones in open/closed states from a zone report.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() ; limits set in zns.c from MAR/MOR.
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: -device nvme-ns,zoned=true,zoned.max_open=2 , then write to 3 empty zones.

name: Invalid Zone State Transition (0xBF) and Invalid Zone Operation Request (0xB6) / ZRWA Resources Unavailable (0xB7)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Zone Management Send (79h) → CQE.
What happens: Zone Management Send asked for a transition the state machine does not allow (e.g. Open a Full zone, Finish an Offline zone) → 0xBF. 0xB6: invalid zone operation (e.g. allocating a ZRWA on a non-empty zone). 0xB7: no Zone Random Write Area available.
How it shows up: 0x1BF → -EIO (Linux has no constant for 0xB6/0xB7 and prints "Unknown").
Spec basis: ZNS Zone Send Actions (Close, Finish, Open, Reset, Offline, Set Zone Descriptor Extension, Flush Explicit ZRWA Range).
Typical causes: Host state cache out of sync; tools sending Open to Full zones. QEMU: nvme_zrm_open_flags() , nvme_zrm_finish() , nvme_zrm_close() , nvme_zrm_reset() , nvme_offline_zone() return NVME_ZONE_INVAL_TRANSITION (no DNR); nvme_open_zone() returns NVME_INVALID_ZONE_OP / NVME_NOZRWA.
How to detect / prove: Zone report before the command; ZNS state diagram.
Linux v7.2 source: Zone ops ( REQ_OP_ZONE_* ) built in zns.c:nvme_setup_zone_mgmt_send() .
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: nvme zns open-zone on a full zone.

name: Write Fault (SCT 2 / SC 0x80)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. The CQE and the full data transfer are visible; whether anything reached the media is not. Use read-back and SMART media_errors. Pattern: Write SQE → device MRd of all data (it was transferred) → after unusually long latency, CQE with SCT 2/SC 0x80.
What happens: The controller could not commit the write data to the media. The data was transferred from the host, but programming failed and the firmware could not place it elsewhere.
How it shows up: SCT 2 / SC 0x80 → Linux BLK_STS_MEDIUM → -ENODATA, dmesg "Write Fault" and "critical medium error ... op 0x1:(WRITE)". SMART "Media and Data Integrity Errors" increments. An Error Information log entry gives the LBA. Repeated faults usually come with Available Spare dropping and possibly critical warning bit 2 or 3 ( S-74 , S-75 ).
Spec basis: Media and Data Integrity Errors "Write Fault"; SMART/Health log Media and Data Integrity Errors counter; Error Information log LBA field.
Typical causes: Program failure with no spare blocks left; power-loss-protection capacitor failure making the drive refuse writes; drive entering read-only end-of-life mode in a vendor-specific way. QEMU: nvme_rw_complete_cb() maps any backend write error (Write, Write Zeroes, Zone Append) to NVME_WRITE_FAULT; nvme_flush_ns_cb() and nvme_copy_out_completed_cb() also return it.
How to detect / prove: nvme smart-log (media_errors, avail_spare, critical_warning); nvme error-log (LBA, NSID, status 0x280 in libnvme form is SCT 2/SC 0x80); read back the LBA. The old data, the new data or garbage can be returned. Record which.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() → BLK_STS_MEDIUM; filesystems usually go read-only on a failed metadata write.
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: attach the namespace through a blkdebug drive with an injected write error (event write_aio , errno 5) to get a real 0x280 CQE on the emulated wire. On hardware only vendor error injection works.

name: Unrecovered Read Error (SCT 2 / SC 0x81)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. The CQE and the missing data MWrs are visible; the media cause is not (use the Error log LBA and SMART). Pattern: Read SQE → long latency (milliseconds instead of ~100 µs, from internal retries) → no data MWr, or partial → CQE SCT 2/0x81. With TLER set, the latency is capped.
What happens: The data could not be recovered from the media even after the controller's full error correction (ECC, read retries, soft decoding, RAID-like die parity). The data at those LBAs is lost unless the host has another copy.
How it shows up: SCT 2 / SC 0x81 on Read, Verify, Compare or Copy. Linux → BLK_STS_MEDIUM → -ENODATA. SMART media_errors increases. The Error Information log has the first failing LBA. Since the controller has already done its internal retries, DNR=1 is common. If DNR=0, Linux retries up to 5 times.
Spec basis: "Unrecovered Read Error"; Error Recovery feature (FID 05h) TLER (Time Limited Error Recovery) limits how long the drive tries before reporting; Write Uncorrectable (04h) marks LBAs to return this error on purpose.
Typical causes: Retention loss (data at rest too long, especially on hot drives), read disturb, worn blocks, firmware mapping bugs that point to the wrong physical page. Field data: Schroeder et al. (FAST '16) found that roughly 20–63% of drives in Google's fleet saw at least one uncorrectable error over four years, and that raw bit error rate was a poor predictor. QEMU: nvme_rw_complete_cb() , nvme_verify_cb() , nvme_compare_*_cb() map backend read errors to NVME_UNRECOVERED_READ.
How to detect / prove: Read the LBA range with nvme read and compare with nvme error-log . Use nvme verify (if ONCS supports it) to scan without moving data. Rewrite the LBA (that usually remaps it), then re-read to confirm.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() ; nvme_log_error() prints "@ LBA x, n blocks" for the whole request (not the exact bad LBA).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION (destroys data in the range): nvme write-uncor /dev/nvme0n1 -s 0x1000 -c 7 , then nvme read ... -s 0x1000 → 0x281. Then nvme write-zeroes or a normal write clears it. In QEMU, use blkdebug read_aio errors.

name: End-to-end PI check errors: Guard (0x82), Application Tag (0x83), Reference Tag (0x84), Storage Tag (0x88)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. If the metadata crosses the link (separate MPTR buffer or extended LBA), the PI tuple is in the payload and the guard can be recomputed offline from the trace. Pattern: Read with PRINFO bits in CDW12 → data and metadata MWr (on read checks the data is often transferred first) → CQE 0x82–0x84.
What happens: On a namespace formatted with Protection Information, a check enabled by PRCHK failed. Guard: CRC of the data does not match the guard field, so the data or metadata was corrupted. App Tag: the tag differs from the expected value (under the mask). Ref Tag: the block is not the LBA the host expected, for example a misdirected write or read. Storage Tag (0x88, libnvme/QEMU only; Linux nvme.h has no constant): the storage tag check failed.
How it shows up: 0x282/0x283/0x284 → Linux BLK_STS_PROTECTION → -EILSEQ ("protection error"). 0x288 → "Unknown" → -EIO. The checks can run on writes (PRACT=0, the controller verifies host-supplied PI) or on reads.
Spec basis: End-to-end Data Protection (Type 1/2/3; 16-bit guard CRC-16 T10-DIF, and 32/64-bit guard formats in newer revisions); PRINFO = PRACT + PRCHK[2:0]; ELBAT/ELBATM/ILBRT fields.
Typical causes: Guard: DMA corruption, controller SRAM/DRAM bit flips, wrong PI generation by the host (bad CRC table, wrong byte order). Ref: host reused a buffer from a different LBA, firmware L2P mapping bug (misdirected write), Type 1 reference tag not incremented across blocks. App: application-tag misuse. QEMU dif.c:nvme_dif_prchk_crc16() shows the exact algorithm and the escape values. For Type 1/2 an app tag of FFFFh disables checking. For Type 3 the app tag FFFFh and ref tag FFFFFFFFh are needed.
How to detect / prove: Read the block with PRCHK cleared plus its metadata ( nvme read ... -y 8 -M meta.bin ), recompute CRC-16 T10-DIF over the data and compare the stored guard; the stored ref tag shows which LBA's data you got. This is one of the few ways to prove a misdirected write.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() → BLK_STS_PROTECTION; PRINFO and reftag setup in core.c:nvme_setup_rw() ; module parameter disable_pi_offsets in core.c changes how PI offsets are handled.
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU ( -device nvme-ns,ms=8,pi=1 ): write with correct PI, then read with PRCHK=ref and a wrong ILBRT ( nvme read ... -p 1 -r 0x1234 ) → 0x284. Write data with a bad guard → 0x282.

name: Compare Failure (SCT 2 / SC 0x85)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Compare SQE → device MRd of the host buffer → CQE 0x285.
What happens: A Compare (05h) found that the media data differs from the host buffer. This is an expected result, not a fault, for compare-and-write locking. As the first half of a fused pair it also aborts the second half (0x09).
How it shows up: 0x285 → Linux BLK_STS_MEDIUM → -ENODATA, so it looks like a medium error in dmesg. Monitoring tools that count "critical medium error" lines over-count on systems using Compare (e.g. VMware-style ATS-like locking over NVMe-oF).
Spec basis: NVM Compare command; Fused Operation; ONCS Compare bit.
Typical causes: Lock contention (expected); stale data after a lost write (unexpected and worth investigating). QEMU: nvme_compare_data_cb() , nvme_compare_mdata_cb() (data and metadata compared separately).
How to detect / prove: Read the LBA and diff it against the compare buffer; check whether the differing data matches an older write (lost-write detection).
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() (BLK_STS_MEDIUM). Compare is not issued by the block layer; it comes from passthrough or targets.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvme compare /dev/nvme0n1 -s 0 -c 0 -z 4096 -d /dev/urandom (random data will not match).

name: Access Denied (SCT 2 / SC 0x86)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: Reads → immediate CQE 0x286 (no media latency).
What happens: Access to the namespace or LBA range is denied because of missing access rights, typically a locked range of a self-encrypting drive.
How it shows up: 0x286 → Linux BLK_STS_MEDIUM → -ENODATA. On boot this looks like a dying disk ("critical medium error" on every read of the partition table) when the drive is simply locked.
Spec basis: Media and Data Integrity "Access Denied"; TCG Storage Opal/Enterprise locking ranges via Security Send/Receive.
Typical causes: Opal locking range locked after power cycle; S3 resume without re-unlock (Linux supports Opal unlock on resume through sed-opal ).
How to detect / prove: sedutil-cli --query /dev/nvme0 shows Locked = Y; all failing LBAs fall inside one locking range.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() ; Opal through core.c:nvme_sec_submit() and block/sed-opal.c .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: lock a range on a test SED and read it. Keep the admin password safe.

name: Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block (SCT 2 / SC 0x87) — DULBE
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. This is one of the few ways a PEX trace can prove a deallocation took effect: with DULBE enabled, a read of the trimmed range returns SC 0x87 and no data MWr. Pattern: Read SQE → immediate CQE 0x287, no data.
What happens: A Read, Verify, Compare or Copy touched a deallocated or never-written LBA, and the host enabled DULBE (Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block Error) in the Error Recovery feature. Without DULBE the drive returns the deallocated read pattern (often zeros; see DLFEAT) with success.
How it shows up: 0x287 → Linux BLK_STS_MEDIUM → -ENODATA. It is a useful error. It is also the only way, other than LBA Status, to prove that a Deallocate actually took effect: after deallocating a range, reads with DULBE on must fail with 0x287.
Spec basis: Error Recovery feature (FID 05h) DULBE bit; Identify Namespace NSFEAT DAE bit (DULBE supported); DLFEAT (read behaviour of deallocated blocks).
Typical causes: Host enabled DULBE and then reads unwritten space (partition probing, filesystem scans). Linux never sets DULBE because it would break partition and filesystem probing (Christoph Hellwig, linux-nvme 2018). Arrays sometimes return it even when DULBE is off, which is a vendor bug (Hannes Reinecke in the same thread). QEMU: nvme_check_dulbe() uses the backend's block status (unallocated → NVME_DULB) when NVME_ERR_REC_DULBE(ns->features.err_rec) is set.
How to detect / prove: nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -f 5 shows whether DULBE is on. As a deallocation proof: write a pattern, nvme dsm -d the range, enable DULBE, read → expect 0x287. If the read returns the old pattern with success, the deallocation was silently ignored.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_error_status() (UNWRITTEN_BLOCK → BLK_STS_MEDIUM).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION (the DSM step destroys data): on a scratch namespace, nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -f 5 -v 0x10000 (DULBE is bit 16 of the Error Recovery value), deallocate a range, read it, then set the feature back to its previous value.

name: Internal Path Error (SCT 3 / SC 0x00)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: On path A: CQE 0x300; the same LBA then appears on path B.
What happens: The command failed because of an internal error specific to the controller processing it, so another controller (path) to the same namespace may succeed (libnvme wording).
How it shows up: 0x300. Multipath: failover, multipath_failover_count increases, and the I/O succeeds on the other path. Single path: retry, then -EIO.
Spec basis: Path Related Status "Internal Path Error".
Typical causes: One controller of a dual-controller array failing its back-end link; one port of a dual-port SSD with an internal fault.
How to detect / prove: nvme list-subsys path states; failover counters per path; correlate with array logs.
Linux v7.2 source: nvme.h:nvme_is_path_error() , multipath.c:nvme_failover_req() ( nvme_mpath_clear_current_path() , requeue on the head).
Test to provoke it: SAFE: fault-inject 0x300 on one path's namespace device (the hidden nvme0c0n1 -style node) and watch I/O continue.

name: ANA path errors: Persistent Loss (0x01), Inaccessible (0x02), Transition (0x03)
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: CQEs with SCT 3 on one controller; Get Log Page LID 0Ch shortly after; I/O moves to the other controller.
What happens: The namespace's ANA group on this controller is in Inaccessible (0x02), Persistent Loss (0x01) or Change/Transition (0x03) state, so the command cannot be served on this path.
How it shows up: 0x301/0x302/0x303. Linux multipath: nvme_failover_req() sets NVME_NS_ANA_PENDING and queues ana_work to re-read the ANA log (LID 0Ch), then resubmits the bios on another path. Usually an ANA Change AEN ( S-83 ) arrives too. Without multipath ( nvme_core.multipath=N ), the code is retried on the same path and ends in -EIO.
Spec basis: Asymmetric Namespace Access: ANA log page (groups, states Optimized 01h, Non-Optimized 02h, Inaccessible 03h, Persistent Loss 04h, Change 0Fh — Linux enum nvme_ana_state ), ANATT (ANA Transition Time, seconds), ANACAP, ANAGRPID.
Typical causes: Array controller failover or firmware upgrade (Transition); a path to a namespace owned by the peer controller (Inaccessible); controller permanently lost access (Persistent Loss).
How to detect / prove: nvme ana-log /dev/nvme0 ; cat /sys/block/nvme0c0n1/ana_state ; failover counters; dmesg "ANATT timeout, resetting controller." if a transition outlasts ANATT.
Linux v7.2 source: multipath.c:nvme_failover_req() , nvme_update_ana_state() , nvme_anatt_timeout() (resets the controller after ANATT×2 seconds of Change state, via mod_timer(&ctrl->anatt_timer, ctrl->anatt * HZ * 2 + jiffies) ); nvme.h:nvme_is_ana_error() .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: Linux nvmet target with two ports; change a port's ANA state through configfs ( ana_groups/<id>/ana_state ) to "inaccessible" or "change" and run fio on the host.

name: Controller Pathing Error (SCT 3 / SC 0x60)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible On NVMe/PCIe the CQE with SCT 3/SC 0x60 is visible like any other; on fabrics (the usual case) it is not on PCIe. Pattern: Response capsule with SCT 3/SC 0x60.
What happens: The controller detected a pathing error, e.g. a fabrics transport problem between itself and the host, or within the subsystem.
How it shows up: 0x360 → failover on multipath; default -EIO otherwise.
Spec basis: Path Related Status "Controller Pathing Error" (controller-detected range 60h–6Fh).
Typical causes: Target-side transport errors; fabric port reset.
How to detect / prove: Target logs; failover counters; network counters on the target side.
Linux v7.2 source: Same path as S-65.
Test to provoke it: SAFE via fault injection 0x360.

name: Host Pathing Error (SCT 3 / SC 0x70) — host-generated
In a PEX trace: Not visible Host-generated: no CQE carries 0x370. At most you see that the command was never submitted (no SQ doorbell MWr) while the controller was being reset. Evidence: the nvme:nvme_complete_rq tracepoint and dmesg. Pattern: Nothing. The command was never submitted, or was submitted to a dead link.
What happens: The host detected that it cannot reach the controller. Linux sets this status itself when a request cannot be queued to a controller that is not live (e.g. during reconnect).
How it shows up: No CQE on the wire. Linux: status 0x370 → FAILOVER on multipath, otherwise BLK_STS_TRANSPORT → -ENOLINK ("recoverable transport error").
Spec basis: Path Related Status "Host Pathing Error" (host-detected range 70h–7Fh).
Typical causes: Fabrics connection lost; PCIe controller in RESETTING/DELETING; the driver's nvme_fail_nonready_command() path for non-ready controllers.
How to detect / prove: dmesg controller state changes ("resetting controller", reconnect attempts) right before; tracepoint status 0x370 with no matching CQE in an analyzer capture.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_host_path_error() , core.c:nvme_fail_nonready_command() , core.c:nvme_error_status() → BLK_STS_TRANSPORT.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: NVMe/TCP loopback, take the target port down ( ip link set ... down ) with fast_io_fail_tmo set, run I/O.

name: Host Aborted Command (SCT 3 / SC 0x71) — host-generated
In a PEX trace: Partly visible 0x371 itself is never on the wire (host-generated). What is visible is the cause and the reset: outstanding SQEs with no CQE, then CC.EN←0 (MWr to BAR0+14h) and re-initialisation. Pattern: No CQE with 0x371. You see the reset itself: CC.EN←0 (MWr to offset 14h), CSTS.RDY→0, re-enable.
What happens: The host cancelled the command because of a host action. Linux sets it on every in-flight request when it tears down a controller's queues (reset after timeout or CSTS.CFS, removal, transport error recovery).
How it shows up: dmesg nvme_log_error lines with "Host Aborted Command (sct 0x3 / sc 0x71)" for many requests at once, usually right after "I/O tag N ... timeout, reset controller" or "controller is down; will reset". Being SCT 3 it fails over on multipath; otherwise it is retried after the reset, or -EIO if the controller is removed.
Spec basis: Path Related Status "Command Aborted By Host" (libnvme NVME_SC_CMD_ABORTED_BY_HOST ).
Typical causes: It is always a symptom . The cause is earlier: a command timeout, a fatal controller status, a PCIe error (AER/DPC), or surprise removal.
How to detect / prove: Read dmesg backwards from the first 0x371 to the first timeout, CFS or AER message. In an analyzer capture, find the last good CQE and what the device stopped doing.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_cancel_request() ( nvme_req(req)->status = NVME_SC_HOST_ABORTED_CMD ), nvme_cancel_tagset() , nvme_cancel_admin_tagset() .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: nvme reset /dev/nvme0 during heavy fio; or echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/remove (EXPERT: device disappears until rescan).

name: Vendor Specific status (SCT 7) and reserved SCT 4–6
In a PEX trace: Visible The status is in DW3 of the 16-byte CQE that the device writes with a device→host MWr to the CQ base address + head×16; the analyzer's NVMe decoder pairs it with the SQE by SQID/CID. Pattern: CQE DW3 bits 27:25 = 111b.
What happens: The controller reports a vendor-defined status (SCT 7). SCT 4–6 are reserved, and receiving one is a device bug.
How it shows up: Linux prints "Unknown (sct 0x7 / sc 0x..)" and maps it to BLK_STS_IOERR → -EIO; retried unless DNR.
Spec basis: Status Code Type 7h = Vendor Specific (libnvme NVME_SCT_VS ).
Typical causes: Vendor commands; firmware debug builds; drives that use SCT 7 for internal faults that should have used Internal Error.
How to detect / prove: Ask the vendor for the code table; capture telemetry right after.
Linux v7.2 source: constants.c:nvme_get_error_status_str() → "Unknown".
Test to provoke it: SAFE via fault injection status 0x7xx.

name: Error Information log entry (LID 01h) — the detail behind More
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The More bit (CQE DW3 bit 30) of the failed command is visible. The entry itself is visible only if a Get Log Page LID 01h is issued inside the capture window: admin SQE (02h, CDW10 LID=01h), then a device→host MWr of 64-byte entries into the host buffer. Decode error_count, SQID, CID, status_field and LBA from that payload.
What happens: For commands that complete with an error (and some errors not tied to a command), the controller records a 64-byte entry: Error Count (unique, increasing), SQID, CID, Status Field, Parameter Error Location, LBA, NSID, Vendor Specific info, Transport Type, Command Specific info, and in newer versions opcode, CSI and log page version (libnvme struct nvme_error_log_page ).
How it shows up: Nothing is pushed unless an Error AEN is raised for errors not tied to a command. The SMART "Number of Error Information Log Entries" counter increases. The CQE's More bit says an entry exists for that command.
Spec basis: Error Information log; Identify Controller ELPE (Error Log Page Entries, 0's based); SMART num_err_log_entries.
Typical causes: Any failing command. The log is a ring of ELPE+1 entries, newest first, so heavy error traffic overwrites the evidence quickly. QEMU's nvme_error_info() returns all-zero entries.
How to detect / prove: nvme error-log /dev/nvme0 -e 64 right after the failure; match SQID/CID to the CQE (or to the nvme_complete_rq tracepoint); use Parameter Error Location (byte in bits 7:0, bit in bits 10:8) to find the offending SQE field.
Linux v7.2 source: The driver never reads LID 01h (no use of NVME_LOG_ERROR in drivers/nvme/host/ ). nvme_log_error() only prints "MORE". struct nvme_error_slot in include/linux/nvme.h defines the entry.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: send an Invalid Field command (e.g. nvme get-feature -f 0x7e ) and read nvme error-log . Check that error_count increased and that SQID=0 and the CID match.

name: SMART critical warning bit 0 — Available Spare below threshold
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Only as (a) an AER CQE on the admin CQ with DW0 type 1 / info 02h / LID 02h, if enabled, or (b) the SMART log payload (byte 0 bit 0; byte 3 avail_spare; byte 4 spare_thresh) in a device→host MWr when the host reads LID 02h during the capture. The underlying wear is not visible.
What happens: Available Spare (percent of remaining spare blocks) fell below Available Spare Threshold. Spare is used when blocks retire. When it runs out the drive usually goes read-only (bit 3).
How it shows up: critical_warning bit 0 set; avail_spare < spare_thresh in nvme smart-log . Linux: no AEN by default (SMART AEN bits not enabled). If enabled, the AEN becomes a uevent NVME_AEN=0x020201 (type 1, info 02h, LID 02h; illustrative encoding) and nothing else.
Spec basis: SMART/Health Information log: Critical Warning, Available Spare, Available Spare Threshold, Percentage Used; Asynchronous Event Configuration bit 0.
Typical causes: End of life (Percentage Used near or over 100%); early block failures in a bad batch; firmware reporting spare wrongly.
How to detect / prove: Poll nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 periodically (smartd / node exporter). Trend avail_spare together with percent_used and media_errors.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_enable_aen() (SMART bits not requested), core.c:nvme_complete_async_event() ( ctrl->aen_result ), core.c:nvme_aen_uevent() .
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: enable SMART AENs (FID 0Bh bit 0), then QMP qom-set /machine/peripheral/<nvme-id> smart_critical_warning 1 ( nvme_set_smart_warning() raises the event only for newly set bits).

name: SMART critical warning bit 1 — Temperature threshold
In a PEX trace: Partly visible AER CQE with type 1 / info 01h (if enabled), or the SMART log payload if read. The temperature itself is not on the wire. The thermal effect (throttling) shows up only as longer command latency between SQE fetch and CQE.
What happens: A temperature sensor crossed the over-temperature (or under-temperature) threshold set with the Temperature Threshold feature (FID 04h). Beyond WCTEMP/CCTEMP (Identify Controller) the drive throttles and counts Warning/Critical Composite Temperature Time.
How it shows up: critical_warning bit 1; SMART temperature (Kelvin), warning_temp_time and critical_comp_time increase, thermal management transition counters change. Linux exposes the bit as hwmon temp1_alarm .
Spec basis: Temperature Threshold feature (TMPTH, TMPSEL, THSEL); Identify WCTEMP/CCTEMP; Host Controlled Thermal Management (FID 10h).
Typical causes: Poor airflow, missing heatsink, sustained writes; a threshold set too low by a tool.
How to detect / prove: sensors / cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/hwmon*/temp1_alarm ; nvme smart-log (temperature, warning_temp_time); correlate latency spikes with temperature.
Linux v7.2 source: hwmon.c : case hwmon_temp_alarm: *val = !!(log->critical_warning & NVME_SMART_CRIT_TEMPERATURE) ; hwmon reads LID 02h through nvme_get_log() .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: lower the over-temperature threshold below the current temperature: nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 4 -v <kelvin> . QEMU raises the event at once ( nvme_set_feature() → nvme_smart_event(n, NVME_SMART_TEMPERATURE) ). Restore the default afterwards.

name: SMART critical warning bit 2 — NVM subsystem reliability degraded
In a PEX trace: Partly visible AER CQE type 1 / info 00h, or SMART log payload bit 2. The preceding SCT 2 CQEs (0x280/0x281) are visible if they happened during the capture. The internal cause is not.
What happens: The controller decided that reliability is degraded because of significant media-related errors or an internal error that degrades reliability.
How it shows up: critical_warning bit 2; usually media_errors rising; possibly endurance group critical warning summary (byte 6) set.
Spec basis: SMART Critical Warning bit 2; Endurance Group Information log (LID 09h) critical warnings.
Typical causes: Die failure, parity/RAIN rebuild exhausted, DRAM ECC problems, controller-internal faults.
How to detect / prove: nvme smart-log , nvme endurance-log , vendor telemetry; Persistent Event log NVM Subsystem Hardware Error events (05h).
Linux v7.2 source: Uevent only ( nvme_aen_uevent() ).
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: smart_critical_warning 4 via QMP.

name: SMART critical warning bit 3 — media placed in read-only mode
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Writes start completing with errors (CQE status visible; often Write Fault or a write-protect status, depending on the vendor impl ). The bit itself is visible only in the SMART log payload or an AER CQE.
What happens: The drive has put all media into read-only mode to protect existing data, typically at end of life or after a critical internal failure.
How it shows up: critical_warning bit 3; writes fail; reads still work. Linux does not mark the block device read-only from this bit. Each write fails individually and filesystems remount read-only.
Spec basis: SMART Critical Warning bit 3.
Typical causes: Spare exhausted; power-loss capacitor failure (some vendors); firmware panic mode.
How to detect / prove: nvme smart-log ; copy the data off immediately with read-only tools.
Linux v7.2 source: No handling beyond the uevent. Read-only state comes only from namespace write protection or NSATTR ( core.c , NVME_NS_ATTR_RO ).
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: smart_critical_warning 8 (QEMU sets the bit only; writes keep working, so this tests monitoring, not the write path).

name: SMART critical warning bit 4 — volatile memory backup device failed
In a PEX trace: Not visible as a failure: power-loss protection health is internal. Only the bit in a SMART log read or an AER CQE is visible. A host-side effect may follow: drives that lose PLP often enable a volatile write cache or slow down (Flush latency). Check Identify VWC and Get Features FID 06h.
What happens: The backup power (capacitors) that protects the volatile write cache has failed, so acknowledged writes may be lost on power failure.
How it shows up: critical_warning bit 4. Behaviour after that is vendor-specific impl : some go read-only, some switch to write-through.
Spec basis: SMART Critical Warning bit 4; Volatile Write Cache feature (FID 06h).
Typical causes: Capacitor ageing or failure; failed PLP self-test at power-on.
How to detect / prove: nvme smart-log ; power-fail test with write verification (fio verify after a power cut) to prove loss of acknowledged data.
Linux v7.2 source: Uevent only. Linux learns cache state from Identify VWC at scan time, not from this bit.
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU: smart_critical_warning 16 .

name: SMART critical warning bit 5 — Persistent Memory Region read-only/unreliable
In a PEX trace: Partly visible PMR accesses are MWr/MRd to the PMR BAR and are visible, but a failure shows only as the SMART bit (log read) or AER CQE. PMRSTS register reads (MRd + CplD) show its status if the host reads it.
What happens: The PMR became read-only or unreliable.
How it shows up: critical_warning bit 5 (libnvme NVME_SMART_CRIT_PMR_RO ; not in Linux nvme.h ). QEMU only accepts this bit when CAP.PMRS is set.
Spec basis: SMART Critical Warning bit 5; PMRCAP/PMRCTL/PMRSTS registers.
Typical causes: Backing NVRAM failure.
How to detect / prove: nvme smart-log , nvme show-regs -H PMRSTS.
Linux v7.2 source: No PMR consumer in the NVMe host driver; uevent only.
Test to provoke it: SAFE in QEMU with pmrdev= : smart_critical_warning 32 .

name: AEN Error: Invalid Doorbell Register (00h) / Invalid Doorbell Write Value (01h)
In a PEX trace: Visible This is one of the best PEX cases: the bad doorbell MWr (host→device to BAR0 + 1000h + …) with its value is in the trace, and so is the AER CQE (type 0, info 00h/01h, LID 01h) that follows. Check that the written value is less than the queue size and that the doorbell belongs to an existing queue.
What happens: The host wrote a doorbell for a queue that does not exist (00h), or wrote a value that is invalid, e.g. tail ≥ queue size, or a CQ head that moves past entries not yet posted (01h).
How it shows up: Error-type AEN; the Error Information log has an entry. The controller may ignore the write. The affected queue can stall, which the host then sees as I/O timeouts.
Spec basis: Doorbell registers (SQyTDBL, CQyHDBL; stride from CAP.DSTRD); Asynchronous Event Information – Error Status.
Typical causes: Driver bug in a new host or user-space driver; doorbell offsets computed with the wrong DSTRD; shadow doorbell (Doorbell Buffer Config) misuse. QEMU: nvme_process_db() enqueues NVME_AER_INFO_ERR_INVALID_DB_REGISTER for an invalid qid and NVME_AER_INFO_ERR_INVALID_DB_VALUE for new_tail >= sq->size / new_head >= cq->size (only if an AER is outstanding).
How to detect / prove: Analyzer filter on MWr to BAR0+1000h…; decode qid = (offset−1000h)/(4<<DSTRD)/2 and SQ vs CQ from parity; compare the value with the queue size from the Create command.
Linux v7.2 source: Not handled specially (uevent). The Linux PCIe driver computes doorbells from dev->db_stride in pci.c .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: user-space driver writing a tail value of queue size. Or in QEMU, write to an unconfigured doorbell through /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/resource0 (CAUTION: only with the kernel driver unbound).

name: AEN Error: Diagnostic Failure (02h), Persistent Internal Error (03h), Transient Internal Error (04h), Firmware Image Load Error (05h)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The AER CQE on the admin CQ (DW0 type 0 with info 02h–05h) is visible. For 03h under Linux, the reset that follows within milliseconds is visible: MWr CC.EN=0 to BAR0+14h, CSTS polling MRds, re-initialisation. The internal failure is not visible.
What happens: 02h: a diagnostic (e.g. power-on self-test) failed. 03h: a persistent internal error, so the controller needs a reset (or is broken). 04h: an internal error that the controller recovered from. 05h: the firmware image could not be loaded at activation (the drive fell back to another image).
How it shows up: Linux, 03h: dmesg "resetting controller due to persistent internal error" and a full controller reset; I/O in flight completes with 0x371 and is retried. Other subtypes: uevent only. 05h: firmware_rev after reset is not the version you committed.
Spec basis: Asynchronous Event Information – Error Status (libnvme NVME_AER_ERROR_* ).
Typical causes: Firmware asserts; failed internal memory test; corrupt firmware slot.
How to detect / prove: nvme error-log , nvme persistent-event-log (NVM Subsystem Hardware Error and Firmware Commit events), nvme fw-log ; capture nvme telemetry-log right after (before a reset clears volatile state).
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_complete_async_event() : if (aer_subtype == NVME_AER_ERROR_PERSIST_INT_ERR) { nvme_handle_aer_persistent_error(ctrl); return; } (no AER resubmit; the reset re-arms it).
Test to provoke it: Not provokable from a standard host; vendor injection only.

name: AEN Notice: Namespace Attribute Changed (00h)
In a PEX trace: Visible AER CQE DW0 = type 2 / info 00h / LID 04h, then Linux's Get Log Page LID 04h (Changed Namespace List, data MWr) and a burst of Identify commands (CNS 00h/05h/…) as it rescans.
What happens: A namespace was attached, detached, resized, formatted or changed in an Identify-visible way (by this host, another host, or the device itself).
How it shows up: Linux rescans: block devices appear or disappear or change capacity; dmesg capacity-change messages. If identifiers changed: "identifiers changed for nsid N" and the namespace is removed.
Spec basis: Notice 00h; Changed Namespace List log (up to 1024 NSIDs; FFFFFFFFh in the first entry means "more than 1024 changed"); OAES bit 8.
Typical causes: Namespace management from another host; thin-provisioned growth; vendor tools reformatting.
How to detect / prove: udev events; nvme list before/after; nvme_async_event tracepoint.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_handle_aen_notice() → set_bit(NVME_AER_NOTICE_NS_CHANGED, &ctrl->events) , nvme_queue_scan() ; nvme_scan_work() → nvme_clear_changed_ns_log() ; nvme_validate_ns() .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: nvme detach-ns / attach-ns on a test namespace (QEMU nvme-subsys ).

name: AEN Notice: Firmware Activation Starting (01h) and CSTS.PP
In a PEX trace: Visible AER CQE type 2 / info 01h / LID 03h, then a run of host MRds of CSTS (BAR0+1Ch) every ~100 ms whose CplD has PP (bit 5) set, then no I/O SQ doorbells (queues quiesced) until PP clears, then Get Log Page LID 03h. The gap length versus MTFA is directly measurable.
What happens: The controller begins activating new firmware without a reset (Firmware Commit CA=3). It sets CSTS.PP (Processing Paused) and stops processing commands until activation finishes.
How it shows up: Linux: controller state goes to RESETTING (to block recovery actions), I/O queues are quiesced, CSTS.PP is polled every 100 ms until clear or until MTFA×100 ms (or admin_timeout if MTFA=0). On timeout: "Fw activation timeout, reset controller". Afterwards it reads the FW Slot log to update firmware_rev .
Spec basis: Notice 01h; CSTS.PP; Identify MTFA; OAES bit 9.
Typical causes: Planned online firmware update. Trouble comes when activation takes longer than MTFA (I/O latency spike or a reset) or the drive never clears PP.
How to detect / prove: dmesg; fio latency log during the update; PEX gap measurement.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_handle_aen_notice() ( NVME_AER_NOTICE_FW_ACT_STARTING ), nvme_fw_act_work() , nvme_ctrl_pp_status() , nvme_get_fw_slot_info() .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: nvme fw-download + nvme fw-commit -a 3 with a vendor-approved image during a fio run; measure the I/O pause.

name: AEN Notice: Telemetry Log Changed (02h) — controller-initiated telemetry available
In a PEX trace: Partly visible AER CQE type 2 / info 02h / LID 08h is visible. The telemetry contents are vendor-encoded and visible as raw payload only if read (Get Log Page LID 08h, possibly many MiB of data MWrs).
What happens: The controller captured an internal snapshot (Controller-Initiated Telemetry), usually because it hit an internal error worth debugging. Header byte ctrlavail = 1 and ctrldgn (generation number) increments (libnvme struct nvme_telemetry_log ).
How it shows up: Linux: dev_warn(ctrl->device, "async event result %08x\n", result) (default case of nvme_handle_aen_notice() ). This is often the only sign of an internal firmware problem.
Spec basis: Telemetry Host-Initiated (07h) and Controller-Initiated (08h) logs; data areas 1–3 (4 with extended); reason identifier.
Typical causes: Firmware assertion recovered internally; vendor-defined triggers.
How to detect / prove: Save it for the vendor: nvme telemetry-log /dev/nvme0 --output-file=tele.bin (check your nvme-cli version for the controller-initiated option). Compare ctrldgn across time.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_handle_aen_notice() default branch.
Test to provoke it: Host-initiated variant only: Get Log Page LID 07h with LSP Create (libnvme NVME_LOG_TELEM_HOST_LSP_CREATE ) — SAFE.

name: AEN Notice: Asymmetric Namespace Access Change (03h)
In a PEX trace: Visible on NVMe/PCIe dual-port: AER CQE type 2 / info 03h / LID 0Ch, then Get Log Page LID 0Ch with group descriptors in the data MWr. Note that each port is a different link, so you need both links probed to follow the failover.
What happens: The ANA state of one or more ANA groups changed on this controller.
How it shows up: Linux (CONFIG_NVME_MULTIPATH): ana_work re-reads the ANA log and updates ana_state per path; I/O policy re-selects paths.
Spec basis: Notice 03h; ANA log; OAES bit 11; ANATT.
Typical causes: Array failover/failback, maintenance, path loss.
How to detect / prove: nvme ana-log ; /sys/block/nvme*c*n*/ana_state ; see the synthetic trace in Chapter II.4.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_handle_aen_notice() → queue_work(nvme_wq, &ctrl->ana_work) ; multipath.c:nvme_update_ana_state() , nvme_anatt_timeout() .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvmet configfs ANA state change.

name: AEN Notices Linux does not act on: Predictable Latency (04h), LBA Status Information Alert (05h), Endurance Group Event (06h); Discovery Log Change (F0h)
In a PEX trace: Visible AER CQE type 2 with info 04h/05h/06h. Since Linux does not read the indicated log, the event type stays masked and no later events of that kind show up on the wire. Absence of later AENs is therefore not evidence of health.
What happens: 04h: Predictable Latency per-NVM-set event (deterministic window violated). 05h: the controller found LBAs that are or may become unrecoverable (LBA Status Information log, LID 0Eh). This is a proactive media warning. 06h: an endurance group crossed a threshold. F0h: fabrics discovery log changed.
How it shows up: Linux: "async event result %08x" warning for 04h–06h; F0h → uevent for nvme-cli's autoconnect rules. Linux does not enable 04h–06h in FID 0Bh, so they arrive only if the controller has them enabled by default or user space enables them.
Spec basis: Notice event info values (libnvme NVME_AER_NOTICE_* ); LBA Status Information log; Predictable Latency Event Aggregate log; Endurance Group Event Aggregate log.
Typical causes: 05h: background media scan found weak blocks. 04h: garbage collection breaking the deterministic window.
How to detect / prove: nvme get-log -i 0x0e for LBA status, then rewrite or relocate the listed LBAs; nvme get-log -i 0x0b (Predictable Latency aggregate).
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_handle_aen_notice() default case; NVME_AEN_SUPPORTED mask.
Test to provoke it: Vendor-specific; not provokable from the host on most drives.

name: AEN I/O Command Set specific: Reservation Log Page Available (00h), Sanitize Completed (01h), Sanitize Completed With Unexpected Deallocation (02h)
In a PEX trace: Visible AER CQE DW0 type 6 with info 00h/01h/02h; the log page (80h or 81h) only if read.
What happens: 00h: a reservation notification is queued (registration preempted, reservation released or preempted). 01h: a sanitize finished. 02h: a sanitize finished but the media was deallocated in a way the host did not request (e.g. No-Deallocate After Sanitize could not be honoured) verify exact semantics in spec .
How it shows up: Linux: uevent NVME_AEN=... only.
Spec basis: libnvme NVME_AER_CSS_NVM_* ; Reservation Notification log (80h); Sanitize Status log (81h).
Typical causes: Cluster fencing (00h); decommission workflows (01h/02h).
How to detect / prove: nvme get-log -i 0x80 , nvme sanitize-log .
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_complete_async_event() ( NVME_AER_CSS → ctrl->aen_result ).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: reservation preempt from a second controller; DESTRUCTIVE: sanitize a scratch drive.

name: Persistent Event log (LID 0Dh) entries that indicate failure
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Only when read during the capture: Get Log Page LID 0Dh with LSP establishing a reporting context, then data MWrs with event headers. Events from before the capture are visible this way, which makes the log a time machine for things the trace missed.
What happens: The controller keeps a timestamped, power-cycle-persistent history: SMART/Health snapshot (01h), Firmware Commit (02h), Timestamp Change (03h), Power-on or Reset (04h), NVM Subsystem Hardware Error (05h), Change Namespace (06h), Format Start/Completion (07h/08h), Sanitize Start/Completion (09h/0Ah), Set Feature (0Bh), Telemetry Log Create (0Ch), Thermal Excursion (0Dh), Sanitize Media Verification (0Eh), vendor (DEh), TCG (DFh) (libnvme NVME_PEL_* ).
How it shows up: Nothing is pushed. You must read it. Header has total events (TNEV), log length (TLL), timestamp, power-on hours, power cycle count, reporting context (RCI).
Spec basis: Persistent Event log; LSP actions read/establish/release context; Identify PELS (log size).
Typical causes: Read it after any unexplained reset, power event, firmware change or data-loss report. "Power-on or Reset" events with unexpected reasons and "NVM Subsystem Hardware Error" events are the highest-value entries.
How to detect / prove: nvme persistent-event-log /dev/nvme0 (establish context, read, release; see nvme-cli help for the action option). Correlate timestamps with host logs. Set the Timestamp feature (FID 0Eh) so the drive's clock matches.
Linux v7.2 source: Not read by the driver. Linux sets the Timestamp feature at init ( core.c:nvme_configure_timestamp() ), which makes PEL timestamps meaningful.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: nvme reset /dev/nvme0 , then read the log and find the new Power-on or Reset event.

name: Telemetry logs (LID 07h host-initiated, 08h controller-initiated) — failure evidence for the vendor
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The transfer is visible (large Get Log Page with offsets; many data MWrs). The content is vendor-opaque. Note that collecting telemetry during a capture inflates the trace and may disturb timing.
What happens: Host-initiated: the host asks the controller to capture internal state now (LSP Create). Controller-initiated: the controller saved state itself (see S-82 ).
How it shows up: Header fields: lpi, IEEE OUI, last block of data areas 1–4 (dalb1–dalb4), ctrlavail, ctrldgn, reason identifier (128 bytes).
Spec basis: Telemetry logs; LPA bit for telemetry; Identify MDTS limits transfer chunking.
Typical causes: Collect after any firmware-suspected failure, before resetting or power-cycling (volatile data may be lost).
How to detect / prove: nvme telemetry-log /dev/nvme0 --output-file=t.bin ; send it to the vendor together with the trace and time of failure.
Linux v7.2 source: Not used by the driver ( NVME_LOG_TELEMETRY_HOST / _CTRL are only defined).
Test to provoke it: SAFE: host-initiated capture with nvme-cli.

name: Device Self-test log (LID 06h) failure results
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The Device Self-test command (14h) and its immediate CQE are visible. The test runs internally for minutes. The result is visible only when LID 06h is read: a 564-byte payload, 20 result entries of 28 bytes.
What happens: A short or extended self-test finished with a failure. Result codes (low nibble of DSTS, libnvme NVME_ST_RESULT_* ): 0 no error, 1 aborted by Device Self-test command, 2 aborted by Controller Level Reset, 3 aborted by namespace removal, 4 aborted by Format NVM, 5 fatal or unknown test error, 6 completed with a failed segment (segment unknown), 7 completed with failed segment(s), first failing segment in SEG, 8 aborted for unknown reason, 9 aborted by sanitize, F entry unused.
How it shows up: Entry fields: dsts (result + test code), seg, vdi (which of NSID/FLBA/SCT/SC are valid), poh, nsid, flba (failing LBA), sct, sc.
Spec basis: Device Self-test command and log; EDSTT; DSTO (one test at a time per subsystem or per controller).
Typical causes: Results 5–7 are hardware/media failures; 2/3/4/8/9 mean the test was interrupted and is not a health verdict.
How to detect / prove: nvme device-self-test /dev/nvme0 -s 2 , wait EDSTT minutes, nvme self-test-log /dev/nvme0 ; read the FLBA it reports with nvme read .
Linux v7.2 source: Not used by the driver.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: start an extended test and abort it ( -s 0xf ) → result 1. Run a test then reset → result 2.

name: Sanitize Status log (LID 81h): sanitize completed with failure / interrupted
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The Sanitize SQE (84h) and its fast CQE (the operation runs in the background) are visible, and so are later 0x1D/0x1C CQEs on I/O. SSTAT/SPROG are visible only as payload of a LID 81h read. Whether the media was really erased is never visible (prove it by reading back).
What happens: SSTAT bits 2:0 (libnvme NVME_SANITIZE_SSTAT_STATUS_* ): 0 never sanitized, 1 completed successfully, 2 in progress, 3 completed with failure, 4 completed successfully with No-Deallocate (ND). Bits 7:3 completed overwrite passes, bit 8 Global Data Erased, bit 9 media verification cancelled. SPROG = progress ×65536.
How it shows up: SSTAT=3 → commands fail with Sanitize Failed (0x1C, S-18 ) until recovery.
Spec basis: Sanitize command and Sanitize Status log (sprog, sstat, scdw10, eto, etbe, etce, etond, etbend, etcend, etpvds, ssi).
Typical causes: Power interruption with an implementation that fails rather than resumes; die failures during block erase.
How to detect / prove: nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0 ; after "success", read random LBAs and verify they contain the expected pattern (zeros, the overwrite pattern, or deallocated data per DLFEAT). A sanitize can report success without erasing everything, and only read-back proves it.
Linux v7.2 source: Not used by the driver.
Test to provoke it: DESTRUCTIVE / EXPERT: sanitize a sacrificial drive, cut power mid-way, read the log after power-up.

name: Controller Fatal Status — CSTS.CFS = 1
In a PEX trace: Partly visible CFS is visible only in the CplD payload of a host MRd to BAR0+1Ch (bit 1 set). The controller sends nothing when it enters fatal state. What you see first is silence : SQ doorbells with no SQE fetch MRds and no CQEs. Then, 30 s later (io_timeout), Linux's CSTS read and the reset sequence. A CSTS read returning FFFFFFFFh means the device did not answer (the root complex synthesised all-ones for a UR/timeout), which is a link/device-gone case, not CFS.
What happens: The controller hit a fatal error it cannot report through a CQE and stopped processing. Only a controller reset (CC.EN 1→0→1) or a deeper reset recovers it.
How it shows up: Linux does not poll CSTS. It finds CFS when a command times out: nvme_timeout() reads CSTS, nvme_should_reset() returns true for CFS, and nvme_warn_reset() prints "controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0x%x, PCI_STATUS=0x%hx". If CSTS reads all-ones it adds "Does your device have a faulty power saving mode enabled?" and suggests nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off . All in-flight commands are cancelled (0x371) and retried after the reset.
Spec basis: CSTS.CFS (bit 1); controller reset (CC.EN); CAP.TO for ready timeouts.
Typical causes: Firmware crash/watchdog, internal hardware fault, power-state transition bugs (APST), thermal shutdown.
How to detect / prove: dmesg line above (CSTS value: 0x3 = RDY|CFS); PEX shows the stall start time precisely. Afterwards read nvme error-log , persistent-event-log and telemetry. Check /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/state transitions.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_timeout() , nvme_should_reset() , nvme_warn_reset() , nvme_pci_ctrl_is_dead() ( (csts & NVME_CSTS_CFS) || !(csts & NVME_CSTS_RDY) ).
Test to provoke it: Not host-provokable on real drives without vendor commands. Simulate the host side with fault injection plus io_timeout , or with an exerciser that answers CSTS reads with CFS set.

name: NVM Subsystem Reset Occurred — CSTS.NSSRO = 1
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The NSSR write itself (host MWr of 4E564D65h to BAR0+20h) is visible if it came over this link, and so is the link going through Recovery/re-training afterwards. NSSRO is visible in a CSTS read CplD (bit 4), and its clearing as a host MWr of 1 to CSTS bit 4.
What happens: An NVM subsystem reset happened (host-initiated through NSSR, or by the subsystem itself). All controllers in the subsystem were reset, possibly including other ports or hosts.
How it shows up: Linux: when dev->subsystem is set, NSSRO counts as a reason to reset in nvme_should_reset() ("loss of adapter communication, possibly by a NVMe Subsystem reset"); the driver clears NSSRO during reset.
Spec basis: CAP.NSSRS (NSSR supported); NSSR register (20h); CSTS.NSSRO (write 1 to clear).
Typical causes: Firmware activation needing a subsystem reset (0x110); nvme subsystem-reset ; the other host on a dual-port drive resetting the subsystem.
How to detect / prove: dmesg reset messages on both hosts; Persistent Event log Power-on or Reset event.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_should_reset() ; NSSRO cleared in pci.c ( writel(NVME_CSTS_NSSRO, dev->bar + NVME_REG_CSTS) ); nvme_pci_subsystem_reset() .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: nvme subsystem-reset /dev/nvme0 on a drive with CAP.NSSRS=1 (the link drops; some platforms report it as a surprise-down error).

name: Firmware Commit outcome hidden in the Firmware Slot log (LID 03h): activation pending or reverted
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The Firmware Image Download chunks (opcode 11h; host buffers fetched by device MRd), the Commit SQE and its CQE status are visible. Which image is actually running after reset is visible only from a LID 03h read (AFI byte) or Identify Controller FR field (bytes 64–71) in a data MWr.
What happens: After a commit the running firmware may not be what you expect: activation pending until the next reset (AFI bits 6:4 ≠ bits 2:0), image rejected at boot and the old slot used (Firmware Image Load Error AEN), or a successful commit reported with a "requires reset" status (S-40).
How it shows up: Linux: "Firmware is activated after next Controller Level Reset" ( nvme_get_fw_slot_info() ), and /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/firmware_rev keeps the old revision until reset.
Spec basis: Firmware Slot Information log (AFI, FRS1–FRS7); Firmware Commit CA values; Identify FR.
Typical causes: Fleet tools reporting "updated" without resetting; images that fail secure-boot checks and roll back silently.
How to detect / prove: nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0 + nvme id-ctrl | grep '^fr ' after every update and after the reset; Persistent Event log Firmware Commit events (02h) with old/new revision.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_get_fw_slot_info() ( cur_fw_slot = log->afi & 0x7; next_fw_slot = (log->afi & 0x70) >> 4 ).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: commit with CA=2 (activate at next reset) and read the slot log before and after nvme reset .

name: SMART counters creeping up without a critical warning: media_errors, num_err_log_entries, unsafe_shutdowns, percent_used
In a PEX trace: Not visible as a trend. A capture covers seconds; counters change over days. Two SMART reads inside a capture can be diffed from their payloads. Otherwise use periodic nvme smart-log collection (smartd, Prometheus exporters).
What happens: The drive is still "healthy" (critical_warning = 0) but the counters show trouble: media_errors (unrecovered data-integrity errors), num_err_log_entries (lifetime error log entries), unsafe_shutdowns (power lost without a shutdown notification, so data in a volatile cache may be gone), percent_used (wear estimate, may exceed 100), warning/critical temperature time.
How it shows up: Nothing is pushed. These counters never raise an AEN on their own.
Spec basis: SMART/Health log counters (128-bit fields; Linux struct nvme_smart_log ).
Typical causes: Ageing media; host shutting down without CC.SHN (unsafe_shutdowns increasing on every reboot points to a platform or driver shutdown bug); thermal design problems. Field studies (Meza et al., SIGMETRICS 2015; Schroeder et al., FAST 2016) found that uncorrectable errors are common across fleets and that wear alone predicts them poorly, so trend counters per drive instead of trusting a single threshold.
How to detect / prove: Store nvme smart-log -o json daily and alert on deltas; after a clean reboot unsafe_shutdowns must not change (if it does, the shutdown path is broken; check that CC.SHN was written, which is visible in a PEX trace of the shutdown).
Linux v7.2 source: Linux uses the SMART log only for hwmon temperatures ( hwmon.c ). Shutdown notification is sent from core.c:nvme_disable_ctrl() with shutdown=true (CC.SHN) and polled with shutdown_timeout (default 5 s).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: hard power-off a test machine and verify unsafe_shutdowns increments by exactly one. A clean poweroff must not increment it.

name: Command submitted but never completed
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Visible as an absence: measure from the SQ tail doorbell MWr (BAR0+1000h+...) to the CQE MWr carrying that CID. Missing CQE plus the Abort SQE fetch ~30 s later proves the stall; the first missing packet (SQE fetch MRd, data, CQE MWr or MSI-X MWr) locates it. Why firmware stopped is not visible.
What happens: The host writes an SQE and rings the doorbell; the controller fetches it (or not) but never posts a CQE. No status code exists because there is no completion.
How it shows up: Nothing until the host timer fires. Linux v7.2: nvme nvme0: I/O tag 17 (0011) opcode 0x2 (Read) QID 3 timeout, aborting req_op:READ(0) size:4096 after 30 s; if the abort also fails, ... timeout, reset controller .
Spec basis: NVMe Base: every command submitted shall be completed with a CQE (unless the controller is reset or the queue deleted). The spec gives no general per-command time limit; host timeouts are policy.
Typical causes: Firmware hang or deadlock on one command type; command lost in the controller after a malformed SQE; device DMA read of the SQE hit a Completion Timeout and firmware dropped the command; MSI-X interrupt lost (command completed but host never noticed); queue stuck behind a long-running background operation.
How to detect / prove: dmesg timeout lines carry tag, CID, opcode, QID. Compare with an analyzer trace: was the SQE fetched (device MRd to the SQ address)? Was a CQE written (device MWr to the CQ address)? Was the MSI-X MWr sent? The first missing packet locates the fault. nvme error-log may show an entry for the CID if firmware noticed.
Linux v7.2 source: block/blk-mq.c:blk_mq_timeout_work() , blk_mq_rq_timed_out() ; drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_timeout() .
Test to provoke it: Use the kernel NVMe fault-injection ( drivers/nvme/host/fault_inject.c , CONFIG_FAULT_INJECTION_DEBUG_FS) or a QEMU NVMe model with a patched delay; on real hardware, a vendor "hang command" debug hook. synthetic Lower /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/io_timeout (ms) to make the ladder fast. SAFE on a scratch device.

name: CSTS.RDY does not become 1 within CAP.TO after CC.EN=1
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = MWr to CC (BAR0+14h) with EN=1 → first CplD of a CSTS (BAR0+1Ch) MRd showing RDY=1. Compare with CAP.TO×500 ms (CAP itself is visible in an earlier CplD of a BAR0+00h read). Expiry = polling series that ends without RDY=1.
What happens: The host enables the controller (CC.EN 0→1) and polls CSTS.RDY. The controller stays not-ready for longer than the worst-case time it advertised in CAP.TO.
How it shows up: No status at all; only a host timer. Linux v7.2 prints Device not ready; aborting initialisation, CSTS=0x0 and the probe or reset fails with -ENODEV. If CSTS reads 0xffffffff the loop exits immediately with -ENODEV (device gone from the bus).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: CAP.TO (bits 31:24) is the worst-case time, in 500 ms units, the host should wait for CSTS.RDY to change after CC.EN changes. Maximum 0xFF = 127.5 s.
Typical causes: Firmware boot slower than advertised (e.g. large mapping-table rebuild after unsafe shutdown); media or NAND not responding; CAP.TO set too small by firmware; controller waiting on a dependency (power, clocks, PERST# timing); host started polling before the device was out of reset.
How to detect / prove: Measure: dmesg -T timestamps of driver bind vs failure; with an analyzer, find the MWr to CC (offset 14h) and the last MRd of CSTS (offset 1Ch) and compare the gap with CAP.TO×500 ms. Read CAP with nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 (read-only) and decode bits 31:24.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_enable_ctrl() computes the limit as (CAP.TO + 1) / 2 seconds and calls nvme_wait_ready() , which polls every 1–2 ms (usleep_range(1000, 2000)), aborts on fatal signal, and fails with -ENODEV on timeout or CSTS = ~0.
Test to provoke it: In QEMU, CAP.TO is 0Fh (7.5 s) in hw/nvme/ctrl.c ; patch the model to delay setting RDY beyond that. On hardware, force an unsafe power cut during heavy writes (CAUTION: data-loss risk on that drive) and time the next initialisation against CAP.TO.

name: CRTO inconsistent with CAP.TO, or media not ready in time
In a PEX trace: Partly visible CAP (BAR0+00h) and CRTO (BAR0+68h) values are visible in the host's MRd/CplD pairs, so CRWMT < CAP.TO can be checked; CC.CRIME is in the CC MWr payload. Interval CC MWr EN=1 → CSTS RDY=1 as in T-02. Media readiness inside the drive is not visible; SC 24h/82h is visible in CQE MWr payloads.
What happens: Controllers that support Controller Ready Modes (CAP.CRMS) report two timeouts in the CRTO register: CRWMT (ready with media) and CRIMT (ready independent of media). If CRWMT is smaller than CAP.TO, or the media is not ready within CRWMT, the host either waits too little or gives up.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2 logs once bad crto:<value> cap:<value> when CRWMT < CAP.TO and falls back to CAP.TO. If the controller then still misses the deadline, the T-02 message appears. When CC.CRIME=1 is used by a host, media commands issued too early complete with Admin Command Media Not Ready (generic 24h) or Namespace Not Ready (82h).
Spec basis: NVMe Base 2.x: CAP.CRMS (CRWMS bit 59, CRIMS bit 60), CC.CRIME (bit 24), CRTO register at offset 68h with CRWMT (bits 15:0) and CRIMT (bits 31:16), both in 500 ms units.
Typical causes: Firmware fills CRTO but forgets that CAP.TO must stay consistent; large-capacity drives whose media becomes ready much later than the controller.
How to detect / prove: nvme show-regs to read CAP and CRTO; compare CRWMT with CAP.TO. In dmesg , look for bad crto . Time the CC.EN→RDY gap on an analyzer.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_enable_ctrl() reads NVME_REG_CRTO if NVME_CAP_CRMS_CRWMS , uses the larger of CAP.TO and CRWMT, and always clears NVME_CC_CRIME ("Until the driver is restructured to handle retries, disable CC.CRIME").
Test to provoke it: QEMU or a device simulator: set CAP.CRMS and an inconsistent CRTO; check for the bad crto warning. SAFE.

name: CSTS.RDY does not return to 0 after CC.EN=0 (reset hangs)
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = MWr CC with EN=0 → first CSTS CplD with RDY=0; limit CAP.TO×500 ms (+2.3 s host quirk delay if applied, seen as silence before polling). Also check for device DMA TLPs after EN=0.
What happens: To reset, the host clears CC.EN and waits for CSTS.RDY to go to 0. The controller keeps RDY=1 beyond CAP.TO, so the reset cannot proceed and the controller cannot be re-enabled.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2: Device not ready; aborting reset, CSTS=0x1 ; the controller is then marked dead and its namespaces are removed. Every outstanding I/O fails.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: after CC.EN 1→0 the controller shall bring CSTS.RDY to 0 within CAP.TO. Some devices need an extra delay before the host starts checking RDY (see NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_BEFORE_CHK_RDY).
Typical causes: Firmware stuck in the very operation that caused the reset (a hung command, a media operation that cannot be interrupted); internal deadlock; PCIe link lost (CSTS reads all-ones instead, a different failure).
How to detect / prove: dmesg shows the "aborting reset" line after a timeout or nvme reset . Analyzer: MWr CC with EN=0, then MRd CSTS returning RDY=1 for longer than CAP.TO×500 ms. Check whether the device sent any TLPs in between (DMA still running after EN=0 is itself a bug).
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_disable_ctrl(ctrl, false) : optional msleep(NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_AMOUNT) (2300 ms), then nvme_wait_ready(ctrl, NVME_CSTS_RDY, 0, (NVME_CAP_TIMEOUT(cap)+1)/2, "reset") . Note: v7.2 uses CAP.TO, not CRTO, for the disable direction.
Test to provoke it: Issue nvme reset /dev/nvme0 while a vendor debug hook keeps the firmware busy, or during a long Format. CAUTION: may leave the drive needing a power cycle.

name: Shutdown not complete (CSTS.SHST ≠ 10b) before power is removed
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Interval = MWr CC with SHN=01b → CSTS CplD with SHST=10b; compare with RTD3E (visible in the Identify data the device DMA-writes to host memory). Trace shows if the host stopped polling or power/link went away first; whether the cache was actually flushed is not visible — use the SMART Unsafe Shutdowns counter.
What happens: At power-off, suspend or driver unload the host writes CC.SHN=01b (normal shutdown) and waits for CSTS.SHST=10b (shutdown processing complete). If the controller takes longer than the host waits, power may be removed while the write cache and mapping tables are still being saved.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2: Device not ready; aborting shutdown, CSTS=0x... . At the next boot the drive's SMART / Health log Unsafe Shutdowns counter has increased, and initialisation may be slower (rebuild), possibly exceeding CAP.TO (T-02).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: CC.SHN (01b normal, 10b abrupt), CSTS.SHST (00b normal operation, 01b processing, 10b complete). Identify Controller RTD3E gives the typical time in microseconds to enter Runtime D3 (shutdown); RTD3R the expected resume time.
Typical causes: Large volatile cache to flush; RTD3E under-reported; host value too small (Linux default 5 s); platform cuts power on a fixed timer regardless of SHST.
How to detect / prove: nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 before and after a clean reboot: unsafe_shutdowns must not increase. nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -i rtd3 for RTD3E. dmesg for D3 entry latency set to N seconds (Linux applied RTD3E) and for the aborting-shutdown line.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_init_identify() sets ctrl->shutdown_timeout = clamp(RTD3E/1e6, shutdown_timeout, 60) seconds; module parameter nvme_core.shutdown_timeout (default 5). nvme_disable_ctrl(ctrl, true) sets NVME_CC_SHN_NORMAL and waits for NVME_CSTS_SHST_CMPLT .
Test to provoke it: Fill the write cache (sustained writes with volatile write cache on), then reboot and compare unsafe_shutdowns . Try nvme_core.shutdown_timeout=1 on a test machine to see how a too-short host limit shows up. CAUTION: risk of losing cached data on that drive.

name: Resume from runtime D3 slower than RTD3R
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Interval = link leaves electrical idle / LTSSM reaches L0 after resume → CSTS CplD with RDY=1 (or first I/O CQE MWr). Compare with RTD3R from Identify data. Platform power-ramp time before the link exists is not on the trace.
What happens: After a runtime-D3 or system suspend, the controller takes much longer to resume than the RTD3R value it advertises. Nothing fails, but the first I/O after resume stalls.
How it shows up: No error. Applications see a multi-second stall after resume; if it exceeds CAP.TO the re-enable fails (T-02). dmesg timestamps between resume start and the controller becoming live show the gap.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Identify Controller RTD3R (Runtime D3 Resume Latency, µs, expected) and RTD3E (entry latency). These are informational: the host uses them to decide whether runtime D3 is worth it.
Typical causes: Mapping table reload from NAND; firmware re-training of internal components; platform delays on the PCIe side (D3cold power ramp, link training, see T-40 and T-41).
How to detect / prove: Measure with dmesg -T or ftrace on the PM callbacks ( pci_pm_resume , nvme_resume ) and compare with nvme id-ctrl RTD3R. Run fio with latency logging across a suspend cycle.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux v7.2 does not use RTD3R in the NVMe host driver (only RTD3E, for the shutdown timeout). Resume paths: pci.c:nvme_resume() , core.c:nvme_enable_ctrl() .
Test to provoke it: rtcwake -m mem -s 10 on a laptop with a fio latency log running. SAFE.

name: Keep Alive Timer expires in the controller
In a PEX trace: Not visible NVMe over Fabrics runs over Ethernet/InfiniBand, not the probed PCIe link (only the NIC's DMA is). Use a network capture: interval between consecutive Keep Alive capsules (admin opcode 18h) vs KATO. For NVMe over PCIe with KATO set, the Keep Alive SQE fetches (MRd of admin SQ, opcode 18h in CplD payload) are visible and their spacing can be measured.
What happens: The host sets a Keep Alive Timeout (KATO) at connect time or via Set Features (FID 0Fh). If the controller does not receive a Keep Alive command (or, with Traffic Based Keep Alive, any command) within KATO, it concludes the host is gone.
How it shows up: On the controller: the association is torn down, outstanding commands may complete with Keep Alive Timer Expired (generic status 19h) and the host's resources (reservations held by the host, queues) are released. On the host: the transport connection drops, the controller goes to RESETTING/CONNECTING and reconnects (T-28).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Keep Alive command (admin opcode 18h); Keep Alive Timer feature (FID 0Fh), KATO in milliseconds; Identify Controller KAS = timer granularity in 100 ms units; CTRATT.TBKAS = Traffic Based Keep Alive support. The host should send Keep Alive at a rate that allows for round-trip time (Linux comment quotes "at half of the Keep Alive Timeout").
Typical causes: Host CPU starvation or a stalled admin queue (the Keep Alive itself is queued behind blocked admin commands); network congestion or packet loss; a target that processes admin commands slowly; KATO set close to the network RTT.
How to detect / prove: Host dmesg : reconnect messages, long keepalive RTT (N ms) . Target-side logs (e.g. Linux nvmet prints keep-alive expiry). Packet capture: interval between Keep Alive capsules (admin opcode 18h) versus KATO.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_keep_alive_work_period() = KATO/2 (halved again if TBKAS); nvme_keep_alive_work() sends the command with rq->timeout = kato * HZ ; fabrics.c:nvmf_parse_options() defaults KATO to NVME_DEFAULT_KATO (5 s) for I/O controllers; fabrics.c:nvmf_connect_cmd_prep() puts KATO×1000 into the Connect command.
Test to provoke it: nvme-tcp to a Linux nvmet target; add delay with tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 3000ms on the host (CAUTION: affects all traffic on that interface). Watch the target drop the association after KATO.

name: Keep Alive command itself slow or failing (host side)
In a PEX trace: Not visible Fabrics traffic is not on a PCIe trace; use a packet capture (Keep Alive capsule → response capsule = RTT) and dmesg.
What happens: The host's Keep Alive command takes most of the keep-alive period to complete, or fails. The host cannot keep the controller's timer refreshed in time.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2 warns long keepalive RTT (N ms) when the round trip exceeds the work period, and failed nvme_keep_alive_end_io error=N on failure. If the request cannot even be allocated: keep-alive failed: N followed by a controller reset.
Spec basis: NVMe Base Keep Alive; the host-side scheduling is implementation policy.
Typical causes: Reserved admin tags exhausted; admin queue blocked by long commands (Format, Sanitize start, Firmware Commit); network latency; target overloaded.
How to detect / prove: dmesg | grep -i keepalive ; trace with nvme_setup_cmd / nvme_complete_rq tracepoints ( /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme ) filtering admin opcode 0x18.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_keep_alive_end_io() subtracts the measured RTT from the next delay and logs the warning; nvme_keep_alive_work() resets the controller if blk_mq_alloc_request() fails. A Set Features KATO passed through user space is applied by nvme_update_keep_alive() ("keep alive interval updated from ... ms to ... ms").
Test to provoke it: Same netem setup as T-07, with delays between KATO/2 and KATO. SAFE on a lab network.

name: Abort does not abort (or cannot be sent)
In a PEX trace: Visible Abort SQE (opcode 08h, CDW10 = SQID/CID) appears in the CplD payload of the admin SQ fetch; its CQE MWr shows DW0 bit 0 (1 = not aborted). Check for a CQE with SC 07h for the victim CID. Interval timeout-to-abort = victim doorbell MWr → Abort doorbell MWr.
What happens: After an I/O timeout the host sends Abort (admin 08h) naming the SQID and CID. Abort is best-effort: the controller may complete it without aborting anything, or the host may have no Abort credits left.
How it shows up: Abort CQE Dword 0 bit 0 = 1 means "command not aborted". Linux v7.2 logs only Abort status: 0x0 and does not inspect Dword 0; it relies on the second timeout to reset. If more Aborts are outstanding than ACL+1, the controller returns Abort Command Limit Exceeded (103h); Linux avoids that by keeping its own budget and simply re-arming the timer.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Abort command; Identify Controller ACL (0's based; the specification recommends 3, i.e. four concurrent Aborts); command-specific status 103h; an aborted command completes with Command Abort Requested (generic 07h).
Typical causes: Firmware cannot locate the command (already inside the media pipeline); controller ignores Abort entirely; Abort itself stuck behind the hung command on the admin queue.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: Abort SQE fetched from the admin SQ, its CQE written with DW0 bit 0 = 1, and no CQE for the target CID. dmesg : "aborting" followed ~io_timeout later by "reset controller" for the same tag.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_timeout() : atomic_dec_return(&dev->ctrl.abort_limit) (initialised to ACL+1 in core.c:nvme_init_identify() ), sets IOD_ABORTED , sends Abort with abort_endio() ; a second timeout on an IOD_ABORTED request resets. QEMU hw/nvme/ctrl.c:nvme_abort() sets result=1 by default and only reports 0 when it aborts an AER.
Test to provoke it: QEMU with a stalled backend (e.g. a blkdebug or throttled image) and a low io_timeout; watch the Abort CQE result. SAFE.

name: Firmware activation takes longer than MTFA
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = CQE MWr for Firmware Commit (or the AER CQE announcing activation) → first CSTS CplD with PP=0, or → first I/O CQE MWr after the pause. Compare with MTFA×100 ms from Identify data. Status 112h is visible in the Commit CQE.
What happens: Firmware Commit with activation without reset pauses command processing (CSTS.PP=1) while the new image starts. If the pause lasts longer than MTFA, every I/O on the host stalls for that time and the host may reset the controller.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2: Fw activation timeout, reset controller . Applications see an I/O pause of up to MTFA (or up to admin_timeout when MTFA=0). If the controller knows activation would exceed MTFA it should refuse up front with Firmware Activation Requires Maximum Time Violation (command-specific 112h).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Identify Controller MTFA (100 ms units); CSTS.PP (Processing Paused, bit 5); Firmware Activation Notice asynchronous event; status 112h.
Typical causes: New firmware image with longer init; image upgrade that migrates internal data structures; MTFA left at an optimistic value.
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ctrl | grep -i mtfa ; run fio with --write_lat_log during nvme fw-commit -a 3 and measure the pause; analyzer: CSTS MRd showing PP=1 and its duration.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_fw_act_work() : quiesces I/O queues, polls nvme_ctrl_pp_status() every 100 ms until mtfa * 100 ms (or admin_timeout seconds if MTFA=0), then nvme_try_sched_reset() .
Test to provoke it: Activate a firmware image with commit action 3 (activate without reset) under load. EXPERT: firmware updates can brick a drive; use vendor-approved images only.

name: Format NVM outlasts the host admin timeout
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = admin SQ doorbell MWr for the Format SQE (opcode 80h in the fetched CplD) → its CQE MWr. If the host gives up first you see CC.EN=0 ~60 s after the doorbell with no CQE. Whether media was actually erased is not visible.
What happens: Format NVM (80h) runs synchronously: the CQE is posted when the format is done. On a large drive or with Secure Erase Settings = user data erase, that can take minutes. The host's admin timeout (60 s in Linux) fires first.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2 times out an admin command and goes straight to reset: I/O tag N (....) opcode 0x80 (Format NVM) QID 0 timeout, reset controller . The reset interrupts the format; afterwards the namespace may report Format In Progress (84h) or be unusable until a new format.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Format NVM has no advertised duration. Commands to the affected namespace during the format complete with Format In Progress (84h). FNA in Identify Controller describes the scope of a format/secure erase.
Typical causes: Using the default admin timeout for a long operation; tools that do not pass a longer timeout.
How to detect / prove: dmesg line with opcode 0x80 on QID 0. Pass an explicit timeout: nvme format /dev/nvme0n1 --timeout=600000 (milliseconds; check your nvme-cli version's default).
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_timeout() : if (!nvmeq->qid || ...) → reset for any admin-queue timeout, no Abort. Passthrough timeout: ioctl.c uses cmd.timeout_ms when non-zero.
Test to provoke it: Format a large namespace with SES=1 with --timeout=60000 on a lab drive. EXPERT/DESTRUCTIVE: erases all data on the namespace.

name: Sanitize runs far longer than its estimate (or never finishes)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Sanitize SQE and its fast CQE are visible; progress is visible only as Get Log Page 81h data (SPROG, SSTAT, ETO/ETBE/ETCE) DMA-written to host memory. Interval = Sanitize CQE → first log read with SSTAT = completed; compare with the estimate. Internal erase work is not visible.
What happens: Sanitize (84h) completes immediately and the operation continues in the background. The controller publishes estimated durations in the Sanitize Status log. If the operation takes much longer than estimated, or SPROG stops moving, the drive is unusable for that time and no timer fires.
How it shows up: No error. Most I/O and many admin commands fail with Sanitize In Progress (generic 1Dh) for the whole duration. Sanitize Status log: SSTAT = in progress, SPROG (numerator over 65536) stuck. On failure SSTAT reports "failed" and later commands get Sanitize Failed (1Ch).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Sanitize Status log (LID 81h) fields SPROG, SSTAT, SCDW10, ETO, ETBE, ETCE and the No-Deallocate variants ETOND, ETBEND, ETCEND (seconds; 0 = completes in the background when the command completes; FFFFFFFFh = not reported). A sanitize continues across resets and power cycles.
Typical causes: Block erase on a drive with many bad blocks; overwrite passes; firmware estimate based on a different capacity; firmware hang.
