How to detect / prove: Poll nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0 and record SPROG versus time; compare the elapsed time with the relevant estimate. A tool should flag "elapsed > k × estimate" (pick k, e.g. 2).
Linux v7.2 source: Linux v7.2 has no Sanitize timer; the CQE arrives quickly. The driver records failures in passthrough logs only.
Test to provoke it: nvme sanitize /dev/nvme0 -a 2 (block erase) and poll the log. EXPERT/DESTRUCTIVE: erases the whole NVM subsystem's user data.

name: Device self-test exceeds EDSTT (or short test exceeds its limit)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Self-test SQE (opcode 14h) and CQE visible; progress only through Get Log Page 06h payloads. Interval = self-test CQE → log showing current operation = not running; compare with EDSTT (minutes). Test internals are not visible.
What happens: Device Self-test (admin 14h) runs in the background. The extended test should finish in about EDSTT minutes; the short test has a fixed upper bound in the specification. A test that keeps running hides a slow or failing internal component.
How it shows up: No error while it runs; a second self-test request gets Device Self-test In Progress (command-specific 11Dh). The Device Self-test log shows Current Operation and Current Completion percentage. The final result entry records abort reasons or a failing segment.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Identify Controller EDSTT (minutes, extended test in power state 0); short self-test time limit (two minutes in NVMe Base; verify in your spec revision); Device Self-test log (LID 06h).
Typical causes: Media with many weak blocks; self-test throttled by host I/O (allowed); thermal throttling (T-49).
How to detect / prove: Start nvme device-self-test /dev/nvme0 -s 2 ; poll nvme self-test-log /dev/nvme0 and compare elapsed time with nvme id-ctrl | grep edstt .
Linux v7.2 source: Linux v7.2 does not time self-tests; the command completes immediately.
Test to provoke it: Run the extended test idle and again under full fio load; compare durations. SAFE (self-test is non-destructive by definition; still avoid on production drives).

name: Power-state exit slower than EXLAT (latency spike after idle)
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = SQ doorbell MWr after an idle period → device's SQE fetch MRd (exit latency incl. any L1 exit, visible as electrical idle exit and LTSSM Recovery/L0 entries); compare with EXLAT (+ link exit latency). APST table visible in the Set Features 0Ch data the device reads.
What happens: With Autonomous Power State Transition (APST) the controller drops into non-operational power states after an idle period. The first command after idle waits for the exit. If the real exit latency exceeds the advertised EXLAT, the host's latency budget is broken without any error.
How it shows up: No error. A periodic latency outlier on the first I/O after idle (often tens of milliseconds). Linux excludes states whose EXLAT > ps_max_latency_us, so a device that under-reports EXLAT defeats that protection.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Power State Descriptor ENLAT/EXLAT (µs, 0 = not reported), NON-OP flag; Autonomous Power State Transition feature (FID 0Ch) entries with Idle Time Prior to Transition (ms) and Idle Transition Power State; Identify Controller APSTA, NPSS.
Typical causes: Firmware under-reports EXLAT; platform adds PCIe L1/L1.2 exit on top (T-45, T-46); host idle timeout too short (thrashing between states).
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ctrl -H /dev/nvme0 for power state table; nvme get-feature -f 0x0c -H /dev/nvme0 for the APST table Linux programmed; fio with --thinktime larger than the idle time, recording clat; compare outlier size with EXLAT. Disable APST ( nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 ) to confirm the outliers disappear.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_configure_apst() walks states from deepest up, skips states with exit_lat > ps_max_latency_us or quirked deepest, uses apst_primary_timeout_ms (100 ms) for states with total latency ≤ 15 ms and apst_secondary_timeout_ms (2000 ms) for ≤ 100 ms; without those parameters it uses (ENLAT+EXLAT)/20 ms ("50 × (enlat + exlat) microseconds"). Per-device limit via PM QoS ( /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/power/pm_qos_latency_tolerance_us , nvme_set_latency_tolerance() ).
Test to provoke it: Sweep fio --thinktime across the APST idle times and plot first-I/O latency. SAFE.

name: Controller never wakes from a deep power state (falls off the bus)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Visible: link enters L1/L1.2 (electrical idle), host doorbell, failed exit (TS1s then Detect, or no response) and all-ones/CTO behaviour of subsequent reads. Not visible: which internal NVMe power state the drive was in or why it did not wake.
What happens: After entering a deep non-operational state (often combined with PCIe ASPM L1 substates), the device fails to come back: config and MMIO reads return all-ones.
How it shows up: The next I/O times out (30 s). Linux v7.2 then reads CSTS = 0xffffffff and prints controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff, PCI_STATUS=0x... followed by Does your device have a faulty power saving mode enabled? and Try "nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off" and report a bug . The reset usually fails and the namespace disappears.
Spec basis: NVMe Base APST and power states; PCIe ASPM and L1 PM substates. No timer in either spec catches this; only the host I/O timer does.
Typical causes: Firmware bugs in the deepest power state; platform BIOS/ACPI problems; L1.2 timing parameters wrong (T-46). Linux carries DMI-based quirks for specific laptop/board and SSD combinations (Samsung SM951/PM951 on Dell XPS 15 9550, Samsung 960 EVO on some ASUS boards, a Lenovo N60z board).
How to detect / prove: The all-ones CSTS line in dmesg. Reproduce with APST disabled (default_ps_max_latency_us=0) and with ASPM off; if the problem disappears, it is a power-state exit failure. lspci -vvv after the event: "Unknown header type 7f" or all-ones config space means the device is gone.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_warn_reset() prints the hints; pci.c:check_vendor_combination_bug() returns NVME_QUIRK_NO_DEEPEST_PS or NVME_QUIRK_NO_APST by DMI; core.c quirk table entries for specific models.
Test to provoke it: Idle the system for long periods (hours) with APST and ASPM enabled, polling with a cron job that issues one read every N minutes. SAFE, but may require a power cycle to recover.

name: Host Memory Buffer missing or disabled: DRAM-less drive becomes slow
In a PEX trace: Partly visible With HMB enabled the drive issues MRd/MWr into the HMB address ranges (descriptor list is visible in the Set Features 0Dh data). Their disappearance is visible; the latency effect inside the drive is only visible as longer doorbell → CQE intervals.
What happens: DRAM-less SSDs ask the host for a Host Memory Buffer (HMB) to cache mapping tables. If the host gives less than requested, or disables the HMB (for example across suspend), the drive keeps working but random-access latency rises.
How it shows up: No error. Linux may log min host memory (N MiB) above limit (128 MiB). and run without HMB, or failed to allocate host memory buffer. ("controller must work without HMB"). Random 4 KiB reads get markedly slower; the effect is device-specific.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Host Memory Buffer feature (FID 0Dh); Identify Controller HMPRE (preferred size) and HMMIN (minimum), both in 4 KiB units, HMMINDS, HMMAXD.
Typical causes: Host limit lower than HMMIN; memory fragmentation; host disables HMB on suspend and the drive has to rebuild its cache on resume.
How to detect / prove: dmesg | grep -i "host memory" ; nvme get-feature -f 0x0d -H /dev/nvme0 shows whether HMB is enabled; sysfs /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/hmb (present when HMPRE ≠ 0). Compare fio random-read latency with and without HMB.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_setup_host_mem() caps the size at max_host_mem_size_mb (module parameter, default 128); pci.c:nvme_suspend() calls nvme_set_host_mem(ndev, 0) before suspend ("Host memory access may not be successful in a system suspend state").
Test to provoke it: Load nvme with max_host_mem_size_mb=0 on a DRAM-less drive and compare 4 KiB random-read latency. SAFE.

name: Command Retry Delay ignored, missing or too long
In a PEX trace: Visible CQE MWr payload shows status with CRD bits and DNR=0; interval = that CQE MWr → doorbell MWr of the resubmitted command (new CID, same LBA) should be ≥ CRDTn×100 ms. CRDT values and ACRE are visible in Identify data and the Set Features 16h payload.
What happens: A controller can ask the host to wait before retrying: it sets the CRD field in the CQE status (1–3) and the host waits CRDT1/2/3 × 100 ms. If CRDT is zero while CRD is used, the host retries instantly and burns its retry budget; if CRDT is very large, every retry adds seconds of latency.
How it shows up: Completions with DNR=0 and a non-zero CRD (e.g. Namespace Not Ready 82h, Command Interrupted 21h). With Linux, each retry increments command_retries_count in sysfs; after max_retries (5) the error reaches the application.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: CQE Status field CRD (bits 12:11 of the status word as Linux stores it, mask 0x1800); Identify Controller CRDT1–CRDT3 (100 ms units); Host Behavior Support feature (FID 16h) ACRE bit enables the mechanism.
Typical causes: Firmware returning CRD before the host enabled ACRE; CRDT left at 0; CRDT set to many seconds for a transient condition.
How to detect / prove: Tracepoint nvme:nvme_complete_rq shows status and retries; nvme id-ctrl | grep -i crdt ; nvme get-feature -f 0x16 -H for ACRE.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_retry_req() : delay = ctrl->crdt[crd - 1] * 100 ms, then blk_mq_delay_kick_requeue_list() ; nvme_configure_host_options() sets ACRE only when CRDT1 ≠ 0; nvme_decide_disposition() stops retrying on DNR or retries >= nvme_max_retries .
Test to provoke it: QEMU or a target with a hook returning 82h with CRD=1; vary CRDT1 and measure added latency. SAFE.

name: Namespace stays "not ready" longer than the host retries
In a PEX trace: Visible Repeated CQE MWr payloads with SC 82h or 24h; interval = CSTS RDY=1 CplD → first successful I/O CQE gives the real "media ready" time.
What happens: After a reset, resume or capacity change, the namespace answers with Namespace Not Ready (82h) or Admin Command Media Not Ready (24h) for longer than the host is willing to retry.
How it shows up: First a few retried commands, then I/O errors reported to the application ( blk_update_request: I/O error -style messages, the NVMe status in nvme_log_error() output).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: generic status 82h (Namespace Not Ready, retry allowed when DNR=0) and 24h (Admin Command Media Not Ready, used with CC.CRIME=1).
Typical causes: Media initialisation slower than the controller ready time; controller sets RDY too early; host retry budget (5 × CRDT) shorter than the real wait.
How to detect / prove: dmesg NVMe error lines with status 0x82; /sys/block/nvme0n1/device/.../command_retries_count ; correlate with time since controller enable.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_decide_disposition() , nvme_retry_req() , nvme_error_status() maps the status to a block error. CRIME is kept off in nvme_enable_ctrl() , which avoids most 24h cases.
Test to provoke it: Power-cycle a large drive after an unsafe shutdown and start I/O immediately when the block device appears. CAUTION.

name: ANA transition exceeds ANATT
In a PEX trace: Not visible ANA is used mainly over fabrics (not on a PCIe trace). For PCIe multi-controller drives: AER/AEN CQE and Get Log Page 0Ch payloads with ANA state "change" are visible; interval = first log showing change → log showing a stable state, vs ANATT seconds.
What happens: In Asymmetric Namespace Access (ANA), a group can report the "change" state while it moves between optimized, non-optimized and inaccessible. ANATT is the maximum time the controller promises to stay in that state. If it stays longer, the host cannot use the path.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2 arms a timer at 2 × ANATT when any group is in change state; on expiry: ANATT timeout, resetting controller. I/O on that path completes with ANA Transition (path-related status 303h) and is failed over.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Identify Controller ANATT (seconds), ANACAP; ANA log page; path-related statuses ANA Persistent Loss 301h, ANA Inaccessible 302h, ANA Transition 303h.
Typical causes: Target failover taking longer than declared (storage array controller takeover); target bug that never leaves change state.
How to detect / prove: nvme ana-log /dev/nvme0 repeatedly; sysfs ana_state per namespace path; dmesg for the ANATT line; multipath_failover_count in sysfs.
Linux v7.2 source: multipath.c:nvme_read_ana_log() (and nvme_mpath_update() ): mod_timer(&ctrl->anatt_timer, ctrl->anatt * HZ * 2 + jiffies) ("double the ANATT value to provide some slack"); nvme_anatt_timeout() calls nvme_reset_ctrl() .
Test to provoke it: Linux nvmet: set a port's ANA group to change (configfs ana_groups/N/ana_state ) and leave it there. SAFE in a lab.

name: Controller timestamp drifts or stops
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The Set Features 0Eh data (8 bytes) read by the device and the Get Features data written back are visible, so drift can be computed between two captures; the device clock itself is not.
What happens: The host sets the controller clock with the Timestamp feature; the controller keeps counting. Over long uptimes the device clock can drift, and in some power states it may stop. Device-side logs (Persistent Event Log, telemetry) then carry wrong times.
How it shows up: Nothing. Log entries cannot be correlated with host logs; a device event appears minutes away from the host symptom it caused.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Timestamp feature (FID 0Eh): 48-bit milliseconds since midnight 1 January 1970 UTC, plus attribute bits giving the timestamp origin and a "Synch" indication that the count may have stopped (exact semantics: verify ). ONCS bit indicates support.
Typical causes: Oscillator tolerance; clock not counting in non-operational power states; host sets it only at controller initialisation.
How to detect / prove: nvme get-feature -f 0x0e -H /dev/nvme0 and compare with date +%s%3N ; repeat a day later to measure drift.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_configure_timestamp() is called from nvme_init_ctrl_finish() , i.e. on every controller (re)initialisation, with ktime_get_real() in ms; failure logs could not set timestamp . QEMU computes the value from its virtual clock ( nvme_get_timestamp() ).
Test to provoke it: Read the timestamp periodically over a week of uptime; plot device minus host. SAFE.

name: Missed interrupt: completion found only by polling
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = CQE MWr → MSI-X MWr (should be microseconds unless coalescing is set). A CQE MWr with no MSI-X MWr (or an MSI-X MWr to the wrong address/data) and a CQ head doorbell MWr only ~30 s later proves a missed interrupt. Host-side IRQ handling is not visible.
What happens: The controller posted the CQE and (maybe) sent the MSI-X message, but the host never ran the completion handler. The command sits "in flight" until the timeout handler polls the CQ and finds it.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2: I/O tag N (CID) QID Q timeout, completion polled . The command succeeds, but 30 s late. No reset.
Spec basis: NVMe over PCIe: MSI-X vector per CQ, interrupt coalescing (Feature 08h), INTMS/INTMC registers for pin/MSI. PCIe: MSI-X is a posted MWr to the address in the MSI-X table.
Typical causes: MSI-X table or address programmed wrong (e.g. after a VM migration or IOMMU remap); interrupt remapping fault; CPU hot-unplug with vector affinity; device bug that writes the CQE but skips the MSI-X write; interrupt coalescing that never fires because the threshold is not reached and the timer is broken.
How to detect / prove: Count "completion polled" lines in dmesg ; check /proc/interrupts for the nvme queue vector not incrementing; IOMMU fault messages ( DMAR: ... fault ). On an analyzer, find the CQE MWr and check for the following MSI-X MWr to the APIC address range.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_timeout() : nvme_poll() for polled queues or nvme_poll_irqdisable() ; if blk_mq_rq_state(req) != MQ_RQ_IN_FLIGHT afterwards, logs "completion polled" and returns BLK_EH_DONE .
Test to provoke it: Mask the queue's MSI-X vector through a debug interface, or use QEMU and drop interrupts in the model; with a short io_timeout the message appears. SAFE in a VM.

name: I/O command timeout: poll, Abort, then reset
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The ladder is visible packet by packet: doorbell MWr → (no CQE) → Abort SQE fetch at +io_timeout → CC.EN=0 MWr at +2×io_timeout. The host's CQ polling reads only host memory and is not on the link.
What happens: An I/O command passes its block-layer deadline (io_timeout, 30 s). Linux escalates: check for a dead or offline device, poll the CQ, send an NVMe Abort, and on the second expiry reset the controller.
How it shows up: I/O tag N (CID) opcode 0x.. (Name) QID Q timeout, aborting req_op:... size:... , then possibly ... timeout, reset controller . If PCI error recovery is in progress ( pci_channel_offline() ), the timer is simply re-armed. If CSTS.CFS=1 or NSSRO is set, the driver resets at once with controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0x..., PCI_STATUS=0x... .
Spec basis: Host policy; NVMe Abort and controller reset are spec mechanisms used by the policy.
Typical causes: Any device stall (see T-01); a firmware bug affecting a specific opcode or LBA; Completion Timeouts on the device's DMA (T-33); a device that is in a long internal operation (GC, T-48) exceeding 30 s.
How to detect / prove: dmesg timeout lines (tag, CID, opcode, QID, size); nvme error-log ; AER status of the device and Root Port for the same time window; tracepoints nvme:nvme_setup_cmd and nvme:nvme_complete_rq to measure per-command latency before the failure.
Linux v7.2 source: block/blk-mq.c:blk_mq_timeout_work() → blk_mq_rq_timed_out() → pci.c:nvme_timeout() ; helpers nvme_should_reset() , nvme_warn_reset() , abort_endio() , nvme_dev_disable() , nvme_try_sched_reset() . Timeout value set by core.c:nvme_alloc_io_tag_set() ( NVME_IO_TIMEOUT ).
Test to provoke it: echo 2000 > /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/io_timeout on a test box, then generate long commands (e.g. very large Write Zeroes or Verify ranges on a slow device) to see the ladder quickly. CAUTION: resets interrupt other I/O.

name: Admin command timeout: immediate controller reset
In a PEX trace: Visible Admin doorbell MWr (SQ0 tail, BAR0+1000h) → no CQE → MWr CC EN=0 about admin_timeout later; no Abort in between distinguishes admin from I/O timeouts.
What happens: Any command on the admin queue (QID 0) that exceeds admin_timeout (60 s) causes a controller reset straight away; Linux never sends an Abort for an admin command.
How it shows up: I/O tag N (CID) opcode 0x.. (Name) QID 0 timeout, reset controller . Typical opcodes: Format NVM (0x80), Sanitize (0x84), Firmware Commit (0x10), Get Log Page of a large telemetry log (0x02), vendor-specific commands.
Spec basis: Host policy.
Typical causes: Long synchronous admin commands; controller stuck in an internal operation; a firmware path that blocks the admin queue while background work runs.
How to detect / prove: QID 0 in the timeout message. For tools: pass an explicit timeout ( nvme ... --timeout=<ms> ) for long operations.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_timeout() : if (!nvmeq->qid || (iod->flags & IOD_ABORTED)) → reset. Admin timeout configured in core.c:nvme_alloc_admin_tag_set() ( NVME_ADMIN_TIMEOUT ); changeable through sysfs admin_timeout ( sysfs.c:nvme_admin_timeout_store() ).
Test to provoke it: See T-11. EXPERT when the command is destructive.

name: Retry budget exhausted (max_retries)
In a PEX trace: Visible The same command (same opcode/SLBA/NLB in the SQE payload) fetched repeatedly with new CIDs; CQE status DNR bit visible; count retries and spacing between them.
What happens: Retryable errors (DNR=0) and cancelled commands after a reset are retried. After max_retries (5) attempts, or immediately when DNR=1, the error reaches the block layer and the application.
How it shows up: An application I/O error; kernel NVMe error log line with the final status; sysfs command_retries_count and command_error_count per namespace increase.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: DNR bit, CRD field. Retry count is host policy.
Typical causes: Repeated resets (each reset cancels and retries all in-flight commands); a namespace that stays not-ready (T-18); transient transport errors on fabrics.
How to detect / prove: cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/device/../nvme0n1/command_retries_count (path varies; find with find /sys -name command_retries_count ); tracepoint nvme:nvme_complete_rq prints retries.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_decide_disposition() ( retries >= nvme_max_retries ), nvme_retry_req() , nvme_cancel_request() (sets NVME_SC_HOST_ABORTED_CMD on reset).
Test to provoke it: Inject errors with drivers/nvme/host/fault_inject.c (debugfs directory per disk with status and dont_retry files plus the standard fault-attr controls); clear dont_retry to watch retries. SAFE.

name: Timeout while the controller is resetting or connecting
In a PEX trace: Visible Reset sequence visible (CC EN=0/EN=1, AQA/ASQ/ACQ writes, Identify/Set Features/Create queue SQEs); the admin SQE that never gets a CQE, then CC writes stop and config/MMIO traffic ceases as the host disables the device.
What happens: A command (often an admin command issued during re-initialisation) times out while the controller is already in RESETTING or CONNECTING. The host cannot reset again, so it gives up on the controller.
How it shows up: I/O tag N (CID) QID Q timeout, disable controller (CONNECTING or DELETING); the controller is marked for deletion and the namespaces disappear. During RESETTING the timer is just re-armed.
Spec basis: Host policy.
Typical causes: Device fails during its own recovery: Identify or Create I/O Queue never completes after a reset; flaky link that drops again during re-init.
How to detect / prove: dmesg sequence: a reset, then "timeout, disable controller", then the device node vanishes ( nvme list ).
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_timeout() state switch: NVME_CTRL_CONNECTING → change to DELETING, nvme_dev_disable(dev, true) ; NVME_CTRL_RESETTING → BLK_EH_RESET_TIMER . For fabrics, tcp.c:nvme_tcp_timeout() and rdma.c:nvme_rdma_timeout() complete the request immediately when not LIVE.
Test to provoke it: Make the device fail a second time during reset (vendor hook or QEMU model). CAUTION.

name: Multipath failover delayed by the full timeout
In a PEX trace: Not visible Path switch happens in the host; a PCIe trace of one path shows its I/O stopping and, if you probe the second path (dual-port drive or second drive), the same LBAs resuming. Measure the gap between the last CQE on path A and the first SQE fetch on path B.
What happens: With native NVMe multipath, a path-related status (SCT 3h) fails over immediately. A path that simply stops answering gives no status, so failover waits for the command timeout (and for fabrics, the transport's error recovery).
How it shows up: I/O pauses for about io_timeout (30 s) — or KATO / transport detection time on fabrics — then continues on the other path. multipath_failover_count in sysfs increases. No application error.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: path-related status codes (Host Path Error 370h, Host Aborted Command 371h, ANA statuses 301h–303h).
Typical causes: Hung path rather than failed path; long io_timeout chosen for single-path use left in place on multipath systems.
How to detect / prove: Latency log shows a gap equal to the timeout when one path is pulled; dmesg timeout on the failed path followed by successful I/O. Compare iopolicy (numa, round-robin, queue-depth) behaviour.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_decide_disposition() returns FAILOVER for REQ_NVME_MPATH with nvme_is_path_error() ; multipath.c:nvme_failover_req() moves the bios to the head's requeue list and kicks nvme_requeue_work() ; cancelled requests carry NVME_SC_HOST_ABORTED_CMD (a path error) so they fail over after a reset.
Test to provoke it: Two-port NVMe-oF setup; block one path with iptables -j DROP (not REJECT) and measure the I/O gap. SAFE in a lab.

name: All paths gone: I/O queued, then failed (or held forever)
In a PEX trace: Not visible Host queueing is not on the wire; the trace only shows silence. Use dmesg and sysfs counters.
What happens: When no path is usable, the multipath head either fails I/O immediately or queues it. Queued I/O waits for a path to return, for delayed_removal_secs , or for every controller to be deleted (ctrl_loss_tmo).
How it shows up: Applications block in D state; after the hold time, I/O errors. sysfs io_fail_no_available_path_count increases.
Spec basis: Host policy.
Typical causes: Network outage longer than expected; all controllers in CONNECTING with failfast not expired; misconfigured ctrl_loss_tmo=-1 (reconnect forever).
How to detect / prove: nvme list-subsys shows all paths connecting or missing; hung-task warnings in dmesg; sysfs counters above.
Linux v7.2 source: multipath.c:nvme_available_path() treats LIVE, RESETTING and CONNECTING controllers as available unless NVME_CTRL_FAILFAST_EXPIRED is set; otherwise nvme_mpath_queue_if_no_path() (driven by delayed_removal_secs ) decides.
Test to provoke it: Disconnect all target ports and watch blocked tasks; vary fast_io_fail_tmo. SAFE in a lab.

name: Fabrics controller lost: reconnect loop ends (ctrl_loss_tmo) or fails fast
In a PEX trace: Not visible Fabrics reconnects are network events; use a packet capture (TCP SYN/ICReq spacing = reconnect_delay).
What happens: After a transport error the host reconnects every reconnect_delay seconds. After ctrl_loss_tmo it gives up and deletes the controller. If fast_io_fail_tmo is set, queued I/O is failed after that time even while reconnects continue.
How it shows up: Reconnecting in 10 seconds... repeated; finally Removing controller (N)... . With fast_io_fail_tmo: failfast expired and queued I/O fails with a host path error.
Spec basis: NVMe over Fabrics: association, Connect command. Timer values are host policy.
Typical causes: Target down longer than ctrl_loss_tmo (default 600 s); authentication failure (no retry); Connect rejected with DNR.
How to detect / prove: dmesg | grep -E "Reconnecting|Removing controller|failfast" ; sysfs ctrl_loss_tmo , reconnect_delay , fast_io_fail_tmo for the controller.
Linux v7.2 source: fabrics.c:nvmf_parse_options() : max_reconnects = DIV_ROUND_UP(ctrl_loss_tmo, reconnect_delay) , warns failfast tmo (N) larger than controller loss tmo (M) ; fabrics.c:nvmf_should_reconnect() (no reconnect on DNR or key rejection); tcp.c:nvme_tcp_reconnect_or_remove() ; core.c:nvme_failfast_work() , nvme_fail_nonready_command() . Defaults in fabrics.h : NVMF_DEF_RECONNECT_DELAY 10, NVMF_DEF_CTRL_LOSS_TMO 600, NVMF_DEF_FAIL_FAST_TMO -1.
Test to provoke it: nvme connect -t tcp ... --ctrl-loss-tmo=30 --reconnect-delay=5 --fast_io_fail_tmo=10 , then stop the target for 60 s. SAFE in a lab.

name: NVMe/TCP or RDMA request timeout triggers error recovery
In a PEX trace: Not visible NVMe/TCP or RDMA PDUs are on the network, not the PCIe link; use a packet capture (CapsuleCmd without CapsuleResp for io_timeout).
What happens: On fabrics there is no Abort escalation: a request timeout in LIVE state starts transport error recovery, which tears down all queues and reconnects.
How it shows up: I/O tag N (CID) type T opcode 0x.. (Name) QID Q timeout (TCP) followed by reconnect messages; all in-flight I/O is retried or failed over.
Spec basis: NVMe over Fabrics / NVMe/TCP transport; host policy.
Typical causes: Target stall; lost PDU; network partition shorter than KATO but longer than io_timeout.
How to detect / prove: dmesg; packet capture showing a command capsule without a response capsule.
Linux v7.2 source: tcp.c:nvme_tcp_timeout() → nvme_tcp_error_recovery() → nvme_tcp_error_recovery_work() ; when not LIVE, nvme_tcp_complete_timed_out() . RDMA: rdma.c:nvme_rdma_timeout() , nvme_rdma_error_recovery() . FC: fc.c:nvme_fc_timeout() .
Test to provoke it: Drop only response packets for one queue with a targeted firewall rule. SAFE in a lab.

name: TLS handshake does not complete in time (NVMe/TCP)
In a PEX trace: Not visible TLS handshake is network traffic; use a packet capture.
What happens: With TLS-secured NVMe/TCP, the in-kernel handshake upcall must finish within tls_handshake_timeout. If not, the connect attempt fails and the reconnect loop continues.
How it shows up: Connect failure with a timeout error; repeated "Reconnecting in N seconds".
Spec basis: NVMe/TCP transport TLS support; timeout is host policy.
Typical causes: tlshd user-space daemon not running or slow; key lookup failing; network latency.
How to detect / prove: dmesg and tlshd logs; /sys/module/nvme_tcp/parameters/tls_handshake_timeout .
Linux v7.2 source: tcp.c : tls_handshake_timeout (default 10 s) used as tmo = tls_handshake_timeout * HZ and args.ta_timeout_ms .
Test to provoke it: Stop tlshd and attempt a TLS connect. SAFE.

name: Device needs a delay before CSTS.RDY is checked (quirk)
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = MWr CC EN=0 → first CSTS MRd: ~2.3 s of silence with the quirk, immediate polling without it; then the RDY transition as in T-04.
What happens: Some controllers misbehave if the host reads CSTS.RDY immediately after clearing CC.EN. Linux works around them with a fixed 2.3 s sleep. A new device with the same bug but without the quirk fails reset or initialisation.
How it shows up: Without the quirk: reset fails ( Device not ready; aborting reset ) or the controller hangs. With the quirk: every reset is 2.3 s slower.
Spec basis: Not a spec feature; a workaround for non-compliant behaviour.
Typical causes: Firmware that cannot handle register reads during reset.
How to detect / prove: Compare reset time with and without the quirk using the nvme.quirks=VID:DID:delay_before_chk_rdy module parameter (prefix the name with ^ to disable a built-in quirk), parsed in pci.c .
Linux v7.2 source: nvme.h : NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_BEFORE_CHK_RDY , NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_AMOUNT 2300 ("found empirically" for PCI_DEVICE(0x1c58, 0x0003)); used in core.c:nvme_disable_ctrl() . pci.c ID table applies it to e.g. HGST and WDC SN200 adapters, Memblaze Pblaze4, Samsung PM1725/PM1725a, Seagate Nytro; core.c applies it by model string to "Samsung Portable SSD X5".
Test to provoke it: On a device that needs it, load nvme with quirks=VID:DID:^delay_before_chk_rdy and run nvme reset . CAUTION.

name: Host stall mistaken for device timeout
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The trace proves the device side: CQE MWr and MSI-X MWr on time, but the host's CQ head doorbell MWr (and the next SQ doorbells) arrive late. The cause in the host (lockup, VM pause) is not visible.
What happens: The device completed on time, but the host could not process the completion: CPU soft lockup, interrupts disabled for seconds, VM paused or migrated, NUMA memory pressure. The NVMe timeout fires anyway.
How it shows up: NVMe timeout messages, often with "completion polled" (T-21), accompanied by soft-lockup or RCU-stall warnings, or a VM pause in the hypervisor log. The device's own logs show nothing.
Spec basis: None; host behaviour.
Typical causes: Long critical sections in other drivers; hypervisor steal time; firmware SMI storms (System Management Interrupts) on x86 platforms.
How to detect / prove: Correlate timeouts with watchdog: BUG: soft lockup , rcu: INFO: rcu_sched detected stalls , hypervisor steal time ( top "st"), perf sched . An analyzer shows the CQE and MSI-X were sent on time.
Linux v7.2 source: Same paths as T-21/T-22; the driver cannot tell host stalls from device stalls.
Test to provoke it: Pause a VM ( virsh suspend ) for longer than io_timeout during I/O and resume it. SAFE.

name: Completion Timeout: a non-posted request gets no completion
In a PEX trace: Visible Request with tag T (MRd or CfgRd) and no Cpl/CplD with tag T and the same Requester ID within the programmed range; measure MRd → CplD per tag. AER bits themselves are visible only if software reads them (CfgRd of the AER capability) or the device sends ERR_NONFATAL/ERR_FATAL messages.
What happens: A requester sends a non-posted request (memory read, configuration access, I/O) and no completion arrives within the Completion Timeout value. The request is abandoned.
How it shows up: AER Uncorrectable Error Status bit 14 (Completion Timeout, PCI_ERR_UNC_COMP_TIME ) in the requester ; Linux prints the error name "CmpltTO" and identifies the agent as Requester. If the Root Port is the requester (CPU MMIO read of a BAR, e.g. reading CSTS), the CPU receives all-ones data and some platforms escalate to a machine check. With DPC root-port PIO extensions the Root Port logs "Memory Request Completion Timeout" or "Configuration Request Completion Timeout".
Spec basis: PCIe Base: Completion Timeout mechanism; Device Capabilities 2 / Device Control 2 fields; AER uncorrectable bit 14 (default severity non-fatal verify ). The header of the timed-out request is logged only if the function supports Completion Timeout prefix/header logging.
Typical causes: Completer hung (device firmware not answering an MMIO read); completion lost or routed wrongly (bad Requester ID/tag after a switch reset); link went down while requests were outstanding; completer much slower than the requester's range (common with long config accesses during device firmware boot); IOMMU blocked the DMA so the host never returned a completion (usually an Unsupported Request instead).
How to detect / prove: dmesg | grep -i -E "aer|CmpltTO" ; sysfs /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/aer_dev_nonfatal counters; lspci -vvv UESta line shows "CmpltTO+". On an analyzer: find a MRd/CfgRd whose tag never receives a Cpl/CplD within the programmed range.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c ( AER_AGENT_REQUESTER_MASK includes PCI_ERR_UNC_COMP_TIME ; name string "CmpltTO"; header logged only with PCI_ERR_CAP_COMP_TIME_LOG ); recovery via drivers/pci/pcie/err.c ; DPC strings in drivers/pci/pcie/dpc.c . The NVMe driver's nvme_timeout() re-arms its timer while pci_channel_offline() .
Test to provoke it: Hold a device in reset with an exerciser or a programmable switch while the host reads its BAR; or use an exerciser endpoint that withholds completions. On Linux, aer_inject ( drivers/pci/pcie/aer_inject.c ) can inject the error record without real traffic. CAUTION: real CTOs may hang the CPU core on some platforms.

name: Completion Timeout disabled or set longer than upper-layer timers
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The DevCtl2 value is visible if the capture includes the CfgRd/CfgWr of offset 28h of the PCIe capability; then any MRd → CplD gap longer than the upper-layer timeout with no ERR_* message shows the effect.
What happens: If the Completion Timeout is disabled, a lost completion never produces an error and the request (and its tag) is stuck forever. If it is set to Range D (seconds), it fires after the NVMe or application timeout, so the upper layer resets first and the real cause is never logged.
How it shows up: No AER entry; instead an NVMe I/O timeout (T-22), or a CPU stuck on an MMIO load (watchdog soft lockup) when the Root Port has no timeout. Tag exhaustion can stall all further DMA from the device.
Spec basis: PCIe Base: Completion Timeout Disable (Device Control 2 bit 4) is allowed only if Device Capabilities 2 bit 4 says it is supported.
Typical causes: BIOS or firmware sets long ranges to "hide" slow devices; driver for a storage controller disables CTO for long config accesses; test configuration left over.
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv DevCtl2 for the drive and every port on the path: "TimeoutDis+" or a seconds-range value. Read-only check: setpci -s BDF CAP_EXP+28.w . Compare with /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/io_timeout .
Linux v7.2 source: Linux v7.2 PCI core does not normally reprogram the Completion Timeout for endpoints (no reference in the local drivers/pci/pci.c subset); values come from firmware or device defaults.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: writing DevCtl2 with setpci changes live hardware behaviour and can hang the system; only on a lab machine with an exerciser.

name: Replay Timer Timeout: TLP not acknowledged in time
In a PEX trace: Visible TLP with sequence number N retransmitted with no Nak DLLP in between; interval = TLP end → retransmission start equals the replay timer; compare with the spec table for the negotiated width/rate/MPS.
What happens: Each transmitted TLP stays in the replay buffer until the link partner acknowledges it with an Ack DLLP. If the REPLAY_TIMER expires first, the transmitter resends all unacknowledged TLPs.
How it shows up: AER Correctable Error Status bit 12 (Replay Timer Timeout, PCI_ERR_COR_REP_TIMER , Linux name "Timeout", agent Transmitter). Usually masked or rate-limited by platforms; latency of the affected I/O rises by microseconds. Many of them mean the link is marginal.
Spec basis: PCIe Base, Data Link Layer: REPLAY_TIMER, its limit given by tables/formulas depending on maximum payload size, link width and data rate (plus internal delay and L0s adjustments); timer restarts on forward progress.
Typical causes: Ack DLLPs corrupted (bad DLLP at the receiver side) or lost; receiver too slow to send Ack (T-37); electrical problems causing LCRC errors (then usually Bad TLP and Nak first).
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv CESta "Timeout+"; sysfs aer_dev_correctable counters (they include per-bit counts); analyzer: a TLP retransmitted with the same sequence number without an intervening Nak.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c : AER_AGENT_TRANSMITTER_MASK = PCI_ERR_COR_REP_ROLL | PCI_ERR_COR_REP_TIMER ; correctable errors are logged and counted, no recovery action.
Test to provoke it: Signal-integrity stress: lower the transmitter swing or add attenuation on a riser; or an exerciser that drops Ack DLLPs. CAUTION.

name: REPLAY_NUM rollover: four replays without progress force Recovery
In a PEX trace: Visible Same sequence number transmitted four times without an Ack, followed by TS1/TS2 ordered sets (Recovery); count replays per sequence number.
What happens: REPLAY_NUM is a 2-bit counter of replays without forward progress. When it rolls over (the fourth replay attempt of the same TLP), the Data Link Layer tells the Physical Layer to retrain the link (LTSSM Recovery).
How it shows up: AER Correctable bit 8 (REPLAY_NUM Rollover, Linux name "Rollover"); link enters Recovery; if Recovery fails the link goes down (Surprise Down, T-44) and the NVMe device disappears. Bandwidth drops during each retrain.
Spec basis: PCIe Base, Data Link Layer: REPLAY_NUM counter, rollover action (initiate link retraining), correctable error reporting.
Typical causes: Persistent receiver errors in one direction; equalization not converged; a receiver that never acks (firmware or hardware bug).
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv CESta "Rollover+"; the Root Port's LnkSta "Link Training" bit or speed/width change; Linux bandwidth notifications from drivers/pci/pcie/bwctrl.c ; analyzer: repeated identical TLP retransmissions followed by TS1 ordered sets (Recovery).
Linux v7.2 source: Logged by drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c as a correctable error; no driver recovery. Link speed or width changes are tracked by bwctrl.c .
Test to provoke it: As T-35, with stronger impairment. CAUTION: may cause link down.

name: Ack latency too long: unnecessary replays and lost bandwidth
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = end of TLP with sequence N → first Ack DLLP with AckNak_Seq_Num ≥ N; compare with the AckNak latency table; spurious replays follow when it exceeds the partner's replay time.
What happens: The receiver must return an Ack within its AckNak latency limit. A receiver that batches Acks for too long makes the transmitter's replay timer expire although nothing was corrupted.
How it shows up: Correctable Replay Timer Timeouts on the partner (T-35) with no Bad TLP / Bad DLLP on either side; throughput below expectation because the replay buffer fills and the transmitter stalls.
Spec basis: PCIe Base, Data Link Layer: AckNak_LATENCY_TIMER limits (tables by payload size, width, rate); it should be well below the partner's replay limit.
Typical causes: Device Data Link Layer implementation coalescing Acks too aggressively; receive-side backpressure inside the device; L0s entry delaying DLLPs.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: measure time from TLP end to the covering Ack DLLP; compare with the spec table for the negotiated width, rate and MPS. Throughput test with fio sequential reads at high queue depth.
Linux v7.2 source: Not visible to Linux except via the correctable counters ( aer.c ).
Test to provoke it: Run maximum-bandwidth sequential I/O and inspect Ack spacing in an analyzer. SAFE.

name: Flow-control credit starvation (no UpdateFC)
In a PEX trace: Visible Track UpdateFC DLLPs per type (P/NP/Cpl, header/data); interval between consecutive UpdateFC of a type should be ≤ ~30 µs while credits are finite; a credit counter stuck at zero with TLPs pending on the other side proves starvation.
What happens: A transmitter may send a TLP only when the receiver has advertised credits for it. If the receiver stops returning credits (no UpdateFC DLLPs), traffic of that type stops. No error is defined for "slow credits"; only upper-layer timers notice.
How it shows up: Nothing on the starved link itself, unless the optional flow-control update watchdog retrains the link or a Flow Control Protocol Error (AER uncorrectable bit 13, PCI_ERR_UNC_FCP ) is detected for an illegal credit update. Upstream symptoms: Completion Timeouts (T-33), NVMe I/O timeouts (T-22).
Spec basis: PCIe Base: InitFC1/InitFC2/UpdateFC DLLPs per type (Posted, Non-Posted, Completion; header and data credits); UpdateFC sent when credits are freed and periodically (about every 30 µs) while credits are not infinite; an optional 200 µs update watchdog verify .
Typical causes: Device receive buffer stuck (firmware not draining posted writes, e.g. doorbells or CQE writes from the host side); deadlock between posted and non-posted queues violating ordering rules; switch buffer exhaustion.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: credit tracking view (most analyzers compute available credits): the advertised credit counter stays at zero while the partner has TLPs waiting. lspci cannot show credits.
Linux v7.2 source: No direct visibility. Indirect: aer.c for FCP errors and Completion Timeouts, pci.c:nvme_timeout() for stalled commands.
Test to provoke it: Exerciser endpoint configured to withhold UpdateFC for posted credits while the host writes doorbells. EXPERT.

name: LTSSM state timeout: training loops, falls back or downshifts
In a PEX trace: Visible LTSSM state entries/exits (TS1/TS2, EIOS, electrical idle) with timestamps: interval = state entry → exit or fallback; e.g. Polling.Active → Detect after 24 ms. Negotiated width/rate visible in TS ordered sets. Requires an analyzer that records the training (start capture before reset).
What happens: Each LTSSM state has a timeout. If the expected ordered sets are not seen in time, the state machine moves on: Detect repeats every 12 ms while no receiver is detected; Polling and Configuration fall back to Detect; Recovery may fall back to Detect (link down). Repeated partial success shows up as a link trained at lower width or speed.
How it shows up: No AER error for a successful downshift. lspci -vvv LnkSta shows "Speed 8GT/s (downgraded), Width x2 (downgraded)" versus LnkCap. Root Port LnkSta2 equalization bits; Link Bandwidth Management Status. In the worst case the link never reaches L0 and the device is missing.
Spec basis: PCIe Base, LTSSM: Detect.Quiet 12 ms timeout verified ; Polling.Active 24 ms, Polling.Configuration 48 ms, Configuration.Linkwidth.Start 24 ms, other Configuration substates 2 ms, Recovery.RcvrLock 24 ms, Recovery.RcvrCfg 48 ms, Recovery.Idle 2 ms verify in spec ; equalization phase timeouts at 8 GT/s and above verify .
Typical causes: Signal integrity (lane failing receiver detect or symbol lock); lane reversal or polarity issues; equalization failure at 16/32 GT/s; reference clock problems; mis-wired lanes on risers.
How to detect / prove: Compare LnkCap and LnkSta for both ends; analyzer LTSSM view: state durations and which state times out; Linux bwctrl.c link speed change notifications; repeated link-up/down events in dmesg ( pciehp : "Link Down"/"Link Up").
Linux v7.2 source: quirks.c:pcie_failed_link_retrain() handles one known case (link stuck in training; retrain at 2.5 GT/s then lift the limit) — "broken device, retraining non-functional downstream link at 2.5GT/s".
Test to provoke it: Disable lanes with a lane-disabling interposer, or force target speed ( setpci on Link Control 2 — EXPERT, can drop the link) and retrain.

name: Link does not come up in time after reset or power-on
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = PERST# deassertion (if the fixture records sideband) or electrical idle exit → first TS1 → L0 (first DLLP/InitFC); and L0 → first CfgRd from the host (must be ≥ 100 ms above 5 GT/s).
What happens: After a reset the downstream component must enter Detect within 20 ms, and software must not send configuration requests until the link is up and a further 100 ms have passed (above 5 GT/s, measured from Data Link Layer Link Active). If the link is not active within the host's wait, software declares the device missing.
How it shows up: Linux: the device does not enumerate, or not ready Nms after bus reset; giving up ; for hot-plug ports, no "Link Up" event. Without Data Link Layer Link Active reporting Linux simply sleeps 1000 ms + delay and hopes.
Spec basis: PCIe Base reset and link-up timing rules (as quoted in drivers/pci/pci.c comments: enter Detect within 20 ms; 100 ms minimum before configuration requests; at least 1 s before declaring a non-responding device broken). Link Capabilities DLLLARC; Link Status DLLLA and LT bits.
Typical causes: Slow device PHY start; reference clock or PERST# sequencing errors; LTSSM failures (T-39).
How to detect / prove: dmesg with pci=... debug ( dyndbg="file drivers/pci/* +p" ) shows "waiting N ms for downstream link"; analyzer timestamp of PERST# deassertion vs first TS1 and vs L0.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:pci_bridge_wait_for_secondary_bus() , pcie_wait_for_link_delay() (20 ms then poll DLLLA, timeout PCIE_LINK_RETRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS , then pcie_failed_link_retrain() ), pcie_wait_for_link_status() polling every 1 ms.
Test to provoke it: Delay the device's PERST# release with a controllable fixture; secondary bus reset via /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/reset (CAUTION: resets the device).

name: Device not ready after reset: RRS beyond 1 s or no response at all
In a PEX trace: Visible CfgRd0 → Cpl with status RRS (Configuration Request Retry) repeated; interval = reset (or L0) → first CplD with a valid Vendor ID; compare with 1 s. DRS/FRS messages, if sent, are visible as Msg TLPs.
What happens: After a Conventional Reset or D3cold→D0, a function must accept configuration requests within 1 s, but may answer with Request Retry Status (RRS, formerly CRS) to ask for more time. A function that keeps answering RRS, or answers with all-ones, is "not ready".
How it shows up: Linux: pci BDF: not ready 1023ms after FLR; waiting , then ready Nms after ... or, after 60 s, not ready 65535ms after ...; giving up . During enumeration: not ready after Nms; giving up from pci_bus_wait_rrs() . NVMe probe never starts.
Spec basis: PCIe Base: device readiness 1 s after Conventional Reset; RRS completions; Root Control "Configuration RRS Software Visibility Enable" (with it, a Vendor ID read returns the special value 0001h); Readiness Time Reporting extended capability; Device Readiness Status (DRS) and Function Readiness Status (FRS) messages; Immediate Readiness bit in the Status register.
Typical causes: Firmware boot slower than 1 s (large drives loading internal tables); firmware stuck in a boot loop; failed link retrain.
How to detect / prove: dmesg lines above; lspci -s BDF -vvv returning "Unknown header type 7f" (all-ones); analyzer: CfgRd0 answered by Cpl with status RRS repeatedly.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:pci_dev_wait() (uses Vendor ID with RRS SV, otherwise the Command register; PCI_RESET_WAIT 1000 ms, caller timeout PCIE_RESET_READY_POLL_MS 60000 ms); probe.c:pci_enable_rrs_sv() , pci_bus_wait_rrs() , pci_bus_read_dev_vendor_id(..., 60*1000) ; probe.c:pci_imm_ready_init() reads Immediate Readiness. The local v7.2 subset showed no consumer of Readiness Time Reporting, DRS or FRS verify .
Test to provoke it: Trigger FLR via echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/reset (CAUTION: unbind the NVMe driver first, data in flight is lost) and time the "ready Nms" message.

name: D3hot→D0 transition: access before the 10 ms recovery time
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = CfgWr to PMCSR setting D0 → next config/memory request to that function; must be ≥ 10 ms (or the device's value); its completion shows whether the device was ready.
What happens: After writing PowerState=D0 in the PM capability of a function that was in D3hot, software must wait 10 ms before accessing it (unless the function reports otherwise). Accessing earlier, or a function that needs longer, gives undefined results.
How it shows up: Config reads return garbage or all-ones; MMIO reads time out (T-33); the NVMe driver sees CSTS=0xffffffff on resume. Linux increases the delay for known-bad devices (quirks 20 ms or 120 ms).
Spec basis: PCI Power Management: D3hot→D0 recovery time 10 ms; "No Soft Reset" bit determines whether state is preserved.
Typical causes: Device firmware needs longer than 10 ms; platform-specific slowness; driver skipping the wait.
How to detect / prove: dmesg with PM debug; analyzer: CfgWr to PMCSR (D0) followed by CfgRd sooner than 10 ms, answered badly.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:pci_dev_d3_sleep() (max of dev->d3hot_delay and global pci_pm_d3hot_delay ; default PCI_PM_D3HOT_WAIT = 10 ms, defined in drivers/pci/pci.h ); then pci_dev_wait(dev, "power up D3hot->D0uninitialized", PCIE_RESET_READY_POLL_MS) . quirks.c:quirk_d3hot_delay() raises it to 20 ms for some devices; quirk_intel_pcie_pm() sets the global delay to 120 ms; quirk_remove_d3hot_delay() sets 0 for some Intel chipset functions.
Test to provoke it: Runtime PM: echo auto > /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/power/control and idle the device; measure resume. SAFE.

name: Function Level Reset not complete in 100 ms
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = CfgWr to Device Control with Initiate FLR (bit 15) → first CfgRd that completes successfully; must be ≥ 100 ms (unless Immediate Readiness); outstanding non-posted requests at FLR time are visible.
What happens: After Initiate FLR, a function must complete the reset within 100 ms; it may silently drop requests during that time. Software also should wait for outstanding transactions to drain before initiating FLR.
How it shows up: Linux: timed out waiting for pending transaction; performing function level reset anyway (Transaction Pending bit still set after about 700 ms of polling), then readiness messages from pci_dev_wait() (T-41).
Spec basis: PCIe Base: FLR (Device Capabilities FLR bit, Device Control Initiate FLR bit 15); 100 ms completion requirement; Device Status Transactions Pending bit.
Typical causes: DMA engine stuck (completions never returned); firmware slow to reinitialise after FLR.
How to detect / prove: dmesg; lspci -vvv DevSta "TransPend+" before reset; time between CfgWr setting Initiate FLR and the first successful CfgRd.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:pcie_flr() : pci_wait_for_pending_transaction() (polls 4 times with 0, 100, 200, 400 ms sleeps), sets PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_BCR_FLR , msleep(100) unless dev->imm_ready , then pci_dev_wait(dev, "FLR", PCIE_RESET_READY_POLL_MS) .
Test to provoke it: echo flr > /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/reset_method then echo 1 > .../reset with the driver unbound. CAUTION.

name: Surprise link down / hot removal while I/O is in flight
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The link drop is visible (traffic stops, electrical idle, Detect) and outstanding tags never complete; the Surprise Down AER bit and hot-plug slot events are in the port's registers, visible only if read by software over a probed link.
What happens: The link drops without warning (cable pull, power fault, failed Recovery). Outstanding requests can never complete; the port may report a Surprise Down error and hot-plug events.
How it shows up: Port AER uncorrectable bit 5 (Surprise Down, PCI_ERR_UNC_SURPDN ) if the port supports Data Link Layer Link Active reporting; Slot Status Data Link Layer State Changed / Presence Detect Changed; DPC may contain the port. NVMe: reads of CSTS return all-ones, the controller is removed; I/O fails with a host path error and fails over if multipath.
Spec basis: PCIe Base: Surprise Down error, Data Link Layer State Changed, hot-plug slot registers, Downstream Port Containment (DPC).
Typical causes: Physical removal; power loss on the device; REPLAY_NUM rollover followed by failed Recovery (T-36); deep power state not exiting (T-15).
How to detect / prove: dmesg: pciehp "Link Down", AER "Surprise Down", DPC containment messages, NVMe "controller is down" or removal. lspci -vvv on the port: SltSta DLActive-.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_timeout() checks pci_dev_is_disconnected() and moves the controller to DELETING; pci.c:pci_dev_wait() returns early when disconnected; DPC in drivers/pci/pcie/dpc.c , recovery in err.c . (pciehp itself is not in this atlas's source subset.)
Test to provoke it: Hot-plug capable slot: echo 0 > /sys/bus/pci/slots/N/power during I/O (CAUTION), or pull a U.2 drive in a hot-plug backplane (EXPERT).

name: ASPM exit latency larger than the endpoint can accept
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = electrical idle (EIOS) → first TLP after exit, i.e. the L0s/L1 exit time; compare with LnkCap exit latency and DevCap acceptable latency (both visible in config CplD payloads if captured).
What happens: Each port reports how long it needs to leave L0s and L1 (Link Capabilities exit latencies); each endpoint reports how much latency it can accept (Device Capabilities acceptable latencies). If exit latency (plus 1 µs per switch for L1) exceeds acceptable latency, enabling that ASPM state can starve the device.
How it shows up: If enabled anyway (by firmware or by forcing a policy): latency spikes, sometimes Completion Timeouts or replay errors after L1 exit. If Linux detects the mismatch it silently does not enable the state (higher power, no error).
Spec basis: PCIe Base: Link Capabilities L0s/L1 Exit Latency, Device Capabilities Endpoint L0s/L1 Acceptable Latency, Link Control ASPM Control.
Typical causes: Under-reported exit latencies; PLLs that take longer than declared; platform BIOS forcing ASPM.
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv : LnkCap "ASPM L0s L1, Exit Latency L0s <1us, L1 <8us", DevCap "Latency L0s <64ns, L1 <1us", LnkCtl "ASPM L1 Enabled". Compare with /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy . Measure fio latency with ASPM on and off ( pcie_aspm=off ).
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aspm.c:pcie_aspm_check_latency() converts encodings ( calc_l0s_latency() = 64 ns « encoding, calc_l1_latency() = 1 µs « encoding; encoding 7 means "more than"), adds 1 µs per switch for L1 and clears aspm_capable bits that do not fit. It does not check L1 substates ("We assume that the L1 exit latencies advertised by a device include L1 substate latencies").
Test to provoke it: Compare tail latency with pcie_aspm.policy=performance vs powersupersave . SAFE.

name: L1 substates / LTR misprogrammed: wake too slow or link lost
In a PEX trace: Partly visible L1 entry (PM DLLPs / EIOS) and exit timing visible; L1.2 itself turns the PHY off so the analyzer sees only electrical idle and the wake; CLKREQ# is sideband (visible only with a sideband probe). LTR Message TLPs carrying latency values are visible.
What happens: L1.1/L1.2 turn off more of the PHY. Entry depends on the device's Latency Tolerance Reporting (LTR) value versus the LTR_L1.2_THRESHOLD; exit timing depends on T_POWER_ON and Common_Mode_Restore_Time. Wrong values make exit slower than the device tolerates, or make exit fail.
How it shows up: Latency spikes after idle; in bad cases the link fails to retrain after L1.2 and the drive disappears (T-15, T-44). No error is reported for a slow exit.
Spec basis: PCIe Base: L1 PM Substates extended capability (capability ID 1Eh): L1SS capabilities, Control 1 (enables, Common_Mode_Restore_Time, LTR_L1.2_THRESHOLD value/scale), Control 2 (T_POWER_ON scale/value); LTR extended capability (18h): Max Snoop/No-Snoop Latency; Device Control 2 LTR Mechanism Enable.
Typical causes: Inconsistent values programmed on the two ends; T_POWER_ON shorter than the PHY needs; CLKREQ# routing problems; device reporting very large LTR values.
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv : "L1SubCap", "L1SubCtl1: PCI-PM_L1.2+ ASPM_L1.2+ ... T_CommonMode=..us LTR1.2_Threshold=..ns", "L1SubCtl2: T_PwrOn=..us", "LTR+" in DevCtl2. Compare both ends of the link. Reproduce with L1.2 disabled.
Linux v7.2 source: aspm.c:aspm_calc_l12_info() computes T_POWER_ON, Common_Mode_Restore_Time and LTR threshold from both ends; pcie_encode_t_power_on() ; pci_configure_aspm_l1ss() , pci_save_aspm_l1ss_state() / pci_restore_aspm_l1ss_state() across suspend.
Test to provoke it: Toggle L1.2 via the ASPM policy ( powersupersave ) on a laptop and run idle/burst fio patterns. SAFE.

name: Tail-latency SLA miss (p99 / p99.9 / p99.99)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Per-command latency = doorbell MWr → CQE MWr (match CID and SQID) for every command in the capture; build the distribution and compare p99/p99.9 with the SLA. Host-side latency above the driver is not visible.
What happens: Median latency is fine, but a small fraction of commands take tens or hundreds of times longer. A service with a percentile target fails even though every command succeeded.
How it shows up: No error anywhere. Only the latency distribution shows it: fio clat percentiles , application histograms, blk-mq stats.
Spec basis: None. NVMe and PCIe define no per-command latency limit; the SLA is yours. Contributing spec mechanisms: arbitration (CC.AMS, Arbitration feature 01h), interrupt coalescing (feature 08h), APST and ASPM exit latencies.
Typical causes: Garbage collection (T-48), power-state exits (T-14, T-45, T-46), thermal throttling (T-49), read retries on worn NAND (internal error recovery), queue imbalance or head-of-line blocking behind large commands, host interrupt or scheduling delays (T-32).
How to detect / prove: fio --name=t --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=1 --runtime=600 --time_based --lat_percentiles=1 --percentile_list=50:99:99.9:99.99 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 (read-only workload); bpftrace on nvme:nvme_setup_cmd / nvme:nvme_complete_rq for per-command latency; correlate outliers with SMART temperature, power state ( nvme get-feature -f 0x02 ) and AER counters.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux v7.2 does not track SLAs; measurement via tracepoints in drivers/nvme/host/trace.c and block-layer statistics.
Test to provoke it: Run a read-latency probe at QD1 while a second job does sustained random writes; compare percentiles with and without the writer. SAFE for the probe; the writer is DESTRUCTIVE to data on the target range.

name: Garbage-collection stall
In a PEX trace: Partly visible GC itself is internal; visible symptom is a burst of long doorbell → CQE intervals on writes (and reads) under sustained random write, with otherwise normal link behaviour.
What happens: When free blocks run low, the SSD must copy valid pages out of blocks before erasing them. Host commands queue behind this work, producing periodic latency spikes from milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds.
How it shows up: Latency spikes correlated with sustained writes; no error. The Tiny-Tail Flash study (FAST 2017) reports 5–138× GC-induced slowdowns at the 99–99.99th percentiles for a baseline design.
Spec basis: Not specified. Related host hints exist: Deallocate/TRIM (DSM 09h), Write Zeroes, Streams/Flexible Data Placement, Predictable Latency Mode (I/O determinism windows) where supported.
Typical causes: High write amplification (random small writes, low over-provisioning); no TRIM; full drive.
How to detect / prove: Long sustained random-write test with latency logging ( --write_lat_log ); plot latency vs time and vs bytes written. If supported, check Predictable Latency Mode logs and Endurance Group logs.
Linux v7.2 source: No driver involvement; Linux sends Discard as DSM Deallocate when the filesystem issues it ( core.c:nvme_setup_discard() ).
Test to provoke it: Precondition the drive (fill sequentially twice), then 4 KiB random writes at high QD for hours. DESTRUCTIVE to data on the drive; CAUTION wear.

name: Thermal throttling slowdown
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Visible symptom: doorbell → CQE intervals and data throughput dropping over time; temperature and throttling state only in SMART log payloads (Get Log Page 02h data) if the host reads them during the capture.
What happens: As the composite temperature rises past the drive's thermal management thresholds, the controller reduces performance to cool down. Commands still succeed, just slower.
How it shows up: Throughput drops and latency rises after minutes of load. SMART / Health log: Composite Temperature, Warning Composite Temperature Time, Critical Composite Temperature Time, Thermal Management Temperature 1/2 Transition Count and Total Time. An Asynchronous Event (SMART/Health, temperature) may be raised when a threshold is crossed — that part is reported.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: SMART / Health Information log (02h) temperature fields and thermal management counters; Identify WCTEMP/CCTEMP; Host Controlled Thermal Management (feature 10h) with MNTMT/MXTMT; Temperature Threshold feature (04h).
Typical causes: Insufficient airflow or heatsink; sustained writes; host thermal management thresholds set low.
How to detect / prove: Poll nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 every few seconds during a fio run; correlate throughput with temperature and with the thermal transition counters; /sys/class/hwmon NVMe sensors (Linux drivers/nvme/host/hwmon.c ).
Linux v7.2 source: hwmon.c exposes temperatures and thresholds; quirks NVME_QUIRK_NO_TEMP_THRESH_CHANGE , NVME_QUIRK_NO_SECONDARY_TEMP_THRESH exist for devices that misbehave.
Test to provoke it: Run sequential writes with airflow blocked (CAUTION: monitor temperature, stop before the critical threshold).

name: Write cliff: steady-state write performance far below fresh-out-of-box
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Visible as write CQE latency rising and throughput falling after a capacity-sized amount of written data (sum of NLB in Write SQEs); the cause (free-block exhaustion) is internal.
What happens: A new or freshly sanitized drive writes into free blocks (and often an SLC cache). After roughly a drive capacity of writes (or once the cache fills), throughput drops sharply to the steady-state rate.
How it shows up: No error. Throughput vs time graph shows a step down; latency rises. Benchmarks run on an empty drive overstate performance.
Spec basis: Not specified. SNIA Solid State Storage Performance Test Specification defines preconditioning methods (external standard).
Typical causes: SLC cache exhaustion; free-block pool exhaustion leading to GC (T-48).
How to detect / prove: Write the whole drive while logging bandwidth once per second ( --bwavg_time=1000 --write_bw_log ); find the knee; compare with datasheet steady-state numbers.
Linux v7.2 source: No driver involvement.
Test to provoke it: Sanitize or format, then sequential write 2× capacity. DESTRUCTIVE.

name: Flush or FUA write takes far longer than expected
In a PEX trace: Visible Interval = Flush SQE (opcode 00h) doorbell MWr → its CQE MWr; compare with your SLA; whether data was really made durable is not visible.
What happens: With a volatile write cache, a Flush (or a write with Force Unit Access) must wait until cached data is on non-volatile media. On some drives this takes hundreds of milliseconds or more; databases that fsync often stall.
How it shows up: No error; fsync latency spikes. If it exceeds io_timeout, it becomes T-22.
Spec basis: NVMe NVM Command Set: Flush (00h), FUA bit in Write; Identify Controller VWC; Volatile Write Cache feature (06h).
Typical causes: Large dirty cache; flush serialised behind GC; firmware flushing the mapping table too.
How to detect / prove: fio with --fsync=1 or --fdatasync=1 and latency percentiles; tracepoints for opcode 0x00 latency; check VWC with nvme id-ctrl | grep vwc and nvme get-feature -f 0x06 .
Linux v7.2 source: Linux issues Flush for REQ_PREFLUSH when the device reports a volatile cache ( core.c sets the queue write-cache flag from VWC).
Test to provoke it: Mixed write + fsync workload; compare with write cache disabled ( nvme set-feature -f 0x06 -v 0 , CAUTION: changes drive behaviour until reset/power cycle).

name: Deallocate accepted but not performed
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The DSM SQE (OPC 09h, CDW11=4), the range-list fetch with SLBA/NLB, the Success CQE and MSI-X are all visible and look perfect. The failure itself is not. Partial clue: if the capture also holds the Identify Namespace data (DLFEAT RB=001b/010b) and a later Read of the range, a non-zero data payload in that Read proves it. Detail: Identical to a good deallocate: doorbell MWr, MRd of the 64-byte SQE (OPC 09h, CDW11 = 4), MRd of 16×(NR+1) bytes of ranges, MWr of a CQE with status 0, MSI-X. The DSM exchange itself never shows the failure; only the absence of a later effect does.
What happens: The host sends DSM with AD=1 for a range. The controller fetches the range list, completes with status 0, and leaves every LBA in the range mapped. Old data, space accounting and garbage-collection load stay as if nothing happened.
How it shows up: Nothing is reported: CQE status 0, no dmesg line, no Error Information log entry, no AER. blkdiscard / fstrim exit 0. Over time sustained write performance and endurance are worse than expected, because the drive keeps moving data the host no longer needs.
Spec basis: NVM Command Set: Dataset Management, Attribute – Deallocate. Identify Namespace DLFEAT (read behaviour bits 2:0), NSFEAT bit 2 (DULBE), NUSE; Feature 05h DULBE bit. Whether doing nothing is a violation depends on these promises. AD is widely described as advisory verify in spec .
Typical causes: Firmware treats AD as a hint and drops it under load or when the queue of unmap work is full. Ranges smaller than the internal mapping unit are ignored. Firmware feature disabled in a SKU. A bug where a multi-range DSM processes only range 0.
How to detect / prove: 1) Confirm the DSM and its ranges on the wire or with blktrace (rule out D-04 ). 2) If DLFEAT RB = 001b/010b: read back sample LBAs; old data = proven. 3) If NSFEAT.DULBE: enable Feature 05h bit 16 and read; Success instead of status 287h = not deallocated (control: a never-written LBA must give 287h). 4) NUSE before/after (if the drive tracks it). 5) Performance A/B against a run without deallocate.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_setup_discard() builds the command; nvme_update_disk_info() sets discard limits; nvme_cleanup_cmd() frees the range buffer. No code path verifies the effect.
Test to provoke it: Lab IV.1 CAUTION : write a pattern, deallocate an aligned range, read back per DLFEAT, DULBE probe, NUSE delta. Vary the range size (1 granule, 1 GiB, whole namespace), number of ranges (1, 2, 256), and queue depth of concurrent writes. In QEMU, a backend that ignores discards reproduces it on purpose.

name: Deallocate partially performed: ranges or edges silently skipped
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The range descriptors and the length of the range-list MRd are visible, so a device that fetched fewer than 16×(NR+1) bytes is caught. Which ranges took effect is not visible, except through later Read payloads at range edges. Detail: Decode every range descriptor in the range-list CplD. Confirm that NR+1 descriptors were fetched (the MRd length). If the device fetched fewer bytes than 16×(NR+1), it cannot have processed the later ranges. That is the one case where the trace does show a partial deallocate.
What happens: Only part of the request takes effect: the first range of a multi-range DSM, only fully-aligned granules (the unaligned head and tail are kept), or every range except the ones larger than an internal limit. The CQE is still Success.
How it shows up: Silent. Read-back gives zeroes in the middle of the range and old data near the edges, or in whole sub-ranges. NUSE drops by less than NLB.
Spec basis: NPDG/NPDA and NPDGL/NPDAL are preferred granularity and alignment. Unaligned deallocates are allowed, and how much is deallocated is implementation-dependent unless DLFEAT promises a read value for each deallocated LBA. DMRL/DMRSL are limits the host should honour. What a controller must do when they are exceeded: verify in spec .
Typical causes: Internal mapping unit larger than the LBA size (for example 4 KiB map on 512-byte LBAs). Range-count or range-size limits handled with a silent "skip". The QEMU model does exactly this: hw/nvme/ctrl.c:nvme_dsm_cb() skips a range with nlb > dmrsl or out-of-bounds LBAs, emits only a trace event, and completes Success.
How to detect / prove: Read back the first and last LBA of every range, plus one LBA either side of each. With DLFEAT RB = 001b, any non-zero LBA inside a range is a violation, whatever the alignment. Check NUSE delta against Σ NLB. For multi-range, use distinct patterns per range so you can tell which range was skipped.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_update_disk_info() (discard_granularity from NPDG/NPDA/NPDGL/NPDAL; max_discard_segments from DMRL or 256; max_hw_discard_sectors from DMRSL); core.c:nvme_init_non_mdts_limits() reads DMRL/DMRSL.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION With nvme dsm passthrough (bypasses the block layer's rounding): issue ranges that start or end off the NPDA boundary, 256-range DSMs, and a range just above DMRSL. Check every edge LBA. Run on QEMU first to see the skip behaviour in its trace events.

name: Read after deallocate returns old data (DLFEAT promise broken)
In a PEX trace: Visible If the capture includes the Identify Namespace payload (DLFEAT), the DSM, and the later Read, the Read data payload carrying the old pattern instead of the promised 00h/FFh is direct proof on the wire. Detail: The later Read's data MWr TLPs carry the old pattern. This is one of the few silent failures where the proof itself is visible on the wire, in the read data payload.
What happens: The namespace reports DLFEAT read behaviour 001b (zeroes) or 010b (FFh). After a successful deallocate, a Read returns the previous contents of the block. Either the FTL did not unmap it, or it unmapped and a cache (read buffer, write cache, read-ahead) still returns the old page.
How it shows up: Read completes Success with stale data. With PI enabled, the stale PI may still be valid for the old data, so even PI checks pass.
Spec basis: Identify Namespace DLFEAT bits 2:0. With 001b/010b the read result is defined. Returning old data is a conformance failure . Linux relies on this promise: nvme_update_ns_info_block() enables DEAC only when RB = 001b and DLFEAT bit 3 is set.
Typical causes: Deallocate not performed ( D-01 ). Unmap applied to the map but not invalidated in an internal read cache. A race between a write still in the volatile cache and the deallocate (ordering bug). Unmap lost across a power cycle (the unmap journal was not persisted, so after power-on the old mapping comes back). The last case is the nastiest: data deleted for security reasons reappears.
How to detect / prove: Read-back right after the CQE, again after idle, and again after a clean power cycle ( nvme subsystem-reset or a real power cycle). Any non-promised value at any point is proof. Collect: Identify Namespace (DLFEAT), trace of the DSM, and a hex dump of the read.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_update_ns_info_block() (DEAC condition), core.c:nvme_setup_write_zeroes() ; quirk NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES in nvme.h and pci.c:nvme_id_table .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION Write pattern → deallocate → read immediately → idle 10 min → read → power cycle → read. Also overlap: issue a Write and a DSM to the same LBAs back to back at high queue depth, then read. The result must be either the new data or the promised value, consistent with the completion order.

name: Discard never reaches the device (host-side silent drop)
In a PEX trace: Visible Visible as an absence: no SQE with OPC 09h (or 08h) in a capture window long enough to cover the journal commit or fstrim. That proves the drive was never asked. Detail: Nothing: no OPC 09h SQE in the capture window. Note that discards may come long after the truncate (journal commit, periodic fstrim), so capture long enough.
What happens: The user believes the space was trimmed, but no DSM was ever sent. Common reasons: filesystem not mounted with -o discard and no fstrim run; dm-crypt without discard passthrough; LVM/MD layers or a virtual disk that do not forward discards; discard_max_bytes = 0 because ONCS.DSM is clear or the queue limit was changed; the discard was smaller than discard_granularity and rounded away.
How it shows up: Mostly silent. blkdiscard on a device without discard support does fail ( EOPNOTSUPP ), but filesystem truncate and many stacked layers just drop the request. The drive is blamed for keeping data it was never told about.
Spec basis: Not a device issue. Identify Controller ONCS bit 2 decides whether Linux enables discard at all.
Typical causes: Mount options, dm/LVM configuration, virtualization layers, misread fstrim output (its byte count is what it asked for), discards rounded away by granularity.
How to detect / prove: lsblk --discard on every layer of the stack (non-zero DISC-GRAN/DISC-MAX needed on each). blktrace -d /dev/nvme0n1 while truncating or trimming: look for discard requests (RWBS with D ). Enable the nvme:nvme_setup_cmd tracepoint and look for DSM with attributes=4 . Analyzer: no SQE with OPC 09h means nothing was sent.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_update_disk_info() : max_hw_discard_sectors = 0 when ONCS.DSM is clear and DMRSL is 0. core.c:nvme_setup_cmd() is the single point where REQ_OP_DISCARD becomes a DSM, so a probe there catches every discard that leaves the block layer.
Test to provoke it: SAFE on a scratch filesystem: mount without discard , write and delete a file, trace for 2 minutes and observe no DSM. Remount with discard and repeat. Repeat on dm-crypt with and without discard passthrough.

name: Write Zeroes completes but blocks are not zero
In a PEX trace: Visible The Write Zeroes SQE (OPC 08h, DEAC in CDW12 bit 25) and Success CQE, followed by a Read whose data payload is non-zero, are both on the wire, which proves the failure. Detail: SQE OPC 08h with SLBA/NLB in CDW10-12 and DEAC in CDW12 bit 25. No data transfer for the command itself. The later Read data TLPs show the non-zero content.
What happens: Write Zeroes (08h), with or without DEAC, returns Success, but later reads return old data, garbage, or zeroes for only part of the range. Filesystems and databases that rely on zero-out for allocation (for example, unwritten extents converted to written, or BLKZEROOUT used to clear metadata) then see stale structures.
How it shows up: Silent at the NVMe level. Upper layers may later report corruption (filesystem check errors, database page checksum failures) far away from the cause.
Spec basis: NVM Command Set Write Zeroes: after completion the LBAs read as zeroes (and PI per PRACT/PRINFO). DEAC allows the controller to deallocate instead, but the zero read result is still required. Linux's comment in nvme_update_ns_info_block() says DEAC "must be a no-op if reads from deallocated data do not return zeroes".
Typical causes: Firmware implementing DEAC as "deallocate" on a drive whose deallocated read value is not zero. Size-limit handling (WZSL, or WZDSL when ONCS bit 11 applies) silently truncating long commands. Bugs the Linux quirk NVME_QUIRK_DISABLE_WRITE_ZEROES ("Broken Write Zeroes") exists for: in v7.2 it is set for many device IDs in pci.c:nvme_id_table , including the Intel 600P/P3100 and the QEMU 5845h controller.
How to detect / prove: Write a non-zero pattern, Write Zeroes the range (both DEAC=0 and DEAC=1 via nvme write-zeroes … --deac ), read every block back, compare with zeroes. Test sizes around WZSL/WZDSL and MDTS. Any non-zero byte is proof, independent of DLFEAT.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_setup_write_zeroes() , core.c:nvme_init_non_mdts_limits() (WZSL, NVME_QUIRK_DISABLE_WRITE_ZEROES ), core.c:nvme_update_disk_info() ( max_write_zeroes_sectors , NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES ).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION On a spare namespace: pattern-fill 1 GiB; nvme write-zeroes in sizes 1 block, WZSL−1, WZSL, WZSL+1 (expect an error, not silent truncation), with and without --deac . Read back and compare. Also run blkdiscard -z and confirm with blktrace which command Linux actually used.

name: Deallocate reaches too far: live data outside the range lost
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The range descriptors in the range-list CplD show whether the host asked for the right LBAs. Lost guard blocks show up only if the capture also holds the guard writes and a later read of the guards. Detail: Range descriptor values in the CplD. If they are right and guards are still lost, the device is at fault. If they are already wrong, the host is.
What happens: Blocks outside the requested range read back as zeroes/FFh or fail with 287h. The drive rounded the range out to its internal unit, mis-parsed the descriptor (for example, read NLB as 0's based, which adds one block), or the host sent the wrong range.
How it shows up: Silent until the data is read. Filesystems see corrupted files or metadata long after the trim. Host-side cases have happened in practice: a 2019 dm-devel thread reports fstrim discarding too many or the wrong blocks on Linux 5.1 with dm-crypt/LVM, which led to data loss.
Spec basis: Range descriptor: Length in logical blocks (a 1's based count, unlike CDW12 NLB in Read/Write, which is 0's based). Deallocating LBAs not listed in any range is never permitted.
Typical causes: Firmware treating Length as 0's based; rounding unaligned ranges outward instead of inward; host stacking layers translating offsets wrongly; a DSM processed against the wrong namespace (NSID bug).
How to detect / prove: Guard pattern: write distinct "guard" blocks right before and after each range, deallocate, and verify the guards with a checksumming read (fio --verify=crc32c over the guard areas). Decode the range list in the trace to tell host error from device error.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_setup_discard() : nlb = blk_rq_sectors(req) >> (lba_shift - 9) (single segment) or bi_size >> lba_shift per bio, written as a 1's based count.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION For N in {1, 7, 8, 9, 4095, 4096, 4097} blocks: guard–range–guard layout, deallocate the range via nvme dsm , verify guards. Repeat with 2- and 256-range DSMs and with ranges in a second namespace to catch NSID mix-ups.

name: Allocation accounting wrong: NUSE frozen, DULBE not reported
In a PEX trace: Visible The Identify Namespace data payload (NUSE at bytes 16–23) before and after, and the CQE status of a DULBE-enabled Read (287h expected, 0 observed) are on the wire, provided the test commands are captured.
