Detail: Identify Namespace data (4 KiB CplD/MWr to the host) shows NUSE at bytes 16–23. Compare captures before and after. The DULBE read's CQE carries SCT 2h / SC 87h when it works.
What happens: The namespace advertises thin provisioning (NSFEAT bit 0) or DULBE (NSFEAT bit 2), but NUSE never changes after writes or deallocates, or DULBE is enabled and reads of never-written/deallocated blocks still return Success. Management software that relies on NUSE for capacity planning or thin-provisioning alerts gets wrong numbers.
How it shows up: No error. NUSE stays equal to NCAP (or at its value from the factory), and Get Features 05h shows DULBE=1 while reads of unwritten LBAs succeed.
Spec basis: Identify Namespace NUSE ("current number of logical blocks allocated", ≤ NCAP), NSFEAT THIN/DULBE, Feature 05h DULBE bit 16. A drive without thin provisioning may legitimately report NUSE = NCAP. The QEMU model does so on purpose ( hw/nvme/ns.c : "no thin provisioning").
Typical causes: NUSE computed once at format time; DULBE accepted by Set Features but not wired to the read path; DULBE checked for never-written blocks but not for deallocated ones (or the reverse).
How to detect / prove: After a Format (NUSE should drop to about 0 on a tracking drive), write N blocks (NUSE +N), deallocate them (NUSE −N). For DULBE: read a never-written LBA (expect 287h), write it (expect Success), deallocate it (expect 287h). The QEMU controller's nvme_check_dulbe() is a reference: it returns NVME_DULB when the block-status query says the range holds no data.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux does not use NUSE for block I/O. core.c:nvme_error_status() maps NVME_SC_UNWRITTEN_BLOCK (287h) to BLK_STS_MEDIUM ; constants.c names it "Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block".
Test to provoke it: CAUTION Format the test namespace, then run the NUSE/DULBE state table above: never-written → written → deallocated → written again, at both 1-block and 1 GiB scale. Disable DULBE afterwards.

name: Flush ignored / volatile write cache that lies
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Flush SQE (OPC 00h) and its CQE are visible, so you can show the host flushed. A Flush that always completes in microseconds after many MiB of writes is a clue, not proof. With VWC=0 you see no Flushes at all. The data loss needs a power-cut ledger test. Detail: Flush SQE (OPC 00h, NSID) and its Success CQE. How long the Flush took is the only clue: a Flush after many MiB of cached writes that completes in microseconds every time is suspicious, but not proof (the drive may have PLP). With VWC = 0 you will see no Flush commands at all.
What happens: Either (a) Flush completes Success before the cached data is on NAND, or (b) the drive reports VWC = 0 (no volatile cache) while it really buffers writes in DRAM or SRAM without power-loss protection. In case (b) Linux never sends a Flush at all , because the queue is set up without a write cache.
How it shows up: Nothing until an unexpected power loss. Then data that fsync() / fdatasync() reported as durable is missing or old, and journals replay inconsistent states.
Spec basis: NVM Command Set Flush; Identify Controller VWC; Set/Get Features 06h (Volatile Write Cache, WCE bit 0). A completed Flush is a durability promise for all previously completed writes.
Typical causes: Firmware completing Flush early for benchmark scores; a flush that only drains the controller's front-end buffer, not the FTL metadata; a missing VWC report; capacitors (PLP) degraded or absent on a SKU that shares firmware with a PLP model. A widely reported informal 2022 test (by Russ Bishop, covered in the press) claimed that two of four consumer NVMe SSDs lost flushed data on power cuts uncertain (not peer-reviewed; details not independently verified here).
How to detect / prove: Power-cut test with a host-side ledger (see Lab IV.3): write records, fsync/Flush, log the acknowledged sequence number to a different machine, cut power at random points, power up, check that every acknowledged record is present. Any acknowledged-but-missing record after Flush = proof. Check nvme id-ctrl -H VWC and nvme get-feature -f 6 . On Linux, /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_cache shows "write back" or "write through". "write through" on a drive you suspect caches is case (b).
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_update_ns_info_block() sets BLK_FEAT_WRITE_CACHE | BLK_FEAT_FUA only if ctrl->vwc & NVME_CTRL_VWC_PRESENT and not info->no_vwc ; core.c:nvme_setup_flush() builds the Flush; core.c:nvme_ns_info_from_id_cs_indep() reads NVME_NS_VWC_NOT_PRESENT .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT : controlled power interruption (programmable PSU or a PCIe slot power switch / interposer) during a write+fsync workload, hundreds of cycles, varied timing relative to the Flush completion. Compare with the same drive with WCE disabled ( nvme set-feature -f 6 -v 0 ) as a control.

name: FUA not honoured
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The FUA bit (Write CDW12 bit 30) and the completion latency are visible. FUA writes as fast as cached writes on a drive without PLP is a clue. Proof needs a power-cut test. Detail: Write SQE CDW12 bit 30 = 1. FUA writes that complete exactly as fast as non-FUA writes on a drive without PLP are a strong hint.
What happens: A Write with FUA = 1 completes while its data is still only in volatile cache. Filesystems and databases use FUA for journal commit blocks (Linux turns REQ_FUA into NVME_RW_FUA ), so a lost FUA write loses the commit record of a transaction the application already saw as complete.
How it shows up: Only after power loss: the last committed transactions are missing even though the commit write completed.
Spec basis: Read/Write command Force Unit Access bit (CDW12 bit 30). Durable at completion, independent of the write cache.
Typical causes: Firmware treating FUA as a hint, or making the data durable but not the mapping-table update that points to it (after power-up the LBA maps to the old page).
How to detect / prove: Power-cut ledger test using only FUA writes and no Flush (use a small program that writes with O_DIRECT|O_DSYNC ; Linux can then mark the write REQ_FUA when the queue advertises FUA. Confirm with the nvme_setup_cmd tracepoint that the control field has bit 14 set before trusting the test). Any acknowledged FUA write missing after power-up = proof.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_setup_rw() : if (req->cmd_flags & REQ_FUA) control |= NVME_RW_FUA; . FUA is advertised to the block layer only with a write cache ( BLK_FEAT_FUA in nvme_update_ns_info_block() ). Otherwise the block layer never sets it.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT : as D-08 but with O_DSYNC writes. Compare the FUA write latency distribution with WCE on and off: if they are the same and the drive has no PLP, investigate.

name: Acknowledged writes lost on power loss (PLP failure)
In a PEX trace: Not visible Not visible: the trace before the cut is normal, and after power-up you see only a normal (possibly slower) initialization. Use a power-cut ledger and the SMART Unsafe Shutdowns counter. Detail: Nothing before the cut. After power-up: normal initialization, possibly a longer time to CSTS.RDY = 1 (the drive rebuilding its map), then Reads returning old or wrong data.
What happens: On a drive that claims power-loss protection, or with the cache disabled, writes that completed before the power cut are missing or old after power-up. Also includes losing data written long before the cut, when an FTL metadata update in flight corrupts the mapping of older data. Zheng et al. classify this as metadata corruption.
How it shows up: Nothing at power-up in most cases. Sometimes the SMART log Unsafe Shutdowns counter increments (it should on every unexpected power loss), and sometimes Media and Data Integrity Errors rise if the drive notices. A drive that comes back with no namespace, read-only mode, or a Critical Warning bit set is the "total device failure" end of the range.
Spec basis: No single NVMe field promises PLP. Durability rests on Flush/FUA and the VWC report. SMART / Health log: Unsafe Shutdowns, Critical Warning bits (including "volatile memory backup device has failed"), Media and Data Integrity Errors.
Typical causes: Hold-up capacitors aged or out of tolerance; firmware not finishing the dump within the hold-up time; mapping table checkpoint corruption; power cut during an internal operation (GC, wear levelling) that moved live data.
How to detect / prove: Power-cut ledger test with verification of all previously written data, not just the latest records, because older data can be lost too. nvme smart-log before and after each cycle: Unsafe Shutdowns must increase by exactly one per cut (if it does not, the drive's power-loss detection itself is broken). Check the critical warning bits.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux has no visibility. On orderly shutdown it sets CC.SHN and waits for CSTS.SHST (see the shutdown timeout parameter shutdown_timeout in core.c ). An unexpected power loss skips this entirely.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT : hundreds to thousands of randomized power cuts (the FAST '13 study used more than 3,000 cycles across devices) with mixed sequential, random and flush-heavy workloads, including cuts during idle (background GC). Record temperature, as hold-up energy varies with it.

name: Torn (shorn) write: atomicity broken
In a PEX trace: Not visible Not visible: the write traffic is normal and the tear happens inside the drive at the cut. After power-up, Read payloads show mixed old/new blocks only if you read them back and know the expected content. Use record checksums. Detail: Normal Writes. The torn state is visible only in later Read payloads.
What happens: A write that should be atomic persists only partly: some logical blocks new, some old, or even part of one logical block new (a "shorn write" in Zheng et al.'s terms). Databases that rely on atomic 4 KiB or 16 KiB page writes (to skip double-write buffers) then see half-written pages.
How it shows up: After power loss (or after an error/reset during the write), reads return a mix. Page checksums in the application fail, but the drive reports nothing.
Spec basis: AWUN/AWUPF (Identify Controller, 0's based in logical blocks), NAWUN/NAWUPF/NABSPF (Identify Namespace, valid when NSFEAT bit 1 is set). A write ≤ NAWUPF that does not cross an NABSPF boundary must be all-or-nothing even across power failure. A single logical block is always expected to be atomic.
Typical causes: NAND page programming interrupted; firmware splitting a host write across two internal units with separate mapping updates; advertising NAWUPF larger than really guaranteed.
How to detect / prove: Write records of exactly NAWUPF size, aligned to NABSPF, each carrying a sequence number and checksum in every logical block (so a mix is detectable). After a power cut every record must be entirely old or entirely new. Also test records of NAWUPF + 1 blocks to confirm the boundary (tearing is allowed there).
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_configure_atomic_write() uses NAWUPF (and NABSPF as the boundary) only when NSFEAT has the atomics bit. Otherwise it logs "AWUPF ignored, only NAWUPF accepted" and uses one logical block. nvme_update_disk_info() limits physical_block_size to the atomic size, because "Linux filesystems assume writing a single physical block is an atomic operation".
Test to provoke it: EXPERT : power-cut loop with atomic-size records. Also CAUTION : controller reset ( nvme reset ) or an FLR in the middle of large writes, then verify the records, because tearing can also follow resets, not only power loss.

name: Unserializable persistence: write order not preserved across a power cut
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The trace proves the host side of the contract (Writes completed, Flush SQE/CQE, then the commit Write), which is half the evidence. The out-of-order persistence itself is not visible. Detail: Correct ordering on the host side: Writes completed, Flush SQE/CQE, then the commit Write. Capturing the trace proves the host kept its side of the contract.
What happens: After power loss, a later write (acknowledged and followed by Flush) is present, but an earlier one, also flushed before it, is missing. The persisted state matches no order in which the host could have seen the writes complete. Zheng et al. call these "unserializable writes".
How it shows up: Silent. Journaling and log-structured software break, because they assume "if the commit record is there, the data blocks before the flush are there too".
Spec basis: NVMe does not order independent commands, so writes in flight together may persist in any order. But Flush is a barrier: everything completed before it must be durable when it completes. A state with post-flush data present and pre-flush data missing violates the Flush contract.
Typical causes: Flush implemented per internal channel or die rather than globally. Mapping journal entries written out of order. The flush-ignoring behaviour of D-08 combined with a cache that evicts out of order.
How to detect / prove: Ledger with epochs: epoch N data → Flush → commit record N → Flush → epoch N+1. After a cut, if commit record N is present, every block of epoch N must verify. Note the distinction: missing data from an epoch whose Flush had not completed is legal.
Linux v7.2 source: Block layer flush machinery generates REQ_OP_FLUSH → core.c:nvme_setup_flush() . Linux does not wait for anything beyond the Flush CQE.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT : power-cut loop with the epoch ledger. Run it with high queue depth and many concurrent streams so the drive's internal parallelism is busy.

name: Lost write (dropped write) without any power event
In a PEX trace: Visible If the Write and the later Read are both captured: the device fetched the new data (MRd/CplD of the write buffer), posted Success, and later returned the old version in the Read data payload. That is proof on the wire. Detail: Write SQE, data MRd/CplD (the device fetched the new data), Success CQE. The later Read returns the old payload. The trace proves the device received the new data, which pins the fault inside the device.
What happens: A Write completes Success, no power event or reset follows, and a later Read returns the previous content of the block. The write was dropped (never programmed, or programmed but the mapping not updated).
How it shows up: Silent. A per-block checksum stored with the block cannot catch it, because the old block is self-consistent. Only a checksum or version stored elsewhere (in the parent pointer, as in ZFS/Btrfs, or in an application index) catches it. This is the case Krioukov et al. analysed for RAID.
Spec basis: Write command semantics. With PI Type 1, the reference tag only checks the LBA, not the version, so PI does not detect lost writes either.
Typical causes: FTL mapping-update race (two writes to the same LBA in flight, the older one's mapping update applied last); write-cache bugs on overlapping writes; firmware error recovery that retries a failed program and silently gives up.
How to detect / prove: Write a version number into each block and keep the expected version in host memory (fio --verify with --verify_header -style headers, or a custom tool that stores per-LBA generation counters). Read back after overwrites. Old version = lost write. Stress overlapping writes to the same LBA at high queue depth.
Linux v7.2 source: No detection in the driver. Linux allows overlapping writes in flight (the block layer does not serialize them), so an application that issues them must not depend on order.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : fio --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --size=1G --iodepth=64 --verify=crc32c --verify_backlog=1024 with --norandommap (allows overwrites) plus a custom generation-counter checker. Long runs (hours), near-full drive to force GC.

name: Misdirected write: data written to the wrong LBA
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The Write SQE SLBA shows where the host asked to write. The misdirection is visible only if you also capture a Read of the wrong destination returning that data (with an LBA header inside the payload). Detail: The Write SQE's SLBA shows what the host asked for. If the SLBA is already wrong, it is a host bug. If it is right and the data shows up elsewhere, it is the device.
What happens: The data for LBA X lands at LBA Y. Two corruptions result: X keeps old data (a lost write), and Y is overwritten with data that belongs elsewhere. Zheng et al. describe "flying writes" after power faults, data appearing at an unexpected location, which is the power-fault version of this.
How it shows up: Silent at the device. Detectable by checksums that embed the block's own address (a header containing the LBA, or PI reference tag with Type 1/2).
Spec basis: Write semantics; End-to-end Data Protection: with PI Type 1 the Reference Tag must match the lower bits of the LBA and the controller checks it when PRCHK includes the reference tag. A misdirected write then fails with Reference Tag Check Error (status 284h) on the read, or at write time if the controller re-checks.
Typical causes: FTL mapping corruption; namespace offset bugs (multi-namespace); bit flips in internal address paths without parity; on the host side, wrong SLBA from a stacking-driver bug.
How to detect / prove: Write blocks whose content includes their own LBA (fio verify headers include the offset). On read, check that the header offset equals the LBA read. A block containing another block's header = misdirected write, and the header tells you the intended destination.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_set_ref_tag() fills the reference tag for PI Type 1/2 (16-bit and 64-bit guard formats); core.c:nvme_error_status() maps NVME_SC_REFTAG_CHECK to BLK_STS_PROTECTION .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : full-drive fio write with --verify=crc32c (headers carry the offset), then a full read-verify, repeated after GC-heavy random overwrites and after power cuts ( EXPERT ). On a PI-formatted namespace, also confirm that a deliberately wrong SLBA via passthrough is caught.

name: Stale data returned on read
In a PEX trace: Visible With timestamps: the Write CQE MWr is earlier than the Read SQ doorbell MWr, and the Read data payload carries the old version. An analyzer capture gives exactly that ordering proof. Detail: Write CQE MWr timestamp earlier than the Read's SQ doorbell MWr timestamp, and the Read data payload carries the old version. An analyzer with timestamps gives exactly that proof.
What happens: A Read returns an older version of a block although a newer Write to that LBA has completed (no power event). Unlike D-13, the new data may be on media: a later Read, after a cache eviction or a reset, returns the correct new data. So the error comes and goes.
How it shows up: Silent, intermittent, and very hard to reproduce. Applications see "my write disappeared, then came back".
Spec basis: A Read that starts after a Write's completion must return that Write's data (or newer). NVMe does not order commands that are in flight at the same time, so a Read issued before the Write completed may legally return either version.
Typical causes: Read cache / read-ahead buffer not invalidated by a write to the same LBA; multi-queue race in firmware (write on one SQ, read on another); with multi-path/multi-controller subsystems, a second controller serving from a stale cache.
How to detect / prove: Write–complete–read loops with version numbers on the same LBAs from different queues (different CPUs) and, for multi-controller subsystems, via different controllers. Record the completion time of the write and the submission time of the read to show the read started after the write completed. That ordering is what turns "odd" into "proven".
Linux v7.2 source: Requests are spread over per-CPU hardware queues by blk-mq ( block/blk-mq.c ), so cross-queue read-after-write is normal Linux traffic.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : small hot set (for example 64 LBAs), one thread per CPU, each doing write(version)→wait for completion→read from another CPU→compare. Run with the drive both near-empty and full.

name: Wrong data / bit flips returned without an error
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The Read data payload with the wrong bytes is visible, and LCRC protected the hop, so the trace proves the device sent them. Recognising them as wrong needs the expected data (a captured earlier Write or a checksum). Detail: The Read data MWr payload already contains the wrong bytes, which proves the device sent them (PCIe LCRC protected the hop). If the trace shows correct data and the buffer is wrong, the fault is in host memory or an IOMMU/DMA mapping problem.
What happens: A Read completes Success but the data differs from what was written by a few bits or by a whole chunk. The drive's ECC either miscorrected (decoded to a wrong but valid codeword), or the corruption happened outside the ECC-protected path: controller SRAM/DRAM without parity, a firmware buffer handling bug, or the PCIe/host side (very unlikely to be undetected on PCIe because of LCRC, but possible in host memory).
How it shows up: Silent at the drive: no media error status, no SMART Media Errors increment. Only an end-to-end checksum catches it.
Spec basis: Read semantics. SMART/Health log Media and Data Integrity Errors counts only errors the controller detected . End-to-end Data Protection (PI guard CRC) covers the whole path from host buffer to media and back when PRCHK guard is enabled.
Typical causes: ECC miscorrection at high raw bit error rates; DRAM bit flips in the drive's buffer without ECC; firmware bugs in buffer management or in compression/encryption engines; host memory errors (rule out with ECC RAM and EDAC counters).
How to detect / prove: Checksummed reads: fio --verify=crc32c or sha256, a checksumming filesystem (ZFS/Btrfs scrub), PI with guard checking. Keep the bad buffer and compare it bit by bit with the expected one: a few scattered bit flips point to media/ECC, a block-sized chunk of other valid data points to D-14/D-15. Check host memory EDAC counters to rule out the host.
Linux v7.2 source: With a PI namespace and CONFIG_BLK_DEV_INTEGRITY , core.c:nvme_init_integrity() registers the profile so the block layer generates and verifies guard tags. Without it, Linux sets PRACT and the controller handles PI alone ( core.c:nvme_setup_rw() ), so host-to-controller transfer is not covered.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : long fio verify runs at high temperature, after many P/E cycles (endurance tests), and with data retention bakes (write, power off, store warm, read-verify). Compare the detected-error counters with the verify failures: every verify failure without a matching Media Errors increment is a silent corruption.

name: Retries mask failing media
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Device-internal retries are visible only as longer gaps between SQE fetch and data MWr. Host retries are visible as an error CQE (no DNR) followed by re-submission of the same SLBA/NLB. The media wear itself is not visible. Detail: Device-internal retries: only longer gaps between the Read SQE fetch and the data MWr. Host retries: the same command (same SLBA/NLB, new CID or same tag) re-submitted after an error CQE without DNR.
What happens: Data is returned correctly, but only after many internal read retries (read-level shifts, soft decoding) or after the host retried a failed command. Every layer reports success, while the media is wearing out and latency tails grow. Eventually it becomes an uncorrectable error. Schroeder et al. found uncorrectable errors in 20–63% of drives within four years, and that raw bit error rate is a poor predictor of them, so you cannot rely on a single "health" number.
How it shows up: Higher p99/p99.9 read latency on specific LBA ranges. SMART Percentage Used and Available Spare change slowly. On the host side, Linux retries a non-DNR error up to max_retries (default 5) times. A request that eventually succeeds produces no error to the application, and only the per-namespace command_retries_count in sysfs counts it.
Spec basis: CQE status Do Not Retry (DNR) bit and Command Retry Delay (CRD, with CRDT1–3 in Identify Controller). SMART/Health log Media and Data Integrity Errors, Available Spare, Percentage Used. Vendor or OCP logs may expose internal retry and ECC-correction counts impl .
Typical causes: Wear-out, read disturb, retention loss (data written long ago or at temperature extremes); host-visible retries also come from transient link or controller issues.
How to detect / prove: Latency heat map per LBA region (fio with --write_lat_log / --log_avg_msec , or bpftrace on block completion latency by sector). Read the per-path namespace counters in the diag sysfs group, …/diag/command_retries_count and …/diag/command_error_count (Linux v7.2 sysfs.c , nvme_ns_diag_attr_group ; with native multipath they appear on the hidden path disk such as nvme0c0n1 , not on the head nvme0n1 ). Track SMART over time. Compare Verify-command latency (opcode 0Ch, reads media without transfer) across regions.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_decide_disposition() (RETRY unless DNR set, blk_noretry_request() , or retries >= nvme_max_retries ); core.c:nvme_retry_req() (honours CRD via ctrl->crdt[] , increments ns->retries ); sysfs.c:command_retries_count_show() ; module parameter nvme_core.max_retries .
Test to provoke it: SAFE to observe: periodic full-drive read scans with latency logging. CAUTION : use the kernel's NVMe fault injection ( drivers/nvme/host/fault_inject.c , debugfs fault_inject ) to inject retryable status codes and confirm that only the retry counter shows them.

name: Sanitize reports success but user data remains
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The Sanitize SQE (admin OPC 84h, SANACT in CDW10), its quick Success CQE, the Get Log Page 81h polling and the Sanitize Status payload (SPROG, SSTAT) are visible. Read data payloads after the sanitize showing old patterns are visible proof that the logical view still has data. Remaining data in NAND blocks that are no longer mapped is not visible.
What happens: A Sanitize (Block Erase, Overwrite or Crypto Erase) runs to completion. The Sanitize Status log reports the most recent sanitize as completed successfully, but some user data can still be read: from LBAs (an incomplete pass), from areas outside the user LBA space (over-provisioning, retired blocks, caches), or by reading the raw NAND.
How it shows up: SSTAT says success (value 1, or 4 for the No-Deallocate variant), and no error is logged. Only a read-back audit or forensic analysis of the NAND finds the leftovers.
Spec basis: Base spec Sanitize command (84h) and Sanitize Status log (81h). libnvme defines SSTAT status values 0 never sanitized, 1 completed successfully, 2 in progress, 3 failed, 4 completed successfully with No-Deallocate, plus the Global Data Erased bit (bit 8) and completed-passes count. Identify Controller SANICAP (CES, BES, OWS, NDI, NODMMAS). Sanitize is meant to affect all user data, including caches and unallocated media verify exact scope wording in spec .
Typical causes: Firmware erasing only mapped blocks; skipping retired or bad blocks that still hold readable data; host-memory-buffer or controller cache not cleared; a power loss during sanitize followed by a wrong recovery. Wei, Grupp, Spada and Swanson (FAST '11) found that built-in sanitize commands worked on drives where they were implemented correctly, but some implementations were incorrect.
How to detect / prove: Fill the whole namespace with a recognizable, LBA-tagged pattern (including writes over the full capacity several times, so over-provisioned blocks also hold the pattern), sanitize, poll the log to completion, then read every LBA with O_DIRECT and search for the pattern. For the media-level claim, only a lab chip-off/raw-NAND read (as in Wei et al.) or a vendor-supported verification can prove it.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux never issues Sanitize itself. It arrives via the passthrough ioctls; core.c:nvme_init_known_nvm_effects() forces the LBCC and CSE effects for nvme_admin_sanitize_nvm , and core.c:nvme_passthru_end() unfreezes queues afterwards.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION (destroys all data): pattern-fill ×2, nvme sanitize /dev/nvme0 -a 2 (block erase; check nvme sanitize --help for your version), nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0 until done, full O_DIRECT read audit. Repeat for each SANACT the drive supports, and once with a power cut mid-sanitize ( EXPERT ): the drive must resume or report failure, never report success.

name: Crypto erase leaves data readable
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The command (Sanitize SANACT=100b, or Format NVM with SES=010b) and its Success CQE are visible. A later Read whose data payload contains the old plaintext is visible proof. A key that was not really replaced (data still decryptable with the old key, but reads return garbage) is not visible.
What happens: The drive reports a successful cryptographic erase but did not change the media encryption key, or changed it for some ranges only, or kept a copy. Reads either return old plaintext (key unchanged) or random-looking data (key changed). The second case looks correct even if a copy of the old key remains.
How it shows up: Silent. The user's only check, "reads now return something other than my data", passes even when the erase is not cryptographically effective.
Spec basis: Sanitize Crypto Erase (SANICAP.CES) and Format NVM Secure Erase Setting 010b (cryptographic erase), supported when the Identify Controller FNA field says so verify FNA bit . NVMe defines the command, not the key management. TCG Opal/Ruby specs cover encryption ranges.
Typical causes: Drive not actually encrypting media (no self-encryption despite the claim); key wrapped by a constant; per-range keys with one range forgotten; firmware bug that rewrites the old key after power cycle.
How to detect / prove: Read-back immediately after the erase and after a power cycle: old plaintext anywhere = proof. Strong assurance needs vendor documentation, a certification report (for example FIPS 140 validation of the drive's crypto module), or raw-NAND analysis showing ciphertext that changes between two writes of the same plaintext.
Linux v7.2 source: Passthrough only; Format gets LBCC|NCC|CSE effects in core.c:nvme_init_known_nvm_effects() , so the namespace is rescanned after it.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : write pattern, crypto erase, O_DIRECT read audit, power cycle, audit again. Compare against the DLFEAT read behaviour: many drives deallocate after crypto erase, so reads return zeroes. A drive returning ciphertext is fine, and one returning plaintext has failed.

name: Format NVM leaves old data
In a PEX trace: Visible The Format SQE (admin OPC 80h) shows the SES field in CDW10, so the trace proves which erase was requested. If SES=001b or 010b was requested, a later Read data payload with old data is visible proof. With SES=000b the trace also shows that no secure erase was asked for.
What happens: After Format NVM completes, reads return the data written before. Two different situations: (a) SES = 000b (no secure erase) was used. Then the spec does not require the data to be destroyed, only the LBA format to change, and with DLFEAT 000b the old data may still read back. That is a misunderstanding , not a drive failure. (b) SES = 001b (user data erase) or 010b was requested and data remains. That is a real failure.
How it shows up: Silent. Format may complete in milliseconds in either case.
Spec basis: Format NVM CDW10: LBAF, MSET, PI, PIL, SES (000b none, 001b user data erase, 010b cryptographic erase). FNA in Identify Controller says whether Format applies to all namespaces and whether crypto erase is supported verify bit layout .
Typical causes: Tools defaulting to SES=0 (users assume "format = wipe"); firmware implementing SES=1 as "deallocate all" on a drive with DLFEAT 000b, so reads still return old content.
How to detect / prove: Check the SES actually sent (PEX trace, or nvme format … --ses=1 on the command line). Pattern-fill, format, O_DIRECT read audit. With SES ≥ 1, any old pattern = proof. Check the Format completion time against Identify Controller's estimate, if reported.
Linux v7.2 source: Passthrough. After the command, nvme_passthru_end() runs a namespace rescan (NCC effect), which also catches LBA-format changes.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : run the same audit for SES=0, 1 and 2. Expect possible old data only for SES=0 with DLFEAT 000b.

name: Metadata / protection information not checked
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The PRINFO bits (PRACT, PRCHK guard/app/ref in CDW12 bits 29:26) of every Read/Write, and the reference/application tags in CDW14–15, are visible, so you can prove checking was not requested . With separate metadata (MPTR) or extended LBAs the PI bytes themselves cross the link and can be checked offline. Whether the controller really checked is not visible, unless a deliberately bad PI comes back with Success.
What happens: The namespace is formatted with PI, but corrupted data passes because: PI checking was not requested (PRCHK = 0); the host uses PRACT = 1 so the controller generates and strips PI and the host-to-controller path is not covered; the PI type is 0 (metadata only, never checked); application tag FFFFh disables checking for that block (an escape value verify per PI type ); or the controller ignores PRCHK.
How it shows up: No Guard/App/Reference Tag Check Error (282h/283h/284h) even though data or LBA is wrong.
Spec basis: NVM Command Set End-to-end Data Protection: Identify Namespace DPC/DPS, FLBAS/LBA format MS, PRINFO in Read/Write. Status codes Guard Check Error 282h, Application Tag Check Error 283h, Reference Tag Check Error 284h (Linux NVME_SC_GUARD_CHECK etc.).
Typical causes: Kernel without CONFIG_BLK_DEV_INTEGRITY ; integrity profile not registered; the user assuming "formatted with PI" means "protected end to end"; firmware skipping checks for performance.
How to detect / prove: Write with a deliberately wrong guard or reference tag via passthrough ( nvme write … --prinfo with a wrong --ref-tag ) and confirm the error. A Success here proves the check is not done. Check /sys/block/nvme0n1/integrity/ (format, read_verify, write_generate) to see what Linux does.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_init_integrity() (returns PI-capable only if the namespace has PI when integrity support is missing); core.c:nvme_setup_rw() sets PRACT when no integrity payload exists, and PRCHK bits from BIP_CHECK_GUARD/REFTAG/APPTAG ; core.c:nvme_set_ref_tag() ; core.c:nvme_error_status() maps 282h–284h and Invalid PI to BLK_STS_PROTECTION .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION on a test namespace formatted with PI Type 1: wrong ref tag write; correct write then wrong expected ref tag on read; corrupt guard. Each must fail. Repeat with app tag FFFFh to see the documented escape.

name: Bogus or duplicate namespace identifiers (NGUID / EUI64 / UUID)
In a PEX trace: Visible The Identify payloads (Identify Namespace NGUID/EUI64, and the Namespace Identification Descriptor list for CNS 03h) cross the link as MWr data. All-zero, all-FFh, or identical values across namespaces or across drives of the same model can be read straight from the capture.
What happens: The drive reports identifiers that are not unique: the same NGUID for every unit of a model, garbage, or the same ID for two namespaces. Multipath software and /dev/disk/by-id links may then merge two different namespaces into one, or point to the wrong disk.
How it shows up: Silent unless Linux detects the duplicate. Linux v7.2 then prints "clearing duplicate IDs for nsid N" and "use of /dev/disk/by-id/ may cause data corruption" (or "ignoring nsid N because of duplicate IDs" for fabrics or shared multi-controller namespaces) and sets NVME_QUIRK_BOGUS_NID at runtime.
Spec basis: Identify Namespace NGUID/EUI64, Namespace Identification Descriptor list (CNS 03h), NSFEAT bit 3 (identifiers never reused).
Typical causes: Firmware with a constant ID from the reference design; manufacturing step that never programs a unique value. v7.2 pci.c:nvme_id_table has many NVME_QUIRK_BOGUS_NID entries, including Intel 0A54h (P4500/P4600) and both QEMU device IDs.
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 | grep -iE 'nguid|eui64' and nvme ns-descs /dev/nvme0n1 on several units and namespaces; compare. dmesg | grep -i "duplicate IDs\|bogus" .
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_process_ns_desc() (ignores IDs under the quirk), core.c:nvme_identify_ns() ("Ignoring bogus Namespace Identifiers"), core.c:nvme_init_ns_head() (duplicate detection, runtime quirk), core.c:nvme_subsys_check_duplicate_ids() .
Test to provoke it: SAFE : create two namespaces (or use two drives of one model), compare all identifiers, and check that by-id links resolve uniquely.

name: Identify returns wrong data for a CNS value it does not really support
In a PEX trace: Visible The Identify SQE shows CNS in CDW10 bits 7:0. The returned data payload is visible. A controller answering CNS 02h (active namespace list) with the Identify Controller structure, or returning Success with a zero-filled descriptor list, shows up when you compare the payload with what that CNS should contain.
What happens: The controller claims a spec version that includes a CNS value but handles it wrongly: it truncates CNS to one bit (NVMe 1.0 behaviour), so the request is answered as a different structure, or returns Success with an empty structure instead of Invalid Field.
How it shows up: Silent wrong values: missing namespaces, wrong namespace list, garbage descriptors. Sometimes Linux prints "ctrl returned bogus length" for descriptor list entries.
Spec basis: Identify CNS values. NVMe 1.1 widened CNS from one bit to two bits; later versions to a full byte. The Linux comment in nvme_id_cns_ok() explains this history.
Typical causes: Old command decoders kept after raising the reported version. Linux quirks: NVME_QUIRK_IDENTIFY_CNS (only CNS 0/1 handled, QEMU 5845h and Apple controllers in v7.2) and NVME_QUIRK_NO_NS_DESC_LIST (descriptor list not handled despite claiming 1.3).
How to detect / prove: Issue each CNS with nvme admin-passthru --opcode=0x06 --cdw10=<cns> --data-len=4096 -r and compare the structure with what the CNS defines. An unsupported CNS should fail with Invalid Field, not return Success with unrelated data.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_id_cns_ok() (CNS ≤ 3 for ≥ 1.1 unless quirk, else ≤ 1), core.c:nvme_identify_ns_descs() , core.c:nvme_process_ns_desc() ("ctrl returned bogus length"), apple.c sets NVME_QUIRK_IDENTIFY_CNS .
Test to provoke it: SAFE (read-only admin commands): sweep CNS 00h–1Fh with NSID 0, 1 and FFFFFFFFh, log status and payload.

name: Namespace capacity or format mis-reported
In a PEX trace: Partly visible NSZE/NCAP/NUSE (bytes 0–23), FLBAS (byte 26) and the LBA format table are in the Identify Namespace payload, so inconsistent values (NUSE > NCAP, NCAP > NSZE without THIN, a format index beyond NLBAF) are visible. Whether the drive really has that much usable space is not: the failure shows later as writes beyond some LBA failing or wrapping.
What happens: The reported size is larger than the media really backs (counterfeit or mis-configured drives: writes past the real capacity wrap around and overwrite earlier data), or the LBA data size in the format table is wrong, or NCAP/NSZE disagree after namespace management.
How it shows up: Silent at first. Later: data at low LBAs is overwritten by writes to high LBAs (wraparound), or LBA Out of Range errors appear below the reported size.
Spec basis: Identify Namespace NSZE, NCAP, NUSE, NSFEAT THIN, FLBAS, LBAF[]; Identify Controller TNVMCAP/UNVMCAP for totals.
Typical causes: Fake-capacity firmware; namespace-management bugs; reporting the LBA count for 512-byte format while the namespace uses 4096.
How to detect / prove: Full-capacity write with LBA-tagged data (fio --verify=crc32c headers include offset, or f3 -style tools), then full read-verify. Wraparound shows as blocks containing headers of other offsets. Cross-check blockdev --getsize64 with NSZE × LBA size.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_update_ns_info_block() computes capacity and calls set_capacity_and_notify() ; capacity is set to 0 if metadata cannot be handled ( nvme_init_integrity() false).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : full-drive tagged write and verify. Also create, resize and delete namespaces repeatedly and check the Identify values each time.

name: SMART / health counters frozen or wrong; bogus temperature
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Each Get Log Page 02h returns 512 bytes of payload over the link, so values that do not change between two captures, or that are impossible (temperature 0 K, Percentage Used decreasing), are visible. Whether a counter is right needs a reference from the same trace: Host Write Commands must rise by the number of Write SQEs you saw in between.
What happens: Counters do not update (Data Units Written stuck), update at the wrong scale, wrap, or reset at power cycle. Composite Temperature is constant, 0, or far from reality. Critical Warning bits never set even when thresholds are crossed.
How it shows up: Monitoring sees a healthy drive. Wear-out or thermal trouble is missed, or alarms fire falsely.
Spec basis: SMART / Health Information log (02h): Critical Warning, Composite Temperature (Kelvin), Available Spare, Percentage Used, Data Units Read/Written (thousands of 512-byte units, rounded up), Host Read/Write Commands, Power Cycles, Power On Hours, Unsafe Shutdowns, Media and Data Integrity Errors, Number of Error Information Log Entries. Temperature thresholds via Feature 04h.
Typical causes: Counters kept in RAM and only saved occasionally; a broken sensor; firmware that reports a fixed value. Linux has quirks NVME_QUIRK_NO_TEMP_THRESH_CHANGE and NVME_QUIRK_NO_SECONDARY_TEMP_THRESH for drives that misbehave with temperature thresholds.
How to detect / prove: Snapshot nvme smart-log , write exactly N × 512,000 bytes with O_DIRECT, snapshot again: Data Units Written must grow by N (± rounding), Host Write Commands by the number of commands sent. Compare temperature with an external thermocouple and with the hwmon value ( sensors , /sys/class/hwmon/*/temp1_input ). Power cycle and check that counters persist and Power Cycles increments.
Linux v7.2 source: hwmon.c:nvme_hwmon_get_smart_log() , hwmon.c:nvme_hwmon_read() , hwmon.c:nvme_get_temp_thresh() / nvme_set_temp_thresh() .
Test to provoke it: SAFE : counted-write test above; heat the drive with a sustained write and watch temperature and Warning Composite Temperature Time; cool it and check the reverse.

name: Firmware update reports success but the old firmware is still running
In a PEX trace: Visible Firmware Image Download (11h) chunks, Firmware Commit (10h) with its Commit Action and slot in CDW10, the CQE status (Success, or 10Bh/110h/111h "activation requires … reset"), any AER notice for firmware activation, and the Firmware Slot log (03h) and Identify Controller FR payloads afterwards are all on the wire. Comparing FR before and after the reset shows whether activation happened.
What happens: The download and commit succeed, the tool says "updated", but the running firmware revision is unchanged: the commit action only stored the image (CA = 000b), activation was deferred to a reset that did not happen (status 10Bh/110h/111h treated as success by a tool), or activation silently failed and the drive fell back to the old slot.
How it shows up: Silent if the tool ignores the status or the slot log. Linux v7.2 logs "Firmware is activated after next Controller Level Reset" when the slot log's next-active slot differs from the current one.
Spec basis: Firmware Commit (CA values: replace, replace and activate at next reset, activate at next reset, replace and activate immediately), status codes Firmware Activation Requires Conventional Reset (10Bh), Requires NVM Subsystem Reset (110h), Requires Controller Level Reset (111h), Requires Maximum Time Violation (112h), Firmware Slot Information log (AFI: active slot bits 2:0, next slot bits 6:4; FRS1–FRS7), Identify Controller FR and FRMW.
Typical causes: Tool or script not checking the CQE status or not resetting; wrong slot; image verification failing in firmware after the commit returned; a read-only slot 1.
How to detect / prove: nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0 (AFI and slot revisions) and nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -i '^fr ' before and after the activation reset; cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/firmware_rev . The running revision is FR after the reset, not what the tool printed.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_get_fw_slot_info() (reads log 03h, compares afi & 0x7 with (afi & 0x70) >> 4 , updates subsys->firmware_rev ), core.c:nvme_handle_aen_notice() ( NVME_AER_NOTICE_FW_ACT_STARTING ), core.c:nvme_fw_act_work() ; status codes NVME_SC_FW_NEEDS_* in include/linux/nvme.h .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION (vendor image required): commit with each supported CA, check status, slot log and FR before and after a controller reset, a subsystem reset and a power cycle. Also try a corrupted image: the drive must reject it, never report success and keep running old firmware silently.

name: ZNS write pointer does not match the data
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Zone Append CQEs return the assigned LBA in DW0–DW1, and Zone Management Receive (Report Zones) payloads carry each zone's state and write pointer, so a WP that disagrees with the appends you saw complete is visible. Data persisted beyond or below the WP after a power cut is not, until you read it.
What happens: The reported write pointer is ahead of the data actually persisted (reads below the WP return old or unwritten content), or behind it (data written but the WP rolled back, so the host overwrites it with the next append). Usually after a power loss or a reset in the middle of writes.
How it shows up: Silent. Zoned filesystems and applications that rebuild state from the WP (for example to find the end of a log) lose or duplicate records.
Spec basis: Zoned Namespace Command Set: zone states, write pointer, Zone Append (returns the LBA written), Zone Management Send/Receive, errors such as Zone Invalid Write (1BCh) and Zone Boundary Error (1B8h) that Linux names in include/linux/nvme.h .
Typical causes: WP updated before the data is durable; WP recovery after power loss scanning the wrong way; zone state machine bugs on Finish/Reset.
How to detect / prove: Append records with sequence numbers and checksums, cut power or reset, then nvme zns report-zones and read each zone up to and past the WP. All records below the WP must verify; none above it may be valid new data (allowed values above WP per the read rules for unwritten blocks verify in spec ).
Linux v7.2 source: zns.c:nvme_zone_parse_entry() (for zones reported FULL, Linux sets wp = start + len instead of the reported WP; non-sequential zone types fail with "invalid zone type"), zns.c:nvme_ns_report_zones() , zns.c:nvme_setup_zone_mgmt_send() .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT : append workload across many open zones with power cuts; compare WP with the last acknowledged append per zone and with the data.

name: Completion posted with the wrong CID
In a PEX trace: Visible Every SQE fetch (CplD with the CID) and every CQE MWr (DW3 CID, SQID) is captured, so an analyzer script can match them: a CQE whose CID was never submitted on that SQ, or a CID completed while its own command is still outstanding and another's is missing, is directly visible.
What happens: The controller completes command A but writes the CID of command B. If B is outstanding, the host completes B (with A's status) while B's data is not there yet, and A later times out. Buffers can be reused while the device still DMAs into them.
How it shows up: Partly reported. Linux v7.2 encodes a 4-bit generation counter in the CID upper bits (unless NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN ), so a CID with a wrong generation produces "request 0x… genctr mismatch" and "invalid id N completed on queue M". A wrong CID that happens to match another outstanding request with the right generation is silent and completes the wrong request.
Spec basis: CQE DW3 Command Identifier and DW2 SQ Identifier; CID must be unique among outstanding commands on that SQ.
Typical causes: Firmware CQE-assembly bugs under high queue depth; controllers that store only some CID bits (the reason NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN exists: "requires the command_id value be limited").
How to detect / prove: dmesg | grep -E "genctr mismatch|invalid id" . Data verification (fio verify) catches the reads that completed early. Analyzer script: build a map SQID/CID → outstanding from SQE fetches and check every CQE against it.
Linux v7.2 source: nvme.h:nvme_cid() , nvme.h:nvme_find_rq() (genctr check), nvme.h:nvme_try_complete_req() (increments genctr), pci.c:nvme_handle_cqe() ("invalid id %d completed on queue %d").
Test to provoke it: SAFE to observe: high-QD mixed fio with verify while capturing. On QEMU, a modified model that corrupts CIDs shows how Linux reacts.

name: Duplicate completion for one command
In a PEX trace: Visible Two CQE MWr TLPs with the same SQID/CID and no SQE fetch of that CID in between are directly visible in the capture.
What happens: The controller posts two CQEs for the same command, for example after an internal retry or an Abort race. If the host has already reused the tag for a new command, the second CQE completes the new command early.
How it shows up: Usually reported, not silent, on Linux v7.2: nvme_try_complete_req() increments the request's generation counter on the first completion, so the duplicate CQE (carrying the old generation in CID bits 15:12) fails the check in nvme_find_rq() , is logged as "genctr mismatch" / "invalid id … completed on queue …" and ignored. It becomes silent with NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN , or if the duplicate arrives exactly 16 reuses later, and then it can complete an unrelated new I/O early.
Spec basis: Exactly one completion per command.
Typical causes: Abort handling races, error-recovery paths, CQ-wrap bugs (phase tag not flipped, so the host re-reads an old entry as new).
How to detect / prove: dmesg genctr messages; analyzer CID-pairing script; check CQ phase-tag handling at wrap (the duplicate appears exactly at the CQ wrap point if the phase tag is wrong).
Linux v7.2 source: nvme.h:nvme_find_rq() , pci.c:nvme_cqe_pending() (phase tag check), pci.c:nvme_update_cq_head() (phase flip on wrap).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : Abort storms ( nvme_core.io_timeout lowered on a test system) under load; small CQ sizes to force frequent wrap.

name: Missing interrupt or completion hidden by timeout polling
In a PEX trace: Visible Two patterns: (a) the CQE MWr is there but no MSI-X MWr follows (missed interrupt), and about 30 s later (the I/O timeout) the host just resumes; (b) no CQE MWr at all for a fetched CID until the host sends Abort or resets. Timestamps between SQE fetch and CQE show the gap.
What happens: The device posts the CQE but the interrupt is lost (masked vector, wrong MSI-X entry, coalescing bug). After the I/O timeout, Linux polls the CQ, finds the completion and finishes the request normally. The application sees a 30-second stall but no error.
How it shows up: Only a warning: "I/O tag N (CID) QID M timeout, completion polled". No error is returned to the application, so monitoring based on I/O errors never sees it.
Spec basis: Interrupt generation for CQ entries (MSI-X table, Interrupt Vector in Create I/O CQ, interrupt coalescing Feature 08h).
Typical causes: Interrupt coalescing or aggregation firmware bugs; MSI-X table programming races; platform interrupt remapping problems. Linux quirks NVME_QUIRK_BROKEN_MSI and NVME_QUIRK_SINGLE_VECTOR exist for related device problems.
How to detect / prove: dmesg | grep "completion polled" ; latency histograms with a long tail at exactly the timeout value; /proc/interrupts counts for the NVMe vectors not increasing while I/O completes.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c:nvme_timeout() : polls the queue ("Did we miss an interrupt?") with nvme_poll() or nvme_poll_irqdisable() , then logs "completion polled" and returns BLK_EH_DONE ; otherwise aborts ("timeout, aborting") or resets.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : run with interrupt coalescing enabled at extreme settings (Feature 08h), CPU hotplug of the CPUs owning NVMe vectors, and watch for "completion polled".

name: DMA writes outside the data buffer
In a PEX trace: Visible Every device-to-host MWr carries its address and length. Comparing them with the PRP/SGL entries in the captured SQE (and PRP list CplDs) shows a write past the end of the buffer, to a page not in the list, or after the CQE. The analyzer sees it even when nothing in the host notices.
What happens: The device writes data beyond the PRP range, to a stale address from a previous command, or after it already posted the CQE (when the host may have freed the buffer). Without an IOMMU this silently corrupts unrelated kernel or application memory.
How it shows up: Without IOMMU: random crashes, corrupted unrelated data, nothing pointing at the SSD. With IOMMU (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi, Arm SMMU) in translated mode: a DMA fault message naming the device's BDF and the faulting address (wording varies by IOMMU driver, for example "DMAR: [DMA Write] … fault addr …" or "AMD-Vi: Event logged [IO_PAGE_FAULT …]"; illustrative ), and the write is blocked.
Spec basis: PRP/SGL data pointer rules (PRP entries and the transfer length NLB × LBA size); Linux also limits addresses for NVME_QUIRK_DMA_ADDRESS_BITS_48 devices.
Typical causes: Off-by-one in PRP list walking (page boundary at the end of a list page), metadata pointer misuse, firmware reusing a stale PRP after Abort, devices that cannot handle DMA addresses above 48 bits.
How to detect / prove: Boot with the IOMMU in translated (not passthrough) mode ( intel_iommu=on iommu.passthrough=0 or the AMD equivalent) and watch dmesg for faults naming the NVMe BDF. In the analyzer, check every MWr address against the command's PRPs.
Linux v7.2 source: Driver builds PRP/SGL in drivers/nvme/host/pci.c ; DMA mask reduced for NVME_QUIRK_DMA_ADDRESS_BITS_48 . IOMMU fault reporting is in the IOMMU drivers (not in the local snapshot).
Test to provoke it: SAFE with IOMMU strict mode: run fio with odd buffer alignments ( --iomem_align ), transfer sizes that end exactly at PRP-list page boundaries, and Abort under load. Any IOMMU fault is a finding.

name: DSM range list over-read: device ignores Number of Ranges
In a PEX trace: Visible The device's MRd for the range list asks for 4096 bytes (256 × 16) while the SQE's CDW10 NR is 0 (one range). The MRd length versus NR+1 is in the capture.
What happens: The controller DMA-reads the maximum range buffer instead of (NR+1) × 16 bytes. With a small host buffer this reads memory past the end, and with an IOMMU it faults and the DSM fails. Linux v7.2 hides it by always allocating a 4096-byte, zero-filled buffer, so on Linux the over-read is harmless and invisible. If the device then also processes the extra (zero) ranges, it should be harmless (NLB 0). If the buffer held stale ranges, it would deallocate the wrong LBAs (see D-06 ).
How it shows up: Silent on current Linux. Historically visible as failing trims: a 2020 Ubuntu kernel SRU ("Prevent fstrim failure so unused blocks can be discarded", Launchpad bug 1856603) restored the larger allocation after "nvme: rewrite discard support" reduced it, because discard requests failed on a non-compliant device with "FITRIM ioctl failed: Input/output error". Search results connected to that bug also mention IOMMU faults during the trim.
Spec basis: DSM CDW10 Number of Ranges (0's based); data length = (NR+1) × 16 bytes.
Typical causes: Firmware using a fixed-size DMA for the range list.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: compare range-list MRd length with NR. On an OS that allocates exactly (NR+1)×16 bytes (or with a custom passthrough that places the range list at the end of an IOMMU-mapped page), an IOMMU fault proves it.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c:nvme_setup_discard() : alloc_size = sizeof(*range) * NVME_DSM_MAX_RANGES with the comment "Some devices do not consider the DSM 'Number of Ranges' field when determining how much data to DMA"; kzalloc zero-fills it.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : nvme dsm --ad -s <slba> -b <nlb> with one range while capturing; check the MRd length.

name: Verify or Compare returns Success without checking the media
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Verify (0Ch) moves no data, so the trace shows only SQE and CQE, and the completion time is the only clue (a 1 GiB Verify finishing in microseconds every time did not read the media). Compare (05h) is visible: the device fetches the host buffer (MRd/CplD), and a Success CQE for a buffer you know differs from the media is proof.
What happens: Verify is supposed to read and check the data (and PI) without transferring it. A shortcut implementation returns Success without reading, so "scrubbing" with Verify finds nothing. Compare returning Success when the data differs (or Compare Failure, 285h, when it matches) breaks fused compare-and-write users.
How it shows up: Silent: scrubs report clean drives that later return uncorrectable errors on normal reads.
Spec basis: NVM Command Set Verify (ONCS bit 7) and Compare (ONCS bit 0); Compare Failure status 285h; Unrecovered Read Error 281h expected from Verify on bad blocks.
Typical causes: Firmware treating Verify as a no-op; Compare checking only the first block.
How to detect / prove: Use Write Uncorrectable (04h, ONCS bit 1) on a test LBA, then Verify it: it must fail (with Unrecovered Read Error or similar). For Compare: compare a buffer that differs only in the last byte of the last block. Also time Verify of a large range against a Read of the same range.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux does not issue Verify or Compare for normal block I/O; use passthrough. core.c:nvme_init_known_nvm_effects() marks Write Uncorrectable as content-changing (LBCC).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION : nvme write-uncor on an LBA, then nvme verify and nvme read on it (both must fail), then rewrite the LBA to clear it.

name: Receiver Error (RxErr) — physical-layer symbol or framing errors
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The symbol, disparity, framing or sync-header error is a physical-layer analyzer event, covered in the physical-layer part of this atlas. At protocol level you see what follows: a Nak DLLP and replayed TLPs, plus an ERR_COR Message TLP from the receiver to the Root Port. The RxErr bit itself is visible only if software reads the AER registers (CfgRd to Correctable Status at AER+10h) on the probed link. The analyzer's own receiver can disagree with the device's receiver, so treat the device counter as authoritative.
What happens: The receiver sees a bad symbol, disparity or block-encoding error, a framing error, or a lane-to-lane deskew problem. The TLP or DLLP that contained it is dropped and normally replayed.
How it shows up: Correctable Status bit 0 ( PCI_ERR_COR_RCVR ), ERR_COR to the Root Port. Linux v7.2 prints PCIe Bus Error: severity=Correctable, type=Physical Layer, (Receiver ID) and [ 0] RxErr at KERN_WARNING, rate-limited. The RxErr counter in aer_dev_correctable increments. The NVMe layer reports nothing.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, AER Correctable Error Status register, Receiver Error Status. Physical Layer receiver error rules.
Typical causes: Marginal channel: long traces, riser or cable adapters, U.2/U.3 backplanes, missing or misconfigured retimers, poor TX/RX equalization presets at Gen4/Gen5, reference-clock problems (SSC mismatch with separate clocks), contamination or wear on M.2 connectors, thermal drift.
How to detect / prove: Read counters at both ends ( cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/aer_dev_correctable ). lspci -vvv shows CESta: RxErr+ and DevSta: CorrErr+ . For per-lane detail, use the Lane Error Status register of the Secondary PCIe Extended Capability ( setpci read-only) or the platform's lane-margining tool (Gen4+ Lane Margining at the Receiver).
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c : aer_irq , aer_isr_one_error , aer_print_error , pci_dev_aer_stats_incr , pci_aer_handle_error (clears status and calls cor_error_detected if the driver has one; the NVMe driver does not).
Test to provoke it: SAFE: run the workload with the SSD in different slots, with and without an extender. CAUTION: use lane margining (time/voltage offset) to step toward the eye edge on Gen4+ platforms. EXPERT: insert a lossy channel or an attenuating fixture.

name: Bad TLP — LCRC or sequence error, TLP replayed
In a PEX trace: Visible A Nak DLLP whose AckNak_Seq_Num is one less than the failed TLP, followed by replayed TLPs that repeat the same sequence numbers. Most analyzers flag the bad LCRC directly. If ERR_COR reporting is enabled, an ERR_COR Message TLP from the receiver appears shortly after.
What happens: A TLP arrives with a bad LCRC or an unexpected sequence number. The receiver Naks it and the transmitter replays it. The NVMe command is delayed by roughly one replay round trip.
How it shows up: Correctable bit 6 ( PCI_ERR_COR_BAD_TLP ), [ 6] BadTLP , reported by Linux as Data Link Layer / Receiver ID. Counter BadTLP .
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Data Link Layer: LCRC, Sequence Number, Ack/Nak protocol; AER Bad TLP Status.
Typical causes: Same channel problems as L-01 when the error is not caught as a symbol error. Occasionally a controller bug that generates a wrong LCRC on certain payload sizes.
How to detect / prove: Counters at both ends. If BadTLP rises only during large DMA (writes to the SSD stress the RC→EP direction; reads stress EP→RC), the problem is direction-dependent: look at the transmitter on the far side.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : AER_DATA_LINK_LAYER_ERROR_MASK , aer_correctable_error_string ("BadTLP").
Test to provoke it: As L-01. An error-injecting interposer or jammer can corrupt the LCRC of chosen TLPs (EXPERT, needs lab equipment).

name: Bad DLLP — corrupted Ack/Nak/flow-control DLLP
In a PEX trace: Visible The analyzer flags a DLLP with a bad 16-bit CRC. A missing Ack can then lead to a replay on the far side with no Nak before it (see L-05). If enabled, an ERR_COR Message follows from the receiver.
What happens: A DLLP (Ack, Nak, UpdateFC, PM) fails its 16-bit CRC and is discarded. A lost Ack is harmless because later Acks are cumulative, unless the next one is also late, in which case L-05 follows. A lost UpdateFC can briefly starve the transmitter of credits.
How it shows up: Correctable bit 7 ( PCI_ERR_COR_BAD_DLLP ), [ 7] BadDLLP , Data Link Layer.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, DLLP CRC; AER Bad DLLP Status.
Typical causes: Channel quality, as L-01 and L-02. DLLPs are short, so a high BadDLLP count with little BadTLP points to burst errors.
How to detect / prove: Counters. Look for throughput dips that coincide with bursts of BadDLLP, which show credit starvation.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : string "BadDLLP", data-link classification.
Test to provoke it: As L-01 and L-02.

name: REPLAY_NUM Rollover — four replays failed, link forced into Recovery
In a PEX trace: Visible The same sequence number is replayed several times, then TS1/TS2 ordered sets appear in the middle of traffic (LTSSM Recovery). After that, traffic resumes, possibly at a different rate or width. Measure the gap between the last TLP before Recovery and the first one after it. An ERR_COR from the transmitter follows.
What happens: The same TLP has been replayed until the 2-bit REPLAY_NUM counter rolls over. The transmitter starts LTSSM Recovery to retrain the link. No new TLPs move for the length of the retrain, typically microseconds but sometimes much longer. If retraining picks a lower speed, the link stays degraded (see L-25 ).
How it shows up: Correctable bit 8 ( PCI_ERR_COR_REP_ROLL ), [ 8] Rollover , Data Link / Transmitter ID. Because the agent is the transmitter, the device that logs it is the one whose packets were not getting through. If the port supports bandwidth notification, Link Status LBMS may also be set (Linux bwctrl tracks this).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: REPLAY_NUM, Recovery entry; AER REPLAY_NUM Rollover Status.
Typical causes: Severe signal integrity problems, a receiver CDR losing lock, or a lane that stopped working.
How to detect / prove: Counter Rollover . Check LnkSta speed and width before and after. On the analyzer, look for TS1/TS2 ordered sets mid-traffic (Recovery). Repeated Rollovers are the "recovery storm" pattern of L-26 .
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : AER_AGENT_TRANSMITTER_MASK (Rollover, Timeout), string "Rollover". drivers/pci/pcie/bwctrl.c : pcie_bwnotif_irq records LBMS.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an interposer that Naks or corrupts every copy of one TLP; or margin the link until rollovers appear.

name: Replay Timer Timeout — no Ack/Nak in time
In a PEX trace: Visible TLPs go out with no Ack or Nak returning within the replay-timer window, then the transmitter replays them without any preceding Nak. Use the timestamps to compare the gap with the REPLAY_TIMER limit for that link width and payload size. Look for an ERR_COR afterwards.
What happens: The transmitter's replay timer expires before any Ack or Nak arrives for outstanding TLPs, so it replays them all. This is "timer only" at link level, but AER does report it.
How it shows up: Correctable bit 12 ( PCI_ERR_COR_REP_TIMER ), [12] Timeout , Data Link / Transmitter ID. Do not confuse it with Completion Timeout (uncorrectable bit 14, L-14 ).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: REPLAY_TIMER, its limit formula (depends on link width, max payload, and L0s exit latency); AER Replay Timer Timeout Status.
Typical causes: Lost or corrupted Acks (L-03). Receiver Ack-coalescing that is too slow. Long ASPM L0s/L1 exit latency on the receiver side so Acks leave late. A link partner stalled internally.
How to detect / prove: Counter Timeout . If it correlates with ASPM being enabled (it disappears with pcie_aspm=off as a diagnostic boot), suspect power-management exit latency (see L-37 ).
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : string "Timeout", transmitter agent mask.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: enable aggressive ASPM ( /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy set to powersupersave ) with bursty, low-QD I/O. Compare counts with ASPM off.

name: Advisory Non-Fatal Error — an uncorrectable error handled as correctable
In a PEX trace: Partly visible You see the request and its Cpl with status UR or CA (or a dropped posted request), then an ERR_COR Message instead of an ERR_NONFATAL. Whether the device classed it as advisory is visible only in its AER registers (CfgRd).
What happens: The PCIe spec allows certain uncorrectable non-fatal errors to be signalled as "advisory" when the detecting agent is not the one that has to act. A typical case is a completer that returns UR to a request and also logs the error: it signals ERR_COR instead of ERR_NONFATAL, because the requester will handle the failed completion. The uncorrectable status bit (for example UR) is still set as well.
How it shows up: Correctable bit 13 ( PCI_ERR_COR_ADV_NFAT ), [13] NonFatalErr , plus the underlying uncorrectable bit in the same device's uncorrectable status, which Linux does not print on this path. Masked by default per spec, so many systems never show it.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Advisory Non-Fatal Error cases; AER Advisory Non-Fatal Error Status and Mask.
Typical causes: Config reads of absent functions during enumeration (UR, advisory). An endpoint receiving a request it does not support, for example an MMIO read to an unimplemented register.
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv : look for CESta: AdvNonFatalErr+ together with UESta: UnsupReq+ on the same device. Read both registers with setpci (read-only).
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : string "NonFatalErr". Handled like every correctable error: cleared, no recovery.
Test to provoke it: SAFE (if unmasked): lspci scans of absent functions. CAUTION: unmasking the bit with setpci changes platform configuration.

name: Corrected Internal Error — controller fixed its own internal fault
In a PEX trace: Not visible The internal correction happens inside the device. At most an ERR_COR Message TLP appears, if the error is unmasked, and it does not say which error. To identify it, read the device's AER registers or vendor telemetry.
What happens: The function detected and corrected an internal error, for example single-bit ECC in a buffer RAM of the PCIe or NVMe front end. What counts as an internal error is up to the device.
How it shows up: Correctable bit 14 ( PCI_ERR_COR_INTERNAL ), [14] CorrIntErr . Masked by default. Linux v7.2 unmasks internal errors only for CXL devices ( pci_aer_unmask_internal_errors() , exported only to cxl_core ; its comment says internal errors are "too device-specific to enable generally").
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Corrected Internal Error Status/Mask (optional).
Typical causes: SRAM soft errors, aging, temperature. A rising rate can come before an uncorrectable internal error ( L-22 ) or an NVMe-level Persistent Internal Error event.
How to detect / prove: Unmask it in a lab with setpci (CAUTION), then watch the counter. Correlate with the NVMe SMART "Media and Data Integrity Errors" field and with vendor telemetry.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : pci_aer_unmask_internal_errors , is_aer_internal_error (CXL RAS only).
Test to provoke it: Vendor-specific error injection only.

name: Header Log Overflow — more errors than the log can hold
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The burst of erroneous transactions that filled the log is visible. The overflow itself is a register bit, readable only through a CfgRd of the AER capability.
What happens: With multiple-header recording enabled, the device's header log is full, so the next error's TLP header is lost. Diagnosis loses information exactly when errors are arriving fastest.
How it shows up: Correctable bit 15 ( PCI_ERR_COR_LOG_OVER ), [15] HeaderOF . Masked by default.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Multiple Header Recording, Header Log Overflow Status.
Typical causes: A burst of UR or CA from a misbehaving DMA engine. Software that does not clear status fast enough.
How to detect / prove: Treat it as a sign that the logged header is not necessarily representative. Look at the first error, not the last.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : string "HeaderOF".
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: error injection while multiple-header recording is enabled.

name: Undefined (bit 0) set — legacy "Training Error" bit
In a PEX trace: Not visible Nothing on the wire identifies bit 0. You might see an ERR_* Message. To identify the bit, read UESta (CfgRd).
What happens: Bit 0 of Uncorrectable Status was "Training Error" in early PCIe revisions. It is now undefined. A device that sets it is either very old or buggy.
How it shows up: [ 0] Undefined in the AER log ( PCI_ERR_UNC_UND ).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Uncorrectable Error Status bit 0 is Undefined in current revisions.
Typical causes: Legacy IP, or firmware that writes the wrong bit.
How to detect / prove: Read UESta with lspci -vvv . Report it to the vendor as a compliance issue.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : aer_uncorrectable_error_string[0] = "Undefined".

name: Data Link Protocol Error (DLP)
In a PEX trace: Visible An Ack or Nak DLLP whose AckNak_Seq_Num refers to a sequence number the transmitter never sent, or one already acknowledged. Then an ERR_FATAL Message (if the link still works) and, after Linux recovery, a link-down followed by retraining (secondary bus reset: Hot Reset TS1s).
What happens: The Data Link Layer received an Ack or Nak whose sequence number does not match any unacknowledged TLP, or another DL-protocol violation. The replay state can no longer be trusted. The default severity is Fatal.
How it shows up: [ 4] DLP , severity=Uncorrectable (Fatal), type=Data Link Layer . Linux v7.2 calls pcie_do_recovery(..., pci_channel_io_frozen, aer_root_reset) , which brings the link down and up again. The NVMe driver logs frozen state error detected, reset controller then restart after slot reset , and in-flight I/O is retried or failed.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Data Link Protocol Error, AckNak_Seq_Num checks.
Typical causes: Data Link Layer bugs in the port or SSD IP. Retimer bugs. Interaction with link power-management entry and exit.
How to detect / prove: The AER log and the counter aer_dev_fatal DLP. An analyzer capture with a trigger on "Ack/Nak sequence out of range".
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : AER_DATA_LINK_LAYER_ERROR_MASK (DLP); err.c : pcie_do_recovery ; nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_error_detected , nvme_slot_reset , nvme_error_resume .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser or interposer that injects bad AckNak_Seq_Num values. Software injection: aer-inject with CONFIG_PCIEAER_INJECT exercises the recovery path only, not the hardware.

name: Surprise Down Error (SDES)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Visible only if the probe sits on the SSD's link: traffic stops, electrical idle with no PM_Enter DLLPs and no Hot Reset or Disabled TS first, then possibly Detect and Polling. The SDES bit is set in the Downstream Port's registers. The port's ERR_FATAL travels on the upstream link, which a probe on the SSD link cannot see.
What happens: A Downstream Port (Root Port or switch DSP) that supports Surprise Down reporting sees its link go from DL_Active to DL_Inactive without being told to. To the host, the SSD has vanished. Every MMIO read returns all-ones, posted writes are dropped, and DMA in flight is lost.
How it shows up: Uncorrectable bit 5 on the Downstream Port , not on the SSD. Default severity Fatal. Linux prints [ 5] SDES as "Transaction Layer" (see 20.4). If DPC is enabled and the port is a hot-plug bridge, dpc_is_surprise_removal() treats it as an expected removal and quietly cleans up ( dpc_handle_surprise_removal() ). Otherwise DPC or AER recovery runs. The NVMe driver then sees CSTS == ~0 on its next register read or in nvme_timeout() , and logs controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff, PCI_STATUS=0xffff or PCI_STATUS read failed , followed by the hint lines about power saving ( C-01 ).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Surprise Down Error, Data Link Layer Link Active reporting, Hot-Plug surprise.
Typical causes: Physical removal. Power loss to the slot or a brown-out. An SSD firmware crash or watchdog reset that drops the link. An ASPM L1 or L1-substate exit failure (see L-37 ). Thermal shutdown. A loose M.2 or U.2 connector.
How to detect / prove: On the port: lspci -vvv -s <port> shows UESta: SDES+ and LnkSta DLActive- . On the SSD, config reads return ff . Afterwards, check the drive's nvme smart-log "unsafe shutdowns" counter: if it went up by one, the drive lost power or reset without a shutdown notification.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/dpc.c : dpc_is_surprise_removal , dpc_handle_surprise_removal , pci_clear_surpdn_errors ; nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_should_reset , nvme_warn_reset , nvme_timeout (checks pci_dev_is_disconnected ), nvme_remove (checks pci_device_is_present ).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: surprise-remove a hot-plug-capable U.2/E3.S drive in a hot-plug bay under I/O. EXPERT: cut slot power with a controllable riser or power interposer. Never do this on a non-hot-plug M.2 slot.

name: Poisoned TLP received
In a PEX trace: Visible A TLP with the EP (poisoned) bit set: usually a CplD toward the SSD carrying write data, or an MWr from the SSD carrying read data. An ERR_NONFATAL Message from the receiver follows. The CQE that follows for the affected command shows whether the controller failed it.
What happens: A TLP arrives with the EP (Error Poisoned) bit set. Its data payload is known to be bad. Most often the host memory controller found an uncorrectable ECC error while serving the SSD's DMA read of write data, and returned the CplD poisoned. The opposite case is the SSD sending poisoned read data because of an internal uncorrectable error.
How it shows up: Uncorrectable bit 12 at the receiver , default Non-fatal, with the TLP header logged. Linux prints [12] TLP and a TLP Header: line. Recovery runs with pci_channel_io_normal , and nvme_error_detected() returns CAN_RECOVER (no reset). What happens to the NVMe command is up to the controller. A well-behaved SSD fails the write with a data-transfer or internal-error status and does not commit poisoned data impl . A poor one may write it. When the host receives poisoned read data, platform RAS policy decides the outcome (machine check, data dropped, or poison propagated in memory) impl .
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Data Poisoning, EP bit, Poisoned TLP Received Status. NVMe Base Specification: generic status codes such as Data Transfer Error and Internal Error are what a controller can return. Check which one your device uses.
Typical causes: Host DRAM uncorrectable errors. Errors in the SSD's internal SRAM or DRAM on the read path. Switch internal parity errors (some switches poison rather than drop).
How to detect / prove: The AER log with the header (decode it: a CplD toward the SSD means host memory; an MWr toward the host means SSD data). Correlate with EDAC or MCE logs ( ras-mc-ctl --errors , journalctl -k | grep -i mce ). Read back the affected LBA range and check it.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : AER_LOG_TLP_MASKS includes PCI_ERR_UNC_POISON_TLP ; pci_aer_handle_error → pcie_do_recovery(..., pci_channel_io_normal, ...) ; dpc.c reports whether DPC can trigger on poisoned TLPs ("PoisonedTLP" in the capability line).
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser that sends CplD with EP=1 to the SSD's MRd, or an analyzer with injection. On servers, ACPI EINJ memory error injection into a buffer the SSD then DMA-reads (CAUTION: may cause machine checks).

name: Flow Control Protocol Error (FCP)
In a PEX trace: Visible InitFC1/InitFC2 or UpdateFC DLLPs with illegal credit values, or credit counters that jump beyond the allowed range. Then an ERR_FATAL and a link reset.
What happens: The flow-control credit protocol was violated, for example InitFC advertising illegal values or credits that overflow the counter field. Credit accounting is corrupt. The default severity is Fatal, and the link is reset.
How it shows up: [13] FCP , Fatal, frozen-channel recovery, NVMe controller reset (messages as in L-10).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Flow Control, Flow Control Protocol Error.
Typical causes: Port IP bugs. Very rare in shipping products. More likely on FPGA-based NVMe prototypes.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer capture of InitFC and UpdateFC DLLPs around link-up or the event.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : string "FCP".
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser that injects bad UpdateFC.

name: Completion Timeout — a read request was never answered
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Visible only as an absence. The analyzer shows an MRd (from the SSD for SQE, PRP or data fetch, or from the host to a register) with a given tag and no CplD with that tag within the timeout. The analyzer's 'outstanding request' or 'split transaction' view makes this easy to spot. Next comes an ERR_NONFATAL from the requester, and possibly a late CplD (L-16). If the request was dropped on another link (inside the root complex or IOMMU), the trace cannot show why.
What happens: A requester sent a non-posted request (MRd, CfgRd, ...) and no completion arrived within its Completion Timeout range. In NVMe there are two cases. (a) The SSD's DMA read of an SQE, PRP or SGL list, or write data is never answered by the host: an IOMMU silently dropping it, a root complex deadlock, or a switch problem.
