The SSD logs CmpltTO and usually ends the command with an error status, or hangs. (b) The host CPU's MMIO read of an SSD register is not answered because the controller's PCIe front end is hung. The root port logs CmpltTO, and the CPU receives all-ones (or, on some platforms, a machine check impl ).
How it shows up: Uncorrectable bit 14 on the requester , default Non-fatal, agent "Requester ID". A header is logged only if the device advertises PCI_ERR_CAP_COMP_TIME_LOG . Downstream NVMe effects: case (a) gives a CQE error or an NVMe I/O timeout ( I/O tag N (cid) opcode 0x.. (...) QID n timeout, aborting ... ). Case (b) gives CSTS=0xffffffff → controller is down; will reset .
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Completion Timeout mechanism, Device Control 2 "Completion Timeout Value" and "Completion Timeout Disable", Device Capabilities 2 "Completion Timeout Ranges Supported". The timeout value is configurable. A 50 µs–50 ms default range is commonly cited (verify in spec).
Typical causes: IOMMU faults where the platform drops the request (see L-36 ). DPC or containment upstream. Host memory power states that stall. P2P targets that never answer. A hung SSD front end.
How to detect / prove: See which device logged it: the SSD (case a) or the Root Port (case b). lspci -vvv DevCtl2 shows "Completion Timeout: 50us to 50ms" or similar, and whether it is disabled. Correlate with IOMMU fault logs and the NVMe timeout messages.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : AER_AGENT_REQUESTER_MASK (CmpltTO, UR), tlp_header_logged ; nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_timeout , nvme_warn_reset .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser acting as host memory that withholds CplD for chosen tags. CAUTION: shorten the SSD's Completion Timeout Value through Device Control 2 with setpci on a test system to make marginal latency visible.

name: Completer Abort (CA)
In a PEX trace: Visible A Cpl (no data) with Completion Status = CA (100b), matching the tag of a preceding request. The completer then sends an ERR_NONFATAL, or ERR_COR if advisory.
What happens: The completer understood the request but refused it because of an internal rule: an access violation, an unsupported access size to a register, or a device in a state where it cannot serve it. It returns a completion with status CA and logs bit 15. The requester sees an "unsuccessful completion".
How it shows up: [15] CmpltAbrt , agent "Completer ID", header logged, default Non-fatal. If the SSD aborts a host MMIO read, the CPU usually sees all-ones data. If the root complex aborts an SSD DMA read, the SSD's command fails.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Completion Status CA, Completer Abort Status.
Typical causes: Host side: MMIO accesses that cross register boundaries or use unsupported sizes (for example, 64-bit reads of registers some controllers accept only as 32-bit; Linux uses lo_hi_readq for CAP for this reason). Root complex: some platforms use CA for IOMMU-blocked requests impl .
How to detect / prove: Decode the logged header: address and requester. If the address is inside the SSD's BAR0, look at the access size and offset.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : AER_AGENT_COMPLETER_MASK ; nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_pci_reg_read64 uses lo_hi_readq .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: issue unusual-size MMIO reads to reserved BAR offsets from a test tool, on a disposable system only.

name: Unexpected Completion — completion for a request nobody is waiting for
In a PEX trace: Visible A CplD or Cpl whose Requester ID and Tag do not match any outstanding request on the link. Typically it arrives after the analyzer already shows that request as timed out. An ERR_NONFATAL or ERR_COR follows.
What happens: A completion arrives whose Requester ID and Tag do not match any outstanding request. The usual case is a completion that arrives after the requester already gave up (Completion Timeout). Another is a completion routed to the wrong function. The receiver drops it.
How it shows up: [16] UnxCmplt , header logged, default Non-fatal. Often seen right after an L-14 on the same device. Can be handled as advisory (L-06).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Unexpected Completion Status, completion matching rules.
Typical causes: A late completion from slow host memory or a switch. Tag reuse bugs, especially with 10-bit tags when one side does not support them properly. A completer returning the wrong Requester ID (for example a function-alias DMA bug; see the Marvell quirk in Chapter VI.3).
How to detect / prove: Decode the header's Tag and Requester ID. Check whether 10-Bit Tag Requester Enable is set ( lspci -vvv DevCtl2 "10BitTagReq") and whether every hop supports it.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : string "UnxCmplt"; probe.c "enabling Extended Tags" and "disabling Extended Tags" messages.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser that delays a completion past the SSD's completion timeout.

name: Receiver Overflow (RxOF)
In a PEX trace: Visible Compare the credits advertised in UpdateFC DLLPs with the headers and data sent. The analyzer's flow-control tracking flags the TLP that overran the credit limit. ERR_FATAL follows.
What happens: The receiver got more TLPs or data than the credits it advertised, so its buffer overflowed. Data is lost and credit state is broken. Default Fatal.
How it shows up: [17] RxOF , Fatal, link reset, NVMe controller reset.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Receiver Overflow, flow-control rules (optional checking).
Typical causes: Transmitter credit-accounting bugs, often after a link Recovery or power-state transition.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: compare the credits advertised with the TLPs sent.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : string "RxOF".
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser that ignores credits.

name: Malformed TLP
In a PEX trace: Visible The analyzer decodes and flags the offending TLP: a payload longer than the receiver's MPS (Length field × 4 bytes), a request crossing a 4 KB boundary, or a Length/payload mismatch. The receiver's MPS comes from a CfgWr to Device Control earlier in the capture, or from your notes. ERR_FATAL follows.
What happens: A TLP breaks format rules. Examples: payload longer than the receiver's Max_Payload_Size, Length field not matching the actual payload, a request crossing a 4 KB boundary, illegal byte enables, an undefined Type, or TC/VC mapping violations. Default Fatal.
How it shows up: [18] MalfTLP with the header logged, Fatal, frozen recovery, NVMe reset. If it repeats at every large transfer, Linux keeps resetting (a reset loop, C-06 ).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: TLP formation rules, Malformed TLP, Max_Payload_Size rules.
Typical causes: MPS mismatch is the classic case: the SSD is configured for 512 B and sends 512-byte MWr to a Root Port set to 256 B ( L-32 ). DMA engine bugs that cross 4 KB with an unaligned PRP offset. Firmware bugs in CQE or MSI-X write formation.
How to detect / prove: Decode the logged header. Compare its Length with the MPS of the receiving device ( lspci -vvv DevCtl "MaxPayload"). Check that the whole path has a consistent MPS.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : AER_LOG_TLP_MASKS includes MALF_TLP; probe.c : MPS configuration ( pcie_bus_configure_settings path; messages "Max Payload Size set to ...", "can't set Max Payload Size to ...").
Test to provoke it: CAUTION/EXPERT: on a test system, set the Root Port's MPS lower than the SSD's with setpci , then run large reads. This deliberately creates a fatal error, so use a disposable system with no valuable data.

name: ECRC Error — end-to-end CRC mismatch
In a PEX trace: Visible A TLP with TD=1 whose digest the analyzer's own ECRC check also finds wrong. Corruption inside a switch shows up only on the egress link, so probe both sides of the switch to localise it. Without ECRC (TD=0) the same corruption is invisible as an error.
What happens: When ECRC generation and checking are enabled, the receiver found the 32-bit end-to-end CRC (TLP Digest) wrong. LCRC protects each hop, but a TLP can be corrupted inside a switch or retimer buffer between hops. ECRC catches that.
How it shows up: [19] ECRC with the header, default Non-fatal. Without ECRC enabled, the same corruption is silent : the switch regenerates a valid LCRC around corrupted data.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: ECRC, TLP Digest (TD bit), AER ECRC Generation/Check Capable/Enable.
Typical causes: Switch or retimer internal memory errors.
How to detect / prove: Check whether ECRC is on at all. lspci -vvv AERCap shows "GenCap+ CGenEn- ChkCap+ ChkEn-". Linux v7.2 has an ecrc= boot policy, "bios" (default), "off" or "on" ( ecrc_policy_str ; pcie_set_ecrc_checking ), passed as pci=ecrc=on .
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : enable_ecrc_checking , disable_ecrc_checking , pcie_set_ecrc_checking , pcie_ecrc_get_policy .
Test to provoke it: SAFE to enable ( pci=ecrc=on ) on a test system. EXPERT: inject digest errors with an exerciser.

name: Unsupported Request (UR)
In a PEX trace: Visible For non-posted requests: a Cpl with Completion Status UR (001b). For posted requests (the SSD's MWr of data or a CQE to an unmapped address): the MWr is visible, but its rejection happens inside the root complex, so only the root's ERR message on another link, or the missing host reaction, shows it. Check the MWr address against the PRPs and queue bases earlier in the trace.
What happens: The completer does not support the request at all: an address no BAR or window claims, a disabled Memory Space Enable, a message type it does not know, or a config request to a function that does not exist. Non-posted requests get a Cpl with UR status. Posted ones (DMA writes, doorbells) are dropped.
How it shows up: [20] UnsupReq , agent "Requester ID", header logged, default Non-fatal. The kernel documentation example is exactly this line: severity=Uncorrectable (Fatal), type=Transaction Layer, (Requester ID) ... [20] UnsupReq (First) , on a platform where severity was set to fatal. NVMe consequences: an SSD DMA write of read data or a CQE to an unmapped host address is dropped, and the command "completes" from the SSD's view while the host never sees the CQE, so it times out. A doorbell write while Memory Space is disabled is dropped silently.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Unsupported Request, completion status UR, address decoding.
Typical causes: DMA to a stale or unmapped IOVA when the IOMMU is in a mode that returns UR impl . PRP entries pointing at garbage (a host driver bug or a corrupted PRP list). MMIO after the BAR was moved or disabled by hot-plug or reset. Enumeration probing absent functions (expected, normally masked or advisory).
How to detect / prove: Decode the header address. Look for a matching IOMMU fault ( L-36 ). Check lspci -vvv Control: "Mem+ BusMaster+" on the SSD.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : AER_AGENT_REQUESTER_MASK ; Documentation/PCI/pcieaer-howto.rst example output.
Test to provoke it: SAFE-ish: setpci read of a non-existent function (normally masked). EXPERT: a deliberately wrong PRP in a user-space NVMe test driver (SPDK/vfio) with the IOMMU on. The IOMMU should block it, which proves the protection works.

name: ACS Violation
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Visible if the probe is on the link where the P2P TLP enters the switch: the TLP goes in and never comes out on the peer's link. The violation is detected inside the switch and logged in its registers. Its ERR_NONFATAL goes upstream.
What happens: A switch Downstream Port or root port with Access Control Services (ACS) enabled blocked a TLP that violated its policy. Typically this is peer-to-peer traffic (SSD → GPU or NIC BAR) that ACS Source Validation, P2P Request Redirect or Egress Control forbids, or a TLP with a spoofed Requester ID. See also the configuration-level card L-33 .
How it shows up: [21] ACSViol with the header, logged at the port, default Non-fatal. The P2P DMA fails, and the NVMe command using a P2P buffer times out or returns an error.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Access Control Services, ACS Violation Status.
Typical causes: P2PDMA (NVMe CMB as a target, GPUDirect Storage) through a switch with ACS redirect enabled for IOMMU isolation. VFs using the wrong Requester ID.
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv ACSCtl on each port. Linux logs Configured ACS to %#06x ( pci_std_enable_acs path), and the pci=config_acs= parameter changes it.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pci.c : pci_enable_acs , pci_acs_enabled , pci_acs_path_enabled , messages "Invalid ACS flags specified", "Configured ACS to %#06x".
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: attempt P2PDMA between two devices under one switch with ACS P2P redirect on.

name: Uncorrectable Internal Error
In a PEX trace: Not visible The fault is internal to the device. At most an ERR_FATAL Message appears, and only if unmasked. Afterwards the device may stop responding (MRd with no completion). Use the AER registers, CSTS.CFS and vendor telemetry.
What happens: The function detected an internal error it could not correct: a parity or ECC error in internal SRAM or an internal bus fault inside the PCIe or NVMe front end. Default Fatal, but masked by default , so most systems never see it as AER. The NVMe controller may instead set CSTS.CFS ( C-01 ) or post a Persistent Internal Error asynchronous event ( C-11 ).
How it shows up: If unmasked: [22] UncorrIntErr , Fatal recovery. If masked: nothing in AER. Look at the NVMe-level symptoms.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Uncorrectable Internal Error Status/Mask/Severity (optional).
Typical causes: SRAM soft errors, silicon defects, overheating.
How to detect / prove: Check UEMsk in lspci -vvv . For a lab, unmask and watch (CAUTION). Correlate with NVMe telemetry and the error log.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : pci_aer_unmask_internal_errors (CXL only), string "UncorrIntErr".
Test to provoke it: Vendor-specific injection only.

name: Egress-blocked family: MC Blocked, AtomicOp Egress Blocked, TLP Prefix Blocked, Poisoned TLP Egress Blocked, DMWr Request Egress Blocked, TLP Translation Egress Blocked
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The originating TLP (AtomicOp, prefixed TLP, poisoned TLP, DMWr) is visible on the ingress link. The blocking happens inside the port. On the requester's link, you then see a UR/CA completion or no completion.
What happens: A port refused to forward a TLP out of an egress port because the next hop cannot accept that TLP type, or because policy says to block it. Bit 23 is a multicast TLP blocked. Bit 24 is an AtomicOp toward a port without AtomicOp routing or support. Bit 25 is an End-End TLP Prefix (such as PASID in some forms) toward a port that does not support prefixes. Bit 26 is a poisoned TLP blocked by policy. Bit 27 is a Deferrable Memory Write blocked. Bit 31 is translation-related egress blocking.
How it shows up: Bits 23–27 and 31, all in AER_LOG_TLP_MASKS (header logged). Linux strings: "BlockedTLP", "AtomicOpBlocked", "TLPBlockedErr", "PoisonTLPBlocked", "DMWrReqBlocked", "TLPXlatBlocked". The originator's request fails, usually as a Completion Timeout or UR from its point of view.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: AtomicOp routing/egress blocking, End-End TLP Prefix rules, Poisoned TLP Egress Blocking, Deferrable Memory Write. Default severity and mask values for bits 26, 27 and 31: verify in spec uncertain .
Typical causes: Rare for plain NVMe I/O. Possible with PASID or SVA-capable NVMe controllers, computational storage using AtomicOps toward host memory, and poisoned-TLP containment policies on server root ports.
How to detect / prove: Decode the logged header (prefix present? Fmt/Type = AtomicOp?). Check DevCap2 AtomicOpsCap and AtomicOp routing on each port, and End-End TLP Prefix support.
Linux v7.2 source: pci_regs.h : PCI_ERR_UNC_MCBTLP , _ATOMEG , _TLPPRE , _POISON_BLK , _DMWR_BLK , _XLAT_BLK ; aer.c : strings and AER_LOG_TLP_MASKS .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser sending AtomicOps or prefixed TLPs through a port without support.

name: IDE family: IDE Check Failed, Misrouted IDE TLP, PCRC Check Failed
In a PEX trace: Partly visible IDE TLPs are visible with their IDE prefix and stream ID, but their payload is encrypted. Integrity failures can be decoded only if the analyzer has the keys. Otherwise you see only the error message or the device stopping DMA.
What happens: With PCIe Integrity and Data Encryption (IDE) active, used for confidential computing and TDISP-style device assignment, a received TLP failed its integrity (MAC) check (bit 28), arrived on the wrong IDE stream or port (bit 29), or failed the optional plaintext CRC (PCRC) check (bit 30). IDE treats integrity failure as a security event. The spec defines how the IDE stream is affected (for example, the stream is torn down and must be re-keyed) uncertain — verify in spec.
How it shows up: "IDECheck", "MisIDETLP", "PCRC_CHECK", with the header logged. The NVMe device's DMA stops working until the stream is re-established.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: IDE (introduced in 6.0-era ECNs). Severity defaults: verify in spec.
Typical causes: Key-programming mismatches, stream ID misconfiguration, real tampering, or (more likely) firmware bugs in early IDE implementations.
How to detect / prove: The AER log plus the platform security or TSM logs. IDE-capable analyzers need the keys to decode traffic.
Linux v7.2 source: pci_regs.h : PCI_ERR_UNC_IDE_CHECK , _MISR_IDE , _PCRC_CHECK ; aer.c strings.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: program mismatched keys on a test setup.

name: Link trained at lower speed or narrower width than capable
In a PEX trace: Visible The training sequence shows it: TS1/TS2 ordered sets advertise data rates and link/lane numbers, lanes that do not respond are marked PAD, and a failed speed change appears as Recovery.Speed reverting. In L0, the analyzer's link-status display shows the negotiated width and rate. The capture must include link-up, or a retrain, for the reason to be visible.
What happens: The LTSSM settled on a lower data rate (for example 8 GT/s instead of 16 GT/s) or fewer lanes (x2 instead of x4). Everything works and nothing is logged as an error, but sequential bandwidth is capped. A Gen4 x4 link carries roughly 7–7.5 GB/s of payload, while Gen3 x2 manages under 2 GB/s.
How it shows up: No AER bit and no NVMe status. Linux v7.2 prints an informational line once at enumeration , from pcie_report_downtraining() → __pcie_print_link_status(dev, false) , only when available bandwidth is less than capable: "%u.%03u Gb/s available PCIe bandwidth, limited by %s x%d link at %s (capable of %u.%03u Gb/s with %s x%d link)" . The at %s part names the limiting device, which may be an upstream switch port or Root Port and not the SSD. A downgrade after boot (retraining at runtime) does not print this line. bwctrl updates the cached speed in sysfs when the port supports Link Bandwidth Notification.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Link Capabilities (Max Link Speed, Maximum Link Width), Link Status (Current Link Speed, Negotiated Link Width), Link Control 2 (Target Link Speed), LTSSM Configuration and Recovery (speed change, equalization).
Typical causes: Width: a damaged lane or connector pin; M.2 slots wired x2 on the board; bifurcation set wrong in BIOS; a riser that carries only some lanes. Speed: equalization failure at Gen3+ that falls back to a lower rate; BIOS "Link Speed" set to GenN; a retimer or redriver not rated for the rate; a slot sharing lanes through a slower switch; Linux or firmware lowered Target Link Speed (a thermal cooling device through bwctrl, or the 2.5 GT/s retrain quirk, L-39).
How to detect / prove: Compare LnkCap with LnkSta at each hop under load. dmesg | grep 'limited by' . Prove the performance impact with fio sequential read at high queue depth (bandwidth close to the lower link's ceiling). Re-seat the drive or swap slots. Check LnkCtl2 Target Link Speed. Check BIOS settings.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pci.c : __pcie_print_link_status , pcie_print_link_status (verbose variant, exported for drivers), pcie_bandwidth_available , pcie_bandwidth_capable ; drivers/pci/probe.c : pcie_report_downtraining (only for Endpoints, Legacy Endpoints and Upstream Ports, function 0, not VFs); drivers/pci/pcie/bwctrl.c : pcie_bwnotif_irq , pcie_set_target_speed .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: limit speed in BIOS, then confirm the log line appears and fio bandwidth drops. CAUTION: write LnkCtl2 Target Link Speed with setpci on the Root Port and set Retrain Link. This changes the live link and may drop it.

name: Link flapping / recovery storm — only correctable errors, endless retraining
In a PEX trace: Visible Repeated TS1/TS2 bursts (Recovery) between TLPs, usually after Naks or replays. Count Recovery entries per second and correlate them with gaps in NVMe traffic. The underlying physical-layer errors are covered in the physical-layer part of this atlas.
What happens: The link keeps entering LTSSM Recovery: after Replay Rollover, after receiver errors, or after an electrical-idle glitch. Each retrain stalls all traffic for microseconds to milliseconds. Data is never lost, so no uncorrectable error appears. The only symptoms are correctable counts (RxErr, BadTLP, BadDLLP, Rollover, Timeout), periodic latency spikes, and sometimes a speed or width that changes over time.
How it shows up: Rate-limited severity=Correctable lines (10 per 5 s per device by default, so the log hides the true rate; the aer_dev_correctable counters show it). LnkSta LBMS (Link Bandwidth Management Status) set by hardware when it changes speed or width "to correct unreliable link operation". Linux bwctrl records it ( PCI_LINK_LBMS_SEEN ). The NVMe layer shows no errors, only p99.9 latency spikes and lower throughput.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Recovery state, Link Bandwidth Management Status / Link Autonomous Bandwidth Status, Link Bandwidth Management Interrupt Enable.
Typical causes: Marginal signal integrity near the eye limit (temperature dependent). Spread-spectrum clocking mismatch. Failing retimers. ASPM exit problems (L-37).
How to detect / prove: Sample aer_dev_correctable on both ends every second and plot the deltas. Sample LnkSta. Run fio --percentile_list=99:99.9:99.99 latency. A storm shows as all queues stalling together. An analyzer with a trigger on TS1 ordered sets in L0 shows each Recovery entry.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : aer_ratelimit , pci_dev_aer_stats_incr ; bwctrl.c : pcie_bwnotif_irq , pcie_reset_lbms ; Documentation/PCI/pcieaer-howto.rst "AER Ratelimits".
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: thermal cycling of the riser or SSD under load. EXPERT: lane-margining at an offset that produces occasional errors.

name: Surprise link down without Surprise Down reporting
In a PEX trace: Partly visible On the SSD link: abrupt electrical idle with no PM or Hot Reset first. The host's later requests appear on the Root Port side, but the Root Port drops them once the link is down, so they are not on this link. The 30-second NVMe timeout and the CSTS read returning all-ones are host-side, and visible only if the probe is upstream.
What happens: The link drops (DL_Active goes to 0), but the Downstream Port does not support Surprise Down error reporting, or the error is masked, or there is no hot-plug or DPC service on that port. Nothing is signalled. The host finds out the next time it touches the device: MMIO reads return all-ones (after a Completion Timeout at the Root Port, if that is logged), doorbell writes vanish, and every outstanding NVMe command waits for its timer.
How it shows up: Up to io_timeout (30 s default in Linux v7.2) or admin_timeout (60 s) later: nvme_timeout() reads CSTS = 0xffffffff , nvme_should_reset() decides it must reset (CFS bit appears set in all-ones), and the driver logs controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff, PCI_STATUS=0xffff plus Does your device have a faulty power saving mode enabled? and Try "nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off" and report a bug . The reset then fails ( nvme_pci_enable sees CSTS == -1), and Disabling device after reset failure: -19 follows ( C-17 ).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Data Link Layer Link Active Reporting Capable, Surprise Down Error Reporting Capable (both optional); a read to a non-responding device ends in a Completion Timeout at the requester.
Typical causes: SSD firmware hang or crash that takes down the PHY. Power-state exit failures (APST, L1.2). Power delivery dips. Connector problems.
How to detect / prove: Read the port's LnkSta ( DLActive- ) and LnkCap ("Surprise-" / "DLActive-" capability flags). Cross-check the time of the first NVMe timeout with the kernel timestamps of earlier traffic. An analyzer left armed on electrical idle catches the moment.
Linux v7.2 source: nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_timeout , nvme_should_reset , nvme_warn_reset , nvme_pci_enable , nvme_reset_work ; core.c : admin_timeout , nvme_io_timeout .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: cut SSD power with an interposer on a slot without Surprise Down reporting; or force a firmware crash with a vendor debug command.

name: DPC containment event — the port cut the link on purpose
In a PEX trace: Partly visible On the SSD link: the port forces the link down (electrical idle, no TLPs), then after software clears DPC a fresh Detect, Polling, Configuration, L0 and the re-enumeration CfgRd/CfgWr sequence. The trigger reason is in the port's DPC registers. If the trigger was an ERR_FATAL from the SSD, that message is visible just before the link goes down.
What happens: A Downstream Port with Downstream Port Containment (DPC) enabled saw an uncorrectable error. Linux v7.2 configures DPC to trigger only on ERR_FATAL, as the dpc_handler comment says. The port immediately disables its link, so no possibly-corrupt TLPs travel further upstream, and it interrupts the OS. Every request to the SSD fails until software clears the trigger and the link retrains.
How it shows up: dpc_process_error() logs one of: containment event, status:%#06x: unmasked uncorrectable error detected (the port's own error, followed by the AER details); containment event, status:%#06x, ERR_FATAL received from DDDD:BB:DD.F (an error message from the SSD); or containment event, status:%#06x: RP PIO error detected / software trigger detected . With RP extensions, RP PIO details follow, for example [18] Memory Request Completion Timeout . Then pcie_do_recovery(pdev, pci_channel_io_frozen, dpc_reset_link) : the NVMe driver logs frozen state error detected, reset controller then restart after slot reset . If the link does not come back: Data Link Layer Link Active not cleared in 1000 msec , root port still busy , or device recovery failed .
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Downstream Port Containment, DPC Status Trigger Reason, RP PIO extensions.
Typical causes: Any fatal error from the SSD (L-10, L-13, L-17, L-18, L-11). Completion Timeouts of host MMIO reads when RP PIO is enabled. Software trigger by firmware (EDR).
How to detect / prove: dmesg | grep -E 'DPC|containment' . lspci -vvv -s <port> shows the DPC capability and DpcSta. On probe, Linux prints enabled with IRQ and an error containment capabilities: Int Msg #%d, RPExt%c PoisonedTLP%c SwTrigger%c RP PIO Log %d, DL_ActiveErr%c line, which tells you what is enabled.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/dpc.c : dpc_irq , dpc_handler , dpc_process_error , dpc_process_rp_pio_error , dpc_reset_link , dpc_wait_rp_inactive , pci_dpc_recovered ; err.c : pcie_do_recovery .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: software trigger via DPC Control (setpci) on a test port. EXPERT: inject a fatal error with an exerciser. The effect is a full SSD reset, and data in flight is lost.

name: Hot-plug removal under I/O (surprise or orderly)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible For orderly removal: the CC write with SHN set, CSTS polling, then the link going down. For surprise removal: only the abrupt end of traffic. Presence-detect and slot events are sideband signals, not TLPs.
What happens: The SSD is removed or powered off in a hot-plug slot. In an orderly removal (attention button or echo 0 > /sys/bus/pci/slots/N/power ) the OS unbinds the driver first. In a surprise removal the device is already gone when the driver is told. The PCI core marks it disconnected, and pending I/O must fail rather than hang.
How it shows up: The hot-plug driver (pciehp, not in the local source tree used here) logs slot link-down and presence-change events uncertain wording. Linux v7.2 NVMe: nvme_remove() sets the state to DELETING and, if !pci_device_is_present() , sets DEAD and calls nvme_dev_disable(dev, true) at once, so outstanding requests are cancelled and namespaces are marked dead ( nvme_mark_namespaces_dead → blk_mark_disk_dead ). Filesystems see I/O errors. In nvme_timeout() , if pci_dev_is_disconnected() is true, the controller goes straight to DELETING and is disabled. The source comment says this unblocks a deadlock between error recovery and removal.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Hot-Plug (Presence Detect, Data Link Layer State Changed, Attention Button); NVMe transport behaviour is up to the host.
Typical causes: Operator removal, drive failure that triggers presence-detect change, backplane faults.
How to detect / prove: dmesg around removal; lspci no longer lists the BDF; /sys/block/nvme* disappears. Check that no task is left in D state ( ps -eo stat,pid,cmd | grep '^D' ), which would mean an I/O path hang.
Linux v7.2 source: nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_remove , nvme_timeout , nvme_dev_disable , nvme_pci_ctrl_is_dead ; core.c : nvme_mark_namespaces_dead , nvme_remove_namespaces .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: orderly hot-remove through sysfs slot power with fio running on a scratch namespace, then check for hung tasks. EXPERT: physical surprise removal in a certified hot-plug bay.

name: Configuration RRS (CRS) loop — device answers "retry" forever
In a PEX trace: Visible CfgRd0 to the Vendor ID register answered with a Cpl with Completion Status RRS (Configuration Request Retry Status), repeated with growing gaps (Linux doubles its delay). If the device never returns Successful Completion within the timeout, the loop is the evidence.
What happens: After reset or power-up, a function may return Configuration Request Retry Status (RRS, formerly CRS) completions while it initializes. If its firmware never finishes booting, it keeps answering RRS. Enumeration or post-reset restore waits and then gives up. The device is missing from lspci , or present but unusable.
How it shows up: With Configuration RRS Software Visibility enabled on the Root Port (Linux enables it if supported: PCI_EXP_RTCAP_RRS_SV → PCI_EXP_RTCTL_RRS_SVE ), a Vendor ID read returns a special value, which Linux recognises with pci_bus_rrs_vendor_id() . During enumeration, pci_bus_wait_rrs() doubles its delay each time and logs pci DDDD:BB:DD.F: not ready after %dms; waiting once past 1000 ms, then ready after %dms or not ready after %dms; giving up . After resets, pci_dev_wait() logs not ready %dms after %s; waiting / giving up (the timeout for reset waits is PCIE_RESET_READY_POLL_MS = 60000 ms). Past PCI_RESET_WAIT (1000 ms) it tries one link retrain through pcie_failed_link_retrain() . Without RRS visibility, the hardware retries silently and eventually returns all-ones.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Configuration Request Retry Status, Configuration RRS Software Visibility, the rule that a device must be ready for configuration requests after reset within the specified time (with Readiness Notifications as an optional speed-up).
Typical causes: SSD firmware stuck in its boot ROM (corrupt firmware image, failed update). Very slow boot after unsafe shutdown with a large mapping-table rebuild. Power sequencing problems.
How to detect / prove: dmesg | grep -E 'not ready|ready after' . A long "ready after" (several seconds) on every boot is a latent problem even when it works. Time the SSD's boot after power-on with an analyzer: count the RRS completions.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/probe.c : pci_bus_wait_rrs , RRS SV enable around line 1304; drivers/pci/pci.c : pci_dev_wait , PCI_RESET_WAIT , PCIE_RESET_READY_POLL_MS ; quirks.c : pcie_failed_link_retrain .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser as endpoint that answers RRS for N seconds; or a vendor command that holds the SSD in its boot loader.

name: BAR not assigned / resource conflict — driver cannot map registers
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The enumeration CfgWr sequence to BAR0/BAR1 and the readback show the sizing and the assigned address. Later MMIO TLPs are either missing or go to an address outside the SSD's BAR. The OS's decision not to assign the BAR is host-side.
What happens: The SSD's BAR0 (registers and doorbells) has no address assigned, or has one that conflicts with another device or lies outside the upstream bridge window. The NVMe driver's probe fails, or MMIO goes to the wrong place.
How it shows up: Enumeration messages from probe.c such as %s: can't handle BAR larger than 4GB , %s: can't handle BAR above 4GB , initial BAR value %#010llx invalid , device has non-compliant BARs; disabling IO/MEM decoding , or devices behind bridge are unusable because %pR cannot be assigned for them . Resource-assignment failure messages come from setup-res.c, which is not in the local tree, so treat their wording as uncertain . NVMe probe then fails in nvme_dev_map() / pci_request_mem_regions or reads all-ones; nvme_pci_enable logs reading CSTS register failed at debug level only, and probe ends with probe failed ( dev_err_probe ).
Spec basis: PCI/PCIe configuration space: BARs, bridge memory windows. NVMe: BAR0/BAR1 hold the controller registers (the 64-bit MLBAR/MUBAR pair).
Typical causes: Too little 32-bit MMIO space with many devices. BIOS not reserving hot-plug windows. Thunderbolt or USB4 enclosures. SR-IOV VF BARs exhausting space. "Above 4G decoding" disabled.
How to detect / prove: lspci -vv -s <BDF> showing "Region 0: Memory at <unassigned>" or "[disabled]"; cat /proc/iomem ; dmesg | grep -i 'BAR\|bridge window' . Try pci=realloc as a diagnostic boot option.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/probe.c : BAR sizing messages (lines ~264–320), "devices behind bridge are unusable..." ; nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_dev_map , nvme_remap_bar , nvme_pci_enable .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: boot with many devices and BIOS "above 4G decoding" off, then inspect. CAUTION: hot-plug into a slot whose bridge window is too small.

name: Link never reaches DL_Active — training fails or oscillates between speeds
In a PEX trace: Visible Repeated TS1/TS2 ordered sets alternating between data rates, the link never reaching L0 or dropping back to Recovery straight away, and no DLLPs or TLPs ever exchanged. A Linux retrain at 2.5 GT/s appears as a new training sequence advertising only 2.5 GT/s.
What happens: Training never completes. The LTSSM cycles between Detect, Polling, Configuration and Recovery, or keeps switching speed. The pcie_failed_link_retrain() comment in quirks.c describes a real case (ASMedia ASM2824 switches) where the link "continues switching between the two speeds indefinitely and the data link layer never reaches the active state, with link training reported repeatedly active ~84% of the time". The SSD never appears.
How it shows up: The SSD is not enumerated. Linux v7.2 may log broken device, retraining non-functional downstream link at 2.5GT/s , then removing 2.5GT/s downstream link speed restriction on success or retraining failed on failure. Also Data Link Layer Link Active not set in %d msec from pci_bridge_wait_for_secondary_bus() in pci.c (after pcie_wait_for_link_delay() fails).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: LTSSM, Data Link Layer Link Active, Link Bandwidth Management Status, Target Link Speed.
Typical causes: Speed-negotiation interoperability bugs. Bad equalization. A broken lane 0. Missing reference clock. PERST# timing.
How to detect / prove: Port LnkSta shows Link Training set or toggling, DLActive-, and LBMS+. The quirk uses exactly this: DLLLA clear plus LBMS seen. Try forcing 2.5 GT/s Target Link Speed to see whether the link comes up.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/quirks.c : pcie_failed_link_retrain ; bwctrl.c : pcie_set_target_speed ; pci.c : pci_dev_wait .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser that refuses speed change, or a degraded channel at the target rate.

name: MPS / MRRS mismatch along the path
In a PEX trace: Visible The CfgWr to Device Control during enumeration shows the MPS and MRRS values programmed on each device whose link you probe. A TLP whose payload exceeds the receiver's MPS is flagged as malformed. MRd sizes show the effective MRRS.
What happens: Max_Payload_Size (MPS) must not exceed what each receiver on the path accepts. If the SSD's MPS is larger than the Root Port's or a switch's, its large MWr (read data to host) are Malformed at the receiver ( L-18 ), which is fatal by default. Max_Read_Request_Size (MRRS) mismatches are legal but can hurt performance (too small) or fairness (too large). Some devices mishandle certain MRRS values, as the comment in pcie_write_mrrs() says: "issues with setting MRRS to 0 on a number of devices".
How it shows up: Fatal MalfTLP during the first large read, then a reset loop. Or, with consistent but small MPS/MRRS, a quiet bandwidth deficit (Degraded). Linux v7.2 messages: Max Payload Size set to %d (was %d, max %d) , Upstream bridge's Max Payload Size set to %d ... , Max Payload Size %d, but upstream %s set to %d; if necessary, use "pci=pcie_bus_safe" and report a bug (with pci=pcie_bus_tune_off ), can't set Max Payload Size to %d ... , Failed attempting to set the MPS , Failed attempting to set the MRRS , MRRS was unable to be configured with a safe value. If problems are experienced, try running with pci=pcie_bus_safe , and in non-default modes Max Payload Size set to %4d/%4d (was %4d), Max Read Rq %4d .
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Device Capabilities Max_Payload_Size Supported, Device Control Max_Payload_Size and Max_Read_Request_Size, the rule that TLP payloads must not exceed the receiver's MPS.
Typical causes: Hot-plugged SSDs under a port configured for a different MPS. Firmware that programs the root ports differently from Linux's policy. P2P ( pci=pcie_bus_peer2peer forces 128 B). Settings changed by user tools with setpci .
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv | grep -E 'MaxPayload|MaxReadReq' on every device on the path. Each DevCtl line lists "MaxPayload N bytes, MaxReadReq M bytes". Each must be ≤ its partner's capability, and the payload size must be consistent across the path. Boot-option tests: pci=pcie_bus_safe , pcie_bus_perf , pcie_bus_tune_off , pcie_bus_peer2peer .
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/probe.c : pci_configure_mps , pcie_write_mps , pcie_write_mrrs , pcie_bus_configure_set , pcie_bus_configure_settings ; drivers/pci/pci.c : pcie_bus_config and parsing of pcie_bus_* . Quirk: fixup_mpss_256 in quirks.c (limits MPSS to 256 for listed devices, including an ASMedia 0x0612 storage controller).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION/EXPERT: set mismatched MPS with setpci on a test machine and run a large read. Expect MalfTLP and a fatal reset.

name: ACS misconfiguration — P2P blocked, redirected, or isolation silently missing
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Too strict: P2P TLPs travelling up to the root port and back down (visible only if both links are probed). Too loose: P2P TLPs turning around inside the switch, which an upstream probe cannot see at all. ACS settings appear only as CfgWr to the ACS Control register.
What happens: ACS has two failure directions. Too strict: P2P traffic (SSD ↔ GPU or NIC) is redirected upstream to the root complex, where it may be refused (UR or ACS Violation) or just run slowly through the IOMMU. Too loose: a switch without ACS lets an SSD DMA straight into a peer's BAR, bypassing the IOMMU. Isolation is broken with no error anywhere. A misprogrammed PRP that points at a peer BAR then corrupts that device silently.
How it shows up: Too strict: L-21 ACSViol, or P2P performance far below expectation. Too loose: nothing, apart from IOMMU groups that contain several devices ( /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/*/devices ).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: ACS Source Validation, Translation Blocking, P2P Request Redirect, P2P Completion Redirect, Upstream Forwarding, P2P Egress Control, Direct Translated P2P.
Typical causes: Switches without an ACS capability. Firmware ACS settings that differ from what the OS expects. The pci=config_acs= override. VFIO setups.
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv : ACSCap and ACSCtl on every downstream port. Linux logs Configured ACS to %#06x when it applies an override. Check IOMMU group membership.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pci.c : pci_request_acs , pci_std_enable_acs , pci_enable_acs , pci_acs_enabled , pci_acs_path_enabled , pci_acs_init .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: inventory ACS capabilities and IOMMU groups. CAUTION: P2PDMA tests with ACS on and off.

name: ATS / PRI errors — translated-address or page-request failures
In a PEX trace: Visible Translation Requests (MRd with AT=01b), Translated requests (AT=10b), Invalidate Request and Invalidate Completion messages, Page Request messages and PRG Responses are all TLPs. A missing Invalidate Completion or PRG Response is visible as an absence with timestamps. A stale translation is visible only by comparing addresses against the earlier invalidation.
What happens: With Address Translation Services (ATS) the device caches IOVA→physical translations (in its ATC) and sends "translated" requests that the IOMMU does not check again. Failure modes: a stale ATC entry after the host unmapped and invalidated, where the device misses or acknowledges the invalidation too late, so DMA goes to freed memory ( silent corruption ). An Invalidate Completion that never arrives, so the IOMMU invalidation times out. With Page Request Interface (PRI), a page request that is never answered or that fails, so DMA waits forever.
How it shows up: Invalidation timeouts and page-request failures are reported by the IOMMU driver (Intel VT-d / AMD-Vi / Arm SMMU), not by AER. Exact message wording is uncertain here because those drivers are not in the local source tree. Stale-ATC DMA is silent . Most NVMe SSDs do not implement ATS or PRI, so this matters mainly for SVA/PASID-capable or computational storage devices impl .
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: ATS (Translation Request/Completion, Invalidate Request/Completion), PRI (Page Request Message, PRG Response), PASID.
Typical causes: ATC invalidation bugs in device firmware. Invalidation queues saturated in the IOMMU. Page-request group bookkeeping bugs.
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv : ATSCap/ATSCtl "Enable+", PRI capability, PASID capability. IOMMU fault logs. For stale-translation corruption: a read-back verify test (fio verify=crc32c ) during heavy map/unmap churn (for example with the IOMMU in strict mode, iommu.strict=1 ).
Linux v7.2 source: ATS/PRI core ( drivers/pci/ats.c ) and IOMMU drivers are not in the local tree. Not verified here.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser that delays Invalidate Completions; IOMMU stress with frequent unmaps during DMA.

name: MSI / MSI-X misconfiguration — lost or misrouted interrupts
In a PEX trace: Visible A CQE MWr to the CQ base address, then the expected MSI-X MWr (on x86 to the 0xFEExxxxx range) with the data value from the MSI-X table that the host programmed (CfgWr or MWr to the table BAR). The bug is a missing interrupt MWr after a CQE, or one with the wrong address or data. Whether the CPU acted on it is host-side.
What happens: The SSD posts a CQE, then sends its interrupt as an MWr to the MSI or MSI-X address. If the vector is masked, has the wrong address or data, is blocked by interrupt remapping, or is never sent (a device bug), the CPU never runs the completion handler. The CQE sits in host memory, already written.
How it shows up: After io_timeout , Linux v7.2's nvme_timeout() first polls the CQ ("Did we miss an interrupt?" in the source). If the request was in fact completed, it logs I/O tag %d (%04x) QID %d timeout, completion polled and finishes the request with no reset. A single occurrence means a lost interrupt. Many mean systematic interrupt failure. Other signs: /proc/interrupts counts for the nvme0qN vectors that stay flat while I/O is issued; the MSI core's arch assigned 64-bit MSI address %#llx above device MSI address mask %#llx .
Spec basis: PCI/PCIe: MSI and MSI-X capability, MSI-X Table and Pending Bit Array, Function Mask, per-vector Mask. NVMe: the INTMS/INTMC registers mask pin-based and single-message MSI only (not MSI-X). The Create I/O CQ "IV" field selects the vector.
Typical causes: Devices whose MSI (not MSI-X) does not work at all. Linux has NVME_QUIRK_BROKEN_MSI for two SanDisk models (Chapter VI.3). Controllers that require all queues on vector 0 ( NVME_QUIRK_SINGLE_VECTOR , Apple). Interrupt-remapping table errors. CPU hot-unplug with affinity mistakes. A device that sends the MWr before its CQE write is visible (an ordering bug), so the handler finds nothing and the next interrupt never comes. Coalescing settings too aggressive (Set Features Interrupt Coalescing).
How to detect / prove: Search dmesg for "completion polled". Compare /proc/interrupts deltas with I/O counts. lspci -vvv "MSI-X: Enable+ Count=N Masked-". Boot with nvme.use_threaded_interrupts=1 or use poll queues ( nvme.poll_queues=N , with io_uring hipri) to see whether the problem disappears when interrupts are bypassed.
Linux v7.2 source: nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_timeout (poll then "completion polled"), nvme_irq , nvme_irq_check , nvme_poll_irqdisable , nvme_setup_irqs (BROKEN_MSI clears PCI_IRQ_MSI ; SINGLE_VECTOR uses one vector), nvme_pci_enable ; drivers/pci/msi/msi.c : msi_verify_entries .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: mask an MSI-X vector through the table (with a debug tool) while I/O runs; expect "completion polled" after the timeout. SAFE: run with nvme.io_timeout lowered on a test box to shorten the experiment.

name: IOMMU / DMAR fault — SSD DMA to an address the host did not map
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The SSD's MRd or MWr to the faulting address is visible. Check its address against the PRP entries and queue bases seen earlier in the trace. The IOMMU's decision and its fault log are inside the root complex. A blocked read shows up as a UR/CA Cpl or no Cpl. A blocked write is indistinguishable from a successful one.
What happens: The SSD issues DMA (SQ fetch, PRP-list fetch, data read or write, CQE write, or the MSI address when not remapped) to an IOVA that has no valid mapping or no permission. The IOMMU blocks it. Blocked reads complete with an error (UR or CA, or a timeout at the device). Blocked writes are dropped. The NVMe command fails, or more often its CQE is lost and the host times out.
How it shows up: An IOMMU fault message naming the device's Requester ID and the faulting address. On Intel the message is commonly of the form DMAR: [DMA Read/Write] Request device [bb:dd.f] ... fault addr 0x... [fault reason 0xNN] ... , on AMD AMD-Vi: Event logged [IO_PAGE_FAULT device=... address=...] . These IOMMU driver strings were not verified against the local tree uncertain . The QEMU NVMe model shows what a careful device does when its own SQ or CQ DMA fails: nvme_process_sq() and nvme_post_cqes() trace pci_nvme_err_addr_read / _write and pci_nvme_err_cfs , then set CSTS to NVME_CSTS_FAILED . Real SSDs may instead set CFS, log an error, or carry on impl .
Spec basis: Platform IOMMU specifications (VT-d, AMD IOMMU, SMMU). NVMe: CSTS.CFS is the controller's way to say it can no longer operate. PCIe: completion statuses UR and CA.
Typical causes: Host driver bugs: use-after-unmap, wrong PRP list length, PRP offsets crossing into unmapped pages. Controller bugs: prefetching past the end of a PRP list, reading SQ entries beyond the queue size, DMA after a reset was requested (stale queue addresses). A device using the wrong Requester ID (see the DMA alias quirks in Chapter VI.3). NVME_QUIRK_DMA_ADDRESS_BITS_48 : controllers that cannot DMA above 48 bits; Linux limits their DMA mask.
How to detect / prove: dmesg | grep -iE 'DMAR|AMD-Vi|iommu|smmu' . Match the fault address to an NVMe structure: run the nvme_setup_cmd tracepoint ( /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/ ) and look for the same IOVA in PRP1/PRP2. Rebooting with iommu=pt or the IOMMU off as a diagnostic can show whether faults turn into silent corruption, so verify the data.
Linux v7.2 source: nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_pci_alloc_dev sets dma_set_mask_and_coherent to 48 or 64 bits; drivers/pci/quirks.c : quirk_dma_func1_alias and related alias quirks; __pci_dev_specific_reset logs failed to stop IOMMU for a PCI reset: %d . QEMU: hw/nvme/ctrl.c nvme_process_sq , nvme_post_cqes .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: a user-space NVMe driver (vfio-based) that submits a command with a PRP pointing outside its mapped buffer. The IOMMU must fault, and the SSD's response (CFS, error status, or hang) is the result of the test.

name: ASPM-related link drop or stall (L0s / L1 / L1 substates)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible PM_Active_State_Request_L1 and PM DLLPs, electrical idle, and the exit TS1s are visible if the analyzer handles electrical idle correctly. L1 substate entry depends on the sideband CLKREQ# signal, which a protocol probe does not capture. Use an extra logic probe for it.
What happens: When idle, the link goes into L0s, L1 or L1.1/L1.2. On the next transaction it must wake up. If exit latency exceeds what the endpoint tolerates, or the exit fails (CLKREQ# handshake, reference clock not restored, a PHY bug), the link either stalls (replay timeouts, Recovery) or goes down entirely. Often this happens only after minutes or hours of idle, which makes it look random.
How it shows up: Mild cases: correctable Replay Timer Timeout and Receiver Errors after idle periods. Severe cases: SSD drops off, and the first I/O after idle times out with CSTS=0xffffffff and the driver hint Try "nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off" and report a bug . NVMe APST (controller power states) often combines with ASPM, and the quirk table (Chapter VI.3) has many "drops off the PCIe bus" entries for APST. Linux ASPM messages: ASPM: current common clock configuration is inconsistent, reconfiguring , ASPM: Could not configure common clock , ASPM: Link Capabilities L0s/L1 treated as unsupported to avoid device defect (from pcie_aspm_remove_cap() via quirks), can't disable ASPM; OS doesn't have ASPM control .
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: ASPM L0s/L1, L1 PM Substates (L1.1, L1.2), LTR, exit latencies in Link Capabilities and Device Capabilities (acceptable latencies), Common Clock Configuration.
Typical causes: Platform firmware advertising L1.2 without proper CLKREQ# routing. Wrong T_POWER_ON or LTR values (Linux logs Invalid T_PwrOn scale ). Device PHY bugs. Missing LTR restore after resume ( no suspend buffer for LTR; ASPM issues possible after resume ).
How to detect / prove: Diagnostic boots: pcie_aspm=off , or set /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy to performance . Per-link control is under /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/link/ (for example l1_2_aspm ; availability varies) version . lspci -vvv : LnkCtl "ASPM L1 Enabled", L1SubCtl1. An idle-then-burst test loop: sleep N seconds, issue a 4 KiB read, measure latency, raise N.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aspm.c : pcie_aspm_remove_cap , common-clock configuration, policy parameter; quirks.c : quirk_disable_aspm_l0s , quirk_disable_aspm_l0s_l1 (including ASMedia 0x1080); nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_warn_reset .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: idle-burst loop with ASPM policy powersupersave versus performance , counting timeouts. CAUTION: run for hours; a drop may need a power cycle to recover.

name: Poisoned data accepted and committed — poison "handled" by writing it
In a PEX trace: Visible A CplD with EP=1 answering the SSD's MRd for write data, then a successful CQE for the same Write command (match the CID). This is the proof. Whether the bad data reached NAND is not visible, so a read-back is still needed.
What happens: The SSD receives a poisoned CplD carrying write data ( L-12 ). AER logs it at the SSD, but the controller's data path ignores the poison, writes the bad data to NAND and completes the Write with success. Later reads return the corrupt data with good status.
How it shows up: One AER Poisoned TLP line (non-fatal, no reset, and possibly rate-limited). NVMe CQE status Success. Nothing else.
Spec basis: PCIe says a receiver of a poisoned TLP must not use the data as if it were good (Data Poisoning rules). How an NVMe controller then fails the command is implementation-defined impl .
Typical causes: Firmware that does not propagate the poison indication from the PCIe core to the command engine.
How to detect / prove: Inject a poisoned completion for a known write (exerciser), then read back the LBA and check that either the write failed or the data is intact. Correlate field AER poison events with later application checksum errors.
Linux v7.2 source: aer.c : pcie_do_recovery(..., pci_channel_io_normal, ...) for non-fatal; nvme_error_detected returns CAN_RECOVER, so the NVMe layer does nothing.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: exerciser or analyzer injection of EP on the CplD path; destructive to the target LBAs.

name: Tag and ordering capability mismatch: Extended/10-bit tags, Relaxed Ordering errata
In a PEX trace: Visible TLP headers carry the Tag field (count the distinct outstanding MRd tags and check the 10-bit tag bits) and the RO attribute bit. The CfgWr to Device Control and Device Control 2 shows what was enabled.
What happens: Two related failures. (1) Tags: a requester using 8-bit (Extended) or 10-bit tags toward a completer or root that mishandles them gives wrong-tag completions (Unexpected Completion, Completion Timeout). Disabling them limits outstanding reads, so SSD read bandwidth drops at high queue depth. (2) Relaxed Ordering: some root complexes have errata with Relaxed Ordering (RO) TLPs. Linux disables RO for listed root ports and prints Disable Relaxed Ordering Attributes to avoid PCIe Completion erratum (the quirks.c comment cites a Flow Control credit issue on Broadwell/Haswell Xeon root complexes causing "performance problems").
How it shows up: probe.c messages enabling Extended Tags / disabling Extended Tags , Relaxed Ordering disabled because the Root Port didn't support it . Otherwise only lower bandwidth.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification: Extended Tag Field Enable, 10-Bit Tag Requester/Completer, Relaxed Ordering attribute, Enable Relaxed Ordering in Device Control.
Typical causes: Root complex errata; host-bridge flags ( no_ext_tags ); devices with limited completion buffers.
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv DevCtl "ExtTag+ RlxdOrd+", DevCtl2 "10BitTagReq+". Compare fio random-read bandwidth at QD128 with and without those settings.
Linux v7.2 source: probe.c : pci_configure_extended_tags , Relaxed Ordering configuration; quirks.c : quirk_relaxedordering_disable .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: measure; CAUTION: toggle with setpci on a test system.

name: Controller Fatal Status (CSTS.CFS) — controller declares itself failed
In a PEX trace: Visible The CplD for an MRd to BAR0+1Ch carries data with bit 1 set (for example 0x00000003), usually after a period with no CQE MWr from the controller. The CC write that follows (EN=0) and the recovery are visible too. Why the controller failed is internal and not visible.
What happens: The controller hit an error it cannot recover from by itself and set CFS. Outstanding commands will not complete. The host must reset it (CC.EN 1→0, or something stronger).
How it shows up: Linux v7.2 reads CSTS in nvme_timeout() . nvme_should_reset() returns true when CFS is set (or NSSRO on an NSSR-capable controller) and the controller is not already RESETTING or CONNECTING. nvme_warn_reset() logs controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0x%x, PCI_STATUS=0x%hx . If CSTS reads ~0 , that means the device is gone rather than CFS, and two more lines follow: Does your device have a faulty power saving mode enabled? and Try "nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off" and report a bug . The driver then disables the controller and schedules a reset. CFS is noticed only when a command times out. Linux v7.2 does not poll CSTS periodically for PCIe controllers.
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: CSTS.CFS, controller reset, "Controller Fatal Status" handling (host should reset the controller).
Typical causes: Firmware assert or watchdog. DMA failure on queue memory (the QEMU model sets NVME_CSTS_FAILED when it cannot read an SQE or write a CQE: nvme_process_sq , nvme_post_cqes ). Invalid CC values at enable (QEMU fails nvme_start_ctrl on misaligned ASQ/ACQ, unsupported CSS, page size out of range, or zero queue entry sizes, and sets CFS). Internal uncorrectable errors (L-22).
How to detect / prove: dmesg | grep 'controller is down' (the CSTS value is in the message: 0x3 = RDY+CFS, 0xffffffff = gone). nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 (read-only register dump). After recovery, collect nvme error-log , the persistent event log, and vendor telemetry ( nvme telemetry-log ) before any further reset overwrites them.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_timeout , nvme_should_reset , nvme_warn_reset , nvme_pci_ctrl_is_dead (CFS or !RDY ⇒ dead, so nvme_dev_disable skips deleting queues on the device); QEMU hw/nvme/ctrl.c : nvme_start_ctrl failure paths ( trace_pci_nvme_err_startfail_* ).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: on QEMU, enable the controller with a misaligned ASQ from a user-space test driver; the model sets CFS. EXPERT: vendor fault-injection commands on real SSDs.

name: CSTS.RDY never sets after CC.EN=1
In a PEX trace: Visible An MWr to BAR0+14h with EN=1, then a series of CSTS MRd/CplD pairs every 1–2 ms that all return RDY=0, lasting until about CAP.TO×500 ms (or the CRTO-derived value). After that the host stops polling. The timestamps prove the timeout.
What happens: The host enabled the controller, but it never reports ready within the advertised time. The admin queue cannot be used.
How it shows up: nvme_enable_ctrl() → nvme_wait_ready(ctrl, NVME_CSTS_RDY, NVME_CSTS_RDY, (timeout + 1) / 2, "initialisation") logs Device not ready; aborting initialisation, CSTS=0x%x and returns -ENODEV. Note the unit conversion: the wait is in seconds, and CAP.TO is in 500 ms units. If CAP.CRMS indicates CRTO support, the driver reads CRTO and uses the larger of CRTO.CRWMT and CAP.TO. When CRTO is smaller, it logs bad crto:%x cap:%llx once (C-13). The reset then fails with Disabling device after reset failure: -19 .
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: CAP.TO ("worst-case time that host software should wait for CSTS.RDY to transition"), CRTO and CC.CRIME (Controller Ready Independent of Media Enable), controller initialization sequence.
Typical causes: Firmware boot slower than CAP.TO after an unsafe shutdown (mapping-table rebuild). Media not ready. Note that Linux v7.2 always clears CC.CRIME ( ctrl->ctrl_config &= ~NVME_CC_CRIME , with the comment that the driver cannot yet handle "Admin Command Media Not Ready"), so the controller must wait for media before setting RDY. Invalid CC field values; the controller may instead set CFS (C-01).
How to detect / prove: The dmesg line gives the final CSTS. Compare the elapsed time with CAP.TO ( nvme show-regs : "cap" field, TO bits 31:24). Repeat cold-boot and warm-reset tests, and especially after an unsafe power loss.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/core.c : nvme_enable_ctrl , nvme_wait_ready ; quirk NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_BEFORE_CHK_RDY (C-27).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: power-cut during heavy writes (unsafe shutdown), then time the next enable. Repeat 100+ times and plot time-to-RDY against CAP.TO.

name: CSTS.RDY never clears after CC.EN=0 (controller reset hangs)
In a PEX trace: Visible An MWr to CC with EN=0, then repeated CSTS reads with RDY=1 for the whole timeout. In Linux v7.2 that is followed by an FLR: a CfgWr to Device Control with the Initiate FLR bit set, the link quiet period, config-space restore CfgWrs, then a second CC EN=0 write and polling.
What happens: The host asked for a controller reset and the controller never acknowledged it by clearing RDY. Its internal state is stuck.
How it shows up: nvme_disable_ctrl(ctrl, false) → nvme_wait_ready(..., NVME_CSTS_RDY, 0, (CAP.TO + 1)/2, "reset") logs Device not ready; aborting reset, CSTS=0x%x . In nvme_pci_configure_admin_queue() , Linux v7.2 then escalates: the source comment says "The NVMe Controller Reset method did not get an expected CSTS.RDY transition... Use the lower level and bigger hammer PCIe Function Level Reset". It calls pcie_reset_flr() , restores state, retries the disable, and on success logs controller reset completed after pcie flr .
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: controller reset via CC.EN, CAP.TO. PCIe: Function Level Reset.
Typical causes: Firmware stuck on an outstanding internal operation (a long command that cannot be aborted, background media work). A controller left enabled by firmware or a previous OS (kexec, boot loader). Linux deliberately does not send a shutdown notification in that case, for fear the device "may cause the device to complete commands to the admin queue ... and we don't know what memory that might be pointing at!"
How to detect / prove: dmesg: "aborting reset" followed by "controller reset completed after pcie flr" means CC reset is broken and FLR works around it. Report it to the vendor even though the system recovered.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_disable_ctrl , nvme_wait_ready ; pci.c : nvme_pci_configure_admin_queue ; drivers/pci/quirks.c : nvme_disable_and_flr (generic NVMe pre-FLR disable used for Samsung 0xa804, logging Timeout waiting for NVMe ready status to clear after disable ).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: issue a long-running admin command (for example a sanitize or self-test, where allowed) and immediately reset the controller ( nvme reset /dev/nvme0 ) on a test drive; measure the time for RDY to clear.

name: Shutdown never completes (SHST never reaches 10b)
In a PEX trace: Visible An MWr to CC with SHN=01b, then CSTS reads returning SHST=01b (processing) or 00b for the whole timeout, then the host giving up: on power-off, the link goes down or power is cut while SHST≠10b. Whether the controller flushed its cache is not visible.
What happens: The host notified the controller of shutdown, and the controller did not report completion in time. The host powers off anyway. Volatile write cache contents or FTL metadata may not be saved, which can cause data loss or a long recovery on the next boot.
How it shows up: nvme_disable_ctrl(ctrl, true) → nvme_wait_ready(ctrl, NVME_CSTS_SHST_MASK, NVME_CSTS_SHST_CMPLT, ctrl->shutdown_timeout, "shutdown") logs Device not ready; aborting shutdown, CSTS=0x%x . shutdown_timeout is a module parameter (default 5 s in Linux v7.2: nvme_core.shutdown_timeout ). If the controller reports RTD3 Entry Latency (RTD3E, Identify Controller), Linux uses it clamped between shutdown_timeout and 60 s, and logs D3 entry latency set to %u seconds when that differs from the parameter. A controller that under-reports RTD3E gets only the default 5 s. On the next boot, SMART "Unsafe Shutdowns" goes up by one.
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: CC.SHN, CSTS.SHST, RTD3E, Unsafe Shutdowns in the SMART / Health Information log.
Typical causes: Large volatile caches that take longer than the host waits. Firmware that ignores SHN while busy. Host timeout lower than RTD3E.
How to detect / prove: Compare nvme smart-log unsafe_shutdowns before and after a clean reboot: it must not increase. Check nvme id-ctrl rtd3e against the effective host timeout. A data-integrity test: write with a known pattern, Flush, clean reboot, read back.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_disable_ctrl , nvme_wait_ready , shutdown_timeout ; pci.c : nvme_shutdown → nvme_disable_prepare_reset(dev, true) , nvme_dev_disable .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: 500 reboot cycles while writing, checking unsafe_shutdowns each time. CAUTION: lower nvme_core.shutdown_timeout to 1 on a test system to expose slow shutdowns.

name: NVM Subsystem Reset (NSSR) side effects — link drop and lost state
In a PEX trace: Visible An MWr to BAR0+20h with data 0x4E564D65 ("NVMe"), then the link going down (electrical idle) and retraining, because an NVM subsystem reset resets the PCIe port too. The host's CSTS MRd right after it gets no completion, or all-ones. After re-link, a CSTS read shows NSSRO=1.
What happens: Writing "NVMe" to the NSSR register resets the entire NVM subsystem, including the PCIe link of every controller in it. Every in-flight command on every controller (all ports of a dual-port drive) is lost. The host sees what looks like a surprise link down (L-11 or L-27). After recovery, CSTS.NSSRO=1 tells the host what happened.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2 nvme_pci_subsystem_reset() moves the controller to RESETTING, writes NVME_SUBSYS_RESET to NVME_REG_NSSR , moves it through CONNECTING to LIVE, and then reads CSTS on purpose "to flush the previous write and trigger a pcie read error". Recovery comes from AER, DPC or the timeout path: nvme_should_reset() treats NSSRO as "loss of adapter communication". At init, nvme_pci_configure_admin_queue() clears a stale NSSRO (write-1-to-clear). Expect AER Surprise Down or DPC containment on the port, and "controller is down; will reset".
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: NSSR register (offset 20h), CAP.NSSRS, CSTS.NSSRO, NVM Subsystem Reset scope.
Typical causes: Deliberate test actions ( nvme subsystem-reset ). Firmware activation methods that need a subsystem reset. Unexpected NSSR from another host on a shared dual-port subsystem.
How to detect / prove: After the event, nvme show-regs shows NSSRO=1 (if not yet cleared). The QEMU model does not implement it: writing the magic value only traces pci_nvme_ub_mmiowr_ssreset_unsupported , and W1C of NSSRO traces ..._ssreset_w1c_unsupported . Do not validate NSSR handling on QEMU.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_pci_subsystem_reset , nvme_should_reset , nvme_pci_configure_admin_queue ; nvme.h : nvme_reset_subsystem (requires ctrl->subsystem , which is set only if VS ≥ 1.1 and CAP.NSSRS).
Test to provoke it: EXPERT / destructive to in-flight I/O: nvme subsystem-reset /dev/nvme0 on a test system under load, while capturing the link and the AER/DPC logs.

name: Controller reset loop
In a PEX trace: Visible A repeating macro-pattern: CC EN=0 → RDY=0 polls → AQA/ASQ/ACQ writes → CC EN=1 → RDY=1 → Identify, Set Features (Number of Queues), Create CQ/SQ commands → I/O → (timeout gap) → CC EN=0 again. The analyzer's NVMe-over-PCIe decode makes each cycle easy to spot, and the last command before each reset is the suspect.
What happens: Every reset succeeds, but the same trigger hits again soon after: a command that always times out, a fatal AER on the first large transfer (MPS mismatch), or an APST transition that drops the device. The system spends its time resetting, and the I/O that keeps failing after retries reaches applications as errors.
How it shows up: Repeated I/O tag ... timeout, reset controller or controller is down; will reset lines. The controller's reset counter ( nr_reset , incremented in nvme_change_ctrl_state() on each transition to RESETTING) keeps rising. Linux has no generic "give up after N resets" for PCIe impl ; per-request retries are limited by nvme_core.max_retries . The loop ends only when a reset itself fails (C-17).
Spec basis: Host behaviour; not defined by the NVMe spec.
Typical causes: A poisoned command that is retried after each reset (same LBA, same opcode). Fatal PCIe errors on a specific transfer pattern (L-18). Power-state bugs (C-07). Firmware asserts on a specific command.
How to detect / prove: Count resets per hour from dmesg. The NVMe tracepoints ( nvme:nvme_setup_cmd , nvme:nvme_complete_rq ) show the last command before each timeout. Find whether the same opcode and LBA appear every time.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_change_ctrl_state ( atomic_long_inc(&ctrl->nr_reset) ), nvme_reset_ctrl , max_retries ; pci.c : nvme_timeout , nvme_reset_work .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: replay the suspected command in a loop with nvme io-passthru on a scratch namespace.

name: Controller stuck in a low-power state / drops off the bus after APST or D3
In a PEX trace: Partly visible APST is configured with a Set Features (FID 0Ch) admin command whose table is a DMA'd payload, which is visible. Autonomous transitions are internal and invisible. A failed wake shows as the next doorbell MWr followed by no SQE-fetch MRd from the device, or as the link never leaving electrical idle (L-37). For D3hot, the CfgWr to PMCSR is visible.
What happens: The controller enters a non-operational power state (APST or host-requested) or the function goes to D3, and does not come back correctly. It either answers nothing (link down, CSTS all-ones) or wakes with lost state. The quirk table (Chapter VI.3) records this as the most common shipping-device bug class: NVME_QUIRK_NO_DEEPEST_PS (10 PCI IDs, plus DMI-matched Samsung cases) and NVME_QUIRK_NO_APST (core quirks for a Toshiba and a Kioxia model, plus DMI-matched cases), with comments such as "seem to drop off the PCIe bus randomly when APST is on and uses the deepest sleep state", and the Kioxia CD6 entry "times out and aborts I/O during any load, but more easily reproducible with discards".
How it shows up: An I/O timeout after an idle period, then controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff and the power-saving hint lines. Configuration messages: NPSS is invalid; not using APST , failed to set APST feature (%d) , forcibly allowing APST due to nvme_core.force_apst -- use at your own risk .
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: Power State Descriptors (ENLAT, EXLAT, NOPS), Autonomous Power State Transition feature (FID 0Ch), Power Management feature (FID 02h), Non-Operational Power States.
Typical causes: Firmware wake-up bugs. Interaction with platform L1.2 or CLKREQ#. Exit latency longer than advertised.
How to detect / prove: Diagnostic boot with nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 (disables APST). nvme get-feature -f 0x0c -H /dev/nvme0 shows the APST table. nvme id-ctrl -H shows the power-state descriptors. Idle/burst loop tests with increasing idle time.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_configure_apst (APST table construction; honours NVME_QUIRK_NO_DEEPEST_PS ), default_ps_max_latency_us , force_apst , apst_primary_timeout_ms and related parameters, core_quirks[] ; pci.c : check_vendor_combination_bug , nvme_suspend , nvme_set_power_state .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: idle soak (hours) with default APST, then a single read; repeat with APST off. CAUTION: suspend/resume cycling (s2idle) 500 times.

name: Admin queue hang — admin command never completes
In a PEX trace: Visible An MWr to the SQ0 tail doorbell (BAR0+1000h), then the controller's MRd fetching the 64-byte admin SQE (visible with its opcode and CID), and then no CQE MWr to the admin CQ for that CID within the timeout. If the controller never even fetches the SQE, the hang is in its front end.
What happens: An admin command (Identify, Get Log Page, Format, Sanitize, Firmware Commit, Set Features) never completes. Linux does not abort admin commands. A timeout on QID 0 goes straight to a controller reset.
How it shows up: After admin_timeout (60 s default, nvme_core.admin_timeout ): I/O tag %d (%04x) opcode %#x (%s) QID 0 timeout, reset controller . The nvme_timeout() branch is if (!nvmeq->qid || (iod->flags & IOD_ABORTED)) . The submitting tool (nvme-cli) gets an error such as EINTR or ENODEV after the reset cancels it.
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: admin queue; some admin commands have long, implementation-defined durations (Format NVM, Sanitize runs in the background with its own log, Device Self-test).
Typical causes: Long Format NVM with a user timeout shorter than its duration (nvme-cli's --timeout ). Firmware deadlocks between admin and I/O paths. Get Log Page of large telemetry. Identify CNS values the controller mishandles: Linux's NVME_QUIRK_IDENTIFY_CNS for QEMU's old model and an Apple controller means "doesn't handle Identify value others than 0 or 1 correctly".
How to detect / prove: Read the opcode from the dmesg line (the %s part is nvme_opcode_str() ). Re-issue it alone with a long timeout to separate "slow" from "hung".
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_timeout ; core.c : admin_timeout , nvme_alloc_admin_tag_set ( set->timeout = NVME_ADMIN_TIMEOUT ).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: nvme format with a deliberately short --timeout on a large scratch drive (destroys data on the namespace).

name: Invalid Doorbell async event — host wrote a bad doorbell
In a PEX trace: Visible The bad doorbell MWr is visible: offset 1000h + (2y or 2y+1)×(4<<DSTRD) for a queue that was never created, or a value ≥ the queue size from its Create command. If an Async Event Request is outstanding, a CQE MWr on the admin CQ for that AER CID follows, with DW0 type 0 (Error) and info 0 (Invalid Doorbell Register) or 1 (Invalid Doorbell Write Value).
What happens: The host (driver bug, or a user-space driver) writes a doorbell for a non-existent queue or a value beyond the queue size. The controller ignores the write and, if an AER command is outstanding, posts an Error-type asynchronous event. Some controllers then also need a reset.
How it shows up: The AEN. Linux v7.2 nvme_complete_async_event() stores the result in ctrl->aen_result for Error-type events and re-arms. It sends a uevent (through nvme_aen_uevent , carrying NVME_AEN=%#08x ) rather than logging a kernel message, so check udevadm monitor --kernel . QEMU's model posts NVME_AER_INFO_ERR_INVALID_DB_REGISTER / _VALUE with log page Error Information and traces pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_cq , ..._invalid_cqhead , ..._invalid_sq , ..._invalid_sqtail .
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: Asynchronous Event Information for Error Status (Invalid Doorbell Register, Invalid Doorbell Write Value), doorbell register rules. The QEMU source quotes NVMe 1.3d section 4.1 on this behaviour.
Typical causes: Host bugs in custom or user-space drivers (SPDK-style, test tools). Using the wrong CAP.DSTRD stride. Writing a doorbell after the queue was deleted. Shadow-doorbell (DBBUF) mismatches.
How to detect / prove: nvme error-log (error information entries, if the device logs them). udev events. The trace (above) is the definitive proof.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_complete_async_event , nvme_aer_type , nvme_aer_subtype ; QEMU hw/nvme/ctrl.c : doorbell write handling (around the NVME_AER_INFO_ERR_INVALID_DB_* sites).
Test to provoke it: SAFE on QEMU / CAUTION on hardware: from a user-space driver, write the SQ tail doorbell of QID 99 with an AER outstanding. Verify the event and that the controller keeps working.

name: Keep-alive loss (fabrics / KATO-enabled controllers)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible For a PCIe controller that uses KATO, the Keep Alive admin commands (opcode 18h) and their CQEs are visible with timestamps, so gaps longer than KATO are provable. For NVMe over Fabrics the keep-alive travels on the network, not on PCIe, so it is not in a PEX trace.
What happens: The Keep Alive Timer expires on the controller because the host did not send a Keep Alive in time (or, with Traffic Based Keep Alive, no traffic was seen). The controller then treats the host as gone, which on fabrics means tearing down the association. On the host side, a keep-alive command that fails or times out leads to a reset.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2: long keepalive RTT (%u ms) when a keep-alive took longer than its period; failed nvme_keep_alive_end_io error=%d ; keep-alive failed: %ld (allocation failure, followed by nvme_reset_ctrl() ); keep alive interval updated from %u ms to %u ms . For fabrics, KATO is mandatory ( keep-alive support is mandatory for fabrics ). PCIe controllers usually run with KATO=0, so keep-alive is not started ( nvme_start_keep_alive returns early when kato == 0 ).
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: Keep Alive Timer feature (FID 0Fh), Keep Alive command, Traffic Based Keep Alive (CTRATT.TBKAS).
Typical causes: Host CPU stalls (softlockups), admin-queue saturation, network partitions (fabrics), controllers that count time differently.
How to detect / prove: nvme get-feature -f 0x0f /dev/nvmeX ; dmesg strings above; on fabrics, a network capture.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_keep_alive_work , nvme_keep_alive_end_io , nvme_start_keep_alive , nvme_stop_keep_alive , nvme_update_keep_alive .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION (fabrics): block traffic with a firewall rule for longer than KATO and watch the reconnect.

name: Persistent Internal Error async event
In a PEX trace: Visible A CQE MWr on the admin CQ completing the outstanding Async Event Request with DW0 type 0 (Error), info 03h. Then, from Linux, a controller reset sequence (CC EN=0 ...) without any timeout gap in between. The internal fault itself is not visible.
What happens: The controller reports a persistent internal error, one that will not go away without intervention.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2 handles this subtype specially in nvme_complete_async_event() : for NVME_AER_ERROR_PERSIST_INT_ERR it calls nvme_handle_aer_persistent_error() , which logs resetting controller due to persistent internal error and calls nvme_reset_ctrl() (without re-arming the AER; the reset does that).
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: Asynchronous Event Type Error Status, Persistent Internal Error (03h); QEMU defines the same value ( NVME_AER_INFO_ERR_PERS_INTERNAL_ERR = 3 ).
Typical causes: Internal memory errors, firmware faults, media controller failures.
How to detect / prove: dmesg; nvme error-log ; SMART critical warnings; telemetry captured immediately.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_complete_async_event , nvme_handle_aer_persistent_error .
Test to provoke it: Vendor-specific injection; on QEMU it would require modifying the model.

name: Firmware activation never finishes (CSTS.PP stays set)
In a PEX trace: Visible The Firmware Commit admin command, the AEN CQE (Notice, Firmware Activation Starting), then Linux polling CSTS every 100 ms with PP=1 in the CplD data. If PP never clears within MTFA×100 ms (or admin_timeout when MTFA=0), the host stops polling and a controller reset sequence follows.
What happens: On activation without reset, the controller pauses command processing (CSTS.PP=1) while it switches firmware. If it never resumes within its advertised Maximum Time for Firmware Activation (MTFA), the host must reset it.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2 nvme_handle_aen_notice() on NVME_AER_NOTICE_FW_ACT_STARTING moves the controller to RESETTING ("(ab)using the RESETTING state to prevent subsequent recovery actions from interfering") and runs nvme_fw_act_work() . That quiesces I/O and polls nvme_ctrl_pp_status() . On timeout it logs Fw activation timeout, reset controller . Related: Firmware is activated after next Controller Level Reset (from the firmware slot log handling) and Get FW SLOT INFO log error .
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: Firmware Commit actions, CSTS.PP, MTFA in Identify Controller, Firmware Activation Notices.
Typical causes: Firmware images whose activation exceeds MTFA. MTFA reported as 0 or too small.
How to detect / prove: Compare measured PP=1 time with nvme id-ctrl mtfa. Check that I/O resumes without a reset.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_handle_aen_notice , nvme_fw_act_work , nvme_get_fw_slot_info .
