Test to provoke it: CAUTION/EXPERT: firmware download and commit with action "activate immediately" on a test drive, under I/O, while capturing the trace. Risk of bricking with an incorrect image.

name: CRTO smaller than CAP.TO — inconsistent ready-timeout advertisement
In a PEX trace: Visible The MRd of CAP (64-bit, read as two 32-bit reads) and of CRTO (BAR0+68h) and their CplD data show the inconsistent values directly.
What happens: The controller advertises a CRTO (Controller Ready With Media Timeout) smaller than CAP.TO. A host that trusts CRTO alone may give up too early.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2 logs bad crto:%x cap:%llx once and uses the larger value. The source comment says "CRTO should always be greater or equal to CAP.TO, but some devices are known to get this wrong."
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: CAP.CRMS, CRTO register (CRWMT/CRIMT).
Typical causes: Firmware filling the newer register incorrectly.
How to detect / prove: nvme show-regs ; dmesg.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_enable_ctrl .
Test to provoke it: Inspection only.

name: I/O command timeout handled by Abort
In a PEX trace: Visible The original SQE (fetched by the device with its CID), no CQE for that CID for about 30 s, then an admin SQ doorbell, the device fetching an Abort SQE (opcode 08h, CDW10 = SQID | CID<<16), the Abort's CQE (DW0 bit 0 = 1 means "not aborted"), and ideally a CQE for the original CID with status Command Abort Requested (generic 07h). Measure the gap from the SQE fetch to the Abort.
What happens: An I/O command does not complete within io_timeout . The driver asks the controller to abort it. Abort is best effort, and the controller may decline.
How it shows up: The "aborting req_op" line, then Abort status: 0x0 (or an error). If the original command completes with "Command Abort Requested", blk-mq retries it up to nvme_core.max_retries (default 5) unless DNR is set. If it does not complete within another timeout, the second-timeout branch resets the controller.
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: Abort command, Abort Command Limit (ACL), status Command Abort Requested.
Typical causes: A slow internal operation (GC, read-retry ladders on worn NAND). A lost doorbell (L-20, L-27). A device that fetched the SQE and lost it.
How to detect / prove: dmesg. The trace (above) separates "never fetched" from "fetched but not completed" from "completed but CQE lost or misdirected".
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_timeout , abort_endio ; core.c : abort_limit from id->acl + 1 , nvme_decide_disposition , nvme_retry_req .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: lower nvme_core.io_timeout on a test box and run a workload that triggers long internal operations. The NVMe fault-injection framework ( CONFIG_FAULT_INJECTION_DEBUG_FS , drivers/nvme/host/fault_inject.c ) injects status errors, not timeouts.

name: Lost interrupt — "completion polled"
In a PEX trace: Visible A CQE MWr to the CQ for the CID, and then no MSI-X MWr (or an MSI-X MWr to a vector the host did not expect). About 30 s later, the CQ head doorbell write from the host's poll. If the MSI-X MWr is present, the loss happened in the host (interrupt remapping or CPU), which a PEX trace cannot see.
What happens: The device completed the command, but the host never processed the CQE until the timeout handler polled the CQ.
How it shows up: I/O tag %d (%04x) QID %d timeout, completion polled , a 30-second latency for that I/O, and no reset.
Spec basis: NVMe: interrupts per CQ (Create I/O CQ IEN/IV). PCIe: MSI-X.
Typical causes: See L-35 : broken MSI (quirked devices), vector affinity bugs, a CQE write after the interrupt (ordering bug), interrupt coalescing.
How to detect / prove: Count "completion polled" occurrences. Check /proc/interrupts . Bisect with poll queues.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_timeout , nvme_poll_irqdisable , nvme_poll .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: mask a vector from a debug tool.

name: Device gone: CSTS reads all-ones
In a PEX trace: Partly visible On the Root Port side of the link, the CSTS MRd from the host and then either no CplD (Completion Timeout) or a Cpl with UR. The all-ones value is synthesised by the root complex and is never on the wire. On the SSD side you see the link down. The CfgRd of PCI_STATUS has the same pattern.
What happens: The driver reads 0xFFFFFFFF from CSTS. The PCIe read failed, so the device is not responding at all.
How it shows up: In nvme_timeout : controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff, PCI_STATUS=0xffff plus the two power-saving hint lines. In nvme_wait_ready() , all-ones returns -ENODEV at once with no message. In nvme_pci_enable() : debug-level reading CSTS register failed and -ENODEV. The reset therefore fails (C-17).
Spec basis: PCIe: unsuccessful completions return all-ones on most platforms impl .
Typical causes: Surprise link down (L-11, L-27), DPC containment (L-28), power loss, firmware crash, power-state exit failure (C-07, L-37).
How to detect / prove: lspci -s <BDF> -vv shows "!!! Unknown header type 7f" or all-ff. Check the upstream port's LnkSta for DLActive.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_warn_reset , nvme_pci_enable , nvme_pci_ctrl_is_dead ; core.c : nvme_wait_ready .
Test to provoke it: See L-11 and L-27.

name: Reset fails — controller marked DEAD, namespaces fail all I/O
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The failed re-init is visible (CC EN=1 with RDY never set, or no completions at all, or an admin command that fails). The driver's decision to give up is host-side. Afterwards, no traffic reaches the device.
What happens: nvme_reset_work() fails at any step: PCI enable, admin queue setup, enable, Identify, HMB setup, I/O queue creation, or a state change. The controller is moved to DELETING, disabled with shutdown, its namespaces are marked dead ( blk_mark_disk_dead ) and its state becomes DEAD. Applications get I/O errors and the block devices stay present but unusable until the device is removed and rescanned.
How it shows up: Disabling device after reset failure: %d (-19 = ENODEV is typical for a missing device). This is often preceded by Device not ready; aborting initialisation , Identify Controller failed (%d) , Could not set queue count (%d) or IO queues lost .
Spec basis: Host behaviour.
Typical causes: Device gone (C-16), a controller that cannot complete re-initialisation (firmware hung), repeated fatal PCIe errors.
How to detect / prove: cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/state shows dead (or deleting ). dmesg. Recovery attempt: echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/remove then echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/rescan (CAUTION: removes the device).
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_reset_work (out: path), nvme_dev_disable ; core.c : nvme_mark_namespaces_dead , nvme_change_ctrl_state .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: power off the slot (sysfs slot power) without removing the driver, then trigger I/O.

name: PCI error recovery of the NVMe function (error_detected / slot_reset / resume)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The cause (an ERR_FATAL message, a malformed TLP and so on) is visible if it crossed the probed link. Then the secondary bus reset (Hot Reset TS1s, or the link going down for DPC), link retraining, config-space restore CfgWrs, and a full NVMe init sequence. The callbacks themselves are software.
What happens: AER or DPC decides the channel is frozen. The NVMe driver shuts the controller down, the link is reset, and the driver re-initialises. In-flight requests are cancelled and retried.
How it shows up: frozen state error detected, reset controller → (port) Root Port link has been reset (0) or DPC messages → restart after slot reset → device recovery successful . On failure: failure state error detected, request disconnect , device recovery failed . Non-fatal errors: nvme_error_detected returns CAN_RECOVER, no NVMe log line, nothing is reset. Also reset_prepare / reset_done ( nvme_reset_prepare , nvme_reset_done ) for user-initiated resets via /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/reset .
Spec basis: Linux PCI error recovery ( Documentation/PCI/pci-error-recovery.rst ); PCIe secondary bus reset, DPC.
Typical causes: Any fatal AER (Chapter V.3) or DPC trigger (L-28).
How to detect / prove: dmesg sequence; pci_uevent_ers uevents; AER counters.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_error_detected , nvme_slot_reset , nvme_error_resume , nvme_err_handler ; drivers/pci/pcie/err.c : pcie_do_recovery , report_error_detected (logs can't recover (no error_detected callback) for drivers without one).
Test to provoke it: SAFE-ish: aer-inject (CONFIG_PCIEAER_INJECT) a fatal error at the SSD's BDF on a test system; this exercises the software path only.

name: Completion for an unknown or stale command ID
In a PEX trace: Visible A CQE MWr whose CID (DW3 bits 15:0) does not match any outstanding SQE on that queue, or matches one that already completed (a duplicate CQE). Compare it with the SQE CIDs in the trace. Check the phase tag too: a stale phase means a CQE the host should have ignored.
What happens: The controller posts a CQE whose CID the host cannot match. Linux v7.2 encodes a 4-bit generation counter in the upper CID bits (unless NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN is set), so late or duplicate completions for a reused tag are caught instead of completing the wrong request.
How it shows up: request %#x genctr mismatch (got %#x expected %#x) , could not locate request for tag %#x , then invalid id %d completed on queue %d . The CQE is dropped, and the real request (if any) later times out.
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: CID uniqueness per SQ for outstanding commands; CQE format (SQ ID, CID, phase).
Typical causes: Controller firmware bugs (duplicate completions, wrong CID after an abort). A controller limiting CID values (the Apple quirk). Memory corruption of the CQ.
How to detect / prove: dmesg; the trace.
Linux v7.2 source: nvme.h : nvme_find_rq , nvme_cid ; pci.c : nvme_handle_cqe .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: a modified QEMU model that posts a duplicate CQE.

name: Controller comes back with no I/O queues
In a PEX trace: Visible After re-init, the Set Features Number of Queues (FID 07h) CQE reports 0 queues allocated, or Create I/O CQ/SQ commands complete with an error status. Both are admin CQEs on the wire.
What happens: After a reset, the controller accepts admin commands but grants no I/O queues, or queue creation fails. Linux keeps the controller for investigation ("If only admin queue live, keep it") but removes the namespaces.
How it shows up: IO queues lost (reset) or IO queues not created (probe); Could not set queue count (%d) . nvme list shows the controller but no namespaces, and admin passthrough still works.
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: Number of Queues feature, Create I/O Submission/Completion Queue.
Typical causes: Firmware in a degraded or read-only "safe mode" (often after media failure). Controller resources leaked across resets.
How to detect / prove: nvme get-feature -f 7 /dev/nvme0 ; nvme smart-log critical warning; vendor logs.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_reset_work , nvme_setup_io_queues ; core.c : nvme_set_queue_count .
Test to provoke it: Vendor-specific (force safe mode).

name: Abort Command Limit exhausted — abort requests deferred
In a PEX trace: Partly visible You see up to ACL+1 outstanding Abort commands and further timed-out commands with no Abort issued for them. The driver's counter is host-side, and only the absence of Aborts is visible.
What happens: Many commands time out at once (typically when the controller has stalled). Linux v7.2 has only ACL+1 aborts available. When none are left, nvme_timeout just re-arms the timer (RESET_TIMER), so recovery for the rest is delayed by whole timeout periods until an abort finishes or a reset happens.
How it shows up: A few "aborting" lines followed by silence. Long multi-minute stalls before the eventual "reset controller".
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: Abort Command Limit (ACL, 0's based) in Identify Controller; "Abort Command Limit Exceeded" status.
Typical causes: Controller-wide stall with many commands outstanding. Very small ACL (e.g. 0, meaning one abort).
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep acl ; timestamps of timeouts versus resets.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_timeout ( atomic_dec_return(&dev->ctrl.abort_limit) ), abort_endio ; core.c : atomic_set(&ctrl->abort_limit, id->acl + 1) .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: stall a QEMU controller (for example by pausing its I/O thread with a debugger) under QD128 load.

name: Drive drops off the bus in its deepest power state (APST / deepest PS)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The Set Features APST command and its table payload are visible. The autonomous entry into the deepest state is not. A failed exit appears as link electrical idle that never ends, or as the first doorbell after idle getting no SQE fetch. See C-07 and L-37.
What happens: The kernel comments describe it: Samsung SM951/PM951/950 PRO on two Dell laptops "drop off the PCIe bus randomly when APST is on and uses the deepest sleep state"; Samsung 960 EVO "drops off the PCIe bus after system suspend" on two ASUS boards; the Toshiba THNSF5256GPUK "seems to die using any APST states"; "NVMe SSD drops off the PCIe bus after system idle for 10 hours on a Lenovo N60z board".
How it shows up: After idle: an I/O timeout, then controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff ... and the power-saving hint. The reset fails, and the device is gone until power-cycled.
Spec basis: NVMe: APST, power state descriptors (non-operational states, ENLAT/EXLAT).
Typical causes: Firmware or PHY bugs in the deepest state, often only with particular platform clocking or power delivery. That is why several quirks are DMI-matched.
How to detect / prove: Reproduce with a long idle soak. Confirm the fix with nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us set to just below the deepest state's exit latency (Linux picks APST targets using this limit), or with nvme.quirks=VID:DID:no_deepest_ps .
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : check_vendor_combination_bug ; core.c : core_quirks[] , nvme_configure_apst .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: idle soaks of 1, 4 and 12 hours, then I/O. CAUTION: 500× s2idle suspend/resume.

name: Write Zeroes (or Deallocate-as-zero) reported successful but data not zeroed
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The Write Zeroes SQE (opcode 08h: SLBA, NLB, DEAC bit) or DSM Deallocate SQE (09h with the range list as a DMA payload) and its successful CQE are visible. Whether the media was zeroed is not . Only a later Read's CplD/MWr payload crossing the link (non-zero data where zeros were promised) proves it.
What happens: 19 ID-table entries carry NVME_QUIRK_DISABLE_WRITE_ZEROES ("Broken Write Zeroes"): Linux stops issuing Write Zeroes to them. Two older Intel IDs carry NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES ("deterministically returns 0's on reads to logical blocks that deallocate was called on"). For those, Linux v7.2 implements block-layer write-zeroes with a Deallocate ( nvme_setup_write_zeroes calls nvme_setup_discard ) and advertises unlimited write-zeroes size. If such a device stopped returning zeroes after deallocate (a firmware change, or a partial-block range), write-zeroes would be silently wrong. This is the user's "trim completes but nothing happens" scenario, with the kernel depending on it.
How it shows up: Nothing. Both commands return Success. On a quirked drive, /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_zeroes_max_bytes is 0 (DISABLE) or very large (DEALLOCATE_ZEROES).
Spec basis: NVMe NVM Command Set: Write Zeroes (DEAC), Dataset Management Deallocate, deallocated logical block read behaviour (DLFEAT in Identify Namespace).
Typical causes: Firmware implementing Write Zeroes as a metadata-only operation with bugs at range boundaries. Deallocate granularity larger than the request.
How to detect / prove: Write a pattern, issue Write Zeroes ( nvme write-zeroes ) or blkdiscard -z , read back, compare. Vary alignment and length, including sub-granularity ranges. Do it across a power cycle too.
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_setup_write_zeroes , the NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES check in queue-limit setup, NVME_QUIRK_DISABLE_WRITE_ZEROES checks around max_zeroes_sectors .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION (destroys data in range): fio verify pattern write, blkdiscard -z -o OFF -l LEN , read-back verify; repeat for 4 KiB-misaligned ranges.

name: Bogus or duplicate namespace identifiers (EUI-64 / NGUID / UUID)
In a PEX trace: Visible The Identify Namespace (CNS 00h) and Namespace Identification Descriptor list (CNS 03h) data are DMA'd to the host as MWr payloads, so the duplicate or garbage EUI-64/NGUID/UUID bytes can be read directly. Compare captures from two drives of the same model.
What happens: The most-quirked bug in the table (30 IDs): drives report all-zero, constant or duplicated identifiers. Two drives of the same model then look like the same namespace, which breaks /dev/disk/by-id , multipath and RAID membership.
How it shows up: With the quirk: Ignoring bogus Namespace Identifiers . Without it, Linux v7.2 detects duplicates in the subsystem and, for non-shared PCIe namespaces, logs clearing duplicate IDs for nsid %d and use of /dev/disk/by-id/ may cause data corruption , then sets NVME_QUIRK_BOGUS_NID itself. For fabrics or shared namespaces it refuses the namespace: ignoring nsid %d because of duplicate IDs . Also: missing or invalid SUBNQN field. (IGNORE_DEV_SUBNQN cases).
Spec basis: NVMe Base Specification: namespace identifiers must be globally unique (EUI-64, NGUID, UUID), Namespace Identification Descriptors, SUBNQN.
Typical causes: Controller vendors' reference firmware shipping with placeholder IDs. OEMs not programming unique values.
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 | grep -E 'nguid|eui64' on two drives; nvme ns-descs ; ls -l /dev/disk/by-id/ .
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_identify_ns_descs paths ( NVME_QUIRK_BOGUS_NID checks), nvme_global_check_duplicate_ids / namespace-head checks around "clearing duplicate IDs".
Test to provoke it: SAFE: install two identical drives and compare identifiers.

name: MSI (not MSI-X) never fires
In a PEX trace: Visible The CfgWr enabling MSI (MSI Control Enable=1, address/data programmed), then CQE MWrs with no following MSI MWr to the programmed address.
What happens: NVME_QUIRK_BROKEN_MSI : "MSI (but not MSI-X) interrupts are broken and never fire" (SanDisk SN530, SN550). If the platform falls back to MSI (for example a vector shortage, or MSI-X disabled), every completion relies on timeout polling.
How it shows up: Without the quirk: "completion polled" for every command, and probe takes minutes. With it, Linux clears PCI_IRQ_MSI so only MSI-X or INTx are used.
Spec basis: PCI: MSI capability is optional when MSI-X exists, but if advertised it must work.
Typical causes: Untested MSI path in firmware.
How to detect / prove: Force MSI ( pci=nomsi forces INTx instead; to test MSI specifically, disable MSI-X on a test kernel or with the nvme.quirks parameter on another drive). Watch /proc/interrupts .
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_pci_enable , nvme_setup_irqs .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: test-kernel modification.

name: DMA above 48 bits mishandled
In a PEX trace: Visible Compare the 64-bit addresses in PRP entries (in the SQE and PRP lists) with the addresses of the device's MRd/MWr. A device that truncates the upper bits issues TLPs to the wrong (lower) address.
What happens: NVME_QUIRK_DMA_ADDRESS_BITS_48 : "does not properly handle DMA addresses over 48 bits" (six Amazon device IDs). Without the quirk, a buffer above 2 48 could be read from or written to a truncated address: silent corruption of unrelated memory, or an IOMMU fault if one is present.
How it shows up: With the quirk, Linux sets a 48-bit DMA mask ( dma_set_mask_and_coherent(..., DMA_BIT_MASK(48)) ) and nothing is visible. Without it, corruption or IOMMU faults appear only on systems with very large IOVA/physical spaces.
Spec basis: NVMe PRP/SGL entries are 64-bit addresses. PCIe supports 64-bit addressing.
Typical causes: Hardware DMA engines with truncated address registers.
How to detect / prove: Force IOVAs above 2 48 (IOMMU with a large address width, or a test DMA allocator), then data-verify.
Linux v7.2 source: pci.c : nvme_pci_alloc_dev .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: platform-specific.

name: Controller needs a delay before CSTS.RDY can be checked
In a PEX trace: Visible The CC EN=0 MWr followed by a CSTS MRd within milliseconds. On an affected device that read misbehaves: it returns stale RDY=1 forever, gets no completion, or is followed by a failed enable. With the quirk the gap is about 2.3 s.
What happens: NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_BEFORE_CHK_RDY : "needs a delay before starts checking the device readiness" (Seagate Nytro, HGST and WDC SN200 adapters, Memblaze Pblaze4, Samsung PM1725/PM1725a, and the Samsung Portable SSD X5 by string). Linux sleeps NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_AMOUNT = 2300 ms after clearing CC.EN, before polling. The core quirk comment adds that the X5 "fails initialization without a delay ... and has a whole set of other problems" and shares a PCI ID with the internal 970 Evo Plus, which does not need the quirk. That is why it is matched by model string.
How it shows up: Without the quirk: Device not ready; aborting reset or initialisation failures at probe.
Spec basis: NVMe: CSTS must reflect state transitions within CAP.TO, and register reads should always be valid.
Typical causes: Controllers that reset their register block asynchronously after CC.EN=0.
How to detect / prove: Repeated resets ( nvme reset ) with dmesg monitoring; test with the quirk disabled through nvme.quirks=VID:DID:^delay_before_chk_rdy .
Linux v7.2 source: core.c : nvme_disable_ctrl ; nvme.h : NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_AMOUNT ; drivers/pci/quirks.c nvme_disable_and_flr notes these devices are not supported by its generic path.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: 1000 controller resets on a test drive.

name: Device unusable after Function Level Reset
In a PEX trace: Visible The CfgWr setting Initiate FLR in Device Control, then (for the failing case) every subsequent CfgRd returning Cpl with RRS or all-ones data, or an enable sequence with RDY never set. With Linux's workaround: a CC EN=0 MWr and RDY polls before the FLR (Samsung), or a 250 ms gap after it (Intel, Solidigm).
What happens: Two PCI-core quirks in drivers/pci/quirks.c . (1) "The Samsung SM961/PM961 controller can sometimes enter a fatal state after FLR where config space reads from the device return -1. We seem to be able to avoid this condition if we disable the NVMe controller prior to FLR." This is nvme_disable_and_flr() , registered for Samsung 0xa804, which logs Timeout waiting for NVMe ready status to clear after disable if RDY does not clear. (2) "Some NVMe controllers such as Intel DC P3700 and Solidigm P44 Pro will timeout waiting for ready status to change after NVMe enable if the driver starts interacting with the device too soon after FLR": delay_250ms_after_flr() for Intel 0x0953, 0x0a54 and Solidigm 0xf1ac.
How it shows up: Without the quirks: VFIO passthrough or /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/reset leaves the device dead (config reads all-ones) or the next enable fails with Device not ready; aborting initialisation .
Spec basis: PCIe: FLR, a function must be ready for config requests within the post-reset period (or use RRS). NVMe: controller state after FLR is equivalent to a controller reset.
Typical causes: Controllers whose FLR handling races with in-progress internal operations.
How to detect / prove: Loop echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/reset (CAUTION: unbinds traffic) followed by nvme id-ctrl ; watch for "not ready ... after FLR" messages from pci_dev_wait .
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/quirks.c : nvme_disable_and_flr , delay_250ms_after_flr , pci_dev_reset_methods[] , __pci_dev_specific_reset .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: 1000 FLR cycles with the device unbound from the nvme driver (or under VFIO), checking Identify after each.

name: Invalid 10b symbol (code violation) on a Gen1/Gen2 lane
In a PEX trace: Visible The analyzer flags a symbol that is not a valid 10b code word on lane N in one direction. Look for the TLP or DLLP containing it, then a Nak (for a TLP) or a missing Ack and replay-timer replay, from the receiver in the opposite direction.
What happens: One or more bits flip on a lane, so the 10-bit group decodes to no valid 8-bit value. The receiver reports a Receiver Error and discards the packet containing the symbol. The transmitter replays it.
How it shows up: On the receiving device: AER Correctable Error Status Receiver Error ( PCI_ERR_COR_RCVR , "RxErr"), ERR_COR message, often Bad TLP as well. Nothing at the NVMe level.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Physical Layer 8b/10b decode rules and Receiver Error reporting; AER Correctable Error Status.
Typical causes: Marginal channel (long trace, worn connector, riser), crosstalk, a reference-clock problem, a failing transmitter, or the analyzer's own probe ( X-27 ).
How to detect / prove: Count flagged symbols per lane and direction over a fixed workload. Real errors on the link match: the receiver in the opposite direction sends a Nak and the device's AER RxErr counter rises ( /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/aer_dev_correctable ). Errors on one lane only point to that lane's channel. If the analyzer can show raw 10b codes, a single-bit difference from a valid code suggests noise, while a whole-symbol garble suggests a lock or alignment problem.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c : aer_irq , aer_isr_one_error , aer_print_error , pci_dev_aer_stats_incr , aer_ratelimit . See also L-01 .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: run the same workload through different slots or extenders and compare counts. EXPERT: add a lossy fixture to the channel, or force Gen2 on a channel built for Gen1.

name: Running-disparity error (Gen1/Gen2)
In a PEX trace: Visible The analyzer flags a valid 10b code with the wrong disparity for the current running disparity on lane N. Often a symbol error on a nearby symbol accompanies it, because the actual bit error can be several symbols before the place disparity catches it.
What happens: 8b/10b keeps the count of ones and zeros balanced. Each code word has a positive and a negative form, chosen by the running disparity. A bit error can produce a valid code word of the wrong form, which the receiver detects only as a disparity violation.
How it shows up: Receiver Error in AER on the receiving side, like X-01. The packet is discarded and replayed.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification 8b/10b rules (inherited from the IBM 8b/10b code); Receiver Error.
Typical causes: Same as X-01. A disparity error with no symbol error nearby is a strong hint of a single bit flip.
How to detect / prove: Because the error position is uncertain, look at the packet that the receiver Nak'd, not only the flagged symbol. A cluster of disparity errors right after electrical-idle exit, on every lane at once, is usually the analyzer regaining lock ( X-28 ), not a link problem.
Linux v7.2 source: As X-01 ( PCI_ERR_COR_RCVR in include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h ).
Test to provoke it: As X-01. Disparity errors cannot be injected from software on standard hardware. Use an exerciser that can send bad disparity on purpose (EXPERT).

name: Invalid sync header in a 128b/130b block (Gen3–Gen5)
In a PEX trace: Visible The analyzer flags a block on lane N whose 2-bit sync header is 00b or 11b. Then look for what the link does: Recovery (TS1 ordered sets in both directions) usually follows within microseconds, and TLPs in flight are Nak'd or replayed after Recovery.
What happens: Each 130-bit block starts with a sync header that says "data block" or "ordered-set block". Only two of the four values are valid. A bit error in the header means the receiver cannot tell how to interpret the next 128 bits, so the data stream is lost on that lane.
How it shows up: Receiver Error (RxErr) on the receiving device. The receiver typically treats it as a framing error and directs the LTSSM to Recovery verify in spec . Linux sees an RxErr burst and possibly a link-speed or width change notice.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, 128b/130b encoding, sync header and data-stream framing rules. A vendor PHY register guide (Efinix) lists "00 and 11 are Invalid Sync Headers".
Typical causes: Gen3+ channel margin, bad equalization result ( X-13 ), retimer problems, block-alignment loss after L0s/L1 exit.
How to detect / prove: Count invalid sync headers per lane. Check that each one is followed by a Recovery entry. If the analyzer reports invalid sync headers and the link stays in L0 without any Recovery, the analyzer lost block alignment ( X-28 ). Use Lane Margining at the Receiver (Gen4+) to measure margin on the suspect lane.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c (RxErr), drivers/pci/pcie/bwctrl.c : pcie_bwnotif_irq (records speed/width changes after Recovery).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: step receiver margining toward the eye edge on a Gen4+ platform that supports it. EXPERT: insert a lossy channel.

name: Invalid or malformed ordered set (TS1/TS2, EIEOS, EIOS, SDS, SKP)
In a PEX trace: Visible The analyzer shows an ordered set whose identifier symbols, length or fields are wrong. Examples: a TS1 with a lane number that differs from the other lanes' pattern, reserved bits set, an EIEOS with the wrong pattern, an ordered-set block in the middle of a data stream without a preceding EDS (Gen3+).
What happens: Ordered sets drive link training and maintenance. A malformed one is ignored by a robust receiver. If it is ignored too often, training takes longer, falls back to a lower speed or width, or times out.
How it shows up: Often nothing directly. Indirectly: longer link-up time, Recovery entries, LnkSta lower than LnkCap, or RxErr when the ordered set breaks framing rules (Gen3+).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, ordered-set definitions (TS1/TS2 fields: Link Number, Lane Number, N_FTS, data-rate identifier, training control, equalization fields) and Gen3+ data-stream rules (EDS before an ordered set).
Typical causes: Firmware or PHY bugs in one link partner (often a new controller or retimer), wrong lane numbering on a board, bit errors in ordered sets.
How to detect / prove: Compare the same ordered set across lanes. All lanes of a link must agree on the link number and the training fields, and lane numbers must be consecutive. Repeated identical malformed ordered sets point to a design bug. Random ones point to bit errors. Use the analyzer's LTSSM view to see which state each one belongs to.
Linux v7.2 source: No direct visibility. Effects appear through drivers/pci/pci.c : pcie_wait_for_link / pcie_retrain_link and drivers/pci/probe.c : pcie_update_link_speed .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: use an exerciser to send TS1/TS2 with bad fields and watch whether the DUT ignores them correctly.

name: Framing error: bad STP/SDP/END/EDB placement or token (TLP or DLLP boundaries lost)
In a PEX trace: Visible The analyzer flags a packet with no valid end, a start token in an illegal lane or position, an STP whose length field does not match the data that follows, an STP frame-CRC or parity mismatch (Gen3+), or an invalid token in a data block. The partial packet is shown truncated or as an error item. Look for Recovery (Gen3+) and a replay afterwards.
What happens: The receiver loses track of where packets start and end. In 8b/10b mode framing uses K symbols (STP…END for TLPs, SDP…END for DLLPs). In 128b/130b mode the STP token carries the TLP length, protected by a small CRC and a parity bit. Any inconsistency means the rest of the data stream on that link cannot be trusted.
How it shows up: Receiver Error on the receiving side. In 128b/130b mode the receiver must also enter Recovery to re-establish the data stream verify in spec . Packets in flight are replayed after Recovery.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, packet-framing rules for 8b/10b and 128b/130b (framing tokens STP, SDP, END, EDB, EDS, IDL; Gen3+ framing-error rules).
Typical causes: Bit errors that hit a framing symbol or token; a transmitter bug (wrong STP length, packing tokens into illegal positions on wide links); lane-to-lane skew beyond the deskew buffer ( X-07 ).
How to detect / prove: Separate random from systematic. A framing error that recurs with the same TLP type and length is a transmitter bug. Prove it with the exact bytes: STP length versus the actual number of Dwords up to the next token. A random framing error with a physical error on the same lane just before it is a channel problem.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c (RxErr, BadTLP). See L-01 , L-02 .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser sending a TLP with a mismatched STP length, or an END-less packet, then checking that the DUT recovers and replays.

name: Nullified TLP (EDB end, inverted LCRC): legal by design, wrong when unexpected
In a PEX trace: Visible A TLP ending with EDB (8b/10b) or followed by an EDB token (128b/130b) and carrying the bitwise inverse of the correct LCRC. Analyzers show it as "nullified" rather than as an LCRC error. Check that no Ack or Nak refers to it and that the next TLP reuses the same sequence number.
What happens: A switch or retimer that forwards a TLP before it has fully arrived (cut-through) may discover an error at the end. It then ends the packet with EDB and inverts the LCRC. The receiver silently drops it: no Nak, no error, and the sequence number is not consumed.
How it shows up: Normally nothing, by design. If the nullified TLP's LCRC is not exactly inverted, the receiver treats it as a Bad TLP (Receiver Error / Bad TLP in AER).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Data Link Layer rules for nullified TLPs; framing (EDB).
Typical causes: Legitimate: cut-through forwarding in a switch that saw an error upstream. Suspicious: an endpoint SSD nullifying its own TLPs (it has no upstream source to forward), or many nullified TLPs in a row.
How to detect / prove: Count nullified TLPs per source. On a direct Root-Port-to-SSD link with no switch, nullified TLPs from the SSD indicate an internal transmit-path problem. Nullified TLPs from a switch indicate errors on the switch's other link. Probe that link next.
Linux v7.2 source: None: nullified TLPs raise no AER bit when correctly formed.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: inject errors on a switch's upstream link with cut-through enabled and capture the downstream link.

name: Lane-to-lane skew beyond the receiver's deskew capability
In a PEX trace: Visible The analyzer measures arrival skew between lanes on ordered sets (SKP, TS, EIEOS, SDS) and flags a deskew failure when the same ordered set does not arrive on all lanes within its window. Symptoms: packets with corrupted Dwords on one lane, framing errors ( X-05 ), training that ends at a narrower width.
What happens: Lanes of one link travel through slightly different lengths of trace, cable and retimer. The receiver aligns them using a common marker (COM in SKP/TS ordered sets for 8b/10b; SKP, SDS or EIEOS block boundaries for 128b/130b). If skew is larger than the receiver's deskew buffer, bytes from different lanes are combined in the wrong order.
How it shows up: Receiver Errors and replays, or the link trains at a reduced width that leaves out the badly skewed lanes ( L-25 ).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, lane-to-lane skew limits for transmitter and receiver (per data rate). One patent summary quotes 20 ns receiver skew tolerance at Gen1 and 8 ns at Gen2 uncertain . Limits for Gen3 and later are tighter; check the spec table for your rate.
Typical causes: Mismatched cable lengths, retimers that add different numbers of SKP symbols per lane, board routing errors, separate-clock (SRIS/SRNS) configurations with dynamic skew.
How to detect / prove: Read the analyzer's per-lane skew report for the same capture at each speed. Skew that grows with speed changes or temperature points to the channel. A constant skew that the analyzer reports but the device tolerates (no RxErr) is within the device's capability. The analyzer's own limit may be tighter ( X-29 ).
Linux v7.2 source: Effects only: drivers/pci/pci.c : __pcie_print_link_status reports reduced bandwidth; AER RxErr counters.
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: insert unequal-length cable pairs on a cabled link (MCIO, OCuLink) and record the width and errors.

name: Lane reversal or polarity inversion not handled (wrong width, failed training)
In a PEX trace: Visible In Polling and Configuration, TS1/TS2 lane numbers show whether lanes are reversed (lane 0 of one partner meets lane N−1 of the other). Inverted symbols in TS1/TS2 on a lane show uncorrected polarity. Failure appears as a link trained at x1 or a reduced width, or a loop in Configuration.
What happens: PCIe lets board designers reverse lane order and swap D+/D−. Every receiver must detect and undo polarity inversion on each lane during Polling. Lane reversal support is optional on one side, so it works only if at least one partner handles it. When neither handles it, or a device bug prevents it, the link trains narrow or not at all.
How it shows up: LnkSta width lower than LnkCap ( lspci -vvv : "LnkSta: … Width x1 (downgraded)"), lower bandwidth, possibly no link at all.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Polling (polarity inversion detection from TS1/TS2 symbols) and Configuration (lane number negotiation, lane reversal).
Typical causes: Board layout reversed on a device that cannot reverse; adapter cards that swap pairs; a known device erratum (for example Intel's advisory that automatic polarity inversion is not guaranteed in one FPGA family under certain conditions).
How to detect / prove: Capture link training from power-on with the analyzer configured for the physical lane map. Compare lane numbers in TS1/TS2 from both ends. Note that the analyzer must also be told about any reversal on the interposer, otherwise it reports false errors ( X-29 ).
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pci.c : __pcie_print_link_status (prints available bandwidth and the limiting link); PCI_EXP_LNKSTA_NLW in include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: use an adapter or interposer that reverses lanes and check both training and analyzer decoding.

name: Unexpected link width or speed renegotiation during operation
In a PEX trace: Visible In the middle of traffic, both directions switch to TS1 ordered sets (Recovery), then TS2 with a changed data-rate field, a speed change (Recovery.Speed), or Configuration with fewer lanes. Traffic resumes at the new speed or width. The analyzer must follow the change; if it does not, the rest of the trace is undecodable.
What happens: A port can change speed or width autonomously (for example after repeated errors, or for power) or because software asked for it. A drop from Gen4 to Gen1, or from x4 to x1, keeps the SSD working at a fraction of its bandwidth.
How it shows up: Link Status bits Link Bandwidth Management Status (LBMS) or Link Autonomous Bandwidth Status (LABS) set on the downstream port. Linux v7.2's bandwidth controller handles that interrupt and updates the cached link speed. No NVMe error, only lower throughput.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, LTSSM Recovery and Configuration; Link Status register (LBMS, LABS), Link Control 2 Target Link Speed.
Typical causes: Hardware autonomous fallback after errors; equalization failure at the higher rate; thermal or power policy; software writes to Target Link Speed followed by Retrain Link.
How to detect / prove: In the trace: find the first TS1 after L0 and look backwards for the physical errors or EIOS that triggered it. Note who started Recovery: the direction where TS1 appears first. On the host: lspci -vvv LnkSta and the sysfs current_link_speed / current_link_width attributes, sampled over time.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/bwctrl.c : pcie_bwnotif_irq (reads PCI_EXP_LNKSTA , records LBMS in PCI_LINK_LBMS_SEEN , calls pcie_update_link_speed ); drivers/pci/quirks.c : pcie_failed_link_retrain (forces 2.5 GT/s when a link fails to come up and LBMS was seen, then tries to lift the restriction). See L-25 .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: on a test system, change the Target Link Speed and retrain through the kernel's bandwidth-control interface, or physically degrade one lane, and capture the transition.

name: SKP ordered-set errors: missing, too frequent, malformed, or inside a packet
In a PEX trace: Visible Only if SKP ordered sets are not filtered. Measure the interval between SKP OS per direction, check their length and format, and look for SKP symbols where they are not allowed (inside a TLP in 8b/10b). The analyzer flags format errors. Interval violations usually need a timing search.
What happens: SKP ordered sets let receivers compensate for small clock-frequency differences between the two ends. Retimers and receivers add or remove SKP symbols. At Gen1/2 a SKP OS is COM followed by SKP symbols. At Gen3+ it is a block of SKP bytes, an end marker and LFSR/parity bytes, and at Gen4+ it can carry margining commands. Too few SKPs over time overflow or underflow the receiver's elastic buffer.
How it shows up: Receiver Errors from elastic-buffer overflow or underflow; with separate reference clocks (SRIS) and wrong SKP interval settings, periodic error bursts.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, clock tolerance compensation: SKP scheduling interval (different for common-clock, SRNS and SRIS modes), SKP OS format for 8b/10b and 128b/130b. The exact intervals depend on mode and rate verify in spec .
Typical causes: SRIS (separate reference clocks with spread spectrum) not enabled on both ends when it is required; retimer bugs; transmitter scheduling bugs under heavy back-to-back traffic.
How to detect / prove: Export SKP timestamps per direction and compute the distribution of intervals; compare with the spec maximum for the clocking mode. Check the platform clocking: whether the SSD uses the slot's reference clock or its own.
Linux v7.2 source: RxErr counters only ( drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c ).
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: run a link with separate spread-spectrum clocks and SRIS disabled, under heavy traffic.

name: Recovery storm: the LTSSM keeps leaving L0
In a PEX trace: Visible Repeated bursts of TS1/TS2 between stretches of traffic: L0 → Recovery.RcvrLock → Recovery.RcvrCfg → Recovery.Idle → L0, many times per second. Each burst stalls all traffic for microseconds to milliseconds. Look at what precedes each entry: physical errors, replay timeouts, REPLAY_NUM rollover, or nothing (a partner's internal decision).
What happens: Recovery re-establishes bit, symbol or block lock and is how a link handles errors and speed changes. A healthy link enters it rarely. A link that enters it constantly works, but with large latency spikes and reduced bandwidth.
How it shows up: Correctable AER errors (RxErr, Replay Timer Timeout, REPLAY_NUM Rollover) on one or both ends, rate-limited in dmesg. NVMe I/O latency spikes, sometimes host timeouts.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, LTSSM Recovery substates and entry conditions.
Typical causes: Marginal channel, equalization that converged to a poor preset, ASPM L1 exit problems, retimer firmware bugs.
How to detect / prove: Count Recovery entries per second from the LTSSM view, and plot them against workload and time. Classify each entry by its trigger (error, rollover, speed change request, idle exit). Confirm with both ends' AER counters over the same period.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c (correctable error handling and rate limiting through aer_ratelimit ). See L-26 .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: enable ASPM L1 on a link with marginal timing, or use receiver margining to reduce margin, and capture.

name: LTSSM stuck or looping in training (Polling.Compliance, Detect/Polling loop, Configuration loop)
In a PEX trace: Visible Instead of TS1/TS2 progressing to L0, the trace shows the compliance pattern on some lanes (Polling.Compliance), TS1 exchanges that never advance to TS2, or the same Detect → Polling → Detect cycle repeating every few tens of milliseconds. No TLPs at all, or none after a certain point.
What happens: Polling.Compliance is a test mode. A port enters it when it detects a receiver on a lane but receives no TS1s there (or when told to by the Enter Compliance bit or a test signal). In normal operation this means one side sees a partner that is not training. Other loops come from mismatched link numbers, lanes that never achieve lock, or timeouts in Configuration.
How it shows up: The SSD never appears in lspci , or appears after a long delay. On the Root Port, Data Link Layer Link Active never sets. Linux waits and then gives up, or applies the 2.5 GT/s retrain quirk.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, LTSSM Detect, Polling (Active, Compliance, Configuration) and Configuration states, including their timeouts.
Typical causes: Broken lane or missing termination on one side, wrong pin assignment, a test strap left asserted (an Altera knowledge-base entry lists a test input bit and PCB pin errors as causes), power sequencing or PERST# timing, an SSD firmware hang during boot.
How to detect / prove: Capture from PERST# deassertion with an analyzer that brings out PERST#. Measure time from PERST# to first TS1 from each side, and find which side stops progressing. Note which lanes show the compliance pattern.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pci.c : pcie_wait_for_link , pcie_wait_for_link_status (polls PCI_EXP_LNKSTA_DLLLA or PCI_EXP_LNKSTA_LT ); drivers/pci/quirks.c : pcie_failed_link_retrain . See L-39 , T-02 .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: tape off or disconnect a lane's receive pair on an adapter, or hold the SSD in reset, and capture training from power-on.

name: Equalization failure or poor preset (Gen3+): fallback to a lower speed, or high error rate
In a PEX trace: Visible Equalization phases appear as TS1 ordered sets in Recovery.Equalization with preset and coefficient fields. A failure shows as phases that time out, repeated requests, lanes finishing on different presets, or a retrain back to the old speed. A Teledyne LeCroy blog notes that lanes ending on different presets (for example P6 on some, P10 on others) are a red flag, since P10 is meant for boost-limit testing.
What happens: At 8 GT/s and above, the two ends tune each other's transmitter equalization in phases 0–3. In phase 2 the upstream port asks the downstream port to adjust its transmitter, and in phase 3 the reverse happens. A bad result leaves a link that works with little margin, or makes the port give up the higher rate.
How it shows up: Link Status 2 equalization status bits (Equalization Complete, Phase 1/2/3 Successful) clear for the failing rate; link at a lower speed; or a link at full speed with steady RxErr counts.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Link Equalization Procedure, Lane Equalization Control registers (Linux: PCI_SECPCI_LE_CTRL , PCI_PL_16GT_LE_CTRL , PCI_PL_32GT_LE_CTRL , PCI_PL_64GT_LE_CTRL ), Link Status 2 equalization bits.
Typical causes: Channel loss outside the budget, wrong preset hints from firmware, retimer equalization bugs, a PHY that does not evaluate requests in time.
How to detect / prove: Trigger on the first TS1 with the equalization bit set after a speed change, or on a speed change, and capture the whole procedure. Tabulate each lane's requested and final preset. Correlate with per-lane errors after equalization. For the analog view, Teledyne LeCroy describes CrossSync PHY, which time-aligns an oscilloscope capture with the protocol trace.
Linux v7.2 source: include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h (Lane Equalization Control registers above); effects through drivers/pci/pcie/bwctrl.c : pcie_bwnotif_irq .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: force a specific preset through platform firmware settings or the device's debug interface, then capture the next equalization and its error rate.

name: Electrical-idle glitches and L0s/L1 entry or exit failures
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Visible: EIOS before idle, the idle period, EIEOS/FTS/TS1 on exit, PM DLLPs (PM_Enter_L1, PM_Request_Ack) and the TLP that woke the link. Not reliable: the exact moment of a short glitch, because the analyzer itself must re-lock after idle and may lose the first symbols ( X-28 ).
What happens: During L0s and L1 the transmitter stops driving the lane. On exit, the receiver must regain lock in a limited time (N_FTS fast training sequences for L0s; Recovery for L1). Problems: idle entered without EIOS, a lane drifting into idle on its own (inferred idle), too few FTS for the receiver to lock, or an exit that fails and falls into Recovery or Detect.
How it shows up: Latency spikes after idle, RxErr bursts at exit, sometimes a link drop. Disabling ASPM makes it go away.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Electrical Idle rules, EIOS/EIEOS, L0s (N_FTS) and L1 entry/exit, ASPM.
Typical causes: N_FTS advertised too small, CLKREQ# handling problems in L1 substates, reference-clock gating issues, PHY bugs at low-power exit.
How to detect / prove: Measure each exit: time from first EIEOS/FTS to the first good TLP, and count errors in that window. Compare with ASPM disabled ( lspci -vvv LnkCtl ASPM field; the kernel parameter pcie_aspm=off ). If errors appear only in the analyzer and not in either device's counters, suspect analyzer re-lock.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aspm.c (ASPM policy). See L-37 , T-14 .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: enable ASPM L0s/L1 (and L1 substates where supported) with a bursty, low-duty workload that makes the link enter and exit idle thousands of times.

name: LCRC error on a TLP
In a PEX trace: Visible The analyzer flags a TLP whose LCRC does not match (and that does not end in EDB, so it is not nullified). Expected follow-up: a Nak in the opposite direction carrying the previous good sequence number, then replay of the bad TLP and everything after it.
What happens: A bit error inside a TLP that the physical layer did not catch (for example in a scrambled data byte, which has no code-level check) breaks the LCRC. The receiver discards the TLP, reports Bad TLP and sends a Nak.
How it shows up: AER Correctable Bad TLP ( PCI_ERR_COR_BAD_TLP , "BadTLP") on the receiving device. Possibly RxErr as well. Nothing at the NVMe level.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Data Link Layer: LCRC, receive rules, Nak scheduling; AER Bad TLP.
Typical causes: Channel noise, equalization margin, retimer bugs; much less often a transmitter that computes LCRC incorrectly for some TLP format (that one repeats exactly).
How to detect / prove: For each flagged TLP, check the receiver's reaction. A Nak, or a replay of the same sequence number, proves the link partner also saw it. If the next Ack covers the flagged TLP with no replay, the receiver accepted it and the flag is an analyzer decode error ( X-27 ). Compute the rate: LCRC errors per 10 9 TLPs by direction.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c : aer_print_error , pci_dev_aer_stats_incr ("BadTLP" counter). See L-02 , V-35 .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser or error-injecting retimer that corrupts LCRC on selected TLPs; or margin the receiver (CAUTION).

name: DLLP CRC error (corrupted Ack, Nak or UpdateFC)
In a PEX trace: Visible The analyzer flags a DLLP whose 16-bit CRC fails. Follow-up depends on its type. A lost Ack is normally covered by a later Ack; if none comes in time, the transmitter's replay timer expires and it replays. A lost UpdateFC is covered by the next UpdateFC of the same type.
What happens: The receiver silently discards a DLLP with a bad CRC and reports Bad DLLP. Because Acks and UpdateFCs are cumulative, one loss is harmless. Many losses cause replays and credit stalls.
How it shows up: AER Correctable Bad DLLP ( PCI_ERR_COR_BAD_DLLP ). Sometimes Replay Timer Timeout on the other side.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, DLLP CRC, Data Link Layer receive rules; AER Bad DLLP.
Typical causes: As X-15. DLLPs are short, so they are hit less often per packet than long TLPs.
How to detect / prove: Count bad DLLPs per direction. Check whether each was followed by a replay-timer replay (the Ack was really lost) or a later DLLP that covered it.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c ("BadDLLP"). See L-03 .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: exerciser that corrupts DLLP CRCs; watch the DUT's replay and credit behaviour.

name: Sequence-number errors: gaps, out-of-order TLPs, Ack/Nak for a number never sent
In a PEX trace: Visible In one direction, list the sequence numbers of new (non-replayed) TLPs. They must increase by one, modulo 4096. Three patterns matter: (1) a number skipped in a new transmission, (2) a TLP with a number lower than expected that is not part of a replay (a duplicate), (3) an Ack or Nak whose number does not belong to any unacknowledged TLP.
What happens: The receiver accepts only the next expected number. A lower number (a duplicate) is discarded and an Ack is scheduled; this is legal after replays. A higher number means TLPs were lost, so the receiver discards it and sends a Nak (Bad TLP). An Ack/Nak whose number is not outstanding at the transmitter is a Data Link Protocol Error.
How it shows up: Pattern 2 (legal duplicate): nothing. Pattern 1: Bad TLP on the receiver plus a Nak. Pattern 3: uncorrectable Data Link Protocol Error ( PCI_ERR_UNC_DLP , "DLP"), which is often set to Fatal severity and leads to link reset or DPC.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Data Link Layer: NEXT_RCV_SEQ, NEXT_TRANSMIT_SEQ, ACKD_SEQ rules; Data Link Protocol Error.
Typical causes: Transmitter bugs after Recovery (sequence state not kept), replay-buffer bugs, a DLLP with a corrupted but CRC-valid number (rare), or analyzer decode errors on a framing boundary.
How to detect / prove: Script it: per direction, keep the next expected number; mark replays (same number and same contents as an earlier TLP); flag new TLPs with unexpected numbers. For pattern 3, keep the set of unacknowledged numbers and check each Ack/Nak. A DLP error in AER right after the event confirms it.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c ("DLP"), recovery through drivers/pci/pcie/err.c . See L-10 .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: exerciser sending TLPs with skipped sequence numbers or Acks for unsent numbers; check that the DUT Naks or reports DLP.

name: Nak storm: frequent Naks and replays on a link that never fails outright
In a PEX trace: Visible Many Naks per millisecond in one direction, each followed by a replay of several TLPs. Throughput drops. Look at what the Nak'd TLPs have in common: size, type, lane errors, time after idle exit, or high utilisation.
What happens: Every Nak costs a replay of all unacknowledged TLPs after the bad one. With large payloads and a deep replay buffer this can waste a large share of the bandwidth while still delivering correct data.
How it shows up: Bad TLP and RxErr correctable counters rising steadily on the receiving side; Linux prints rate-limited correctable error lines. Throughput below expectation; higher latency percentiles. No NVMe error.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Ack/Nak protocol. The spec sets no "maximum Nak rate". This is a quality problem, judged against the expected bit error rate.
Typical causes: Marginal channel, poor equalization, crosstalk under load, a receiver bug for a specific TLP pattern.
How to detect / prove: Compute replay overhead = replayed bytes ÷ total TLP bytes, per direction, per second. Plot it against workload. Errors that grow with traffic on neighbouring lanes or links suggest crosstalk or power-supply noise. Errors concentrated on one TLP type suggest a design bug.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c : aer_ratelimit (why dmesg understates the rate), pci_dev_aer_stats_incr (sysfs counters show the true count).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: run a full-bandwidth sequential workload (for example fio with large blocks) through a marginal extender and capture.

name: REPLAY_NUM rollover: four replays without progress force Recovery
In a PEX trace: Visible The same oldest unacknowledged sequence number is transmitted four times (the original plus replays), with no Ack advancing past it, then the transmitter enters Recovery (TS1s). After Recovery the replay continues. Count the replays per sequence number to see this pattern.
What happens: The transmitter keeps a 2-bit REPLAY_NUM. Each replay without forward progress increments it. When it rolls over, the transmitter assumes the link is in trouble and retrains. Any Ack that advances resets the counter.
How it shows up: AER Correctable REPLAY_NUM Rollover ( PCI_ERR_COR_REP_ROLL , "Rollover") on the transmitter; Recovery; latency spike of the Recovery duration plus all replay time.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Data Link Layer replay mechanism; AER REPLAY_NUM Rollover.
Typical causes: The receiver cannot receive a specific TLP correctly (pattern-dependent error), a receiver that stopped sending Acks, or all Acks lost (DLLP errors in the other direction).
How to detect / prove: Look at the other direction during the replays. No DLLPs at all means the receiver is not sending Acks (a receiver bug or hang). Naks mean it receives the TLP but rejects it every time. Corrupted DLLPs mean the return path is bad.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c ("Rollover"). See L-04 , T-36 .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser that withholds Acks or Naks the same TLP repeatedly.

name: Ack/Nak latency violation: Acks sent too late, causing replay-timer replays
In a PEX trace: Visible Measure, for each TLP, the time from its end to the first Ack or Nak in the opposite direction that covers it. Long tails show a slow receiver. The proof is a replay that happens with no Nak before it (a replay-timer expiry), followed by an Ack for the original that arrives just after the replay started.
What happens: The receiver must send an Ack within a latency limit that the spec gives as a table depending on link width, speed and maximum payload size. The transmitter's replay timer is set to a larger multiple of the same quantity. If the receiver delays Acks (for example because it prioritises sending its own TLPs or UpdateFCs), the transmitter times out and replays TLPs that had arrived fine.
How it shows up: AER Correctable Replay Timer Timeout ( PCI_ERR_COR_REP_TIMER , "Timeout") on the transmitter , although the fault is in the receiver. Duplicate TLPs at the receiver (silently discarded). Wasted bandwidth.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Ack/Nak latency and replay-timer limit tables (depend on width, rate, Max_Payload_Size, and an internal-delay term) exact formula: verify in spec .
Typical causes: Receiver Ack scheduling bugs under heavy bidirectional traffic. An NXP/Mobiveil Linux patch (erratum A-011451) describes a controller that did not prioritise Acks behind many split completions and UpdateFCs, causing Ack-latency timeouts and replays at the link partner. Its workaround reduced the Ack latency timer.
How to detect / prove: Use the Ack-latency script in I-B.7 . Report the distribution per direction and the replays with no preceding Nak. Repeat at different MPS settings: the allowed latency scales with MPS.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c ("Timeout" correctable). See L-05 , T-37 .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: heavy simultaneous read and write traffic (mixed fio workload at high queue depth) so both directions are busy, then capture.

name: Flow-control credit violation: TLP sent without credits, or credits over-advertised
In a PEX trace: Visible Rebuild credits per direction and type. Start from InitFC1/InitFC2 (this needs a capture that includes link-up), add UpdateFC values, subtract each TLP's header credit (1) and data credits (payload ÷ 16 bytes, rounded up). A TLP sent when the required credits exceed the limit is a transmitter violation. An UpdateFC that grants more outstanding credits than the field allows, or changes an infinite (0) advertisement, is a receiver violation.
What happens: Credits prevent buffer overflow at the receiver. A transmitter that ignores them overflows the receiver's buffer and TLPs are lost. A receiver that advertises nonsense credits breaks the transmitter's gating.
How it shows up: Receiver Overflow ( PCI_ERR_UNC_RX_OVER , "RxOF") or Flow Control Protocol Error ( PCI_ERR_UNC_FCP , "FCP"), both uncorrectable, often followed by link reset or DPC.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Flow Control: credit types, InitFC/UpdateFC, credit-limit arithmetic, infinite credits (endpoints must advertise infinite completion credits), Receiver Overflow and Flow Control Protocol Error. A vendor controller guide (Efinix) states the maximum outstanding unused credits without scaling as 2,047 data and 127 header credits and reports violations as FCPE.
Typical causes: Credit-counter bugs (wrap-around of 8-bit header or 12-bit data counters), mis-handled scaled flow control (Gen6), changes in credit accounting after Recovery.
How to detect / prove: Credit arithmetic is modular. Compare (credit limit − credits consumed) mod 2 field size against the needed amount, as the spec describes. An analyzer with credit tracking can do this, or a script over an export with DLLPs and TLP lengths. Any trace starting after InitFC can only check changes , not absolute limits.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c ("RxOF", "FCP"). See L-13 , L-17 .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser that sends TLPs beyond advertised credits, or advertises out-of-range credits, and checks the DUT's error reporting.

name: Missing or stuck UpdateFC: credit starvation stalls one traffic class
In a PEX trace: Visible One TLP type stops flowing in one direction (for example the SSD's posted writes of read data) while others continue. In the opposite direction, UpdateFC for that type has stopped, or keeps repeating the same credit value. Rebuilding credits (X-21) shows the transmitter is at its limit and correctly waiting.
What happens: The receiver returns credits only through UpdateFC. If it stops (because its buffers are full, or because of a bug), the transmitter must wait. Non-posted requests (reads) can then pile up behind it, and the whole device stalls. The spec defines an optional flow-control watchdog that retrains the link when no UpdateFC arrives for a while. One patent summary gives 200 µs for PCIe 2.0 uncertain , and notes that the watchdog cannot catch UpdateFCs that arrive with an unchanged value.
How it shows up: NVMe commands stall and time out with no AER error, unless the optional watchdog is implemented (then it shows as a correctable or uncorrectable error and a retrain, depending on the implementation). Linux shows I/O timeouts and an NVMe controller reset.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, Flow Control update rules and recommended UpdateFC frequency; optional Flow Control Update timer.
Typical causes: Host-side buffers full (the root complex cannot drain posted writes to memory, for example because of a memory-subsystem or IOMMU stall); deadlocks from ordering rules; SSD firmware bugs that never release completion buffers.
How to detect / prove: Plot UpdateFC values per type over time, with TLP counts of that type. A flat UpdateFC with no TLPs of that type, and other types still flowing, identifies the starving type and which side holds the credits. Note the time of the last UpdateFC and compare it with the NVMe command timeout on the host.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c : nvme_timeout (the visible consequence). See T-38 .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: an exerciser that withholds UpdateFC for one credit type and observes whether the DUT stalls, recovers or reports an error.

name: Flit CRC failure / FEC-uncorrectable Flit
In a PEX trace: Visible On a Flit-capable analyzer: Flits flagged as FEC-corrected (with the corrected byte positions) and Flits flagged as CRC-failed. A CRC-failed Flit should be followed by a Nak in the DLP bytes of the opposite direction, then a replay of that Flit (or of it and those after it).
What happens: When more errors hit a Flit than FEC can correct, the CRC fails and the receiver discards the Flit. Its TLPs and DLP content are recovered by replay. A rising FEC-corrected count is the early warning. A rising CRC-failure count costs bandwidth and latency.
How it shows up: Correctable errors in AER on the receiving device (the exact AER bits and any Flit-specific counters depend on the spec version and implementation uncertain ). Linux v7.2 can log TLP headers captured in Flit format ( PCI_ERR_CAP_TLP_LOG_FLIT ). No NVMe-level effect unless replays escalate.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification 6.0 and later, Flit mode: FEC, CRC, Flit replay.
Typical causes: PAM4 channel margin, equalization, crosstalk, retimers; burst errors longer than the FEC can handle.
How to detect / prove: Track FEC-corrected and CRC-failed Flits per lane and per second, and compute the replay overhead. Compare FEC-corrected rates between slots or cables as a margin measure. Confirm CRC failures by the link partner's Nak.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c (Flit-format TLP log handling with PCI_ERR_CAP_TLP_LOG_FLIT ); drivers/pci/pci.c : __pcie_print_link_status . See V-37 .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: Gen6 receiver margining or a lossy channel; error injection with a Gen6 exerciser.

name: Flit sequence and replay anomalies (replay storms, wrong Nak target, missing Ack)
In a PEX trace: Visible Flit sequence numbers and the Ack/Nak information in DLP bytes are decoded by Flit-aware analyzers. Look for replays without a preceding CRC failure, Naks naming a Flit that was received correctly, the same Flit replayed many times, or a gap in sequence numbers of new Flits.
What happens: Flit mode keeps an Ack/Nak replay protocol at Flit granularity. Public material mentions optimisations such as not replaying Flits that carry only NOP content and replaying only the failed Flit uncertain . Implementation bugs in this new protocol show as unnecessary replays or, in the worst case, lost TLPs.
How it shows up: Mostly bandwidth loss and latency. Errors that break the protocol are expected to be reported as Data Link Protocol errors or similar uncorrectable errors verify in spec .
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification 6.0 and later, Flit sequence numbers, Ack/Nak in Flit mode, replay rules.
Typical causes: Early silicon and IP bugs, retimer handling of Flit replay, interaction with L0p (partial-width power state) transitions uncertain .
How to detect / prove: Per direction, list new Flit sequence numbers and replays. Pair each Nak with the CRC-failed Flit it refers to. A Nak with no CRC failure seen by the analyzer is either a receiver bug or an analyzer miss: check lane errors at that moment.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c ("DLP" for protocol errors).
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: Gen6 exerciser injecting CRC errors in chosen Flits and checking the DUT's replay choices.

name: Flit mode or top speed not negotiated: link runs in non-Flit mode or below 64 GT/s
In a PEX trace: Visible In training ordered sets, each side advertises its supported data rates and Flit-mode support. The trace shows who did not advertise it, or at which equalization step the attempt to reach 64 GT/s failed and the link fell back.
What happens: Both ends must support Flit mode for it to be used, and 64 GT/s requires it. A missing capability bit, a firmware setting or an equalization failure leaves a Gen6 SSD running at Gen5 or lower.
How it shows up: lspci -vvv LnkSta speed below LnkCap; Linux v7.2 prints available bandwidth and whether the link is in Flit mode; PCI_EXP_FLAGS_FLIT (Flit Mode Supported) and PCI_EXP_LNKSTA2_FLIT (Flit Mode Status).
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification 6.0 and later, training ordered-set fields for Flit mode, PCI Express Capabilities register Flit Mode Supported, Link Status 2 Flit Mode Status.
Typical causes: One side lacks support, a disabled Flit mode in firmware or BIOS, a retimer in between that does not support it, equalization failure at 64 GT/s ( X-13 ).
How to detect / prove: Capture training from reset and read both sides' advertisements. Compare with config-space capability bits read by software.
Linux v7.2 source: include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h : PCI_EXP_FLAGS_FLIT , PCI_EXP_LNKSTA2_FLIT ; drivers/pci/pci.c : __pcie_print_link_status .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: compare behaviour with and without a retimer/riser; record training each time.

name: Error-message storm on the wire: ERR_COR / ERR_NONFATAL / ERR_FATAL messages
In a PEX trace: Visible Upstream Message TLPs from the SSD with error-message codes (ERR_COR 30h, ERR_NONFATAL 31h, ERR_FATAL 33h). Their rate and timing, relative to physical and link events just before them, show which event the SSD reported. If the host reads the SSD's AER registers during the capture, the config-read completions show which status bits were set.
What happens: An endpoint that detects an error and has reporting enabled sends an error message to the Root Port. A link with constant correctable errors produces a steady stream of ERR_COR messages and AER interrupts on the host.
How it shows up: On the host: AER interrupts, rate-limited dmesg lines, counters in sysfs. Sometimes a message storm costs measurable CPU time.
Spec basis: PCIe Base Specification, error signalling with messages; Device Control error-reporting enables; AER.
Typical causes: Any of the physical or link-layer problems in this part, or device-internal correctable errors (Corrected Internal Error).
How to detect / prove: Count error messages per second in the trace. For each, look back for the triggering event in the opposite direction (errors in TLPs the SSD received). If there is no visible trigger, the error is internal to the SSD or on its receive side below what the analyzer decoded.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c : aer_irq , aer_isr_one_error , aer_ratelimit . See Chapter 20 .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: run a workload on a link with known correctable errors and correlate trace message counts with sysfs counters.

name: Probe or interposer signal-integrity effects (errors caused or hidden by the tap)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Visible: errors flagged by the analyzer. Not visible: whether the link partners saw them. Tell-tale sign of an analyzer-only error: a TLP flagged with a bad LCRC that the receiver Acks with no replay, or symbol errors with no Nak, no Recovery and no AER counter change.
What happens: Two cases. (a) The interposer adds loss or reflections, so the real link gets worse: more errors, lower speed, extra Recovery, only while the probe is installed. (b) The analyzer's own receiver decodes worse than the link partners: the trace shows errors the link does not have.
How it shows up: Case (a): real AER counts and speed changes that disappear without the interposer. Case (b): nothing on the system.
Spec basis: None directly. The spec defines link-partner behaviour, not probes. Use the link-layer reaction rules (Nak on bad LCRC) as the test.
Typical causes: Gen4+ rates through an interposer without redriving; long or damaged probe cables; an interposer for a different form factor revision; analyzer equalization settings that do not match the link.
How to detect / prove: A/B test: the same workload with and without the interposer, comparing AER counters at both ends and LnkSta. In the trace, check the partner's reaction to every flagged error. Classify each error as "confirmed by partner" or "analyzer-only".
Linux v7.2 source: Counters for the A/B comparison: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c sysfs attribute aer_dev_correctable .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: swap interposer cables or slots and repeat the capture; compare error counts.

name: Analyzer re-lock after electrical idle or speed change: lost or garbled first packets
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Bursts of symbol, disparity or sync-header errors on all lanes at once, immediately after an EIEOS/FTS sequence, an L1 exit or a speed change, followed by clean traffic. Or the first TLP after idle missing, while the partner Acks a sequence number the analyzer never saw.
What happens: After electrical idle, every receiver must regain bit, symbol or block lock. The link partners are given training sequences for this. The analyzer, tapping passively, may need longer, especially after a speed change where it must also follow the new rate and equalization. While it re-locks it either drops data or decodes garbage.
How it shows up: Nothing on the system.
Spec basis: None for the analyzer. Link partners follow the L0s/L1/Recovery rules.
Typical causes: Aggressive ASPM (frequent L1 entry/exit), short N_FTS for L0s, analyzer not set to follow speed changes, missing capture of the equalization phase.
How to detect / prove: Check sequence numbers across the idle exit: if the partner's Ack covers numbers that the trace never shows, the analyzer lost packets. Errors confined to the first few hundred nanoseconds after every exit, on all lanes, with no Nak, are re-lock artifacts. Disable ASPM and re-capture to confirm.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aspm.c (ASPM policy that causes the idle transitions).
Test to provoke it: SAFE: capture a lightly loaded link with ASPM L1 enabled, then with it disabled, and compare error flags.

name: Analyzer setup errors: wrong lane map, polarity, speed, clocking or descrambler state
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Systematic nonsense: every packet flagged, impossible TLP headers, framing errors at the same lane boundary every time, ordered sets decoded correctly but data garbled (descrambler not synchronised), or a deskew failure the device clearly does not have (the link runs with no AER errors).
What happens: The analyzer must be told, or must learn, the link's width, lane order, polarity, data rate, clocking mode (common clock, SRNS, SRIS) and, for Gen3+, the scrambler and equalization state. If the capture starts after training, some state cannot be learned from the wire. Its deskew limits may also be tighter than the device's.
How it shows up: Nothing on the system.
Spec basis: None for the analyzer. Lane reversal, polarity and scrambling rules are in the PCIe Base Specification Physical Layer.
Typical causes: Interposer with reversed lanes not configured in the analyzer; capture started mid-traffic at Gen3+; wrong speed selected; spread-spectrum clocking not configured.
How to detect / prove: Re-capture from link training (reset or hot-plug) with automatic link-configuration detection enabled if the analyzer has it. If the errors disappear, they were setup artifacts. A real link with that many errors would not run without AER reports and retraining.
Linux v7.2 source: Not applicable. Use lspci -vvv LnkSta and AER counters to show the real link is healthy.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: deliberately set a wrong lane order in the analyzer on a known-good link to learn what the artifact looks like.

name: Capture gaps, buffer wrap and hardware filters that fake a "missing" packet
In a PEX trace: Partly visible A request with no completion, a CQE with no SQE fetch, no Ack/Nak at all, or no UpdateFC for a long time, where the real cause is that the analyzer did not store it. Signs: a gap in timestamps with no traffic in either direction, an Ack covering sequence numbers that never appear, a trace-start or wrap marker, filter settings that exclude DLLPs or completions.
What happens: Hardware filters drop items before storage. Ring buffers overwrite the oldest data until the trigger. Some analyzers pause storage while the buffer is uploaded or when the internal bandwidth is exceeded impl . The trace then shows an absence that did not happen on the wire.
How it shows up: Nothing on the system. The risk is a false report: "completion timeout", "missing interrupt", "credit starvation".
Spec basis: None for the analyzer. Before claiming any timing violation from an absence (for example a Completion Timeout, L-14 ), prove the window had no gaps.
Typical causes: Aggressive filtering to stretch capture time, too-small pre-trigger, buffer full at high link utilisation.
How to detect / prove: Use sequence numbers as a continuity check. In each direction, new TLP sequence numbers must be continuous (X-17). Ack numbers in the other direction must refer to TLPs present in the trace. A jump with no Nak and no error means the capture, not the link, lost data. Write the filter settings into every report.
Linux v7.2 source: Not applicable. Host-side logs ( dmesg , NVMe timeouts from nvme_timeout in drivers/nvme/host/pci.c ) show whether the host really saw a timeout.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: capture the same workload with and without DLLP filtering and compare what analysis rules report.

name: SQ tail doorbell value beyond queue size
In a PEX trace: Visible Doorbell MWr (host→device, 4 B) to BAR0 + 1000h + 2y·(4<<DSTRD) whose data ≥ QSIZE+1 taken from the captured Create I/O SQ command; afterwards no SQE-fetch MRd from that SQ. A resulting async event is visible as a 16-byte CQE MWr to the admin CQ only if an AER command was outstanding.
What happens: The host writes an SQ y Tail Doorbell with a value ≥ the number of entries of that SQ (for example tail = 70 on a 64-entry queue). The value cannot be a slot index.
How it shows up: The controller ignores the write. If an Asynchronous Event Request is outstanding it may post an Error-type async event "Invalid Doorbell Write Value" and log an entry in the Error Information log. If no AER is outstanding, nothing is reported — commands placed in the SQ are simply never fetched and later time out.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: SQ Tail Doorbell register semantics; asynchronous event information "Invalid Doorbell Write Value" (Error event type). QEMU quotes the rule from NVMe 1.3d in nvme_process_db : "If host software writes an invalid value to the Submission Queue Tail Doorbell or Completion Queue Head Doorbell register and an Asynchronous Event Request command is outstanding, then an asynchronous event is posted…".
Typical causes: Host driver modulo bug (wrap at 2 n instead of queue size); queue resized by a Create I/O SQ with a different QSIZE than the driver uses (QSIZE is 0's based); memory corruption of the driver's tail variable; a user-space driver (SPDK-style) with a stale queue configuration after reset.
How to detect / prove: Checker rule: for each doorbell MWr, decode queue id from offset and compare the value against the QSIZE+1 seen in the Create I/O SQ command (or AQA.ASQS+1 for the admin queue). On Linux, look for nvme_async_event trace events and nvme error-log entries; Linux v7.2 records the result in ctrl->aen_result .
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_write_sq_db writes nvmeq->sq_tail , which nvme_sq_copy_cmd wraps at nvmeq->q_depth ; drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_complete_async_event handles NVME_AER_ERROR .
Test to provoke it: On QEMU (SAFE): use a user-space driver or nvme-cli is not enough — write the doorbell with a raw BAR mapping of an emulated device and watch the QEMU trace event pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_sqtail . On real hardware this is EXPERT: an unbound device, a vfio-based test harness, and an AER posted beforehand.

name: CQ head doorbell value beyond queue size
In a PEX trace: Visible Doorbell MWr to BAR0 + 1000h + (2y+1)·(4<<DSTRD) with data ≥ CQ size; later SQE fetches continue but CQE MWr on that CQ stop after N−1 entries — the "device went quiet" pattern.
What happens: The host writes a CQ y Head Doorbell with a value ≥ the CQ size. The controller cannot interpret how many entries were released.
How it shows up: Write ignored; optional Error async event "Invalid Doorbell Write Value". Because the head is not advanced, the controller eventually sees the CQ as full and stops posting completions: all I/O on every SQ that shares that CQ stalls and then times out.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: CQ Head Doorbell semantics; same asynchronous event as V-01.
