Typical causes: Host increments head past the end instead of wrapping; head computed in bytes instead of entries; CQ created with fewer entries than the driver assumes.
How to detect / prove: Same checker rule as V-01, against the CQ size from Create I/O CQ (QSIZE+1) or AQA.ACQS+1. Correlate: after the bad doorbell, CQE MWr count on that CQ stops at exactly size−1 outstanding entries.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_update_cq_head wraps cq_head at q_depth and flips cq_phase ; nvme_ring_cq_doorbell writes it.
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): raw doorbell write of size+2 on an idle CQ; observe pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_cqhead and, with an AER outstanding, an async event on the admin CQ.

name: Doorbell write for a queue that does not exist
In a PEX trace: Visible Doorbell MWr to an offset whose queue id was never created in the captured admin traffic, or written after the Delete I/O SQ/CQ completion; no fetch MRd follows. Requires the capture to include queue creation (start it before the driver loads, or decode CAP.DSTRD and Create commands from an earlier capture).
What happens: The host writes a doorbell offset belonging to a queue id that was never created, was already deleted, or exceeds the number of queues granted by Set Features Number of Queues.
How it shows up: Ignored by the controller; optional Error async event "Invalid Doorbell Register". QEMU's comment notes that the spec defines this code but "nowhere does it specify when to use it", and QEMU uses it for non-existent queues — so other controllers may report it differently or not at all. impl
Spec basis: NVMe Base: doorbell register layout (1000h + (2y)·(4<<CAP.DSTRD)); asynchronous event information "Invalid Doorbell Register".
Typical causes: Wrong CAP.DSTRD (doorbell stride) used by the host, so every doorbell lands on the wrong queue; queue deleted while another CPU still submits; use-after-teardown during reset; SR-IOV VF using PF queue numbering.
How to detect / prove: Checker keeps the set of live SQ/CQ ids from Create/Delete I/O SQ/CQ commands and their successful CQEs; any doorbell outside the set is flagged. A wrong stride shows as doorbells at offsets that are not multiples of 4<<DSTRD apart.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_create_queue sets up per-queue q_db pointers from dev->db_stride ; teardown paths in nvme_dev_disable .
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): write SQ tail doorbell of queue id conf_ioqpairs+1; QEMU trace pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_sq . A synthetic example appears as rule DB-NOQ in 7.6 .

name: Misaligned or partial doorbell write
In a PEX trace: Visible MWr in the doorbell region with Length ≠ 1 DW, byte enables ≠ Fh, or a 2-DW write spanning SQ tail and CQ head of one pair.
What happens: A doorbell is written with a 1- or 2-byte access, or at an address that is not dword aligned, or a 64-bit write spans two doorbells (SQ tail and CQ head of the same pair).
How it shows up: Nothing is reported. QEMU logs a guest-error trace ( pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_misaligned ) and ignores the write; real controllers may ignore, latch only some bytes, or update both doorbells. impl
Spec basis: NVMe Base: controller registers are accessed with their natural width; doorbells are 32-bit registers. Accesses of other sizes are outside the defined behaviour.
Typical causes: Compiler merging two adjacent 32-bit stores into one 64-bit store on a write-combining mapping; a user-space driver using memcpy to MMIO; byte-wise BAR access tools.
How to detect / prove: Checker: doorbell MWr whose length ≠ 4 bytes, whose first/last byte enables are not 1111b, or whose address is not 4-byte aligned.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_write_sq_db and nvme_ring_cq_doorbell use writel (32-bit).
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): 16-bit write to a doorbell; check QEMU trace output.

name: SQ tail moves backwards or overruns unfetched entries
In a PEX trace: Visible Sequence of SQ tail doorbell values that implies more than N−1 unfetched entries (or a "backwards" move), compared with the SQE-fetch MRd/CplD count and SQHD in CQEs; re-fetched slots whose 64 bytes equal an already-completed SQE.
What happens: The new SQ tail value implies either a negative number of new entries (tail moved "backwards", i.e. the host withdrew entries) or so many new entries that the SQ would hold ≥ N items — the host has overwritten SQEs the controller had not yet fetched.
How it shows up: Nothing reported: the value is in range, so V-01 does not fire. Modulo arithmetic hides the problem — a backwards move looks like "N−k new commands". Consequences range from duplicated commands (the controller re-executes stale SQEs from a previous pass, e.g. a stale Write re-writes old data) to lost commands that time out.
Spec basis: NVMe Base queue model: the host shall not submit to a full SQ (full = tail+1 == head); entries between head and tail are owned by the controller and must not be modified by the host. The host learns the head from SQHD in CQEs.
Typical causes: Two CPUs submitting to one SQ without a lock; driver uses CQ depth for flow control while CQ is shared by several SQs; SQHD ignored and SQ larger than outstanding-request budget assumed; a reset path that zeroes the driver's tail but not the controller's.
How to detect / prove: Checker: keep host tail T, controller head H (from the most recent SQHD and from observed fetches); for a new tail T', new = (T'−T) mod N; flag if new > (N−1) − ((T−H) mod N). Also flag if the data of a re-fetched slot is identical to an already-completed SQE (stale replay).
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_sq_copy_cmd under nvmeq->sq_lock ; nvme_commit_rqs rings only when sq_tail != last_sq_tail . Linux sizes SQ and CQ identically and limits outstanding requests via blk-mq tags, so it does not need SQHD for flow control (it only passes it to trace_nvme_sq ).
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): QEMU does not check this (see 7.1.3) — write tail values out of order and observe re-executed commands; a good negative test for your checker.

name: CQ head released past the controller's tail
In a PEX trace: Visible CQ head doorbell value ahead of the number of 16-byte CQE MWr written to that CQ since the previous head.
What happens: The host writes a CQ head that releases more entries than the controller has posted. The controller now believes there is free space that actually contains its own future slots; its full/empty calculation is corrupted.
How it shows up: No status. Later the controller may overwrite CQEs the host has not yet consumed (because it thinks they were released), producing lost completions (timeouts) or, combined with phase-tag reuse, stale completions processed twice.
Spec basis: NVMe Base queue model: the host releases only entries it has consumed (entries with the current phase).
Typical causes: Host consumes entries by index without checking the phase tag (polling bug); host and controller disagree on CQ size; a missed wrap in the host.
How to detect / prove: Checker counts CQE MWr per CQ (device tail) and compares every CQ head doorbell: released = (H'−H) mod N must be ≤ (Tail−H) mod N. Rule CQDB-PAST-TAIL in 7.6 .
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_poll_cq consumes entries only while nvme_cqe_pending (phase match) and rings the head once, after the loop.
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE) with a test harness: post one command, write CQ head = 3. QEMU will not complain; your checker should.

name: CQ overflow: head not advancing, or controller posts into a full CQ
In a PEX trace: Visible (a) N−1 CQE MWr then no CQ head doorbell for a long time; (b) a CQE MWr to the slot just before the current head. Timeout is visible only as absence plus timestamps (a fetched command with no CQE within the host timeout).
What happens: Two variants. (a) The host stops advancing the CQ head (interrupt lost, CPU stuck, driver bug); the CQ fills to N−1 entries and the controller must stop posting — I/O stalls. (b) The controller posts while the CQ is full, overwriting an entry the host has not consumed.
How it shows up: (a) Only the host's I/O timeout, often with Linux "completion polled" if the CQE was actually there (see V-15). (b) Nothing; the overwritten completion is lost and its command times out; the overwriting entry may carry the "wrong" phase from the host's point of view.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: CQ full condition (head == tail+1); the controller does not post to a full CQ and the host is responsible for sizing CQs so that the commands that can be outstanding on its SQs fit. QEMU nvme_post_cqes breaks out of its loop when nvme_cq_full .
Typical causes: (a) Missing MSI-X (V-15), interrupt affinity to an offline CPU, softirq starvation. (b) Controller firmware not tracking the CQ head doorbell; several SQs mapped to one small CQ.
How to detect / prove: Checker: keep CQ tail (count of CQE writes) and head (doorbells); flag a CQE write when (tail+1) mod N == head. For (a), flag "CQ head unchanged for X ms while CQ non-empty".
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_timeout polls the CQ first and prints "I/O tag %d (%04x) QID %d timeout, completion polled" when the CQE was present.
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): issue N commands while never writing the CQ head; verify QEMU stops at N−1 CQEs. On hardware, the (b) variant needs an analyzer to prove.

name: Command Identifier reused while still outstanding
In a PEX trace: Visible Two SQE-fetch CplDs on the same SQ carrying the same CID (DW0 bits 31:16) with no CQE MWr for that CID between them.
What happens: The host submits a command whose CID equals that of a command still outstanding on the same SQ. Completions become ambiguous: the host cannot tell which of the two finished, and Abort (which names SQID+CID) becomes ambiguous too.
How it shows up: Usually nothing. A controller may detect it and complete the new command with Generic status 03h "Command ID Conflict" (Linux NVME_SC_CMDID_CONFLICT ); many controllers do not check. QEMU does not check (its nvme_abort would match the first request with that CID). impl
Spec basis: NVMe Base: the Command Identifier together with the SQ Identifier uniquely identifies a command outstanding at the controller; Generic Command Status "Command ID Conflict".
Typical causes: Host reusing a tag before its completion was processed; driver completing a request on timeout and reusing the tag while the controller still owns the original; user-space drivers with fixed CIDs.
How to detect / prove: Checker keeps the outstanding set per SQ: add (SQID,CID) on SQE fetch, remove on CQE. Flag duplicates (rule CID-REUSE in 7.6). Linux encodes a 4-bit generation counter into the top bits of the CID, so a reused tag normally has a different CID — a duplicate in a Linux trace is strong evidence of a real bug.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/nvme.h:nvme_cid = nvme_cid_install_genctr(genctr) | rq->tag ; nvme_find_rq checks the generation counter.
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE) user-space harness: submit two long reads with the same CID; verify the checker flags it; on hardware, check whether the controller returns status 03h.

name: CQE for an unknown or already-completed CID
In a PEX trace: Visible A CQE MWr whose DW3 CID matches no earlier SQE fetch on that SQ, or matches a CID that already completed. The host's "invalid id" log line is NOT in the trace.
What happens: The controller writes a completion whose CID matches no outstanding command on that SQ — a duplicate completion, a corrupted CID, or a completion for a command the host already aborted/timed out.
How it shows up: Linux v7.2 logs "invalid id %d completed on queue %d" (or "request %#x genctr mismatch (got … expected …)") and drops the entry. Other drivers may complete the wrong request — a silent data-integrity hazard (the wrong buffer is declared ready).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: each command is completed exactly once by one CQE identifying it by SQID+CID.
Typical causes: Controller firmware posting a completion twice (retry path); CQE corrupted in flight (bit flip in DRAM or a poisoned TLP ignored); host timeout handling that freed the tag while the command was still executing.
How to detect / prove: Checker rule CQE-UNKNOWN. In Linux, grep dmesg for "invalid id" and "genctr mismatch". A trace distinguishes "duplicate" (CID seen in an earlier CQE) from "never submitted" (CID never fetched).
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_handle_cqe ; drivers/nvme/host/nvme.h:nvme_find_rq .
Test to provoke it: QEMU fault injection is not built in; use a modified QEMU or an FPGA/emulator that duplicates a CQE (EXPERT). In the synthetic example, CID 0x99 triggers it.

name: Wrong SQID or non-advancing SQHD in a CQE
In a PEX trace: Visible CQE MWr whose DW2 SQID differs from the queue the CID was fetched from, or whose SQHD sequence does not advance while SQE fetches proceed.
What happens: The CQE's SQ Identifier (DW2 bits 31:16) names a different SQ than the one the command came from, or SQ Head Pointer (DW2 bits 15:0) moves backwards, beyond the tail, or never advances although commands are being consumed.
How it shows up: With a shared CQ, a wrong SQID makes the host look up the CID in the wrong SQ — wrong request completed or "invalid id". A frozen SQHD makes a host that uses SQHD for flow control believe the SQ is full: throughput collapses to zero without any error. Linux, which does not use SQHD for flow control, is unaffected — so the same SSD "works on Linux, hangs on another OS".
Spec basis: NVMe Base: CQE DW2 SQID and SQHD semantics — SQHD indicates the current SQ head pointer for the SQ named by SQID.
Typical causes: Firmware filling SQHD from a stale variable; CQE template reused across queues; SQHD reported before the fetch actually advanced the head.
How to detect / prove: Checker: SQID must equal the SQ the CID was fetched from; SQHD must satisfy (SQHD − previous SQHD) mod N ≤ number of fetches since, and must never pass the host tail.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_handle_cqe passes cqe->sq_head to trace_nvme_sq only and uses cqe->sq_id in the "invalid id" message.
Test to provoke it: Use a driver that honours SQHD (e.g. a user-space test harness) and an SQ much smaller than the outstanding-command budget; a broken SQHD will deadlock it quickly.

name: Phase tag not inverted on CQ wrap
In a PEX trace: Visible CQE MWr to slot 0 after a wrap carrying the same phase bit as the previous pass (decode bit 16 of DW3 / bit 0 of the status half).
What happens: After the controller wraps from the last CQ slot to slot 0 it must invert the Phase Tag (P, bit 0 of the status half of DW3). If it keeps the old value, the host — which expects the new phase — sees the new entry as "old" and does not consume it; if it inverts too early, the host consumes stale entries.
How it shows up: Missing inversion: completions invisible to the host → I/O timeout (Linux may report "completion polled" only if the phase matches; here it does not, so a plain timeout and abort/reset follow). Early inversion: stale CQEs processed twice → "invalid id" messages or double completion.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Phase Tag "identifies whether a completion queue entry is new"; it is inverted each pass through the CQ; host initialises the CQ memory to zero so the first pass uses P=1.
Typical causes: Firmware wrap logic off by one; CQ size mismatch between host and controller; controller reset without the host re-zeroing CQ memory.
How to detect / prove: Checker keeps tail and expected phase per CQ (start 1, invert at wrap) and compares every CQE (rule PHASE in 7.6). Note that a phase error is often the symptom of an earlier V-07(b) overflow; always report the first abnormal event.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_cqe_pending compares status & 1 with nvmeq->cq_phase ; nvme_update_cq_head flips cq_phase at wrap.
Test to provoke it: Run enough I/O to wrap a small CQ many times (e.g. io_queue_depth=2 module parameter — the minimum Linux accepts — on a test system, SAFE) and verify no phase findings in the capture.

name: Shadow doorbell buffer out of sync with the MMIO doorbell
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Controller MRd of the shadow-doorbell buffer and the CplD values it returns are visible, as are MMIO doorbells; the host's own writes to the shadow buffer are CPU-to-DRAM and never cross the link. Only a mismatch between returned shadow values and later MMIO doorbells can be shown.
What happens: With the Doorbell Buffer Config admin command (used mainly by emulated/virtual controllers), the host writes doorbell values into a shadow buffer in host memory and only rings the real MMIO doorbell when the controller's EventIdx says so. If the host updates one but not the other, or ignores EventIdx, the controller works from a stale tail/head.
How it shows up: Stalls that recover when any later doorbell is rung; latency spikes; no error. QEMU's nvme_process_db comments that "various drivers including ones that run on Linux, are not updating Admin Queues" in the shadow buffer, so QEMU writes the admin values back itself. impl
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Doorbell Buffer Config command — Shadow Doorbell buffer and EventIdx buffer; QEMU quotes "the host shall also update the controller's corresponding doorbell property to match the value of that entry in the Shadow Doorbell buffer".
Typical causes: Missing memory barrier between the shadow write and the EventIdx read; admin queue excluded from shadowing in the driver; migration of a VM between hosts.
How to detect / prove: In a VM, the "trace" is QEMU's own tracing ( pci_nvme_* events) or a vhost/vfio capture. Compare shadow value reads (DMA reads of the shadow buffer) with MMIO doorbells.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_dbbuf_update_and_check_event , called from nvme_write_sq_db and nvme_ring_cq_doorbell .
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): enable shadow doorbells (they are used automatically when the controller supports the command) and stress small-queue workloads while tracing pci_nvme_mmio_doorbell_sq .

name: Completion posted before the data writes (ordering)
In a PEX trace: Visible CQE MWr for CID X timestamped before the last data MWr whose address lies in CID X's PRP/SGL ranges (decoded from the SQE and PRP-list CplDs); or RO=1 in the CQE TLP attributes. This proves the order the device sent; whether a switch reordered further upstream needs a second probe.
What happens: For a Read, the controller writes the CQE (or sets RO on data or CQE TLPs in a way that lets the CQE overtake) before all data MWr TLPs for that command have been sent. The host sees "success", hands the buffer to the application, and the application reads stale bytes; the real data arrives microseconds later, after the application has already used the buffer.
How it shows up: Nothing in any log. Symptoms are intermittent data corruption that disappears when tracing is enabled (timing changes) and checksum failures at the application level, typically on the last TLP(s) of a transfer.
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: ordering rules for posted requests (a posted request must not pass another posted request unless RO is set) and the Relaxed Ordering attribute; NVMe Base: a completion indicates the command's data transfer is complete.
Typical causes: Controller DMA engine with several parallel channels and the CQE sent from a different channel; RO set on the CQE write; a switch or root complex that reorders RO TLPs (legally) combined with the device setting RO where it must not.
How to detect / prove: Checker: map each data MWr to its CID (address ∈ the command's PRP/SGL ranges); at each CQE, require delivered bytes == transfer length (rule CQE-BEFORE-DATA in 7.6). Also flag RO=1 on any CQE or MSI-X TLP. Prove at the application level with fio --verify=crc32c --verify_fatal=1 on reads of data written earlier.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_poll_cq issues dma_rmb() between the phase check and reading the rest of the CQE — this protects against CPU reordering of the CQE fields, not against a device that wrote the CQE too early. Relaxed ordering enable bit: include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h:PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_RELAX_EN .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: toggle Device Control "Enable Relaxed Ordering" with setpci on an idle test device and run a verify workload with an analyzer attached; never on a system with data you care about.

name: MSI-X sent before the CQE it announces
In a PEX trace: Visible MWr to the MSI-X message address (vector identified from the captured MSI-X table writes) with no preceding CQE MWr on a CQ mapped to that vector, or the CQE MWr arriving after it.
What happens: The interrupt MWr reaches the host before the CQE MWr (or there is no new CQE at all). The interrupt handler polls the CQ, finds nothing with the expected phase, and returns.
How it shows up: Spurious interrupts: Linux nvme_irq returns IRQ_NONE ; if this happens very often the kernel's spurious-interrupt detector can disable the IRQ line ("nobody cared"), after which completions are found only by the timeout handler — then V-07(a) and "completion polled" messages. Before that point: extra latency, because the real CQE waits for the next interrupt.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: interrupts are generated for new CQ entries; PCI Express Base posted-write ordering ensures the MSI-X MWr cannot pass the earlier CQE MWr if the device sends them in order without RO.
Typical causes: Interrupt sent from a different internal engine than the CQE; interrupt coalescing logic counting submissions instead of completions; RO set on the MSI-X write.
How to detect / prove: Checker rule MSIX-NO-CQE: each MSI-X for vector v must be preceded by at least one new CQE on a CQ mapped to v since the previous MSI-X. On Linux, compare per-vector counts in /proc/interrupts with completions; spurious counts show in /proc/irq/<n>/spurious .
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_irq (returns IRQ_NONE when nvme_poll_cq finds nothing), nvme_irq_check for threaded interrupts.
Test to provoke it: Device-side bug; to validate the checker, use the synthetic trace in 7.6 (line with MSI-X at t=1500 ns).

name: CQE posted but no MSI-X ever sent
In a PEX trace: Visible CQE MWr followed by no MSI-X MWr for that vector; the host's MSI-X table/PBA MMIO writes and reads are on the link too, so a mask bit set by the host is visible. The eventual timeout appears only as a long gap, then Abort or controller reset traffic.
What happens: The controller writes a CQE but never sends the interrupt (vector masked in the MSI-X table, wrong vector programmed in Create I/O CQ, function-mask bit set, or firmware bug).
How it shows up: Linux v7.2: the request times out; nvme_timeout polls the CQ, finds the completion and prints "I/O tag … QID … timeout, completion polled" — the signature of a lost interrupt. Latency equals the timeout (default 30 s for I/O).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Create I/O Completion Queue Interrupt Vector (IV) and Interrupts Enabled (IEN) fields; PCI MSI-X table and Pending Bit Array semantics (a masked vector sets its pending bit instead of sending).
Typical causes: MSI-X vector masked during CPU hotplug or IRQ migration and never unmasked; IV out of range of the MSI-X table size; interrupt remapping (IOMMU) misconfiguration so the write is blocked.
How to detect / prove: Checker: CQE written, no MSI-X for the vector within a window (e.g. 1 ms) while IEN=1 for that CQ. Host-side: "completion polled" in dmesg; read the MSI-X PBA through the BAR (read-only inspection) to see pending bits.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_timeout ; vector assignment in nvme_create_queue / queue_irq_offset .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: mask a vector in the MSI-X table of a test device during I/O; expect "completion polled" and recovery.

name: DMA to a command's buffer after its completion
In a PEX trace: Visible Data MWr/MRd into CID X's buffer range after the CQE MWr for CID X. An IOMMU fault caused by it is host-side and not in the trace.
What happens: The controller writes to (or reads from) host memory belonging to a command after it has posted that command's CQE — for example the tail of the data for a read, or a retry of a data read for a write. By then the host may have freed or reused the buffer.
How it shows up: Random memory corruption elsewhere in the system (the page has been reallocated), IOMMU faults if the mapping was torn down (DMAR/AMD-Vi fault messages in dmesg naming the device), or nothing at all.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: posting the completion transfers ownership of the data buffers back to the host; PRP/SGL entries are valid only while the command is outstanding.
Typical causes: Same as V-13 (parallel DMA channels); Abort handling that completes the command while a DMA is still queued; firmware retry after timeout.
How to detect / prove: Checker rule DMA-NOCMD: any data MWr/MRd whose address belongs to a command that has already completed (and no newer command owns that address). With an IOMMU in strict mode, a late DMA produces a translation fault — strong host-side evidence.
Linux v7.2 source: Unmapping on completion in drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_pci_complete_rq / nvme_pci_complete_batch .
Test to provoke it: Boot a test host with iommu.strict=1 (or the platform equivalent) and run high-QD mixed I/O; any IOMMU fault naming the SSD is a finding to correlate with a trace.

name: PRP1 not dword aligned, or PRP list entry with an offset
In a PEX trace: Visible SQE CplD with PRP1 bits 1:0 ≠ 0, or the PRP-list read (device MRd from PRP2, answered by CplD) returning entries with non-zero low bits; then either a CQE with status 13h or data MWr at odd addresses.
What happens: PRP1 has bits 1:0 set, or an entry inside a PRP list (other than as allowed for the list pointer) has a non-zero page offset.
How it shows up: A checking controller completes the command with Generic status 13h "PRP Offset Invalid" (Linux NVME_SC_PRP_INVALID_OFFSET ), usually with DNR. A non-checking controller DMAs to the wrong address — silent corruption of unrelated memory.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: PRP Entry format (offset field; dword alignment), PRP List rules; Generic Command Status "PRP Offset Invalid".
Typical causes: Host builds PRPs from CPU page size (e.g. 16 KiB or 64 KiB pages on arm64/ppc64) while the controller is configured with CC.MPS = 4 KiB, or vice versa; byte-granular user buffers passed through a passthrough interface.
How to detect / prove: Checker: decode DPTR, fetch the PRP list via the MRd/CplD that follows, and test each entry against the rules in the table above. Host-side: nvme error-log shows status 13h with the CID and SQID.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_pci_setup_data_prp builds PRP1 from the first segment's offset and list entries with NVME_CTRL_PAGE_SIZE stride; dma_set_min_align_mask(&pdev->dev, NVME_CTRL_PAGE_SIZE - 1) in probe keeps bounce buffers page-offset-preserving.
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): passthrough command with a crafted PRP list; expect status 13h and QEMU trace pci_nvme_err_invalid_prplist_ent .

name: Offset in PRP2 when it is a data pointer
In a PEX trace: Visible 8 KiB command with PRP1 = …1000h and PRP2 = …0010h, no PRP-list MRd, then a CQE with status 13h — or, for a lenient controller, data MWr starting at …0010h.
What happens: The transfer needs exactly two pages (the remainder after PRP1's page fits in one page), so PRP2 is a data pointer; it must point at the start of a page but contains an offset.
How it shows up: Status 13h PRP Offset Invalid with DNR (QEMU and checking controllers). A lenient controller writes the second part of the data to PRP2 including the offset and then across the next page boundary — corrupting the neighbouring page.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: PRP Entry 2 semantics — data pointer vs PRP List pointer — and the zero-offset requirement for PRP entries other than PRP1 and the list pointer.
Typical causes: Host confusing "two-page transfer" with "list" case; off-by-one in computing whether the remainder fits in one page (e.g. using < instead of ≤).
How to detect / prove: Checker rule PRP2-OFFSET in 7.6: compute first = page − (PRP1 mod page) ; if first < len ≤ first + page then PRP2 mod page must be 0.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_pci_setup_data_prp (the length <= NVME_CTRL_PAGE_SIZE branch places the second page directly in PRP2).
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): passthrough read of 8 KiB with PRP2 offset 10h; expect pci_nvme_err_invalid_prp2_align and status 13h.

name: PRP list crossing or chaining rules broken
In a PEX trace: Visible PRP-list MRd that spans a page boundary, or a data MWr to an address that should have been the next-list pointer; compare described bytes (from list CplDs) with the command length.
What happens: The PRP list is laid out so that entries run past the end of the memory page that holds the list without using the last entry as a pointer to the next list page; or the last entry is used as a data pointer when more entries follow; or the list has fewer entries than the transfer needs.
How it shows up: The controller interprets a data page address as a list pointer (or vice versa): DMA to/from wrong memory, a Data Transfer Error (04h) if the access fails, or 13h when the misinterpreted entry happens to have an offset. Often silent.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: PRP List — a list occupies one memory page; when more entries are required, the last entry in the page is a pointer to the next PRP list.
Typical causes: List allocated from a pool not aligned to the controller page; driver computing entries per page from CPU page size; list allocated at an offset with the "entries per page" count not reduced accordingly (QEMU computes nents from the offset precisely because this is legal for the first list).
How to detect / prove: Checker walks the list exactly as nvme_map_prp does and compares the number of data bytes described with the command length (NLB+1 × LBA size, plus metadata if interleaved).
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_pci_setup_data_prp chains when i == NVME_CTRL_PAGE_SIZE >> 3 ; NVME_MAX_NR_DESCRIPTORS (5) at the top of pci.c bounds the number of list pages per request.
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE) user-space harness: 1 MiB transfer with a PRP list starting at offset FF0h of its page and no chaining; observe misbehaviour and whether status 13h is returned.

name: Transfer longer than MDTS
In a PEX trace: Visible SQE whose NLB implies more bytes than 2^MDTS × MPSMIN; MDTS is visible if the Identify Controller data (device MWr of 4 KiB to the host buffer) is in the capture. Then a CQE with status 02h/DNR — or the oversize data transfer followed by success.
What happens: A command transfers more data than Maximum Data Transfer Size allows: MDTS (Identify Controller) is a power of two in units of the minimum memory page size (CAP.MPSMIN); 0 means no limit. MDTS = 5 with 4 KiB MPSMIN → 128 KiB.
How it shows up: QEMU and most controllers: Generic status 02h "Invalid Field in Command" with DNR. Some controllers transfer the data anyway (and may truncate silently).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Identify Controller MDTS field; applies to the data transfer of a command (NVM Command Set defines how it applies to commands like Write Zeroes, which have no data transfer — they have separate limits such as WZSL in the NVM Command Set Identify Controller structure).
Typical causes: Passthrough tools ignoring MDTS; user-space drivers with hard-coded 1 MiB I/O; kernel limits overridden; MDTS reduced by a firmware update while the host cached the old value.
How to detect / prove: Checker rule MDTS in 7.6: (NLB+1)·LBA size (+ metadata if extended LBA) > 2 MDTS ·MPSMIN. Host: nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep mdts and cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/max_hw_sectors_kb .
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_init_identify derives max_hw_sectors from id->mdts via nvme_mps_to_sectors ; nvme_init_non_mdts_limits handles commands without data transfer.
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): -device nvme,mdts=5 then nvme io-passthru a 256 KiB read; expect status 02h and trace pci_nvme_err_mdts .

name: Reserved fields non-zero
In a PEX trace: Visible SQE bytes with reserved bits set (decode against the opcode's field map for the spec revision in VS, which is visible if the host's config/BAR read of VS is captured).
What happens: The host sets bits that are reserved in the SQE (for example CDW0 bits 13:10, CDW2–3 in commands that do not define them, reserved CDW10–15 bits) or in a data structure it passes (feature data, PRP list padding).
How it shows up: Today usually nothing — most controllers ignore reserved bits. Tomorrow, when a newer spec revision gives those bits a meaning, the same host software suddenly enables a feature it never intended (e.g. a bit that later became a "storage tag" or "directive" field). Some controllers return Invalid Field in Command. impl
Spec basis: NVMe Base conventions: reserved fields shall be cleared to 0 by the writer; receivers are generally not required to check. (Verify the exact wording for your revision in the spec.)
Typical causes: Uninitialised SQE memory (stack garbage) in user-space or firmware hosts; copying a command structure from a newer spec header to an older device.
How to detect / prove: Checker with a per-opcode mask of defined bits, generated from the spec revision the device claims in VS; flag any 1 outside the mask. Re-run the check against the masks of the next spec revision to spot "future meaning" hazards.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux builds commands from a zeroed struct nvme_command (e.g. memset(&c, 0, sizeof(c)) in drivers/nvme/host/ioctl.c:nvme_user_cmd ), so reserved fields are zero unless passthrough users set them via CDW fields.
Test to provoke it: SAFE on a scratch namespace: nvme io-passthru a read with a reserved CDW bit set; record whether the controller ignores it or returns 02h — a good conformance data point.

name: FUSE field misuse (fused operations)
In a PEX trace: Visible SQE with FUSE=01b whose partner slot was not made visible by the same doorbell, or is not FUSE=10b; CQEs with status 09h/0Ah.
What happens: FUSE (CDW0 bits 9:8): 01b = first command of a fused pair, 10b = second, 11b reserved. Violations: first without second; second without first; the two not in adjacent SQ slots; a non-fusable opcode (only Compare + Write is defined for the NVM Command Set); fused commands submitted to a controller that does not report support in Identify Controller FUSES; reserved value 11b.
How it shows up: Defined status codes: Generic 09h "Command Aborted due to Failed Fused Command" and 0Ah "Command Aborted due to Missing Fused Command" (Linux NVME_SC_FUSED_FAIL , NVME_SC_FUSED_MISSING ), or 02h Invalid Field. QEMU returns Invalid Field (without DNR) for any FUSE value because it does not implement fused operations.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Fused Operations; Identify Controller FUSES (Fused Operation Support); NVM Command Set: Compare and Write as the fused pair.
Typical causes: Host sets FUSE but the doorbell is rung between the two commands (so the controller fetches only the first); second command placed after a wrap without considering adjacency; garbage in CDW0.
How to detect / prove: Checker: for FUSE=01b at SQ slot k, require FUSE=10b at slot (k+1) mod N in the same doorbell batch; require FUSES bit 0 set; require opcodes 05h then 01h.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux does not issue fused commands (see the comment in drivers/nvme/host/fc.c : "Linux initiators don't send fused"); drivers/nvme/host/ioctl.c:nvme_user_cmd rejects passthrough commands with non-zero flags (-EINVAL), so FUSE/PSDT cannot be set from user space. Strings for 09h/0Ah are in drivers/nvme/host/constants.c .
Test to provoke it: Requires a user-space driver (SPDK-style, CAUTION on a scratch device): submit a lone FUSE=01b Compare; expect 0Ah or 02h.

name: Admin command placed on an I/O queue (or vice versa)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible The SQE with an admin-looking opcode/CDW layout on an I/O SQ is visible, and so is any data or DSM range-list transfer it triggers; whether the device actually wrote or deallocated media is NOT visible — prove that with a read-back.
What happens: Opcodes are interpreted per queue type: SQ 0 carries Admin opcodes; I/O SQs carry I/O command set opcodes. An admin opcode on an I/O queue is not an admin command — it is whatever I/O command shares that opcode value. Admin 01h Create I/O SQ becomes NVM Write ; 02h Get Log Page becomes Read ; 00h Delete I/O SQ becomes Flush ; 09h Set Features becomes Dataset Management (possibly a deallocate!); 06h Identify, 0Ah Get Features, 10h Firmware Commit map to opcodes that are reserved or optional in the NVM set and normally return Invalid Command Opcode.
How it shows up: When the opcode collides with an implemented I/O command: nothing — the controller executes a real I/O with arguments taken from admin fields (CDW10 = PRP/feature data becomes SLBA/NLB…). Otherwise Generic status 01h "Invalid Command Opcode" with DNR.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Admin command set vs I/O command sets; opcode tables per command set; Commands Supported and Effects log page.
Typical causes: Passthrough tool sending an admin opcode through the namespace I/O passthrough path (e.g. nvme io-passthru with an admin opcode); user-space driver queue-selection bug; test scripts copying opcode tables.
How to detect / prove: Checker: classify each SQE by queue id; for SQ ≠ 0 validate the opcode against the namespace's command set (Commands Supported and Effects log for that CSI); flag admin-only opcodes on I/O queues whose CDW layout looks like an admin command (e.g. NSID = 0 or FFFFFFFFh with opcode 09h). Then read back the affected LBAs.
Linux v7.2 source: QEMU dispatches by queue: nvme_process_sq calls sq->sqid ? nvme_io_cmd(n, req) : nvme_admin_cmd(n, req) , and nvme_io_cmd_nvm rejects unsupported opcodes with NVME_INVALID_OPCODE | NVME_DNR . Linux: drivers/nvme/host/ioctl.c:nvme_cmd_allowed gates passthrough by opcode and capability.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION, scratch namespace only: nvme io-passthru /dev/nvme0n1 --opcode=0x06 … should return Invalid Command Opcode; never try opcodes 01h/09h on a namespace with data.

name: SGL descriptor rules broken
In a PEX trace: Visible SQE with PSDT ≠ 00b on SQ 0; SGL segment MRd/CplD whose descriptors break the rules (length not multiple of 16, wrong last-descriptor type); CQE status 0Dh/0Eh/0Fh/11h with DNR.
What happens: Typical violations: PSDT selects SGL on an Admin command (not allowed for NVMe over PCIe); SGL used although Identify Controller SGLS reports no support; Segment / Last Segment descriptor length zero or not a multiple of 16; a Last Segment whose final descriptor is not a Data Block; a Segment descriptor inside a segment in a position other than last; total data block length smaller than the transfer, or larger without "excess length" support; reserved descriptor type; SGL Data Block with address + length overflowing 64 bits.
How it shows up: QEMU statuses (all with DNR): NVME_INVALID_SGL_SEG_DESCR (0Dh), NVME_INVALID_NUM_SGL_DESCRS (0Eh), NVME_DATA_SGL_LEN_INVALID (0Fh), NVME_SGL_DESCR_TYPE_INVALID (11h); metadata SGL length problems map to NVME_MD_SGL_LEN_INVALID ; SGL on admin → Invalid Field. Linux names for the same generic codes: NVME_SC_SGL_INVALID_LAST 0Dh, _COUNT 0Eh, _DATA 0Fh, _METADATA 10h, _TYPE 11h, _OFFSET 16h, _GRANULARITY 1Eh.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Scatter Gather List — descriptor types (Data Block, Bit Bucket, Segment, Last Segment, Keyed Data Block, Transport), SGLS field, PSDT; NVMe over PCIe transport: Admin commands use PRPs.
Typical causes: Host chaining segments like PRP lists; byte-granular buffers with SGLS "dword alignment required" bit ignored; descriptor arrays allocated without 16-byte alignment.
How to detect / prove: Checker walks SGL segments as QEMU's nvme_map_sgl does, including the "no forward progress" rule QEMU adds to stop pathological loops, and compares described length with the command length.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_pci_use_sgls uses SGLs only when nvmeq->qid ≠ 0 and the controller supports them (forced for page gaps, user commands, multiple integrity segments); nvme_pci_setup_data_sgl ; module parameter sgl_threshold (default 32 KiB).
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): QEMU supports SGLs; a user-space harness can send a Last Segment ending with a Segment descriptor and observe 0Dh.

name: Illegal queue creation parameters
In a PEX trace: Visible Admin SQE opcode 01h/05h with QSIZE > CAP.MQES (CAP visible as a captured BAR read), unaligned PRP1, PC=0; CQE with SCT=1 and SC 00h/01h/02h/08h.
What happens: Create I/O SQ/CQ with: QID 0 or beyond the granted number of queues, or already in use; SQ referencing a CQ that does not exist; QSIZE 0 or greater than CAP.MQES; non-contiguous queue (PC=0) on a controller with CAP.CQR=1; queue base not page aligned; interrupt vector beyond the MSI-X table.
How it shows up: Command Specific status: Completion Queue Invalid (00h), Invalid Queue Identifier (01h), Invalid Queue Size (02h), Invalid Interrupt Vector (08h); or Generic PRP Offset Invalid / Invalid Field. QEMU nvme_create_sq returns NVME_INVALID_CQID , NVME_INVALID_QID , NVME_MAX_QSIZE_EXCEEDED , NVME_INVALID_PRP_OFFSET , NVME_INVALID_FIELD (PC=0) — all with DNR.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Create I/O Submission Queue and Create I/O Completion Queue commands; CAP.MQES (0's based), CAP.CQR.
Typical causes: QSIZE passed as 1's based; ignoring MQES on small embedded controllers; physically discontiguous queue memory on a controller without PRP-list queue support.
How to detect / prove: Checker validates Create commands against CAP (read during init — capture from controller enable) and the queue count granted in the Set Features Number of Queues CQE (DW0).
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_create_queue and the adapter helpers it calls; queue depth clamped against MQES during nvme_pci_enable .
Test to provoke it: QEMU (SAFE): nvme admin-passthru Create I/O SQ with QSIZE beyond MQES on an unused QID; expect status 0102h (SCT 1, SC 02h) in QEMU's encoding.

name: TLP payload larger than Max_Payload_Size
In a PEX trace: Visible MWr or CplD with Length × 4 > the transmitter's programmed MPS (visible from captured config writes to Device Control, or supplied from lspci); typically followed by an ERR_FATAL message TLP from the receiving port.
What happens: Part V card L-18 (Malformed TLP) and L-32 (MPS/MRRS mismatch) covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. A transmitter sends a TLP whose data payload exceeds the MPS programmed in its own Device Control register (for the SSD: data MWr for reads, or CplD for a host read of the CMB). A receiver with a smaller MPS setting cannot accept it.
How it shows up: The receiver treats it as a Malformed TLP: uncorrectable AER bit 18 "MalfTLP", fatal by default severity, which on Linux triggers AER recovery (reset of the link / device) or, with DPC, containment of the downstream port. The NVMe controller disappears briefly and I/O is retried or failed.
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Max_Payload_Size — transmitters must not send TLPs with payload larger than MPS; receivers treat such TLPs as Malformed. All functions on a path must use an MPS no larger than what every element supports.
Typical causes: Firmware ignoring the programmed MPS and using its capability maximum; hot-plugged device behind a switch whose MPS was configured smaller after the device was enumerated; firmware/OS ( pci=pcie_bus_perf ) choices that set MPS per segment inconsistently.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: compare each TLP's Length field with the configured MPS of the transmitter (capture config writes at enumeration or read lspci -vvv of every device on the path). Rule TLP-MPS in 7.6. Host: dmesg AER lines naming MalfTLP; /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/aer_dev_fatal .
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/probe.c:pcie_write_mps , pcie_bus_configure_settings , pcie_bus_configure_set (MPS policy per pcie_bus_config ); drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c string "MalfTLP".
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: lower MPS on the root port with setpci below the device's setting on a test box — this crashes I/O to the device; do it only with no mounted filesystems.

name: Read request larger than Max_Read_Request_Size
In a PEX trace: Visible MRd with Length × 4 > the requester's MRRS (Device Control, from captured config writes or lspci).
What happens: Part V card L-32 covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. The SSD (as requester) issues a memory read (to fetch write data, SQEs or PRP lists) with a length greater than its programmed MRRS.
How it shows up: MRRS is a requester-side limit; whether the completer flags an oversized read is implementation-dependent (verify the receiver rules in the PCIe Base spec). Usually the host bridge just services it — so the violation is silent, but it breaks the fairness and buffer assumptions the OS made when it chose MRRS (e.g. for isochronous or peer devices).
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Max_Read_Request_Size in Device Control — the requester must not generate read requests larger than this value.
Typical causes: Firmware using a fixed 4 KiB read size; MRRS changed by the OS after the device cached it at link-up.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: MRd Length × 4 > MRRS of the requester.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/probe.c:pcie_write_mrrs (calls pcie_set_readrq in performance mode); register field PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_READRQ .
Test to provoke it: SAFE observation: capture a large sequential write and check MRd sizes against lspci -vvv MaxReadReq.

name: Request crossing a 4 KiB address boundary
In a PEX trace: Visible Any MRd/MWr where (address mod 4096) + length > 4096 — a stateless rule the analyzer can evaluate on every packet.
What happens: A memory read or write request whose address + length spans a 4 KiB-aligned boundary (e.g. MWr of 256 B starting at …0F80h).
How it shows up: Receivers may optionally check this rule; if they do, the TLP is Malformed (AER MalfTLP). Many root complexes do not check, so the request is serviced — and the second part may land in a page that belongs to a different IOMMU mapping, causing an IOMMU fault for "half" a TLP or silent access to the wrong page. impl
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: requests must not specify an address/length combination that causes a memory space access to cross a 4 KB boundary.
Typical causes: DMA engine splitting at MPS multiples from the PRP1 offset instead of at page boundaries; PRP1 with an odd offset (V-17) combined with naive splitting.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer rule: (addr mod 4096) + len > 4096 for any MRd/MWr. Cheap and stateless — always enable it.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux cannot see this; IOMMU fault logs are the only host-side hint. dma_set_min_align_mask in drivers/nvme/host/pci.c preserves page offsets, so a correct device never needs to cross.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: send reads with PRP1 offsets such as 0F80h via passthrough and inspect the device's MWr split pattern.

name: Completions not respecting the Read Completion Boundary
In a PEX trace: Visible For one read request answered by several CplDs, a non-final CplD whose end address is not a multiple of the RCB.
What happens: A completer answering one read request with several CplD TLPs must split only at RCB-aligned addresses (64 or 128 B): each partial completion except the last must end on an RCB boundary, and the data must be returned in increasing address order for a single request. A completer that splits at arbitrary points (e.g. 100 bytes) violates this.
How it shows up: A requester that relies on RCB-aligned splits (to size its completion buffers) may mis-assemble data; a strict requester flags a Malformed TLP. Often silent. impl
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Read Completion Boundary (Link Control RCB; root ports 64 B or 128 B) and completion splitting rules for memory read requests.
Typical causes: Device-side CMB / PMR completion logic (when the host reads the SSD's Controller Memory Buffer) with an incorrect splitter; RCB register not programmed consistently with the root port.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: for each request with multiple CplDs, check that each non-final CplD's end address (Lower Address + payload) is a multiple of RCB.
Linux v7.2 source: include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h:PCI_EXP_LNKCTL_RCB ; CMB mapping in drivers/nvme/host/pci.c ( nvme_map_cmb ).
Test to provoke it: SAFE observation on devices with a CMB: read the CMB region with large reads (e.g. via a test harness or dd on a resource file — read-only) while capturing.

name: Byte Count / Lower Address inconsistent in completions
In a PEX trace: Visible Successive CplDs of one tag whose Byte Count does not decrease by the previous payload, or whose Lower Address does not advance accordingly.
What happens: In a completion, Byte Count must equal the number of bytes remaining to satisfy the request (including this completion's bytes), and Lower Address must be the low address bits of the first byte returned in this completion. A completer that reports the wrong values (e.g. Byte Count = payload length on every partial, or Lower Address not advancing) breaks the requester's reassembly.
How it shows up: The requester may treat the completion as malformed or unexpected, or may conclude the request is finished too early and later receive "unexpected" completions — AER "UnxCmplt" (bit 16) or "MalfTLP"; or the read silently returns partial data. impl
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Completion header fields Byte Count and Lower Address and their rules for split completions.
Typical causes: Completer logic that does not track remaining bytes across splits; BCM (Byte Count Modified) misuse by PCI-X bridges in legacy topologies.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: for each tag, track remaining bytes; every CplD must have Byte Count == remaining and Lower Address == (next expected address mod 128).
Linux v7.2 source: Only the AER outcome is visible: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c strings "UnxCmplt", "MalfTLP".
Test to provoke it: Device-side bug; validate with an exerciser that injects wrong Byte Count (EXPERT, lab equipment).

name: Completion for an unknown tag (Unexpected Completion)
In a PEX trace: Visible Cpl/CplD whose Requester ID + Tag matches no outstanding non-posted request seen on the probed link (often a late completion after a long gap). If the request went over a different link (e.g. peer-to-peer through a switch), the matching request is not visible.
What happens: Part V card L-16 covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. A completion arrives whose Transaction ID (Requester ID + Tag) matches no outstanding non-posted request of the receiver — because the request already completed, already timed out, was never sent, or the completer copied the wrong tag/requester ID.
How it shows up: The receiver logs Unexpected Completion: AER uncorrectable bit 16 "UnxCmplt" (non-fatal by default, often handled as an advisory non-fatal error and reported as correctable "NonFatalErr"). Frequently seen as the second half of a Completion Timeout ("CmpltTO", bit 14): the late completion for a request already timed out arrives and is unexpected.
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Transaction ID matching of completions; Unexpected Completion error; Completion Timeout mechanism (range in Device Control 2).
Typical causes: Completion timeout set too short ( PCI_EXP_DEVCTL2_COMP_TIMEOUT ) on a slow path (e.g. through a switch to a busy root port or to a device in a low-power state); tag mismatch after enabling 10-bit tags on only one side; firmware returning completions after FLR.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: maintain outstanding (Requester ID, Tag) per requester; flag CplD/Cpl without a match; measure request→completion latency to see if a timeout explains it.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c strings "UnxCmplt", "CmpltTO"; per-device counters in sysfs aer_dev_nonfatal , aer_dev_correctable .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: shorten the completion timeout range in Device Control 2 with setpci on the requester while the completer is slow (e.g. deep power state), on a test system only.

name: Tag reused while a request is outstanding
In a PEX trace: Visible Second MRd with the same Requester ID + Tag before all CplDs (Byte Count reaching the final value) of the first have arrived.
What happens: Part V card L-40 (tag capability mismatch) covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. A requester issues a new non-posted request with a Tag that is still in use by an outstanding request (same Requester ID). The completer cannot tell them apart; completions may be matched to the wrong request.
How it shows up: Silent data mix-up: the SSD receives data meant for a different read (e.g. PRP list bytes delivered as write data, or one write's data in another write). Possibly Unexpected Completion later when the "second" completion for the tag arrives.
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Transaction ID (Requester ID + Tag) must be unique among a requester's outstanding non-posted requests; 8-bit, 10-bit (optional, Gen4+) and 14-bit (Flit mode) tag spaces.
Typical causes: Tag allocator bug after a completion timeout (tag freed while the completion may still arrive); 10-bit tag requester whose tags are truncated to 8 bits by a component that does not support 10-bit tags.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: per requester, flag a non-posted request whose tag is in the outstanding set. This is the PCIe twin of V-08.
Linux v7.2 source: Not visible to Linux: tags are allocated by the device's hardware. A grep of v7.2 include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h and drivers/pci/ finds no 10-bit-tag enable logic, so check the Device Control 2 setting with lspci -vvv rather than assuming the kernel configured it. impl
Test to provoke it: Device-side; observe with analyzer under deep queue sequential writes (many concurrent MRd) — the scenario where tag exhaustion bugs appear.

name: Posted-write ordering violation
In a PEX trace: Partly visible On one link you see the order the transmitter sent TLPs and their RO/IDO attributes; proving that a switch or root complex reordered them needs probes on both sides of that component, and what the CPU finally observed is not on any link.
What happens: Part V card L-40 (Relaxed Ordering errata) covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. A component reorders TLPs in a way the ordering table forbids: a posted write passes an earlier posted write without RO; a completion passes a posted write in the same direction (which would let a read return before an earlier write is visible); a read passes a posted write. In NVMe terms: host doorbell write overtaking the host's earlier SQE write is impossible on PCIe (the SQE is in host memory, not sent to the device), but device-side reorderings of data/CQE/MSI-X (V-13, V-14) and switch reorderings are possible.
How it shows up: Stale reads, stale data, spurious interrupts; never a status code.
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Transaction Ordering rules (the ordering table for Posted, Non-Posted, Completion), Relaxed Ordering and ID-Based Ordering attributes.
Typical causes: Device setting RO/IDO on TLPs that need strong ordering; a switch or root complex bug; host chipsets that are known to mishandle RO (Linux has quirks that clear RO enable for certain root ports).
How to detect / prove: Two probes (upstream and downstream of a switch) and compare TLP order; on a single link, check that no CQE or MSI-X TLP has RO=1 and that the ordering of device→host MWr matches the NVMe dependency (data → CQE → MSI-X).
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/quirks.c contains relaxed-ordering quirks for root ports (search for PCI_DEV_FLAGS_NO_RELAXED_ORDERING ); enable bit PCI_EXP_DEVCTL_RELAX_EN .
Test to provoke it: Analyzer-only; run fio verify with RO enabled vs disabled on a test system and compare.

name: ECRC mismatch
In a PEX trace: Visible TLP with TD=1 whose digest does not match the analyzer's recomputation. Without ECRC enabled (TD=0) there is nothing to check; corruption inside the root complex after the probe point is not visible.
What happens: Part V card L-19 covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. When end-to-end CRC is enabled, the transmitter appends a 32-bit TLP Digest (TD bit = 1). A receiver with ECRC checking enabled recomputes it; a mismatch means the TLP was corrupted inside a component (e.g. switch internal SRAM) after the link-level LCRC had already been checked and stripped.
How it shows up: AER uncorrectable bit 19 "ECRC"; Linux logs the TLP header from the AER Header Log. Without ECRC enabled (the common default), the same internal corruption is silent.
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: End-to-End CRC (ECRC), TLP Digest, AER ECRC Generation/Check Capable/Enable bits.
Typical causes: Switch or retimer internal memory errors; a component that modifies a TLP header field it is not allowed to modify (some fields are variant and excluded from ECRC); mismatched ECRC enable (TD set by a device whose partner miscomputes).
How to detect / prove: Analyzer recomputes ECRC on every TLP with TD=1 at both ends of a switch; host: lspci -vvv shows "ECRCGenCap/ECRCChkCap" and enables; dmesg AER messages with "ECRC".
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c (ECRC policy via kernel parameter pci=ecrc=on|off , string "ECRC"); PCI_ERR_CAP_ECRC_* in pci_regs.h .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: boot a lab host with pci=ecrc=on and capture; an exerciser can inject ECRC errors (EXPERT).

name: Data Link Layer replay pattern: Nak, replay, missing Ack, REPLAY_NUM rollover
In a PEX trace: Visible Nak DLLP followed by retransmission of TLPs with already-used sequence numbers; or the same sequence number sent four times with no Ack, then training ordered sets (Recovery). Physical-layer root causes are in Part V.
What happens: The individual link-level errors (Bad TLP, Bad DLLP, Replay Timer Timeout, REPLAY_NUM Rollover) are covered as AER errors in Part V ( L-02 , L-03 , L-04 , L-05 ). This card is the checker rule view: the receiver discards a TLP with a bad LCRC or an out-of-order sequence number and sends a Nak; the transmitter replays from its replay buffer; if no Ack/Nak arrives before the replay timer expires it replays anyway; after four replays of the same TLP the link retrains.
How it shows up: Correctable AER bits "BadTLP", "BadDLLP", "Timeout", "Rollover" (Linux names) — if software reads them; otherwise only lower throughput and latency bursts.
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Data Link Layer — sequence numbers, LCRC, Ack/Nak protocol, replay buffer, replay timer, REPLAY_NUM.
Typical causes: Signal-integrity and PHY causes are in Part V; protocol-side causes are a receiver that is slow to return Acks (Ack coalescing too long, firmware stall) or that loses track of its expected sequence number after Recovery.
How to detect / prove: Checker rules: (1) replay count = TLPs whose sequence number was already transmitted; (2) Ack latency = time from a TLP to the first Ack whose AckNak_Seq_Num covers it, compared with the spec's limit for that speed/width (verify the table in the spec); (3) four transmissions of one sequence number → expect Recovery. Report replays per million TLPs per direction.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c:aer_correctable_error_string ("RxErr", "BadTLP", "BadDLLP", "Rollover", "Timeout").
Test to provoke it: Analyzer-only observation under load; exercisers can drop Acks or corrupt LCRC (EXPERT, lab equipment).

name: FLIT errors in PCIe 6.0 Flit mode (FEC/CRC, replay, sequence)
In a PEX trace: Partly visible With a Gen6-capable analyzer and Flit decode: flit sequence numbers, NAKs and retried flits are visible; FEC corrections happen inside the receiver and are visible only as counters the analyzer or device reports (verify for your analyzer version). PHY margins: see Part V.
What happens: At 64 GT/s with PAM4 signalling, Flit mode carries traffic in fixed 256-byte FLITs (vendor overviews: 236 bytes of TLP, 6 of DLP, 8 of CRC, 6 of ECC). A lightweight FEC corrects small symbol errors in-line; a FLIT whose CRC still fails after FEC is retried at FLIT granularity, with flit sequence numbers and standard or selective NAK. Per-TLP LCRC and the classic per-TLP sequence/Ack scheme are replaced by this flit-level mechanism. version
How it shows up: A rising FEC-corrected count costs nothing yet (an early-warning signal); CRC-failed FLITs cause retries (bandwidth/latency loss); persistent failures cause Recovery or link-down. How these are surfaced to software (AER bits, vendor counters, new capability registers) depends on the implementation and spec version — verify in the PCIe 6.x spec and the device's documentation. uncertain
Spec basis: PCI Express Base 6.0 and later: Flit mode, FEC, flit CRC, flit sequence numbers and NAK/retry (names of the specific counters and capability structures: verify in spec).
Typical causes: PAM4 eye margin (reflections, crosstalk, temperature); equalisation; retimers; mixed Flit/non-Flit negotiation issues on links that fall back to lower speeds.
How to detect / prove: Gen6-capable analyzer with Flit decode: count FEC corrections per lane, flit CRC failures and NAKs; correlate with temperature and link speed. Host: lspci -vvv shows speed 64GT/s and Flit mode state when supported by your lspci version.
Linux v7.2 source: Generic AER handling in drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c ; link speed decoding in drivers/pci/pci.c:__pcie_print_link_status . No NVMe-driver-specific handling.
Test to provoke it: Lab-only (EXPERT): margining tools / lane margining at the receiver, cable or channel stress, and compare FEC/CRC counters at different temperatures.

name: Poisoned TLP data accepted as good
In a PEX trace: Visible CplD/MWr with EP=1 (e.g. answering the device's write-data MRd for CID X), later a CQE for CID X with status 0. Whether poisoned data reached the media is not visible — read back to prove it.
What happens: Part V card L-12 and L-38 covers how the receiver reports this; this card is the trace-checker rule. A TLP carries the EP (Error Poisoned) bit, meaning its payload is known to be bad (e.g. a host memory read hit an uncorrectable ECC error). The receiving NVMe controller must not treat the data as valid — e.g. it must not write poisoned write-data to media as if it were good.
How it shows up: Correct behaviour: AER "Poisoned TLP" received (uncorrectable bit 12, shown by Linux as "TLP") and the NVMe command fails (typically Data Transfer Error 04h). Incorrect behaviour: success, and the corrupted bytes are now persistent on media — silent corruption.
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Data Poisoning (EP bit) and Poisoned TLP Received error; NVMe Base: Data Transfer Error generic status.
Typical causes: Controller firmware ignoring EP on CplD; host DRAM UE during a write command; switch forwarding poisoned data.
How to detect / prove: Analyzer: any CplD/MWr with EP=1 must be followed by a failing CQE for the owning command (or by the device's documented poisoned-data handling). A success CQE after a poisoned CplD is a finding.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/pcie/aer.c:aer_uncorrectable_error_string bit 12 "TLP"; status 04h string in drivers/nvme/host/constants.c .
Test to provoke it: EXPERT: error-injection (EINJ on servers that support it) or a PCIe exerciser setting EP on completions.

name: Throughput well below link capability
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Bandwidth over time, TLP payload sizes, gaps between data bursts and the number of SQEs outstanding are all measurable; whether a gap is the host (no doorbells) or the device (doorbells but slow fetch/CQE) is visible — the root cause inside either is not.
What happens: Large sequential reads (128 KiB–1 MiB, QD ≥ 8) reach, say, 4.1 GB/s on a Gen4 x4 drive whose link ceiling at MPS 256 B is ≈7.2 GB/s and whose datasheet says 7.0 GB/s.
How it shows up: Only in the benchmark number. No error, no log.
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: link rate/width, MPS; NVMe Base: MDTS (limits per-command size), queue model. The ceiling is arithmetic, not a spec field.
Typical causes: Link trained below capability (P-11); MPS 128 B (P-12); I/O split into small commands by MDTS or max_sectors_kb ; too few outstanding commands; CPU or single-thread submission limit (P-09); device thermal throttling (P-06); measuring through a filesystem with buffered I/O.
How to detect / prove: Compute the ceiling (8.1.1) from lspci LnkSta and DevCtl MaxPayload; run fio --rw=read --bs=1m --iodepth=32 --direct=1 ; check iostat -x 1 rareq-sz (average request size actually sent) and aqu-sz (average queue size). If rareq-sz is much smaller than bs, the block layer is splitting.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_init_identify (MDTS → max_hw_sectors ); drivers/pci/pci.c:__pcie_print_link_status reports "available PCIe bandwidth, limited by …".
Test to provoke it: SAFE: read-only fio sweep of bs (4k…1m) × iodepth (1…128); plot bandwidth; the plateau should approach the ceiling.

name: IOPS collapse at high queue depth
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Outstanding-command count (fetched SQEs minus CQEs) and per-command SQE-fetch→CQE time are visible, so the curve can be reconstructed from the trace; why the device slows down (FTL contention) is not.
What happens: IOPS rise with queue depth until the device's internal parallelism is saturated; beyond that they should plateau while latency grows linearly (Little's Law). A collapse — IOPS falling as QD rises (e.g. 800k at QD 64, 450k at QD 256) — means something degrades under contention.
How it shows up: QD sweep curve with a peak and a decline; mean latency growing faster than QD/IOPS predicts.
Spec basis: None; queue depth limits come from CAP.MQES and the host driver's queue depth.
Typical causes: Device: firmware arbitration overhead, internal buffer thrashing, read disturb mitigation, too many concurrent streams for the FTL cache. Host: lock contention when many jobs share one hardware queue, nr_requests limits causing requeue storms, interrupts from all queues landing on one CPU.
How to detect / prove: Sweep --iodepth 1…256 at fixed numjobs ; then repeat with jobs pinned to CPUs on the device's NUMA node. If host CPU (fio sys% , perf top ) is saturated at the peak, it's the host; if the device-reported latency (or analyzer SQE→CQE time) rises disproportionately, it's the device.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c module parameter io_queue_depth (default 1024, "should >= 2 and < 4096"); q_depth clamped to CAP.MQES+1 in nvme_pci_enable .
Test to provoke it: SAFE (read-only): for qd in 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 256; do fio --readonly … --iodepth=$qd; done .

name: Latency outliers at p99.9 / p99.99
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Per-command device latency (SQE fetch → CQE MWr) is visible exactly, separating device from host; whether a 12 ms outlier was GC, read retry or a housekeeping task is NOT visible.
What happens: Median read latency is 80 µs but one I/O in a thousand takes 5–50 ms. Averages hide it; databases and distributed storage feel it, because a request that touches many I/Os waits for the slowest.
How it shows up: fio clat percentiles ; application tail latency; occasionally Linux timeouts if outliers exceed 30 s (then it becomes a timing failure, not a performance one).
Spec basis: NVMe defines no latency targets for ordinary I/O; some features exist to manage it (Predictable Latency Mode, Read Recovery Level, I/O Determinism concepts) — check Identify Controller for support.
Typical causes: Garbage collection (P-05), read retry / soft-decode on worn or long-retention NAND, internal firmware housekeeping (SMART update, table flush), power state exit (P-07), host: interrupt on a busy CPU, softirq delay, CPU frequency ramp-up, SMIs.
How to detect / prove: fio --percentile_list=99:99.9:99.99 --write_lat_log to get each slow I/O's timestamp; bpftrace / biolatency -style histograms; correlate outlier timestamps with SMART temperature samples, APST transitions, and other activity. An analyzer gives the device-only latency (SQE fetch → CQE), separating device from host.
Linux v7.2 source: Trace events nvme_setup_cmd and nvme_complete_rq in drivers/nvme/host/trace.h give per-command host-side latency (enable via /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/ ).
Test to provoke it: SAFE: long (≥ 30 min) read-only random read at moderate QD on a drive that has been written full; compare a fresh drive.

name: Write cliff after the SLC cache is exhausted
In a PEX trace: Partly visible A step down in the rate of write-data MRd and a rise in write SQE→CQE time after N GB are visible; the SLC cache itself and folding are device-internal and not visible.
What happens: Many TLC/QLC drives write first into NAND operated in single-bit (pseudo-SLC) mode, which is fast. When that cache fills during a long sequential write, the drive must write to native TLC/QLC — and simultaneously fold the cache — so throughput drops sharply. Reviewers report drops such as from >2.5 GB/s to ≈0.8 GB/s after ≈150 GB on one TLC drive, and to ≈160 MB/s after ≈80 GB on a QLC SATA drive; the cache recovers during idle time.
How it shows up: A bandwidth-over-time plot with a step down; average numbers for short tests look perfect.
Spec basis: Not specified by NVMe; it is FTL design. (Endurance/space reporting fields in SMART do not expose the cache size.)
Typical causes: Dynamic SLC cache sized by free space (shrinks as the drive fills), no idle time to flush, drive nearly full.
How to detect / prove: CAUTION (destructive): sequential write of the full capacity on a scratch drive with --write_bw_log and 1 s averaging; plot GB written vs MB/s. Repeat at 50% and 90% fill to show the cache shrinking.
Linux v7.2 source: Not visible to the driver.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: fio --name=fill --filename=/dev/nvme1n1 --rw=write --bs=1m --iodepth=32 --direct=1 --write_bw_log=fill --log_avg_msec=1000 on a scratch device.

name: Garbage-collection stalls in steady state
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Periods where the device stops fetching SQEs although doorbells advanced, followed by CQE bursts, are visible; garbage collection is inferred, never shown.
What happens: After the drive has been fully written (no free blocks left), every new write needs garbage collection to reclaim space. Random write IOPS fall from the fresh-out-of-box value to a much lower steady-state value, with periodic stalls when GC falls behind.
How it shows up: IOPS-over-time plot: high, then decline, then a noisy plateau with dips; write latency p99.9 in the tens of ms.
Spec basis: Not specified by NVMe. Related features that help: Deallocate/TRIM (DSM), Write Zeroes, over-provisioning, Endurance Group / NVM Sets, Flexible Data Placement (reduces write amplification when supported).
Typical causes: No TRIM (filesystem mounted without discard and no periodic fstrim ), low over-provisioning, mixed hot/cold data, and see the "deallocate completes but does nothing" silent failure elsewhere in this atlas.
How to detect / prove: CAUTION: precondition (2× capacity sequential, then random 4k writes) and use fio --steadystate=iops_slope:0.1% ; record SMART "Data Units Written" before/after to compute host writes; if the vendor log exposes NAND writes, compute write amplification.
Linux v7.2 source: Discard path drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_setup_discard (DSM deallocate).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: the SNIA-style preconditioning workflow on a scratch drive; compare with and without a full-drive deallocate beforehand.

name: Thermal throttling
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Throughput saw-tooth is visible; temperature is visible only if the host reads the SMART/Health log during the capture (Get Log Page 02h data MWr) or sets/reads features 04h/10h — decode those payloads.
What happens: As the composite temperature rises, the controller reduces performance to stay within limits — either its own internal throttling or Host Controlled Thermal Management (HCTM) levels TMT1/TMT2 set by the host.
How it shows up: Throughput saw-tooth that correlates with temperature. Evidence lives in the SMART / Health Information log: Composite Temperature, Warning Composite Temperature Time, Critical Composite Temperature Time, Temperature Sensor 1–8, Thermal Management Temperature 1/2 Transition Count and Total Time. Crossing a temperature threshold can also raise a SMART/Health async event (critical warning temperature bit).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: SMART / Health Information log page fields above; Identify Controller WCTEMP, CCTEMP, MNTMT, MXTMT; Set Features Temperature Threshold (04h) and Host Controlled Thermal Management (10h).
Typical causes: No heatsink or airflow (M.2 under a GPU), Gen5 drives with high controller power, sustained writes, HCTM thresholds set too low by platform software.
How to detect / prove: Sample nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 every second during the workload (temperature, thm_temp1_trans_count , thm_temp1_total_time , warning_temp_time ); the counters increasing during the dips is proof. Linux exposes temperatures through hwmon ( sensors ).
Linux v7.2 source: SMART fields in include/linux/nvme.h struct nvme_smart_log : warning_temp_time , critical_comp_time , temp_sensor[8] , thm_temp1_trans_count , thm_temp2_trans_count , thm_temp1_total_time , thm_temp2_total_time ; feature ids NVME_FEAT_TEMP_THRESH (04h), NVME_FEAT_HCTM (10h); mntmt / mxtmt in Identify Controller.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: sustained sequential write on a scratch drive with airflow blocked for a short, monitored period; stop at WCTEMP. Never exceed the drive's critical temperature.

name: APST / ASPM wake-latency spikes
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Link L1 entry/exit (electrical idle, then training to L0) and the host's Set Features 0Ch (APST table in the data payload) are visible, as is the delay between the first doorbell after idle and its SQE fetch; the device's internal power state is not.
What happens: After idle, the drive enters a non-operational power state via Autonomous Power State Transition (APST), and/or the link enters L1 / L1 substates via ASPM. The first I/O after idle pays the exit latency (the power state descriptor's EXLAT, plus link L1 exit latency) — from tens of µs to tens of ms.
How it shows up: Latency outliers that occur only after idle periods (bursty workloads, interactive desktops); benchmarks with continuous load never see them. Some drive/platform combinations fail to wake at all (then it becomes a controller-fatal/timeout failure, which is why Linux has quirks).
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Power State Descriptors (ENLAT, EXLAT, non-operational flag), Autonomous Power State Transition feature (0Ch), Identify Controller APSTA, NPSS; PCI Express Base: ASPM L0s/L1, L1 PM Substates, exit latencies in Link Capabilities.
Typical causes: Linux v7.2 default default_ps_max_latency_us = 100000 (100 ms) allows deep states; platform ASPM policy "powersave"; drives with optimistic EXLAT values.
How to detect / prove: Read the APST table: nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x0c -H ; the descriptor latencies: nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -H (power states); ASPM state: lspci -vvv "LnkCtl: ASPM …"; cat /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy . Experiment: run fio --thinktime=2s --thinktime_blocks=1 (idle between I/Os) and compare p99 with APST disabled ( nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 ) — a clear difference is proof.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_configure_apst , nvme_apst_get_transition_time , module parameter default_ps_max_latency_us (100000); quirks NVME_QUIRK_NO_APST , NVME_QUIRK_NO_DEEPEST_PS in drivers/nvme/host/nvme.h ; per-device limit via PM QoS latency tolerance in sysfs.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: read-only fio with think time as above, with APST enabled vs disabled; plot first-I/O-after-idle latency.

name: Interrupt storm or interrupt-coalescing misconfiguration
In a PEX trace: Visible Ratio of MSI-X MWr to CQE MWr and the delay from first CQE to MSI-X; Set/Get Features 08h and 09h commands and their values in the SQE/CQE.
What happens: One interrupt per completion at 1M+ IOPS costs a lot of CPU (storm); conversely, aggressive coalescing (Feature 08h aggregation threshold/time) saves CPU but adds latency up to the aggregation time to every I/O at low QD. Misrouted interrupts (all vectors on CPU 0) create a single-core bottleneck.
How it shows up: High %irq / %soft in mpstat ; one CPU at 100%; or a constant added latency (e.g. +100 µs) at QD 1.
Spec basis: NVMe Base: Interrupt Coalescing feature (08h: Aggregation Time in 100 µs units, Aggregation Threshold), Interrupt Vector Configuration feature (09h: Coalescing Disable per vector).
Typical causes: Coalescing set by vendor tools or firmware defaults; irqbalance moving NVMe vectors away from their managed affinity; fewer MSI-X vectors than CPUs.
How to detect / prove: nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -H ; grep nvme /proc/interrupts (per-CPU counts per queue); mpstat -P ALL 1 ; compare IOPS/CPU with poll_queues + --hipri polling.
Linux v7.2 source: Linux v7.2 does not program Feature 08h: NVME_FEAT_IRQ_COALESCE is only defined in include/linux/nvme.h , not used by drivers/nvme/host . Vector setup: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_setup_irqs ; polling queues via module parameter poll_queues .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION (changes device settings, revert afterwards): nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -v <value> on a test system and measure QD 1 latency before/after.

name: CPU-bound submission path
In a PEX trace: Partly visible Slow, irregular doorbell writes and shallow SQ occupancy are visible (the device is waiting); CPU utilisation and where cycles go are not — use perf.
What happens: The host cannot generate I/O fast enough: one fio job on one core saturates at a few hundred thousand IOPS with libaio, so a drive rated for 1.5M IOPS appears "slow".
How it shows up: fio cpu: usr/sys near 100% per job; Little's Law mismatch (8.1.2); adding jobs increases IOPS linearly.
Spec basis: None (host software).
Typical causes: Single job; synchronous engine; buffered I/O; per-I/O syscalls; kernel debug options; security mitigations; IOMMU in strict mode (map/unmap per I/O); CPU in a low-frequency state.
How to detect / prove: perf top / perf record -g during the run to see where cycles go; try --ioengine=io_uring --fixedbufs --registerfiles --hipri , more numjobs , --iodepth_batch_submit ; check cpupower frequency-info .
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:nvme_queue_rq , nvme_commit_rqs (batched doorbells), nvme_poll_cq ; block/blk-mq.c for the submission path.
Test to provoke it: SAFE: read-only 4k random read with numjobs=1 vs 8, libaio vs io_uring; record IOPS per CPU.

name: NUMA misplacement
In a PEX trace: Not visible NUMA placement is a host-internal property; host DRAM latency appears only indirectly (longer CplD latency for device reads of remote memory). Prove with numa_node/local_cpulist and pinned fio runs.
What happens: On a multi-socket (or multi-die) server, the SSD's root port belongs to one NUMA node. Threads and buffers on the other node make every DMA and every MMIO doorbell cross the inter-socket link, adding latency and consuming inter-socket bandwidth.
How it shows up: 10–30% higher latency or lower IOPS depending on which CPUs run the benchmark; results that vary run to run as the scheduler moves threads. impl
Spec basis: None (platform topology).
Typical causes: Benchmark not pinned; application threads on the wrong socket; interrupt affinity crossing nodes; memory allocated on the remote node.
