How to detect / prove: cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/numa_node and local_cpulist ; run fio with --numa_cpu_nodes=N --numa_mem_policy=bind:N (or numactl --cpunodebind=N --membind=N fio … ) for local and remote N and compare; perf stat uncore/inter-socket counters where available.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/pci.c allocates queues with dev_to_node() -based NUMA hints (e.g. the HMB/descriptor allocations pass numa_node ).
Test to provoke it: SAFE: read-only fio pinned locally vs remotely.

name: Link trained below capability (speed or width downgrade)
In a PEX trace: Visible Training sequences and the negotiated rate/width at link-up or Recovery; lanes inactive. See also Part V L-25 for the link-layer card.
What happens: A Gen4 x4 drive links at Gen3 or at x2 (or x1). Everything works, at half or a quarter of the bandwidth.
How it shows up: lspci -vvv : "LnkSta: Speed 8GT/s (downgraded), Width x2 (downgraded)" vs "LnkCap: Speed 16GT/s, Width x4"; Linux at enumeration prints "… available PCIe bandwidth, limited by … link at … (capable of …)". Bandwidth-management interrupts may log autonomous speed changes.
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Link Capabilities (Max Link Speed/Width), Link Status (Current Link Speed, Negotiated Link Width), LTSSM training and Recovery speed changes.
Typical causes: Slot wired with fewer lanes (chipset slot, bifurcation settings), riser cables, BIOS forcing Gen3, signal-integrity problems causing the LTSSM to fall back, thermal or power policy (some laptops lower speed on battery).
How to detect / prove: cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/{current_link_speed,max_link_speed,current_link_width,max_link_width} ; check the upstream port's LnkCap too (the link runs at the lower of the two); dmesg | grep 'limited by' . Bandwidth test: sequential read plateau ≈ the ceiling of the downgraded link.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/probe.c:pcie_report_downtraining → drivers/pci/pci.c:__pcie_print_link_status ("%u.%03u Gb/s available PCIe bandwidth, limited by %s x%d link at %s (capable of …)"); pcie_bandwidth_available ; register fields PCI_EXP_LNKSTA_CLS , PCI_EXP_LNKSTA_NLW .
Test to provoke it: SAFE: move the drive between slots and record LnkSta; CAUTION: forcing the target link speed via Link Control 2 with setpci and retraining on a test system.

name: Small MPS or MRRS limiting throughput
In a PEX trace: Visible All data MWr exactly 128 B, MRd sizes capped at a small MRRS; config writes to Device Control at enumeration if captured. See also Part V L-32 .
What happens: MPS = 128 B costs ≈8% of a Gen4 x4 link versus 256 B and ≈12% versus 512 B (8.1.1). A small MRRS (e.g. 128 B) forces the SSD to issue many more read requests to fetch write data, each needing a tag and a completion; with limited outstanding tags this caps write throughput.
How it shows up: Sequential read or write stuck at ~85–90% of the expected plateau; lspci -vvv "DevCtl: MaxPayload 128 bytes, MaxReadReq 128 bytes".
Spec basis: PCI Express Base: Max_Payload_Size, Max_Read_Request_Size (Device Control).
Typical causes: A device on the same hierarchy that supports only 128 B forcing the "safe" MPS for all; firmware defaults; kernel MPS policy ( pci=pcie_bus_safe , pcie_bus_perf , pcie_bus_peer2peer , pcie_bus_tune_off ).
How to detect / prove: lspci -vvv for every device from root port to SSD (DevCap MaxPayload vs DevCtl MaxPayload); compare sequential bandwidth; analyzer shows TLP payload sizes directly.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/pci/probe.c:pcie_bus_configure_settings , pcie_bus_configure_set , pcie_write_mps , pcie_write_mrrs ; pcie_bus_config values PCIE_BUS_TUNE_OFF , PCIE_BUS_SAFE , PCIE_BUS_PERFORMANCE , PCIE_BUS_PEER2PEER .
Test to provoke it: CAUTION: boot with a different pci=pcie_bus_* policy on a lab machine and compare; never lower MPS on one end only (that is V-26).

name: Misaligned or sub-sector writes causing read-modify-write
In a PEX trace: Partly visible SLBA/NLB values not aligned to the preferred granularity are visible in SQEs; the read-modify-write inside the device is not.
What happens: A namespace formatted with 512-byte LBAs on a drive whose internal mapping unit is 4 KiB (or larger) receives writes that are not 4 KiB aligned or not 4 KiB multiples. The FTL must read the rest of the unit, merge and rewrite: more latency, more NAND writes.
How it shows up: Small-write IOPS far below datasheet; higher write amplification; nothing in logs.
Spec basis: NVM Command Set: LBA formats (Identify Namespace LBAF, "Relative Performance" field), and optimal I/O hints: NPWG (Preferred Write Granularity), NPWA (Preferred Write Alignment), NOWS (Optimal Write Size) when reported.
Typical causes: Partitions not 1 MiB aligned; databases with 512 B or 2 KiB pages; namespace formatted with a non-preferred LBA format.
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 -H (LBA formats with "Relative Performance", npwg/npwa/nows); cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/{physical_block_size,optimal_io_size,minimum_io_size} ; fio with --bs=4k --offset=512 vs aligned on a scratch device.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/core.c derives physical_block_size / io_opt from NPWG/NOWS when the namespace reports them (search for npwg in nvme_update_disk_info -related code).
Test to provoke it: CAUTION (writes): aligned vs misaligned 4k random write on a scratch namespace.

name: Flush/FUA-heavy workload on a drive without (or with disabled) volatile write cache
In a PEX trace: Visible SQE opcode 00h (Flush) or FUA=1 writes after each write, and the long SQE→CQE time of each Flush; VWC is visible in captured Identify Controller data.
What happens: Applications that call fsync after every write generate Flush commands (or FUA writes). On consumer drives with a volatile write cache, each Flush forces cached data to NAND — sync-write latency jumps from tens of µs to milliseconds. Enterprise drives with power-loss protection can acknowledge flushes quickly.
How it shows up: Database commit latency high; iostat shows low throughput but high w_await ; nothing in logs.
Spec basis: NVMe Base / NVM Command Set: Flush command (00h), Force Unit Access bit in Write, Volatile Write Cache feature (06h) and Identify Controller VWC.
Typical causes: Workload design; drive class (no power-loss protection); volatile write cache disabled by a tool (each write then becomes write-through).
How to detect / prove: nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep vwc ; nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x06 ; cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_cache ; fio with --fsync=1 vs none on a scratch device; count Flush commands with the nvme_setup_cmd trace event.
Linux v7.2 source: drivers/nvme/host/core.c:nvme_setup_cmd (flush and FUA paths); write-cache reporting set from VWC.
Test to provoke it: CAUTION (writes): fio --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --fsync=1 on a scratch namespace, compared with --fsync=0 .
